# Carolina Barbecue — every record, flattened

## Eastern North Carolina barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/eastern-nc/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/eastern-nc.json
id: eastern-nc
aliases: Eastern-style · Down East barbecue · whole-hog barbecue · Eastern Carolina barbecue
said: In the east, 'barbecue' is the meat itself: chopped pork from a whole hog. Nobody says 'pulled pork'.
facets: state=NC · meat=whole hog · base=vinegar-pepper · fuel=mixed
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: The whole pig, split and cooked over coals or on a gas or electric cooker, then chopped — skin, ham, shoulder, loin and belly together, 'every part of the hog except the squeal' — and dressed after cooking with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper. No tomato. It is served with mayonnaise slaw, cornbread or hushpuppies, and often boiled potatoes, on a tray or a sandwich with the slaw on the meat. The style belongs to the Coastal Plain east of Raleigh; Ayden, Goldsboro, Wilson, Kinston, Rocky Mount and Greenville are its towns.
story: The whole hog is the older way, across the whole South. *Tradition holds —* it grew out of plantation and farm life, where a pig was killed, cooked over a trench of hardwood coals through the night and eaten by the whole community at church homecomings, political rallies and hog killings. The cooks at those pits were, for most of two centuries, Black men, enslaved and then paid; Adrian Miller's *Black Smoke* traces that labor and its erasure from the menus and legends that followed. The vinegar-and-pepper dressing is the sauce of the English colonial kitchen — vinegar was the preservative and the seasoning both — and the absence of tomato is what the east points to when it explains itself against the Piedmont.

The named lineages start in the twentieth century. Bob Melton opened a pit at Rocky Mount in 1924 and was called the 'king of Southern barbecue' by Life magazine. Adam Scott, a Black cook and preacher in Goldsboro, began selling barbecue from his back yard in 1917 and bottled a sauce that still carries his name. The Jones family of Ayden claims a cooking line back to Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds* sold barbecue from a wagon in 1830; Pete Jones opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, and after a 1979 National Geographic article called his restaurant 'the barbecue capital of the world' he put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on the roof.

The east's argument with the west is a set-piece. Two newspaper columnists ran a mock war over it: Jerry Bledsoe, self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority', for Lexington, and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, 'oracle of the holy grub', for the east — Bledsoe wrote that Rogers 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue'. The joke reached the legislature: bills in 2006 to make the Lexington Barbecue Festival the state's official barbecue festival were defeated, and the 2007 compromise named it the official food festival of the Piedmont Triad instead, so that no one style could be called the state's. Readers still take sides, and the two styles are the axis on which every North Carolina barbecue conversation turns.
how: A hog of 80 to 180 pounds dressed weight is split down the backbone and laid skin-up over the heat, then turned skin-down to crisp at the end; on a wood pit the coals are shoveled in from a burn barrel every half hour through a night. At many eastern pits the cooker is gas or electric, which the state's health rules made easier than a wood pit. The meat is chopped on a block with cleavers, the crisp skin chopped in for texture, and seasoned on the block with the vinegar sauce and salt. A plate is barbecue, slaw and cornbread; a sandwich is barbecue and slaw on a soft bun; a tray is the same without bread.
today: The whole-hog pits of the east are the ones the national press writes about: Skylight Inn and Sam Jones BBQ in Pitt County, B's in Greenville, Grady's in Dudley, Wilber's in Goldsboro (reopened 2021 after a 2019 closure), Parker's in Wilson. Many more eastern places cook shoulders or hams rather than the whole animal and are still called eastern by their sauce.
geo: 35.47, -77.42 (region)
- kin → lexington (style): the other North Carolina: shoulders instead of the whole hog, a red dip instead of clear vinegar, red slaw instead of white. The two define each other.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce, and the one thing every eastern pit agrees on: vinegar, salt, pepper, no tomato.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut it is named for — the entire pig, cooked as one piece and chopped together.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the slaw on its tray, mayonnaise-dressed and pale, against the red slaw of the Piedmont.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the bread of the eastern tray; at Skylight Inn it is a dense skillet cake baked in pork fat.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the social form of the same cooking: the whole hog cooked for a crowd, and the crowd pulling the meat off the bones by hand.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): its best-known pit, in Ayden since 1947, cooking whole hogs over wood.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): its nearest cousin across the state line: the Pee Dee also cooks the whole hog with a vinegar-pepper sauce.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word, which in the east is a noun for this chopped pork and nothing else.
- not to be confused with lexington: Look at the slaw and the sauce. Red slaw and a reddish dip mean Lexington; pale slaw and a clear, thin vinegar sauce mean the east. If the meat has chopped crisp skin through it, it is whole hog.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/eastern-nc/eastern-nc-cooked-and-chopped-hogs-at-b-s-barbecue.jpg · Public domain · City of Greenville, North Carolina · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACooked_and_chopped_hogs_at_B%27s_Barbecue.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/eastern-nc/eastern-nc-northcarolinabarbecuebanner.jpg · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Rastapopulous · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ANorthCarolinaBarbecueBanner.JPG

## Heavy tomato barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/sc-heavy-tomato/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/sc-heavy-tomato.json
id: sc-heavy-tomato
aliases: heavy-tomato style · tomato-and-sugar barbecue · Upstate barbecue · western South Carolina barbecue
said: Menus call it 'sweet', 'mild' or 'house'; 'heavy tomato' is the map's term.
facets: state=SC · meat=shoulder · base=heavy-tomato · fuel=mixed
region: The Upstate, South Carolina
what: Pork shoulders and butts, ribs and chicken cooked over hickory or on cookers and served with a thick, sweet, red sauce of tomato, brown sugar or molasses, vinegar and spices — the sauce the state tourism office says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf, and the one most of the country means by barbecue sauce. The four-sauce map gives it the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina: Greenville, Spartanburg, Anderson, Greenwood, the Savannah River side. Hash here is often beef, or pork and beef with onions, over rice.
story: The heavy tomato sauce is the newcomer. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's history says it 'evolved only recently, that is, in the last sixty or so years', pushed by commercial brands, and the wider record agrees: Heinz bottled the first major-label barbecue sauce in 1940, General Foods' Open Pit followed, Kraft came in around 1960 and advertised its way to first place, and after the war the sugar and the ingredient count of sauces climbed. The typical commercial sauce is Kansas City's, 'thick, reddish-brown, tomato-based, and made with sugar, vinegar, and spices', and Wikipedia's South Carolina article says the heavy tomato sauce of the west is 'more similar to sauces popular in other states'. *Inference —* a sauce that arrived by bottle would settle where the older sauces were thinnest on the ground, at the state's western edge, farthest from the whole-hog coast and the German Midlands.

Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville cooks pork butts twelve hours and ribs more than eight over hickory logs in open pits and puts two sauces out, a tomato-based mild and a mustard-based spicy. Greenwood's Festival of Discovery, each July, hosts a Kansas City Barbeque Society-sanctioned Carolina barbecue and Black Kettle hash competition and the South Carolina state championship cook-off, with a Blues Cruise through the uptown venues.
how: Simmer tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — with brown sugar or molasses, vinegar, salt, black pepper and spices until it thickens. It is a finishing and table sauce: brushed on ribs and chicken near the end of cooking or served alongside, spooned over chopped pork on the plate, where it sits on the meat rather than soaking in. Hash in the Upstate is beef, or pork and beef, cooked with onions and served over rice.
today: Henry's Smokehouse runs rooms in Greenville and Simpsonville and a food truck; the Festival of Discovery brings its cook teams to Greenwood each July (July 8–10 in 2027). National bottles of the same kind share the western shelves with the state's mustard and vinegar sauces.
geo: 34.8611, -82.4133 (region)
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): its sauce: thick, sweet, red, and the one most of the country means by barbecue sauce.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): the thin vinegar-and-ketchup country to its east; the two share a color and little else.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the Midlands to its southeast, whose mustard sauce turns up beside the tomato one on Upstate tables.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the other end of the state, whole hog and clear vinegar, which the SCBA's history counts as the oldest sauce where this is the newest.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the Upstate's hash, of beef or pork and beef with onions, over rice.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut — pork butts twelve hours over hickory at Henry's.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the hickory logs in Henry's open pits.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): Greenville's pits, with a tomato-based mild sauce and a mustard-based spicy one on the table.
- kin → festival-of-discovery (event): Greenwood's July barbecue-and-blues festival, with a KCBS-sanctioned Carolina barbecue and hash competition and the state championship cook-off.
- kin → lake-high (person): whose SCBA history dates the sauce to the last sixty years.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): the association whose map gives the western corner to heavy tomato.
- not to be confused with sc-light-tomato: Heavy tomato clings to the meat and tastes of sugar; light tomato pours and tastes of vinegar. The tourism office's map gives the western and northwestern corner to heavy tomato.
- not to be confused with lexington: Both are red on pork shoulder. Lexington's dip is thin and sour and comes with red slaw; the Upstate's sauce is thick and sweet and comes with hash and rice.
sources: s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:wp-hash-stew — Hash (stew) — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-four-sauces — South Carolina's Four Barbecue Sauces (Gwen Fowler); s:sc-parks-sauce-map — South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism — the four barbecue sauce regions; s:web-scba-bbq-history — BBQ History (Lake E. High Jr.); s:web-henrys-smokehouse — Henry's Smokehouse — official site; s:web-henrys-destination-bbq — Henry's Smokehouse on Wade Hampton in Greenville; s:web-discovergreenwood-festival — SC Festival of Discovery; s:high-sc-barbeque — A History of South Carolina Barbeque

## Lexington-style barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/lexington/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/lexington.json
id: lexington
aliases: Lexington barbecue · Piedmont-style barbecue · Western-style barbecue · Western North Carolina barbecue
said: In the Piedmont the sauce is 'dip' and the slaw is 'red slaw' or 'barbecue slaw'. Barbecue is ordered chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced, and 'brown' means the crusty outside of the shoulder.
facets: state=NC · meat=shoulder · base=lexington-dip · fuel=wood
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Pork shoulders cooked slowly over hardwood coals, usually hickory, then chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced and dressed with a thin red sauce the Piedmont calls dip: vinegar, ketchup or tomato, water, salt, pepper and red pepper, sweeter or hotter by the house. It comes with red slaw — cabbage dressed with the same dip instead of mayonnaise — and hushpuppies, on a tray or a bun. The style belongs to the Piedmont west of Raleigh. Lexington, a Davidson County town of about 20,000 that calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World and counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, is its center; Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and High Point are its other towns.
story: Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent by the old Davidson County courthouse in 1919, and Jess Swicegood ran a stand a few yards from his within the decade. Warner Stamey, born in 1911, boarded with his sister in Lexington for high school and learned the pits from both men; he sold barbecue in Shelby after graduating, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's place and rename it, and in 1953 opened Stamey's on High Point Road in Greensboro. Stamey's own history credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue. Alton Beck, who had worked for Weaver, built the town's first bricks-and-mortar barbecue restaurant on West Center Street in 1938. Wayne Monk, who had worked for Holland Tussey and took Stamey as his model, opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in 1962; in 1983 a politically connected local attorney asked whether he would cook for President Reagan, and he served the heads of government at that year's economic summit in Williamsburg, Virginia — Thatcher and Mitterrand among them. In 2003 the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic.

The east–west argument is a newspaper invention that outlived the columns. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News, self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority', and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, 'oracle of the holy grub', traded columns for decades over whether ketchup belongs in the sauce. Bledsoe said Rogers 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue'; Rogers wrote that people who would put ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children 'are capable of most anything'. The joke reached the General Assembly in the 2005–06 session, when House Bill 21 and Senate Bill 47 would have made the Lexington Barbecue Festival the official barbecue festival of North Carolina; with nearly half the state eating eastern, neither passed. House Bill 433 passed in 2007 with a narrower title — 'Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina' — which named no style official for the state.
how: Shoulders roast for about ten hours over coals from a wood fire beside the pits — at Lexington Barbecue mostly oak, with hickory when it can be had — meat side down over the embers until it browns, then turned. Some Piedmont places cook on gas or electric cookers. The cooked shoulder is chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced to order, and the crusty outside can be asked for as 'brown'. The dip goes on at the block and stands on the table. A tray is barbecue and red slaw; a plate adds hushpuppies; a sandwich is chopped pork and red slaw on a bun.
today: Lexington counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants for about 20,000 people in 2003; Lexington Barbecue, Bar-B-Q Center and Cook's are in and around town, Stamey's in Greensboro, Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge in Shelby. The Lexington Barbecue Festival closes Main Street each October — October 24 in 2026 — and has been the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad since 2007.
geo: 35.797, -80.274 (region)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the other North Carolina: the whole hog with clear vinegar and white slaw, where this is the shoulder with a red dip and red slaw. Each defines itself against the other.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its sauce — the east's vinegar and pepper with ketchup or tomato added, called dip in the Piedmont — and the dressing of its slaw.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): its slaw, red because it is dressed with the dip and not mayonnaise; the sign of the Piedmont on any tray.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the only cut it cooks; the darker, fattier meat of the shoulder is what the style is built on.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its fuel: Lexington shoulders roast over oak and hickory coals, hickory when it can be had.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the crusty outside of the shoulder, chopped through the meat or asked for on its own as 'brown'.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the bread of the Piedmont tray; Stamey's own history credits Warner Stamey with putting them beside barbecue.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the Piedmont order: chopped pork and red slaw, no bread, hushpuppies on the side.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): chopped shoulder and red slaw on a bun; the red slaw is what tells a Lexington sandwich.
- kin → chopped (term): the word for how the shoulder comes off the block — chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced, by the customer's order.
- kin → dip (term): the Piedmont's word for its sauce.
- kin → piedmont (term): the region whose name is this style's other name.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): sold barbecue from a tent by the Lexington courthouse from 1919; the line starts with him.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): ran the stand beside Weaver's; Warner Stamey learned from both and bought his place in 1938.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): carried the method to Shelby and Greensboro and put hushpuppies on the tray; the men he taught run the Piedmont's pits.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): opened Lexington Barbecue in 1962 and cooked the style for the 1983 economic summit at Williamsburg.
- kin → jerry-bledsoe (person): the Piedmont's columnist in the newspaper war with the east.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): the east's columnist, whose ketchup jokes this style answered for decades.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): Wayne Monk's pit beside U.S. 29/70 since 1962, an America's Classic since 2003.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): an uptown Lexington pit; in Lexington, the Southern Foodways Alliance notes, eaters don't squirt sauce, they dip.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): Warner Stamey's Greensboro pit, opened 1953, with the brick pits built in the late 1960s.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): Shelby's pit, one of the state's oldest, cooking shoulders in the Piedmont way.
- kin → cooks-barbecue (place): Doug Cook's stand outside Lexington, built by hand in 1969.
- kin → short-sugars (place): Reidsville's pit, on the north edge of the dip country.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the October street festival, held since 1984, whose 'official' title took three bills to settle.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): its South Carolina cousin: a thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce that the SC Barbeque Association maps as one country with the Piedmont.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word, which in the Piedmont is a noun for chopped shoulder with dip.
- not to be confused with eastern-nc: Red slaw and a reddish dip on chopped or sliced shoulder mean Lexington; pale mayonnaise slaw and a clear vinegar sauce on meat with crisp skin chopped through it mean the east. If the counter understands 'brown', you are in the Piedmont.
- not to be confused with sc-light-tomato: South Carolina's light tomato sauce is the same vinegar-and-ketchup idea, and the SC Barbeque Association maps it with the Piedmont. The tell is on the plate: red slaw and hushpuppies are Lexington; hash over rice is South Carolina.

## Light tomato barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/sc-light-tomato/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/sc-light-tomato.json
id: sc-light-tomato
aliases: light-tomato style · vinegar-and-ketchup barbecue · upper Midlands barbecue
said: Nobody orders 'light tomato'; it is the map's word. At the counter it is the house sauce, mild or hot.
facets: state=SC · meat=mixed · base=light-tomato · fuel=mixed
region: The Pee Dee, The Upstate, South Carolina
what: Pork — whole hog in the Pee Dee, shoulders and hams in the upper Midlands — cooked over coals or on cookers and served with a thin sauce that is the Carolinas' vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup stirred in. On South Carolina's four-sauce map, as the state tourism office and the South Carolina Barbeque Association publish it, it holds the Pee Dee and the upper middle of the state along the North Carolina line. Hash comes with it, of beef as often as pork toward the Upstate. It is the South Carolina twin of Lexington's dip, and the Barbeque Association's history maps the North Carolina Piedmont and the South Carolina Pee Dee as one light-tomato country.
story: The light-tomato sauce is the youngest of the vinegar family. The South Carolina Barbeque Association dates it to about 1900, 'vinegar and pepper with tomato ketchup added', and Wikipedia's account has it born of cheap mass-produced ketchup in the early twentieth century and of North Carolina's influence on the Upstate. The general history of barbecue sauce runs the same way: sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire came into sauces in the 1920s, and everything after the war got sweeter. *Inference —* the Lexington dip and the light-tomato sauce are the same invention made twice, or once and carried; the SCBA's own history treats the North Carolina Piedmont and the South Carolina Pee Dee as one light-tomato country, and the Piedmont's dip is the sauce Wikipedia describes as 'similar to the East Carolina sauce with the addition of tomato paste, tomato sauce, or ketchup'.

Where exactly it lives is argued. Kovacik and Winberry's 1987 geography set the four regions; the tourism office gives light tomato the Pee Dee and the 'upper middle part' of the state; Wikipedia gives it the Upstate; Robert Moss says the state has only two sauces, sweet mustard and spicy vinegar, and the tomato sauces are variations. Union County, in the upper middle, once had nearly fifty hash houses; Midway BBQ at Buffalo, opened around 1941 by Jack O'Dell, is the one left, cooking shoulders and hams over hickory, and its hash is beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper stewed down in a pot — 'Without hash,' its manager Jay Allen told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2012, 'we're done. We're closed.'
how: Vinegar, salt, black and red pepper, and ketchup enough to color it, thinned with water; cayenne or a bottled hot sauce for heat; a little sugar in some houses. It is warmed, not cooked down. It goes on chopped or pulled pork at the block and stands on the table; on a Pee Dee buffet it sits beside the vinegar-and-pepper bottle, and in the upper Midlands it comes with beef hash and rice.
today: Midway BBQ at Buffalo, Union County, sells chopped pork in its house 'Original Sauce', pulled pork with none, and its beef hash; the tourism office still draws the light-tomato band across the Pee Dee and the upper Midlands, and mustard has spread into these counties from the middle of the state.
geo: 34.705, -81.2133 (region)
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): its sauce: vinegar and pepper with ketchup added, thin enough to pour.
- kin → lexington (style): its North Carolina twin — shoulder with a vinegar-and-ketchup dip; the SC Barbeque Association maps the two as one country.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the same sauce under the Piedmont's name, north of the line.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the base it adds ketchup to; the older sauce it grew from about 1900.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): shares the Pee Dee with it; the tourism office puts both sauces there, and the whole hog under both.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): the thick, sweet sauce of the western corner, against this thin one.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the mustard country to its south, now spreading into its counties.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the side toward the Upstate: at Midway a stew of beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper.
- kin → midway-bbq (place): Buffalo, Union County, since about 1941: the last of the county's fifty hash houses, cooking shoulders and hams over hickory.
- kin → lake-high (person): whose SC Barbeque Association history dates the sauce to about 1900.
- kin → robert-moss (person): who counts it as a variation on vinegar sauce, not a region of its own.
- kin → pee-dee (term): the region the map gives it in the northeast.
- kin → piedmont (term): the North Carolina region the SC Barbeque Association pairs it with.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): the association whose map draws the light-tomato band.
- not to be confused with lexington: The sauces are near twins. Red slaw and hushpuppies put you in North Carolina; hash over rice puts you in South Carolina.
- not to be confused with sc-heavy-tomato: Light tomato pours and soaks in; heavy tomato clings and coats. If it looks like the bottle from the grocery shelf, it is heavy.
- not to be confused with sc-pee-dee: On the same Pee Dee buffet, the clear bottle is vinegar-and-pepper and the orange-red one is light tomato.

## Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/sc-pee-dee/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/sc-pee-dee.json
id: sc-pee-dee
aliases: Pee Dee barbecue · vinegar-and-pepper barbecue · Williamsburg County barbecue · South Carolina whole hog
said: In the Pee Dee a place 'cooks hogs'. The sauce is 'the sauce' or 'pepper vinegar'; Brown's in Kingstree calls its own 'barbecue gravy'.
facets: state=SC · meat=whole hog · base=vinegar-pepper · fuel=wood
region: The Pee Dee, The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: Whole hogs cooked overnight over hardwood coals, pulled or chopped, and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and red pepper — the same sauce as eastern North Carolina's across the state line. The skin is taken off and fried into skins sold by the bag. Hash over rice, chicken bog, slaw and white bread fill the plate, often from a buffet. The style belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina along the Pee Dee and Black rivers — Hemingway, Kingstree, Manning, Florence — and runs down the coast, where the state tourism office marks vinegar-and-pepper as the sauce of the shore.
story: The vinegar-and-pepper sauce is the oldest in the Carolinas; the state tourism office calls it 'the oldest sauce, perhaps the oldest in the nation'. The South Carolina Barbeque Association ties it to the Scots who settled Williamsburg County, and Wikipedia's history of barbecue sauce credits enslaved African cooks with popularising the vinegar, black pepper and chili-flake sauce of the eastern Carolinas. *Tradition holds —* the Pee Dee's whole hog is the same cooking as the Coastal Plain's north of the line, one tradition with a border through it.

The pits that carry it are family stores. Theron Burrows opened an Esso station and country store on the new Highway 521 between Manning and Georgetown in 1937; George and Adalyn Cooper took it over in 1974, and Russell Cooper cooks whole hogs there beside the hardware and the hams with a sauce he calls 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper'. Roosevelt and Ella Scott opened a gas station and variety store in an oak grove at Hemingway in 1972 and cooked a hog or two on weekends; their son Rodney cooked his first at eleven, and by 2012 the store cooked eight to ten a night. Thomas Brown, a farmer, began selling plates from a window on his farm outside Kingstree in 1981 and built a dining room a decade later. Kingstree holds a Pig Pickin' Festival each fall, judged on vinegar-based barbecue, and Hemingway a Bar-B-Q Shag Festival each spring.

Rodney Scott left the family business after a quarrel with his father in 2016 and opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis in February 2017; in 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a chef award, and after his Chef's Table episode in 2020 the restaurant set sales records three days running. Roosevelt Scott died in 2010 and Ella in 2023; the Hemingway store closed for five months and reopened in May 2024 under Ella's brother Sam Wilson and grandson Dominic Scott. In May 2026 the Charleston company's locations were reported closed temporarily under lawsuits and liens.
how: At Scott's the wood — freshly cut hickory, pecan and oak — burns down in a barrel of sheet metal with old truck axles for a grate; the embers are scooped from the bottom and hauled into the pit house under cinder-block-and-brick pits to hold the heat for twelve hours or more while the hog cooks overnight. Cooper's cooks chickens on one half of the pit and hogs on the other. The meat is pulled at Scott's, chopped at Brown's, 'picked and mixed' at McCabe's after up to twelve hours; at Brown's the vinegar-and-hot-pepper 'gravy' is mopped on as the hog smokes. It is served as a sandwich on white bread or a plate with beans and slaw, with skins sold on the side.
today: Scott's Bar-B-Que at Hemingway is open Wednesday to Saturday; Cooper's Country Store sells gasoline, groceries, hardware and whole-hog barbecue on Highway 521; Brown's in Kingstree and McCabe's in Manning cook whole hogs for their buffets. Rodney Scott's Charleston restaurants were reported closed temporarily in May 2026.
geo: 33.7517, -79.4464 (region)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the same cooking north of the line: whole hog, vinegar and pepper, no tomato. The Pee Dee is the eastern tradition's southern half.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce: vinegar, salt, black and red pepper, mopped on the hog and poured over the meat.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the other South Carolina: yellow sauce in the middle of the state, where this is clear vinegar in the northeast.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): shares the Pee Dee with it on the tourism office's map — the same sauce with ketchup in it.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, cooked overnight and pulled or chopped whole.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the skin, taken off and fried, sold by the bag at Scott's.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the stew over rice that shares the buffet with the pork.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): the Pee Dee's chicken-and-rice pilaf, most at home from Florence to the coast.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the sheet-metal barrel with truck axles for a grate in which Scott's burns its wood to embers.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the cinder-block-and-brick pits at Scott's, fed with embers through the night.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): coals shovelled under the hog, not smoke from a firebox.
- kin → pee-dee (term): the region: the northeast of the state along the Pee Dee River.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): cooked his first hog at eleven at his parents' Hemingway store and carried the style to Charleston and a James Beard award.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): the Scott family's store and pit house at Hemingway, since 1972.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): Rodney Scott's Charleston restaurant, opened February 2017: whole hog with a spicy vinegar sauce.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): Thomas Brown's farm pit outside Kingstree, since 1981, where the vinegar-and-hot-pepper 'gravy' is mopped onto the hog.
- kin → mccabes-bar-b-q (place): Manning's whole-hog pit: pigs cooked up to twelve hours, then picked and mixed.
- kin → coopers-country-store (place): the 1937 filling station and store on Highway 521 where Russell Cooper cooks whole hogs with 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper'.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): Kingstree's fall Pig Pickin' Festival, a cook-off judged on vinegar-based barbecue.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): whose 2012 oral histories with Rodney Scott, Russell Cooper and the Browns are this page's record.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): pulled pork on white bread at Scott's.
- not to be confused with eastern-nc: Nothing on the tray tells them apart — whole hog, vinegar and pepper, pale slaw on both sides of the line. Hash and rice or chicken bog on the plate, and skins by the bag at the counter, put you in South Carolina.
- not to be confused with sc-mustard: Clear sauce and pale meat is the Pee Dee; yellow is the Midlands. Both may cook whole hogs and both serve hash.

## South Carolina mustard barbecue (style)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/style/sc-mustard/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/style/sc-mustard.json
id: sc-mustard
aliases: Midlands barbecue · mustard-based barbecue · Carolina Gold barbecue · Dutch Fork barbecue
said: Midlands menus say 'barbecue' or 'pork' and let the color of the sauce speak; the bottles say Carolina Gold or Southern Gold.
facets: state=SC · meat=mixed · base=mustard · fuel=mixed
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: Pork — whole hogs at some pits, hams or shoulders at others — cooked over hardwood coals or on cookers, chopped or pulled, and dressed with a yellow sauce of prepared mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices. Hash, a stew of pork and onions that in the Midlands often takes mustard too, comes over white rice beside it, and the meal is often a buffet. The style belongs to the Midlands, the counties around Columbia: a belt the geographers Charles Kovacik and John Winberry drew in 1987 from Newberry and Lexington counties down through Orangeburg toward Charleston, the German-settled country whose fork of the Saluda and Broad rivers is called the Dutch Fork.
story: German Protestants took up land between the Saluda and Broad rivers from the 1730s, in what became Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties — the Dutch Fork, 'Dutch' from deutsch — and at Orangeburg, where a colony of Swiss, German and Dutch families settled in 1735. The state's accounts lay the mustard sauce at their door: the tourism office says they 'brought their love of mustard', and the South Carolina Barbeque Association's history names the families who sell it — Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman, Dukes. *Tradition holds —* the sauce was on farm tables long before any bottle; the earliest name attached to it is Joe Bessinger, who served it with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939, and some accounts credit him with inventing it.

His sons carried it out of Orangeburg County. Maurice opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr.; Thomas opened Bessinger's in Charleston, and Melvin opened Melvin's in Mount Pleasant in 1982; the Dukes family opened buffet restaurants from the 1950s — the two families, Charleston Magazine says, brought Midlands barbecue to the Lowcountry after the war. Maurice bottled the sauce as Carolina Gold, sold it in supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s, and by 1999 ran the largest barbecue business in the country.

The name also carries a civil-rights case. In 1964 Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry to a Piggie Park drive-in and sued under the Civil Rights Act; Bessinger argued that his religion forbade serving Black customers. The Fourth Circuit ordered the restaurants opened to all, and in 1968 the Supreme Court, in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, held that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the State House, he raised it over his restaurants and handed out tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; grocery chains dropped Carolina Gold, his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007, and his children took down the last flag in 2013. He died in 2014.
how: At Sweatman's, whole hogs cook twelve to fourteen hours over oak and hickory coals and are basted with the mustard sauce as they go; at Maurice's, hams cook sixteen hours over hickory and the chopped meat is coated with the sauce for the plate; at Hite's, whole hogs and hams go over oak and hickory coals rendered from a wood fire. The sauce is prepared yellow mustard, vinegar, sugar or brown sugar and pepper — Bessinger's supermarket bottle listed soy sauce too. It goes on at the block, stands on the buffet line, and in the Midlands goes into the hash pot; some Orangeburg places blend it with ketchup into a 'rust' sauce.
today: Mustard sauce has spread from the Midlands to menus across the state this century. Maurice's is open in West Columbia — its offices, pits and side factory burned on October 26, 2024; the restaurant and its sign survived — with Bessinger's in Charleston, Sweatman's at Holly Hill and Hite's in West Columbia on Fridays and Saturdays, Shealy's at Batesburg-Leesville, and Dukes restaurants around Orangeburg.
geo: 34.0006, -81.0347 (region)
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): its sauce, and the thing South Carolina is known for beyond its borders: prepared mustard, vinegar, sugar and pepper.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): its side: the pork-and-onion stew over white rice, which in the German Midlands often takes mustard too.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the other South Carolina: whole hog and clear vinegar-pepper in the northeast, where this is mustard in the middle.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): the band to its north on the four-sauce map, where ketchup goes into the vinegar instead of mustard.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): the western corner, where the sauce is thick and sweet with tomato.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the whole-hog cooking it shares at Sweatman's and Hite's; only the sauce on the hog differs.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut at Sweatman's and Hite's, basted with mustard sauce as it cooks.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut, with hams, at Bessinger's in Charleston and at Maurice's, where hams cook sixteen hours over hickory.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the coals under Sweatman's hogs and Hite's, and the hickory under Maurice's hams.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German-settled fork of the Saluda and Broad whose families the sauce is traced to.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name the sauce is bottled and known under, from Maurice Bessinger's supermarket brand.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): made the sauce a supermarket product and his company the largest barbecue business in the country by 1999; the defendant in Newman v. Piggie Park, and the man who raised Confederate flags over his restaurants in 2000.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): served the sauce with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939; some accounts credit him with inventing it.
- kin → lake-high (person): the SC Barbeque Association's founder, whose history maps the sauce onto the German-settled counties.
- kin → robert-moss (person): the historian who says the state has two sauces, sweet mustard and spicy vinegar, not four.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): West Columbia, since 1953: hams over hickory, chopped and coated with the sauce the family now bottles as Southern Gold.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): Thomas Bessinger's Charleston pit on Savannah Highway, cooking shoulders and hams over wood coals.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): Holly Hill's farmhouse pit, whole hogs basted with mustard sauce over oak and hickory, in its brick pits since 1977.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the Orangeburg-country buffets of Manuel Dukes's descendants, from the 1950s, with mustard and 'rust' sauces.
- kin → hites-bar-b-q (place): West Columbia, since 1957: whole hogs and hams over oak and hickory coals, and a sauce built on a strong yellow mustard.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): the Batesburg-Leesville buffet, established 1969.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): Jackie Hite's pit at Leesville, opened May 1979 by the town's fire chief and later mayor: hickory-smoked pigs, a sauce of mustard, vinegar and pepper.
- kin → cannons-bbq (place): a pit at Little Mountain, in Newberry County's share of the Dutch Fork.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): the association whose sauce map puts mustard in the middle of the state.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): in South Carolina, pulled pork with the yellow sauce and slaw on a bun.
- not to be confused with sc-light-tomato: Yellow on the meat is mustard; a thin orange-red is light tomato; a brownish blend of both is Orangeburg's rust sauce, which is still mustard country.
- not to be confused with sc-pee-dee: Both put hash and rice on the plate and both may cook the whole hog; the Pee Dee's sauce is clear and peppery, the Midlands' is yellow and sweet.

## Bone Suckin' Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/bone-suckin-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/bone-suckin-sauce.json
id: bone-suckin-sauce
aliases: Bone Suckin' Sweet Southern · Ford's Foods sauce
said: Bone Suckin', with the g dropped on the label.
facets: base=heavy-tomato · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A Raleigh line of bottled sauces, of which the one that built the brand is Sweet Southern: cane sugar first, tomato puree second, water third, apple cider vinegar fourth, at six grams of sugar to the tablespoon. The house also bottles an Eastern Vinegar sauce, whose label puts apple cider vinegar and distilled vinegar first and tomato paste sixth, and a mustard whose seven ingredients name no tomato at all. One maker, three readings of the same state's shelf.
story: The company dates the sauce to Raleigh in 1992 and calls the recipe a family one; the Sweet Southern page describes that bottle as the flavor the brand launched with. The mustard's page quotes Mr. Ford, of Ford's Foods, on making a sweet version of the house's sweet-and-spicy mustard without the heat.

The interesting part is on the backs of the bottles. Sweet Southern reads sugar, tomato, water, vinegar — the order of a Kansas City sauce, made in the eastern half of North Carolina, where the sauce a pit puts on a chopped hog has neither sugar nor tomato in it. The Eastern Vinegar bottle, sold alongside it, inverts that: two vinegars, then water, then cane sugar, with tomato paste down at six. The maker's own page for that bottle describes the tomato and molasses in it as a light hint behind the vinegar. *Inference —* a house that sells both is not choosing between the styles; it is selling the distance between them as two products.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): what its Sweet Southern bottle reads as: sugar first, tomato second.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the region it is made in, whose own sauce its Eastern Vinegar bottle is aimed at.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce its Eastern Vinegar bottle reaches for, and stops short of at the sugar and the tomato paste.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the South Carolina sauce its mustard bottle borrows the method of: mustard first, no tomato.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): what a thick sweet sauce is brushed on at the end of a cook.

## Carolina Treet (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/carolina-treet/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/carolina-treet.json
id: carolina-treet
aliases: Carolina Treet Cooking Barbecue Sauce · Carolina Treet Original
said: Treet, in Wilmington; spelled with two e's.
facets: base=other · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A Wilmington sauce that fits none of the four Carolina bases. Its label reads water, vinegar, wheat flour, salt, soybean oil, paprika, garlic, onion, xanthan gum, spices — no tomato, no mustard, no sugar. The wheat flour does what tomato paste does elsewhere: it thickens. What it tastes of is vinegar, smoke and salt, and it carries 536 milligrams of sodium in a tablespoon, the highest figure among the sixty-eight bottles this project measured. The bottle calls itself a cooking barbecue sauce, meaning it goes on during the cook rather than at the table.
story: The label is the document. Ten ingredients, and the four that name a Carolina style — tomato, mustard, sugar, pepper — supply only the pepper, as paprika. A sauce built on vinegar and flour is a gravy's method applied to a barbecue sauce, and it is the only bottle in the harvest that works that way.

The brand is made by Legacy Family Foods, and carolinatreet.com now forwards to that company's site, which sells the Original alongside other lines. *Tradition holds —* the sauce is a Wilmington and Cape Fear fixture, poured over chicken as often as pork; the project has not found a dated founding on the record and does not assert one.
how: Brushed on chicken, pork and ribs during cooking, which is what the words on the label direct. It is thin and it browns, and because there is no sugar in it there is nothing to burn.
today: Sold in eastern North Carolina groceries and from Legacy Family Foods.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the region it is made and sold in, though its label matches none of that region's sauce.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the eastern sauce it shares a first two ingredients with and then leaves, at the wheat flour.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): what a cooking sauce with no sugar in it is brushed on.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the opposite bottle: tomato and sugar first, nothing to soak in.
- not to be confused with vinegar-pepper-sauce: Both pour thin and taste of vinegar. The eastern sauce is vinegar and pepper and nothing else; Carolina Treet is thickened with wheat flour and carries oil, garlic and onion.

A Practical System for Private Families, in Town and Country, Especially Adapted to the Southern States; s:book-virginia-house-wife — The Virginia House-Wife, or Methodical Cook

## George's Barbecue Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/georges-barbecue-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/georges-barbecue-sauce.json
id: georges-barbecue-sauce
aliases: George's Sauce · George's Original · George's of Nashville
said: George's, on shelves across eastern North Carolina; the label says George's Barbecue Sauce.
facets: base=lexington-dip · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A bottled sauce from Nashville, North Carolina, a Nash County town on the edge of the Coastal Plain, sold in three strengths: Original, Hot and Special. The Original's label reads vinegar, water, tomato concentrate, tomato paste, sugar, apples, salt, high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, red pepper and spices — vinegar leading, tomato third and fourth, and a sweetening that runs to three separate entries. It carries 3.5 grams of sugar in a tablespoon and 180 milligrams of sodium. The Special reverses the first four: tomato concentrate and tomato paste come before the water and the vinegar, and jalapenos join the list.
story: The company dates itself to 1975 and names George Stallings as its founder, who worked the recipe out in his outdoor garage; after it caught on at home, he and his brother cooked, bottled and sold it by hand. The maker's own page says the sauces are still made by hand in small batches to that recipe, and that 4,500 bottles a day are poured, packed and shipped by hand from Womble Road in Nashville.

*Inference —* the label is worth reading against the map. Nashville sits in the eastern half of the state, where the sauce that goes on a chopped hog is vinegar and pepper with no tomato in it. George's pours vinegar first, then puts tomato third — the order of the Piedmont dip, not the Coastal Plain's — and sells it as an eastern-style sauce. A bottle that has to keep on a shelf and please a wide market is not the same object as a sauce mixed in a bucket behind a pit, and the reading here describes the bottle.
how: Poured over chopped or pulled pork, brushed on chicken and ribs, used as a mop while a shoulder cooks. It is thin enough to soak rather than coat. Three strengths sit beside each other on the same shelf: Original, Hot, and Special, which is the tomato-first one with jalapenos.
today: Made and shipped from Nashville, North Carolina. The three bottles are sold from the company's site and through eastern North Carolina grocers.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it is sold as, and the region it is made in: the Coastal Plain, where the pits' own sauce carries no tomato.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the order its label actually reads in: vinegar first, tomato behind it, sugar behind that.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce of its own region, which stops where this bottle adds tomato and sugar.
- kin → scotts-barbecue-sauce (sauce): the other eastern North Carolina bottle on the same shelves, sixty miles south at Goldsboro, with four ingredients to this one's ten and no sugar at all.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): what the bottle is bought for.
- not to be confused with scotts-barbecue-sauce: Both are eastern North Carolina bottles. Scott's label names four ingredients and no sugar; George's names ten, of which three are sweeteners.

## Golding Farms Foods (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/golding-farms-sauces/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/golding-farms-sauces.json
id: golding-farms-sauces
aliases: Golding Farms · Golding Blends
said: Golding Farms on the retail label; Golding Blends on the company's own site.
facets: base=mustard · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: A Winston-Salem sauce manufacturer, the second of that city's two, and one whose output mostly reaches a table under someone else's name. It sells a retail line under the Golding Farms label — the Honey Mustard dipping sauce reads distilled vinegar, canola oil, sugar, honey, water, mustard seed, at 3.5 grams of sugar to the tablespoon — and blends and packs sauces for brands, food service and industrial customers.
story: The company says it has been bringing flavor forward since 1972 and describes fifty years of blending for brand, food service and industrial buyers from Winston-Salem, with an in-house development team of a chef, scientists and technicians.

*Inference —* Winston-Salem holds both ends of the bottled-sauce trade. T.W. Garner makes Texas Pete under its own name and sells it in every grocery in the state; Golding blends and packs, and the name on the bottle is often a customer's. Between them the city puts more sauce in circulation than any pit town, which is a fact about the sauce shelf rather than about the pits. No Golding Farms barbecue sauce label turned up on 16 September 2026, so the retail reading on this page is of the honey mustard dipping sauce, which the label does not call a barbecue sauce.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): the other Winston-Salem sauce house, three miles away, whose bottle carries its own name.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the South Carolina sauce its honey mustard shares a first ingredient order with, and none of the history.
- kin → lexington (style): the style of the Piedmont it manufactures in, whose pits mix their own dip and buy no bottles.

## heavy tomato sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/heavy-tomato-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/heavy-tomato-sauce.json
id: heavy-tomato-sauce
aliases: tomato-and-sugar sauce · sweet red sauce · thick tomato barbecue sauce · Kansas City-style sauce
said: 'Sweet' or 'mild' on Upstate menus; 'barbecue sauce', without qualification, to most of the country.
facets: base=heavy-tomato · styles=sc-heavy-tomato
region: The Upstate, South Carolina, The American South
what: A thick red sauce built on tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — sweetened with brown sugar or molasses, soured with vinegar and seasoned with spices, cooked down until it clings. It is the sauce of the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina on the state's four-sauce map: the tourism office's 'tomato-and-sugar sauce', the one it says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf. It goes on after cooking — on the plate, on the bun, on ribs and chicken — and sits on the meat rather than soaking in.
story: This is the national sauce at the state's edge. Heinz put out the first major bottled barbecue sauce in 1940, General Foods' Open Pit followed, Kraft came in around 1960 and advertised its way to first place, and after the war the sugar and the ingredient count of sauces climbed; the typical commercial sauce is the Kansas City kind, 'thick, reddish-brown, tomato-based, and made with sugar, vinegar, and spices', which Wikipedia's sauce history places downstream of the Piedmont's thin dip and Memphis's sauce. The South Carolina Barbeque Association says the heavy tomato sauce 'evolved only recently, that is, in the last sixty or so years', pushed by commercial brands, and Wikipedia's South Carolina article calls it 'more similar to sauces popular in other states'. *Inference —* a sauce that arrived by bottle would settle where the older sauces were thinnest on the ground, at the state's western edge, farthest from the whole-hog coast and the German Midlands. Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville makes its own tomato-based mild sauce by hand and sets a mustard-based spicy one beside it.
how: Simmer tomato with brown sugar or molasses, vinegar, salt, black pepper and spices until it thickens. It is a finishing and table sauce: brushed on ribs and chicken near the end of cooking or served alongside, spooned over chopped pork on the plate. It is the one Carolina sauce that coats rather than soaks.
today: Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville serves its tomato-based mild sauce beside a mustard one; national bottles fill the western shelves. Greenwood's July Festival of Discovery judges Carolina barbecue and hash under Kansas City Barbeque Society rules.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): the style it names: the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): the thin cousin: same color, opposite body.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the Midlands sauce that shares Upstate tables with it.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the Carolinas' oldest sauce, from which this is the furthest departure: tomato and sugar where that is vinegar and pepper.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the Piedmont's thin red sauce; Wikipedia's sauce history places Kansas City's thick one downstream of it.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): on pork butts at Henry's after twelve hours over hickory.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): Greenville's tomato-based mild sauce, made by hand, beside a mustard one.
- kin → festival-of-discovery (event): Greenwood's July cook-off, judged under Kansas City Barbeque Society rules — the sanctioning body of the thick-sauce world.
- not to be confused with light-tomato-sauce: Heavy tomato coats the meat and tastes of sugar; light tomato pours and tastes of vinegar.
- not to be confused with lexington-dip: Both are red. Dip is thin and sour and soaks into the meat; heavy tomato sits on top of it.
sources: s:web-usda-fdc-branded — FoodData Central, Branded Foods; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-four-sauces — South Carolina's Four Barbecue Sauces (Gwen Fowler); s:sc-parks-sauce-map — South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism — the four barbecue sauce regions; s:web-scba-bbq-history — BBQ History (Lake E. High Jr.); s:web-henrys-smokehouse — Henry's Smokehouse — official site; s:web-henrys-destination-bbq — Henry's Smokehouse on Wade Hampton in Greenville; s:web-discovergreenwood-festival — SC Festival of Discovery; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce-kansas-city-style — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce (Kansas City-style) — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce-i — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce I — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce-sweet — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce (Sweet) — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce-ii — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce II — Wikibooks Cookbook

## Lexington dip (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/lexington-dip/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/lexington-dip.json
id: lexington-dip
aliases: dip · Lexington-style sauce · Piedmont sauce · Western sauce · red sauce · barbecue dip
said: 'Dip' is the Piedmont's word; a Lexington counter will not correct you for 'sauce', but the menu says dip.
root: English dip (n.), from the verb dip, Old English dyppan, Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'. The noun 'act of dipping' is recorded from the 1590s and the sense 'a liquid into which something is dipped' by 1825. · first seen: the noun sense 'liquid into which something is dipped' by 1825 (etymonline, dip n.1); no dated first use of 'dip' for the Lexington sauce found by this project · *Tradition holds —* the name is from the use: the chopped meat is dipped in it, and it is thin enough to dip into rather than spread. Etymonline notes that the sense 'thick, savory sauce for dunking pieces of raw vegetables' (by 1962) is a modern re-coinage, so the barbecue dip keeps the older, thinner sense.
facets: base=lexington-dip · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: The Piedmont's sauce: the east's vinegar, salt, pepper and red pepper with ketchup or tomato and water added, sometimes sugar, so that it comes out thin and reddish — tangy, a little sweet or hot by the house, and every restaurant's recipe its own. It is the sauce of pork-shoulder barbecue in Lexington, Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and the rest of the Piedmont. It is basted on the shoulders as they cook, goes on the chopped meat at the block, stands on the table, and, in place of mayonnaise, dresses the red slaw.
story: The dip came out of the Lexington tents. Sid Weaver sold barbecue by the old courthouse from 1919 and Jess Swicegood beside him; Warner Stamey learned from both and carried the sauce to Shelby and Greensboro, and the men he taught — Wayne Monk at Lexington Barbecue among them — carried it further. *Tradition holds —* the tomato came in with cheap ketchup after the First World War, the same years Wikipedia's sauce history gives for ketchup and sugar entering barbecue sauces generally; the South Carolina Barbeque Association dates the same vinegar-and-ketchup idea to about 1900 in the Pee Dee and the North Carolina Piedmont.

The ketchup is what the columnists fought over. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News took the Piedmont's side — 'America loves ketchup' — and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer the east's: 'People who would put ketchup in the sauce they feed to innocent children are capable of most anything.' The joke ran for decades and reached the General Assembly over the Lexington Barbecue Festival's title in 2005–07. In Lexington the sauce is also the slaw dressing: red slaw is cabbage, vinegar, ketchup and black pepper, no mayonnaise, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's note on Bar-B-Q Center says it plainly — in Lexington, barbecue eaters don't squirt sauce, they dip.
how: Vinegar, ketchup, water, salt, pepper and other spices, in the town's own description; red pepper flakes and sugar in many kitchens; simmered and kept warm. On the pit it is a baste for the shoulders through a ten-hour cook. At the block it is spooned into the chopped meat; at the table it comes in a bottle. For red slaw, chopped cabbage is dressed with it — the same vinegar, ketchup and pepper — instead of mayonnaise, so the slaw matches the meat.
today: Every Lexington pit keeps its own recipe; the town's Wikipedia article calls each one 'a closely guarded secret'. Red slaw dressed with it goes on hot dogs across the Piedmont as well as on trays.
- kin → lexington (style): the style it names: pork shoulder with dip and red slaw, in the Piedmont.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): dressed with the dip in place of mayonnaise — that is why it is red.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the east's sauce it grew from: vinegar, salt and pepper, before the ketchup went in.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): its South Carolina twin, which the SC Barbeque Association maps with the Piedmont.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the thick sweet sauce it is not: dip is thin and sour, and soaks in.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the other Carolina sauce with a color: yellow to its red.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): what it is basted on through a ten-hour cook and chopped into at the block.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): on the tray at the block and in the bottle beside it.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): on the chopped pork and in the red slaw on top of it.
- kin → dip (term): the word itself, with its root and its Piedmont sense.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): Wayne Monk's 'dark, rather thin' dip, neither too mild nor too fiery, in Bob Garner's description.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): where, in the Southern Foodways Alliance's line, eaters don't squirt sauce, they dip.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): Warner Stamey's Greensboro pit, which carried the dip out of Lexington in 1953.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): learned it in the courthouse tents and taught it to the Piedmont.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): whose dip went to the 1983 economic summit at Williamsburg.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): the tent by the courthouse where it starts, 1919.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): the stand beside Weaver's, bought by Stamey in 1938.
- kin → jerry-bledsoe (person): its defender in print: 'America loves ketchup'.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): its accuser: ketchup in sauce fed to children.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): the South Carolina style built on the same sauce.
- not to be confused with vinegar-pepper-sauce: Any red in the bottle is dip; the east's sauce is clear. On the tray, red slaw beside the meat settles it.
- not to be confused with heavy-tomato-sauce: Dip pours like vinegar and soaks in; a thick sauce that coats the meat is the grocery-shelf kind, not dip.
sources: s:web-stameys-shop — Shop — bottle of Stamey's Dip, bottle of Stamey's Smokehouse Hot Sauce; s:web-sauce-harvest-2026-09-16 — Bottled Carolina barbecue sauce labels, 68 rows; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-north-carolina-barbecue-society — North Carolina Barbecue Society — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:wp-coleslaw — Coleslaw — Wikipedia; s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:web-ourstate-lexington-cover-up — The Great Lexington Barbecue Cover-Up (Jeremy Markovich, 31 Mar 2015); s:web-ourstate-stameys — Stamey's Old Fashioned Barbecue (Bob Garner, 31 Aug 2012); s:web-stameys-history — History; s:web-ourstate-lexington-barbecue — Lexington Barbecue (Bob Garner, 2012-08-31); s:web-abc-barbecue-feud — Smoke, Fire as BBQ Bigshots Battle Over Ketchup (John Berman, World News Tonight, 2 Jun 2005); s:web-bbqjew-defining-styles — Defining the Styles (30 Nov 2009); s:web-sfa-nc-trail — North Carolina BBQ — Southern BBQ Trail; s:web-scba-bbq-history — BBQ History (Lake E. ## light tomato sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/light-tomato-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/light-tomato-sauce.json
id: light-tomato-sauce
aliases: light-tomato barbecue sauce · vinegar-and-ketchup sauce · thin red sauce
said: It is 'the sauce' at the counter; the map calls it light tomato.
facets: base=light-tomato · styles=sc-light-tomato, lexington
region: The Pee Dee, The Upstate, The North Carolina Piedmont, The Carolinas
what: Vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added — enough to redden and sweeten it a little, not enough to thicken it — and often cayenne or a bottled hot sauce. The state tourism office's description is the whole recipe: 'a vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added for a little sweetness'. It is the sauce of South Carolina's Pee Dee and upper Midlands on the state's four-sauce map, and the same idea as the Lexington dip across the line, which the South Carolina Barbeque Association counts as the same sauce. It goes on chopped pork at the block and stands on the table.
story: The South Carolina Barbeque Association dates the light tomato sauce to about 1900, 'vinegar and pepper with tomato ketchup added'; Wikipedia ties it to the affordability of mass-produced ketchup in the early twentieth century and to North Carolina's influence. The barbecue-sauce article's timeline agrees: sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire entered sauces in the 1920s. Kovacik and Winberry's 1987 geography of the state drew the four regions the tourism office still publishes, and Robert Moss answers that there are really two sauces, mustard and vinegar, of which this is a variant. *Inference —* the sauce is the vinegar tradition's own sweetening, made in the same kitchens that kept the older sauce, which is why on the map it shares the Pee Dee with vinegar-and-pepper rather than displacing it.
how: Cider vinegar, salt, black pepper, crushed red pepper; ketchup by the spoon until it colors; water to thin; cayenne or hot sauce; sugar if the house likes. Warmed, not cooked down. On the block it goes into the chopped meat; on the table it is the second bottle beside vinegar-and-pepper or mustard.
today: On the table at Pee Dee and upper-Midlands pits under the house name; Texas Pete's bottled Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce — apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes, sugar — is, by this map's terms, a light tomato sauce.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): the style it names on the map: the Pee Dee and the upper Midlands.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the same sauce under the Piedmont's name; the SC Barbeque Association maps the two regions as one.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the base: add ketchup and this is what you get.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the thick, sweet sauce it is often taken for at the shelf; this one pours.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the yellow sauce to its south; blended with it in Orangeburg as 'rust'.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the whole-hog country it shares with vinegar-and-pepper.
- kin → lexington (style): the North Carolina style that made the same sauce its own.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): whose bottled Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce — cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes, sugar — is a light tomato sauce by this map's terms.
- kin → midway-bbq (place): the upper-Midlands hash house whose chopped pork comes in its house sauce.
- kin → lake-high (person): whose history dates the sauce to about 1900.
- kin → robert-moss (person): who folds it back into the vinegar family.
- not to be confused with lexington-dip: The same sauce; the state line is the tell, and the slaw — red slaw beside it means Lexington.
- not to be confused with heavy-tomato-sauce: Light tomato pours and soaks in; heavy tomato coats.

## Maurice's Southern Gold (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/maurices-southern-gold/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/maurices-southern-gold.json
id: maurices-southern-gold
aliases: Southern Gold BBQ Sauce · Maurice's Gourmet Blend · Carolina Gold (former name)
said: Southern Gold on the label now; the supermarket bottles of the 1990s said Carolina Gold.
facets: base=mustard · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: The mustard sauce of Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia, sold in bottles, half gallons and gallons alongside the family's Hickory Red, Vinegar and Hot Pepper sauces. It is the bottle that carried the South Carolina mustard sauce onto national supermarket shelves in the 1990s, then off them again in 2000. No ingredient list or Nutrition Facts panel is published for it, so this page can name the sauce and its history but cannot measure it.
story: Maurice Bessinger and his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; by 1968 there were four drive-ins, by 2002 nine restaurants, and the mustard sauce went into supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s under the name Carolina Gold. The chain's refusal to serve Black customers produced Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, decided by the Supreme Court in 1968. On 1 July 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the South Carolina State House, Bessinger raised it over his restaurants and handed out tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; nine grocery chains dropped the sauce, and his suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007. His children took down the last flag in 2013 and he died in 2014. The family sells the sauce as Southern Gold. The mustard sauce record carries that history in full; this page is about the bottle.

*Inference —* the measurement gap has a shape. Of the sixty-eight bottles read on 16 September 2026, every mustard sauce with a published Nutrition Facts panel was made outside South Carolina — in Maryland, Pennsylvania, Illinois, California, North Carolina. Maurice's, Bessinger's, Dukes, Sweatman's, Shealy's, Hite's, Jackie Hite's, Cannon's, Hudson's and Melvin's all sell the sauce the state is known for, and none of them prints the label a chart can read.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce it bottles, and the record that carries its full history.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the Midlands style it sells nationally.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the West Columbia drive-in it is made for and named after.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): the man who put it in supermarkets and whose politics took it out of them.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name the supermarket bottles carried in the 1990s, and a word the state uses for two other things.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the Midlands plate the same sauce goes into.
sources: s:wp-maurice-bessinger — Maurice Bessinger — Wikipedia; s:wp-newman-v-piggie-park — Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, Inc. — Wikipedia; s:web-piggiepark-shop — Southern Gold BBQ Sauce — shop listing; s:web-piggiepark-about — Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ — company site, 'since 1953'; s:web-sc-four-sauces — South Carolina's Four Barbecue Sauces (Gwen Fowler); s:web-sauce-harvest-2026-09-16 — Bottled Carolina barbecue sauce labels, 68 rows; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. A Practical System for Private Families, in Town and Country, Especially Adapted to the Southern States; s:wikibooks-savory-mustard-sauce — Cookbook:Savory Mustard Sauce — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-barbecue-sauce-sweet — Cookbook:Barbecue Sauce (Sweet) — Wikibooks Cookbook

## Melvin's Golden Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/melvins-golden-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/melvins-golden-sauce.json
id: melvins-golden-sauce
aliases: Melvin's Original Golden Secret · Golden Secret Sauce
said: The Golden, at Melvin's counters in Charleston and Mount Pleasant.
facets: base=mustard · styles=sc-mustard
region: The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: The mustard sauce of Melvin's Bar-B-Que in Charleston, sold in 16-ounce glass bottles, half gallons and gallons, beside the house's Southern Red, Sweet Red and Vinegar sauces. The maker publishes no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts for any of the four, so what this page can give is the history the family tells and the shape of its line, not a measurement.
story: The maker's account dates the sauce to 1933 and to Melvin Bessinger's father, Joe Bessinger — Big Joe on the bottle's copy — and says the recipe passed down spoken and was never written. Joe Bessinger's mustard sauce at Holly Hill is the same sauce the mustard record carries as the Midlands origin story, and his sons carried it out of the Midlands in four directions: Maurice to West Columbia, Melvin and Thomas to Charleston, Robert to Charleston too.

The present line is four sauces and reads as a map of the whole subject. Golden is the family mustard. Southern Red the house calls a tangy tomato sauce blending vinegar and tomato. Sweet Red the current owner describes as a Kansas City style he worked out in his own kitchen. Vinegar, the newest, the house says its pitmaster made for the owner's wife, who grew up in North Carolina on vinegar barbecue. *Inference —* a Charleston counter selling all four is not unusual now; what is unusual is that it sells them as four named things rather than as one house sauce.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce its Golden bottle is, and the record that carries the Bessinger family's part in it.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the Midlands style a Lowcountry counter sells, four generations out from Holly Hill.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): the father the maker's page credits the 1933 recipe to.
- kin → melvins-legendary-bar-b-que (place): the Charleston restaurant the sauce is made for.
- kin → maurices-southern-gold (sauce): the brother's bottle, from the same father's recipe, sold as Southern Gold at West Columbia.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): what the house's Sweet Red bottle is, by the owner's own description.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): what the house's newest bottle reaches for, made for a North Carolinian at a Charleston counter.
- not to be confused with maurices-southern-gold: Two brothers, one father's mustard recipe. Melvin's Golden is sold from Charleston, Maurice's Southern Gold from West Columbia.
