## mustard-based barbecue sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/mustard-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/mustard-sauce.json
id: mustard-sauce
aliases: Carolina Gold · South Carolina mustard sauce · yellow sauce · gold sauce · Southern Gold (Maurice's)
said: 'Mustard-based' on the menu; 'Carolina Gold' on the bottle; 'yellow' at the counter.
root: Carolina Gold: Maurice Bessinger's supermarket brand name for his mustard sauce, from the sauce's colour and the state. 'Carolina Gold' is also the name of the Lowcountry's rice variety, popularised in South Carolina in the 1780s and named for the golden colour of its unhulled grain; the sauce and the rice are unrelated, and the rice's name is the older by two centuries. · first seen: no dated first use of 'Carolina Gold' for the sauce found by this project; the rice carries the name from the 1780s · The Bessinger family's restaurants now sell the sauce as Southern Gold, and 'Carolina Gold' has become a generic name for any South Carolina mustard sauce, used that way by Wikipedia's articles on the state's barbecue and on the barbecue sandwich.
facets: base=mustard · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: Prepared yellow mustard thinned with vinegar and sweetened with sugar or brown sugar, with black and red pepper and whatever else the house keeps to itself — Bessinger's bottled version listed mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar. It is yellow to gold, pourable, sweet-sour with a mustard bite. It belongs to the Midlands of South Carolina, the belt of German-settled counties from Newberry and Lexington through Orangeburg toward Charleston, and is the sauce the state is known for elsewhere. It goes on chopped or pulled pork at the block, is basted on whole hogs at some pits, and goes into hash.
story: German settlers took land along the Broad, Saluda and Congaree from the 1730s — Orangeburg's colony of Swiss, German and Dutch families arrived in 1735 — and the mustard sauce is credited to them by the state tourism office, the South Carolina Barbeque Association and Wikipedia alike, on the evidence of the names on the bottles: Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman, Dukes. Wikipedia adds a colonial belief that mustard kept off mosquitoes. *Tradition holds —* the sauce was a farm and church-supper sauce long before anyone bottled it; Joe Bessinger served it with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939, and some accounts name him its inventor.

Maurice Bessinger made it a product. He and his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; by 1968 there were four drive-ins and by 2002 nine restaurants, and the sauce went into supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s as Carolina Gold, until by 1999 his was the largest barbecue business in the country. The same restaurants had refused Black customers until Anne Newman's 1964 suit under the Civil Rights Act; Bessinger argued that his religion required segregation, lost in the Fourth Circuit, and lost again at the Supreme Court in 1968, where Newman v. Piggie Park set the rule that a winning civil-rights plaintiff ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the State House, he raised it over his restaurants and distributed tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce, his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007, and his children took down the last flag in 2013. He died in 2014. The family sells the sauce today as Southern Gold.
how: Whisk yellow mustard with cider vinegar, brown sugar, salt, black and red pepper — and, in Bessinger's bottle, soy sauce — and simmer briefly; it keeps. At Sweatman's it is basted on whole hogs through a twelve-to-fourteen-hour cook over oak and hickory; at Maurice's the chopped ham is coated with it for the plate; at Hite's the base flavour is a stronger yellow mustard without the sweetness. In the Midlands it is stirred into hash; in Orangeburg it is mixed with ketchup into a 'rust' sauce.
today: Restaurants bottle it — Maurice's Southern Gold, Shealy's sold online — and the mustard sauce has become more popular across the state this century, by Wikipedia's account. Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville keeps a mustard-based spicy sauce beside its tomato one.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style it names: Midlands pork, chopped or pulled, under a yellow sauce, with hash and rice.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): it goes into the hash pot in the German Midlands.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the older Carolina sauce it stands against: clear and sour where this is yellow and sweet.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the Piedmont's red sauce; the two are the Carolinas' colored sauces.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): the sauce to its north on the map; some Orangeburg houses blend the two into 'rust'.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the sauce beside it on Upstate tables, as at Henry's in Greenville.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): basted with it through a twelve-to-fourteen-hour cook at Sweatman's.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): its name on the bottle, from Maurice Bessinger's brand; also the name of an unrelated Lowcountry rice.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German-settled country the sauce is traced to.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): bottled it as Carolina Gold, sold it in supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s, and lost those shelves in 2000 over the Confederate flag.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): served it with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939; some accounts credit him with inventing it.
- kin → lake-high (person): whose history lists the German families behind the sauce — Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): where chopped hickory-cooked ham is coated with it, now labelled Southern Gold.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): Thomas Bessinger's Charleston pit, shoulders and hams over wood coals under the family sauce.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): basted on whole hogs over oak and hickory at Holly Hill.
- kin → hites-bar-b-q (place): where the base flavor is a stronger yellow mustard, since 1957.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the Orangeburg buffets, with mustard and the mustard-and-ketchup 'rust'.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): the Batesburg-Leesville buffet, since 1969, which sells its sauce online.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): Leesville, since 1979: mustard, vinegar and pepper on hickory-smoked pigs.
- kin → cannons-bbq (place): Little Mountain, in the Dutch Fork.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): Greenville, where a mustard-based spicy sauce sits beside the tomato one.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): pulled pork with the yellow sauce and slaw on a bun, the South Carolina sandwich.
- not to be confused with light-tomato-sauce: Yellow is mustard; a thin orange-red is light tomato; a brownish blend is Orangeburg's rust, made of both.

## Sam Jones BBQ sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/sam-jones-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/sam-jones-sauce.json
id: sam-jones-sauce
aliases: Sam Jones Sweet BBQ Sauce · Sam Jones Vinegar
said: The sauce from the Ayden family's Winterville restaurant.
facets: base=heavy-tomato · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A bottled line from the whole-hog house Sam Jones opened at Winterville in 2015, third generation of the Skylight Inn family at Ayden. The Sweet bottle's Nutrition Facts give 10 grams of total sugars and 210 milligrams of sodium in a 2-tablespoon serving, which is 5 grams of sugar and 105 milligrams of sodium to the tablespoon, but the record carries no ingredient list, so its order cannot be read and its base is recorded as other.
story: The Jones family cooks whole hogs over wood at Ayden and has since Pete Jones opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, in a line the family traces to Skilton Dennis in 1830. The sauce a whole-hog pit of that kind puts on chopped pork is vinegar, pepper and salt, mixed by the bucket at the block.

*Inference —* the bottle is a separate object from the bucket. A sweet sauce at five grams of sugar to the tablespoon is not what goes on the meat at the pit; it is what a customer takes home, and what ships. The distance between a pit's own sauce and the pit's bottled sauce is one of the things this project can only measure on one side.
today: Sold from the restaurant's online store at Winterville. The Sweet bottle's panel is recorded in Open Food Facts; no ingredient list is published with it.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): the Winterville restaurant whose name the bottle carries.
- kin → sam-jones (person): the third-generation pitmaster the bottle is named for.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style the pit cooks, which the sweet bottle is not a bottling of.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): what goes on the chopped pork at the block, against the five grams of sugar a tablespoon in the bottle.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cook the house is built on.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the Ayden pit the family has cooked at since 1947.

## Scott's Barbecue Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/scotts-barbecue-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/scotts-barbecue-sauce.json
id: scotts-barbecue-sauce
aliases: Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce · Adam Scott's sauce · Scott's of Goldsboro
said: The label says Scott's Barbecue Sauce; in Goldsboro it is Scott's.
facets: base=vinegar-pepper · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A bottled eastern North Carolina sauce — vinegar-based, the recipe kept secret, sold as sugar-free and fat-free — made by the Scott family of Goldsboro since the mid-1940s from a recipe the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black Holiness minister who began selling barbecue there in 1917, said came to him in a dream. His son A. Martel Scott Sr. patented it in 1946. The North Carolina Arts Council's trail page calls it 'believed to be the oldest commercially available barbecue sauce in the country'. It is sold in Harris Teeter and Food Lion and from the family's website, and the label offers it for meats, seafood, poultry and vegetables.
story: Adam Scott was born in Goldsboro in 1890, the grandson of Charles and Mary Scott, who had been enslaved in Johnston County, and the son of Joseph Scott, born in Oberlin, Ohio. He cooked at an Atlantic City hotel in 1911, married Bessie Bright that September, and by 1917 was in the barbecue business at home — cooking whole pigs in his back yard and, as the Arts Council's page puts it, selling chopped 'cue with his vinegar sauce through the back door to white men who knocked. He catered for the Algonquin Club, a whites-only social club. Between 1931 and 1933 the family home on Brazil Street became a restaurant: two hogs a week at first, then four to seven a day. David Cecelski's account has him catering a barbecue for President Franklin Roosevelt in the White House Rose Garden in 1933. He was a minister of the United Holy Church of America and by 1938 pastored three churches.

The sauce came, he said, in a dream, and took three years to work out — sugar-free and fat-free because, his grandson A. Martel Scott Jr. recalled, 'Daddy never believed in putting sweet stuff on meat'. It dressed the restaurant's barbecue for nearly thirty years before A. Martel Scott Sr., who had joined the business in the 1930s, adjusted it and took out a patent in 1946; the Arts Council's page dates the bottling to 1945. The restaurant moved from the house to its own building in 1951. Adam Scott died in 1983 at 93. In June 2001 the restaurant cut back to two lunch days a week and later closed; the sauce, run by A. Martel Scott III, sells about 750,000 bottles a year by the Arts Council's count.
how: It is used as the eastern sauce is used: poured over chopped pork at the block or the table, as a mop on a cooking hog, and — the label's own list — on meats, seafood, poultry and vegetables. It has no sugar to burn, so it can go on early. It is a family recipe, not published; what is known is what it leaves out.
today: Made and shipped from Goldsboro; on the shelves of Harris Teeter and Food Lion and sold from the family's website. The restaurant on the Arts Council's trail is closed.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it bottles: the vinegar sauce of the Coastal Plain, from a Goldsboro whole-hog cook.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce family it belongs to — in a bottle since the mid-1940s, with no sugar and no fat.
- kin → adam-scott (person): the minister and cook who said the recipe came to him in a dream, and sold barbecue in Goldsboro from 1917.
- kin → scotts-famous-barbecue (place): the family's Goldsboro restaurant, in its own building from 1951, now closed; the sauce outlived it.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): what Adam Scott cooked in his back yard, two a week at first, then four to seven a day.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): the other North Carolina bottle on eastern tables — that one a hot sauce from the Piedmont, this one a barbecue sauce from the east.

Adam Scott of Goldsboro, N.C. — David Cecelski (21 Nov 2025); s:web-ncarts-goldsboro — Let's Eat: Goldsboro — African American Music Trails; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue; s:book-virginia-house-wife — The Virginia House-Wife, or Methodical Cook; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. ## Texas Pete (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/texas-pete/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/texas-pete.json
id: texas-pete
aliases: Texas Pete Hot Sauce · Texas Pete Original
said: Asked for by name at the table: 'pass the Texas Pete'.
root: Texas + Pete: 'Texas' for a state known for hot food, chosen over a marketing adviser's 'Mexican Joe' because Sam Garner wanted an American name; 'Pete' was the nickname of his son Harold Garner. · first seen: 1929, when the sauce was introduced (Wikipedia) · The sauce has never had anything to do with Texas; it has been made in Winston-Salem since 1929.
facets: base=other · styles=eastern-nc
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A cayenne-pepper hot sauce made by the T.W. Garner Food Company of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, since 1929 — mild as hot sauces go, 747 on the Scoville scale — in a flip-top bottle with a red cowboy on a white-and-yellow label. It is not a barbecue sauce and is on this list because of where it stands: on the table at eastern North Carolina barbecue houses beside the vinegar, and, at Skylight Inn in Ayden, in the dressing itself, where the chopped hog is seasoned with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
story: Sam Garner ran the Dixie Pig, a barbecue stand in Winston-Salem, with his sons Thad, Ralph and Harold. Customers asked for a spicier sauce, and the family made one from cayenne peppers and put it out in 1929. A marketing adviser proposed 'Mexican Joe', to suggest Mexico's spicy cooking; Sam Garner wanted an American name, so Texas — a state known for hot food — was joined to Pete, Harold's nickname. Thad W. Garner founded the T.W. Garner Food Company the same year, and the company still makes the sauce in Winston-Salem, twenty miles north of Lexington, in dip country. *Inference —* a Piedmont barbecue stand's table sauce became the east's hot sauce because it was the one made in the state and stocked everywhere in it; the bottle joined the vinegar on Coastal Plain tables at some point this project has no date for, and Skylight Inn, cooking whole hogs since 1947, names it in its own seasoning. The company has since made an Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce of its own — apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes and sugar — along with a sriracha, 'Cha!', in 2013 and a Mexican-style sauce, Sabor!, in 2016; it dropped its hot-dog chili sauce in 2015.
how: Shaken over chopped pork at the table for the heat the vinegar sauce lacks; stirred into the house dressing at some pits — Skylight Inn's is vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete; and, *Tradition holds —* the pepper of choice in home versions of the eastern sauce, a few dashes into a cup of vinegar.
today: The seventh-best-selling hot sauce in the United States in 2022 by Instacart's count, in 6-, 12- and 24-ounce bottles, with a Hotter Hot Sauce, a garlic sauce, a sriracha and the Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce beside it. Still made in Winston-Salem.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the tradition whose tables it stands on: shaken over chopped whole hog beside the vinegar.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce it goes into at Skylight Inn and sits beside everywhere else.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the chop is dressed with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): its own Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce — cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes, sugar — is one, by the South Carolina map's terms.
- kin → lexington (style): its home ground: Winston-Salem is twenty miles north of Lexington, in dip country, and the sauce began at a barbecue stand there.
- kin → scotts-barbecue-sauce (sauce): the other North Carolina bottle: Scott's is a barbecue sauce from Goldsboro, this a hot sauce from the Piedmont.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the bottle on the table beside the tray.
sources: s:wp-texas-pete — Texas Pete — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:web-texas-pete-eastern-carolina — Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce — product page; s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue; s:web-texaspete-original — Original Hot Sauce — product page, ingredients and nutrition panel; s:book-virginia-house-wife — The Virginia House-Wife, or Methodical Cook

## vinegar-and-pepper sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/vinegar-pepper-sauce/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/vinegar-pepper-sauce.json
id: vinegar-pepper-sauce
aliases: eastern sauce · Eastern North Carolina sauce · East Carolina sauce · pepper vinegar · vinegar sauce
said: In the east it is 'the sauce' or just 'vinegar'; Brown's in Kingstree calls its own 'barbecue gravy'.
facets: base=vinegar-pepper · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, The Lowcountry, The Carolinas
what: Vinegar — cider or white — with salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper, and nothing else in its plainest form; some houses add sugar, a bottled hot sauce or lemon. It is thin enough to pour, tart, and as hot as the cook likes. It is the sauce of whole-hog barbecue on the Coastal Plain of both Carolinas, from Rocky Mount to the Pee Dee and the coast: used as a mop while the hog cooks, tossed through the chopped meat at the block, and set on the table for more. Wikipedia's history of barbecue sauce calls it the earliest American barbecue sauce and the root of most of the others.
story: Early home barbecue sauces were vinegar, salt and pepper, and stayed so until sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire came in during the 1920s. The sauce of the eastern Carolinas, Wikipedia says, was popularised by enslaved African cooks who also shaped American barbecue itself; the South Carolina tourism office calls vinegar-and-pepper 'the oldest sauce, perhaps the oldest in the nation'; the South Carolina Barbeque Association gives it the coastal plains of both Carolinas and a share in Virginia and Georgia. *Tradition holds —* vinegar was the English kitchen's preservative and its seasoning, and the sauce is what that kitchen did to a pig.

Its recipes are short. Ed Mitchell of Wilson uses apple cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper. Skylight Inn dresses its chop with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. Russell Cooper at Cooper's Country Store calls his 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper', with black, crushed and ground red pepper in it. Adam Scott of Goldsboro sold his from 1917, and his son patented it in 1946 as a sugar-free, fat-free bottle — 'Daddy never believed in putting sweet stuff on meat'. Rodney Scott's Charleston restaurant serves whole hog with a 'spicy vinegar sauce'. What none of them contains is tomato, and that absence is the whole of the east's argument with Lexington: Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer said of the sauce, 'It doesn't need anything else'.
how: Stir salt into vinegar until it dissolves, add black pepper and crushed red pepper, and let it sit; heat is optional. On a whole hog it is mopped on in the last hours or not at all — many pits season only at the block — and the chopped meat, skin and all, is tossed with it and salt until it tastes right. On the tray it sits in a squeeze bottle or a shaker beside the Texas Pete. It soaks into chopped meat and cuts the fat; it is not a glaze and does not thicken.
today: Every eastern pit has its own. Bottled versions include Scott's of Goldsboro, sold in Harris Teeter and Food Lion, and Texas Pete's own Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce, which lists apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes and sugar — a tomato paste the tradition's own recipes leave out.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it dresses: whole hog, chopped, on the Coastal Plain; the one thing every eastern pit agrees on.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the same sauce south of the line, on the Pee Dee's whole hogs and down the coast.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut it was made for; it soaks into chopped meat and cuts the fat of the whole animal.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its Piedmont descendant: the same sauce with ketchup or tomato added.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): its South Carolina descendant: the same sauce with ketchup added, about 1900 by the SC Barbeque Association's dating.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the Midlands' answer to it: yellow where this is clear, sweet where this is sour.
- kin → scotts-barbecue-sauce (sauce): its bottled form from Goldsboro, sold since the 1940s.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): the hot sauce that goes into it at Skylight Inn and stands beside it on eastern tables.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the chop is seasoned at the block with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
- kin → coopers-country-store (place): where Russell Cooper's version is 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper'.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): whose sauce is apple cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper.
- kin → adam-scott (person): who sold his own vinegar sauce with his barbecue in Goldsboro from 1917.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): the columnist who said of it, 'It doesn't need anything else'.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the bottle beside the tray, for more than the block put on.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): where it goes on: tossed through the chopped meat with salt before it is served.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the baste at an eastern pig picking: a light vinegar sauce with red pepper flakes.
- not to be confused with lexington-dip: Hold it to the light: clear or pale amber with pepper flakes is vinegar-and-pepper; any red tint is dip or light tomato.

## Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce (sauce)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/sauce/wells-hog-heaven/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/sauce/wells-hog-heaven.json
id: wells-hog-heaven
aliases: Hog Heaven · Wells Hog Heaven
said: Hog Heaven, in Pender County.
facets: base=vinegar-pepper · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A vinegar-based sauce made at Burgaw, the seat of Pender County in southeastern North Carolina, and sold in that corner of the state. The maker gives no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts on its site, so what is on record is the description rather than the measurement: a vinegar sauce for seasoning chopped and pulled pork.
story: The maker's account sets the sauce in the hog-killing calendar of southeastern North Carolina, when farming families processed several hogs at one event in the autumn and winter, and barbecued pigs between spring and fall for occasions and gatherings. Farmers made their own vinegar sauce to season the pork, and the choice at the grill was pulled or chopped. Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce began in 1982 at Burgaw with the Wells family. The present owners bought the business in 2008 and have since parted from the original meat store, keeping the sauce.

*Inference —* the bottle sits in a gap the harvest file makes visible. Of sixty-eight bottles read on 16 September 2026, the ones a reader can measure are the ones a supermarket chain or a national manufacturer put on a shelf; the ones a pit or a family sells locally almost never publish a panel. Wells is in the second group.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it seasons: the vinegar sauce of the Coastal Plain, here at its southeastern corner.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce it is a bottling of, by the maker's own description.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the autumn and winter event the maker's own history starts from, when several hogs were processed at once.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): one of the two ways the maker's history says the meat came off the grill; chopped is the other.
- kin → chopped (term): the other of the two.

A Practical System for Private Families, in Town and Country, Especially Adapted to the Southern States; s:wikibooks-eastern-north-carolina-barbecue-sauce — Cookbook:Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce — Wikibooks Cookbook

## baked beans (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/baked-beans/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/baked-beans.json
id: baked-beans
aliases: barbecue beans · pit beans
said: 'Beans' on a Carolina barbecue board means these, sweet and brown, not the field peas or butter beans of a vegetable buffet.
facets: course=side · styles=lexington, eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: White beans — navy or pea beans — cooked slow in a sweet brown sauce of molasses or brown sugar with pork in it, and served hot in a cup or a compartment of the tray. On a Carolina barbecue plate they usually come from a large can, warmed and doctored at the pit with more sugar, mustard, onion or a handful of chopped barbecue; the traditional form is dried beans parboiled and then baked for hours in a covered pot, and the canned form is cooked through steam rather than baked at all. They belong to the pig pickin' — the outdoor party where guests pull the meat off a whole hog — as much as to the counter.
story: The dish is North American before it is Southern. Native peoples of the northeast cooked beans with bear fat and maple syrup; British colonists in New England put molasses or brown sugar in place of the syrup and bacon or ham in place of the fat, and simmered the pot over the fire rather than under the ground, and by the nineteenth century each colony had its own bean — navy in Massachusetts, Jacob's Cattle in Maine, yellow-eye in Vermont. Molasses, used from the eighteenth century partly to dodge British sugar duty, is what ties the sweet brown style to Boston. Mrs. A. P. Hill printed a Southern version in 1867 that parboils the beans three times and buries a scored pound of pickled pork in them. What put beans on the barbecue tray was the can: H. J. Heinz began mass canning them in Pennsylvania in 1895, and by the early twentieth century canned beans were among the first convenience foods. *Tradition holds —* the pit adopted them because a number ten can feeds a crowd and needs no cook. *Inference —* the sweet-and-smoky seasoning most pits add is a way of making a Northern factory bean taste like it came off the pit.
how: Dried beans are soaked overnight, parboiled until tender, then baked slowly in a ceramic or cast-iron pot with salt pork, molasses or brown sugar, onion and mustard, until the liquid thickens and the top darkens. The pit version starts from the can: the beans go in a hotel pan with brown sugar, mustard, onion, sometimes ketchup and a scoop of chopped barbecue or the burnt ends of the shoulder, and sit at the back of the pit or in a low oven until the sauce reduces and a skin forms on top. Served hot, in a cup beside the meat or a compartment of the tray.
today: On the tray at Piedmont pits beside hushpuppies and red slaw. At Brown's Bar-B-Que in Kingstree, South Carolina, a whole-hog plate with bread, baked beans and slaw is the take-out order. Beans, slaw and hushpuppies are the standing list for a pig pickin'.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): a compartment of it, beside the slaw.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): one of the three things a pickin' is eaten with: hushpuppies, coleslaw, baked beans.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): where a whole-hog take-out plate is bread, baked beans and slaw.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the bread on the same tray.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): its partner in a Lexington tray, with the hushpuppies.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): the other thing a pickin' serves in a cup, instead of these.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins, in the word the menus use.
- not to be confused with brunswick-stew: Both come in a cup beside the meat. Beans are whole and brown in a sweet sauce; the stew is red, thick with corn and butter beans, and has chicken or pork shredded through it.
sources: s:wp-baked-beans — Baked beans — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:web-sfa-browns-bar-b-q — Brown's Bar-B-Q — Thomas M. Brown Jr. and Angela Brown, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 17, 2012; s:web-destination-bbq-browns — Brown's Bar-B-Q Restaurant in Kingstree, SC; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia

## banana pudding (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/banana-pudding/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/banana-pudding.json
id: banana-pudding
said: Ordered by the small or large cup at the counter; at Allen & Son it was the Friday dessert.
facets: course=sweet · styles=eastern-nc, lexington, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Layers of sweet vanilla custard, vanilla wafers and sliced bananas built up in a dish and topped with meringue or whipped cream, then chilled until the wafers soften and the layers run together. It is the barbecue house's dessert in both Carolinas, whole-hog pits and shoulder pits alike: the Barbecue Center in Lexington sells it by the small or large cup, Sam Jones BBQ lists it beside the whole hog, Sweatman's in Holly Hill serves it after hash and rice, and Rodney Scott's in Charleston listed it with the catfish and ribs. It needs no oven, scales up to a crowd and keeps — one theory of how a dessert with no early Southern tie became Southern.
story: The pudding is older than its Southern accent. Recipes for banana pudding were popular across the United States in the 1890s, most of them built on sponge cake; the vanilla wafer first replaces the ladyfinger in 1920, in a recipe from Mrs. Laura Kerley in the Bloomington, Illinois Pantagraph, and in the 1940s the National Biscuit Company began printing a banana pudding recipe on the Nilla Wafers box, and the box did the rest. Wikipedia finds no consensus on how it became Southern; one theory is the church picnic, the family reunion and the barbecue, where a dessert that needs no cooking, scales to a crowd and keeps has the advantage. *Inference —* the barbecue house is that gathering made permanent, and the pudding came in on the same logic: a pit kitchen has no pastry oven, but it has a cooler. At Buxton Hall in Asheville, which cooked whole hog until it closed in November 2023, the pudding went out under meringue and Our State said its regulars would swear by that; at Allen & Son outside Chapel Hill, where Keith Allen baked the pies and rolled the cobbler crusts himself, banana pudding was the Friday dessert. Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh, which opened in 1938 without it, added it later and calls it a good old Southern thing. Centerville, Tennessee holds a National Banana Pudding Festival on the first weekend of October.
how: A vanilla custard is cooked and cooled. In a deep dish the cook lays wafers, then banana slices, then custard, and repeats to the top; the dish is chilled for hours so the wafers absorb the custard and the layers merge, which is the point. The top is meringue browned in the oven, or whipped cream. Counters sell it by the cup — 10 or 16 ounces at the Barbecue Center — and it comes after the tray, not with it.
today: The Barbecue Center, Lexington: homemade banana pudding, small (10 oz) $4.00, large (16 oz) $6.25 on its online menu (September 2026). Sam Jones BBQ lists it in Winterville and Raleigh; Sweatman's keeps it with hash and rice; Clyde Cooper's keeps it in Raleigh. Lexington Barbecue's dessert list is pies and cobbler, with no pudding.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): on the menu at Sam Jones BBQ beside the whole hog.
- kin → lexington (style): sold by the cup at the Barbecue Center, on the same menu as the banana split.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): at Sweatman's in Holly Hill, after hash and rice.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): on Rodney Scott's Charleston menu with the catfish and ribs.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): homemade, $4.00 small and $6.25 large in September 2026.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): the one dessert on the menu.
- kin → clyde-coopers (place): 'a good old Southern thing', added after the 1938 menu.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): the Friday dessert, beside Keith Allen's pies and cobblers.
- kin → buxton-hall-barbecue (place): under meringue, the house version.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): on the menu with the catfish, the rib-eye sandwich and the ribs.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): the dessert after the hash and rice.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): what comes before it on a South Carolina plate.
- kin → pig-pickin-cake (dish): the other barbecue dessert, and the one that carries the party's name.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): the drink on the same table.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): brought to picnics, reunions and pig pickins because it scales and keeps, which is one theory of how it became Southern.
- not to be confused with pig-pickin-cake: The cake is sliced; the pudding is spooned. Mandarin orange and pineapple in a frosted layer cake, against bananas and wafers in custard.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/banana-pudding/banana-pudding-classic-banana-pudding.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Alabama Extension · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AClassic_Banana_Pudding.jpg

## barbecue chicken (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/barbecue-chicken/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/barbecue-chicken.json
id: barbecue-chicken
aliases: half chicken · barbecued chicken · pit chicken · dipped chicken
said: In the Carolinas it is chicken, not barbecue: 'barbecue' alone means the pork, so the bird keeps its own name.
facets: course=main · meat=chicken · styles=eastern-nc, lexington
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, Eastern North Carolina, The North Carolina Piedmont
what: Half a chicken, cooked on the pit beside the pig or on its own cooker until the skin chars, brushed with the house sauce — vinegar and pepper in the east, a thin tomato-and-vinegar dip in the Piedmont — and sold by the half or the whole bird. At eastern pits it is the one other meat: B's in Greenville sells out of chicken halves by early afternoon, and Skylight Inn lists it beside the whole hog. Keaton's in Cleveland, Rowan County, does it the other way round, frying the chicken and dipping it in a hot vinegar-tomato barbecue sauce. NCpedia notes that North Carolinians seldom use 'barbecue' alone for chicken.
story: Burette Walker Keaton was laid off by the railroad in 1953 and started selling chicken from a cinder-block shack on Cool Springs Road outside Cleveland, in Rowan County. He fried it, then dipped it in a barbecue sauce he said he had worked out 'like a football huddle' with a ninety-two-year-old man, a sauce meant to penetrate the chicken and then the bone; the legend at the counter is that Schlitz offered him $10,000 for the recipe and he said he would think about it at $100,000. He turned down offers to build a proper restaurant in Statesville or Charlotte, and he died in 1989; his niece Kathleen Murray has run Keaton's since 1991, cash only, on hours that change with the season, with the hot vinegar slaw — cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed — beside the chicken. In the east the bird is the pit's second meat. Bill and Peggy McLawhorn opened B's in a former convenience store just inside Greenville in 1978; their three daughters run it now with the pitmaster Dexter Sherrod, the hogs cook eight hours on charcoal in metal pit cookers, the chicken halves cook on their own, and the food is gone by early afternoon. *Tradition holds —* many eastern pits cook chicken only on certain days, and the regulars know which.
how: The chicken is split into halves and laid bone-side down over the coals or on the cooker, turned once, and cooked until the skin blisters and the joints run clear; at B's it gets a light brushing of the vinegar sauce, and in the Piedmont the dip does the same work. Keaton's fries or bakes it first, then dips the whole piece in the hot sauce so the sauce goes through the crust. A half is the portion; it comes on a tray with slaw and the house bread, or by the whole bird to take away.
today: B's Barbecue: chicken half $7, whole $11.50 (Our State, January 2016); the food sells out by early afternoon. Keaton's: closed Sunday and Monday, open Tuesday to Saturday on hours that vary between lunch and an evening sitting, no cards (Our State, 2017). Sam Jones BBQ lists a chicken tray and slow-cooked chicken plates (2026).
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose pits cook a half chicken as the second meat, brushed with the vinegar sauce.
- kin → lexington (style): the Piedmont's chicken takes the same thin tomato-and-vinegar dip as the shoulder.
- kin → keatons-barbecue (place): where the chicken is fried and dipped, since 1953.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): chicken halves on their own cooker, gone by early afternoon.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): lists barbecue chicken as its one meat besides the hog.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): sells a chicken tray beside the whole hog.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): what brushes the eastern half chicken.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): what the Piedmont chicken is dressed with.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): Keaton's hot vinegar slaw — cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed — is the Piedmont red slaw run hot.
- kin → barbecue (term): the noun that excludes it: barbecue is pork, chicken is chicken.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the tray it comes on in place of the pork.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the cooker a half chicken shares with the pig at an eastern pit.
sources: s:web-ourstate-keatons — Keaton's Barbecue: Where the Chicken is Dipped in a Secret Sauce — and Lore (Joe Posnanski, 2017-04-03); s:web-ncfolk-keatons — Keaton's (David Cecelski, 2010-12-08); s:web-ourstate-bs-barbecue — A Day at B's Barbecue (Jeremy Markovich, 2016-01-26); s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-chicken — Barbecue chicken — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:web-samjones-menu — Menu; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. A Practical System for Private Families, in Town and Country, Especially Adapted to the Southern States; s:wikibooks-barbecue-rub — Cookbook:Barbecue Rub — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-north-carolina-style-bbq-chicken — Cookbook:North Carolina Style BBQ Chicken — Wikibooks Cookbook

## barbecue sandwich (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/barbecue-sandwich/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/barbecue-sandwich.json
id: barbecue-sandwich
aliases: chopped barbecue sandwich · barbecue with slaw · Lexington barbecue sandwich · pork sandwich · a barbecue
said: Ordered as 'a barbecue' or 'a chopped sandwich'; the slaw is on it unless you say otherwise.
facets: course=main · meat=whole hog, shoulder · styles=eastern-nc, lexington, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina
what: Chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw laid on the meat. In North Carolina it is the commonest form of the sandwich: whole-hog barbecue dressed with vinegar and pepper in the east, chopped or sliced shoulder with dip and red slaw in the Piedmont. In South Carolina the meat is pulled or chopped and the sauce is mustard, vinegar-pepper or tomato by region, with slaw a common topping. The bun is a plain hamburger roll — at Skylight Inn a white bread roll — and the bread keeps the meat warm and catches the sauce.
story: The whole-hog sandwich is a twentieth-century form: the older barbecue was a plate, or the pig itself, and the bun came with the roadside stand. At Melton's in Rocky Mount a sandwich cost 15 cents in 1929, against 45 cents for a plate with boiled potatoes. Lexington's version has a name of its own, the 'Lexington Barbecue Sandwich', and its mark is the red slaw — cabbage in vinegar and ketchup with no mayonnaise — that sits on the meat. Slaw on the sandwich is a habit the Carolinas share with Memphis, where Leonard Heuberger's restaurant, opened in 1922, put chopped shoulder, tomato sauce and slaw on a bun and other houses followed; the Carolina sandwich is the same idea with its own sauce under the slaw. *Inference —* the slaw goes on the meat rather than beside it because the sandwich was built to be eaten in one hand at a stand or in a car; the tray, with its slaw in the other half of the boat, is the sandwich opened up for people who sat down.
how: The meat is chopped on the block and seasoned there; a spoonful of slaw goes on top and the bun closes over it. Eastern pits use white slaw, Lexington pits red slaw; at Keaton's in Cleveland the hot vinegar slaw goes on. Lexington Barbecue sells a chopped and a sliced sandwich, both with slaw, and a pork skin sandwich with slaw besides; the Barbecue Center adds a coarse chopped one. On a South Carolina buffet the pork comes with loaves of white bread, and the eater builds the sandwich at the table.
today: Lexington Barbecue: chopped sandwich with slaw $5.70 cash, $5.85 card; sliced $5.90 cash (September 2026). The Barbecue Center: chopped $6.00, sliced or coarse chopped $6.35 (September 2026). B's Barbecue in Greenville charged $3.75 in January 2016.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose sandwich is whole hog, vinegar and white slaw on a bun.
- kin → lexington (style): the style whose sandwich carries red slaw, its defining mark.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style whose sandwich is pulled pork under a yellow mustard sauce, slaw optional.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the same meat and slaw without the bun.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): what goes on the meat in Lexington.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): what goes on the meat in the east.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce under the slaw in the Piedmont.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce under the slaw in the east.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce on the South Carolina sandwich.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the sandwich comes on a white bread roll.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): where the sandwich is chopped or sliced, with slaw, and where a pork skin sandwich sits on the same menu.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): where the sandwich comes chopped, sliced or coarse chopped.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): where a sandwich cost 15 cents in 1929.
- kin → keatons-barbecue (place): where the slaw on the bun is a hot vinegar slaw.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): where the buffet puts out white bread and the eater builds the sandwich.
- kin → light-bread (term): the white loaf the sandwich is built on when there is no bun.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): what South Carolina calls the meat in its sandwich; in North Carolina it is chopped.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the eastern filling, chopped skin and all.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the Piedmont filling.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the filling of Lexington Barbecue's other sandwich.
- not to be confused with barbecue-tray: The bun. A tray has none; a sandwich is the same meat and slaw closed in bread.

## barbecue tray (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/barbecue-tray/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/barbecue-tray.json
id: barbecue-tray
aliases: tray · barbecue plate · plate · large tray · chopped tray · sliced tray · coarse chopped tray
said: In Lexington you order a tray, chopped, coarse chopped or sliced; in the east you say plate or tray and the counter knows what comes with it.
facets: course=main · meat=shoulder, whole hog · styles=lexington, eastern-nc
region: The Carolinas, The North Carolina Piedmont, Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: The unit of ordering at a Carolina barbecue counter: a paper boat or a plate with the chopped pork on one side and slaw on the other, and no bun. In Lexington the meat is pork shoulder and the order names the cut — chopped, coarse chopped (small chunks) or sliced — and the size, tray or large tray; in the east it is whole hog, and the tray or plate carries white slaw with cornbread, a corn stick or hushpuppies. A plate adds french fries and a choice of hushpuppies or rolls. A sandwich is the same meat and slaw on a bun.
story: The tray is a counter word. At Melton's in Rocky Mount, the first sit-down barbecue restaurant in the state, a plate of barbecue with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents in 1929 and a sandwich 15 cents; the plate was the eastern form from the start. In Lexington the vocabulary grew around the shoulder. A regular quoted in Carolina Country in 2018 counted ten ways to order — coarse chopped, fine chopped, chopped, chopped brown, sliced — each dressed with the house dip, and the hushpuppies 'round, thin, fat, oblong, dense or light'. Regulars keep the order light, a paper tray with nothing but pork and slaw; the plate with fries is for visitors and big appetites. *Tradition holds —* the tray began as the cheapest way to sell barbecue from a tent or a curb-service window, and the cardboard boat is still the vessel at Lexington Barbecue and the Barbecue Center. In the east the whole hog gives the counter another set of choices: some pits chop the whole pig together, others let the customer ask for white meat, dark meat, or the 'middlin' from the belly, and Jane and Michael Stern wrote that the sound of the cleavers on the block is one of the pleasures of a Carolina whole-hog house.
how: The order names the cut first, then the form. Lexington Barbecue lists chopped, sliced and coarse chop trays in two sizes; the Barbecue Center fills a plate with two sides and hushpuppies or a potato bun. The meat is dressed on the block — with dip in the Piedmont, with the vinegar-pepper sauce in the east — and more comes in a cup on the side. Slaw goes beside the meat, not under it. At Skylight Inn the tray is barbecue, slaw and a square of cornbread; at B's in Greenville a plate is pork, slaw, potatoes, green beans and corn sticks; at Sam Jones BBQ the family tray is pork, cornbread and one side.
today: At Lexington Barbecue in September 2026 a chopped tray is $8.00 cash, a large chopped tray $13.40 and a chopped plate $13.40; sliced and coarse chop run a little more. At the Barbecue Center a small chopped tray is $9.00, a large $12.00 and a chopped plate $13.00. B's Barbecue's dinner was $7.75 in January 2016.
- kin → lexington (style): the style whose counter vocabulary this is: chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, brown, in a tray with red slaw.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the other home of the form: whole hog on a tray or plate with white slaw and cornbread.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the slaw in the other half of a Lexington tray.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the slaw in the other half of an eastern tray.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the bread of the Piedmont tray, or rolls; in the east a third of the pits give corn sticks instead.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the bread of the eastern tray at Skylight Inn and at the corn-stick houses.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the same meat and slaw on a bun; the tray is the sandwich without the bread.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the word that changes the meat in a Lexington tray: extra crust from the outside of the shoulder.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the eastern plate's other side, at Melton's in 1929 and at B's now.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): what the meat in a Lexington tray is dressed with on the block, with a cup on the side.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): what dresses the meat in an eastern tray.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): the pit whose menu fixes the words: chopped, sliced, coarse chop, tray and large tray.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): the other Lexington counter, whose plate is two sides and hushpuppies or a potato bun.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the eastern tray is pork, slaw and cornbread.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): where a plate is pork, slaw, potatoes, green beans and corn sticks.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): where the family tray is pork, cornbread and one side.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): where a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents in 1929.
- kin → chopped (term): the word for the default cut in a tray.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut in a Lexington tray.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut in an eastern tray.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): where the tray's meat is cut and dressed before it is boxed.
- not to be confused with barbecue-sandwich: A sandwich has a bun and the slaw sits on the meat; a tray has no bun, the slaw sits beside the meat, and rolls or hushpuppies come alongside.

## Blenheim Ginger Ale (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/blenheim-ginger-ale/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/blenheim-ginger-ale.json
id: blenheim-ginger-ale
aliases: Blenheim · Old #3 · hot ginger ale
said: Ordered by the cap: pink cap for the hot one, gold for Not As Hot, white for diet.
root: named for Blenheim, Marlboro County, South Carolina, the town that grew up around the mineral spring the drink was first mixed with · first seen: 1903, when Dr. C. R. May and A. J. Matheson opened the Blenheim Bottling Company (Wikipedia) · Bottling moved to Hamer, in Dillon County, in 1993; the name stayed with the spring.
facets: course=drink · styles=sc-pee-dee, sc-mustard
region: South Carolina, The Carolinas, The Pee Dee
what: A ginger ale bottled at Hamer, in Dillon County, South Carolina, made with Jamaica ginger and sugar in mineral water from a spring in Marlboro County, and hot enough that the heat is the point of it. It comes in three strengths: #3 Hot with a pink cap, #5 Not As Hot with a gold cap, and #9 Diet with a white cap. It was made first as a stomach tonic rather than a soft drink, and it sits on Pee Dee barbecue tables the way Cheerwine sits on Piedmont ones.
story: *Tradition holds —* in 1781 a Patriot named James Spears, running from the British, lost a shoe in the mud of a natural spring; when he came back for it he found the hollow full of water, tasted it and found it strongly mineral. Word spread, and by the late 1800s a small town had grown up at the spring. In the late 1890s Dr. C. R. May began sending patients with stomach trouble to drink the water, and because they complained about its iron taste he mixed in Jamaica ginger and sugar. He went into partnership with A. J. Matheson and they opened the Blenheim Bottling Company in 1903; the plant beside the springs was built in 1920, and for ninety years the company made as little as eighteen or twenty cases a day. In 1993 Alan Schafer, who owned the South of the Border roadside attraction at Hamer, bought Blenheim and moved the bottling to a new plant next to it rather than refurbish the old one. Charles Kuralt filmed a segment on it for CBS on 26 June 1983. In February 1998 William Grimes of the New York Times described the first swallow as bringing on a four-sneeze fit.
how: The recipe is the company's and has not changed in over 110 years: Jamaica ginger and sugar in the mineral water, carbonated and bottled. A ginger ale made at home is a ginger syrup — grated ginger boiled with sugar and water, strained — mixed with carbonated water, or a brewed one, in which the sugar solution is fermented briefly with yeast in a sealed vessel until it carbonates itself. The Blenheim heat is in the quantity of ginger rather than in any added pepper.
today: Bottled at Hamer, next to South of the Border. Distribution stayed inside the Carolinas for most of the company's life; the company now ships to 44 states and three international distributors.
- kin → cheerwine (dish): the other Carolina bottle on a barbecue table; that one is sweet and cherry-red, this one is hot.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): what it is drunk instead of.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): a Pee Dee product, from the springs at Blenheim in Marlboro County.
- kin → pee-dee (term): the region the bottle comes from and is named for in its own telling.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): what is set beside the tray in its corner of South Carolina.
- not to be confused with cheerwine: Both are Carolina-made bottles with cult followings. Cheerwine is burgundy, cherry-flavoured and made at Salisbury, North Carolina; Blenheim is pale, hot with ginger and made at Hamer, South Carolina.
sources: s:wp-blenheim-ginger-ale — Blenheim Ginger Ale — Wikipedia; s:wp-hamer-south-carolina — Hamer, South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## boiled potatoes (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/boiled-potatoes/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/boiled-potatoes.json
id: boiled-potatoes
aliases: barbecue potatoes · stewed potatoes · potatoes
said: 'Potatoes' on an eastern plate means these, boiled whole or in halves — not fries and not potato salad.
facets: course=side · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Potatoes boiled whole or in halves until they are soft and served beside chopped whole hog on the eastern North Carolina plate — the side the Piedmont does not have. At Parker's in Wilson and, by Bob Garner's account, most eastern restaurants they are stewed rather than plainly boiled: peeled potatoes, often with onion, simmered in water with ketchup or red sauce, hot sauce, paprika, sugar, salt, pepper and a spoon of bacon grease, so the broth seasons them through. They come on the plate with slaw and the plate's bread, a corn stick or hushpuppies, and they have been there since Melton's in Rocky Mount charged 45 cents for barbecue with boiled potatoes in 1929.
story: The potato is the eastern plate's own vegetable, and the first record of it is a price. When Bob Melton's shed on the Tar River in Rocky Mount — the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant, Wikipedia says — printed its prices in 1929, a plate of barbecue with boiled potatoes was 45 cents and a sandwich 15; by 1988 the plate came with slaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and the potatoes stayed on the side list with the corn sticks until the restaurant closed in 2005. Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh opened on New Year's Day 1938 with boiled potatoes, French fries, coleslaw and Brunswick stew beside the pork, and the core of that menu has not changed. Bob Garner's North Carolina Barbecue: Flavored by Time (1996) prints Tad Everett's barbecue potatoes — potatoes and onions in chunks, bacon drippings, catsup, Texas Pete and a little sugar, covered with water and simmered until soft — as a variation on the boiled potatoes of most eastern restaurants, and places the dish around Palmyra, Hobgood and Oak City. *Tradition holds —* the seasoned broth is the pit's idea of a potato: the pepper and a spoon of ketchup in the pot, so the side tastes of the same table as the meat. A Barbecue Bros writer touring the whole-hog pits in 2022 called B's potatoes a simple side not really found in the Piedmont; in Lexington the tray's starch is the hushpuppy.
how: Small potatoes, scrubbed, whole or halved, or larger ones peeled and cut in chunks, go into a pot with cold water and salt and boil until a fork slides in. The stewed way, as Mandy Rivers reconstructs Parker's version and as Garner prints Tad Everett's, adds onion, a quarter-cup of hot sauce, smoked or sweet paprika, black pepper, bacon grease and half a cup of red sauce or a quarter-cup of ketchup, with a little sugar, and simmers twenty to forty minutes until the potatoes are soft and have drunk the broth. *Inference —* the ketchup and paprika are what tint them. They are served hot beside the slaw and the bread, and take the pork's vinegar sauce spooned over.
today: On the plate at B's in Greenville, where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans and the barbecue dinner was $7.75 in 2016; on Bum's buffet in Ayden with the collards and black-eyed peas; by the bulk order at Parker's in Wilson; on the menu at Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh (2026). Melton's closed in 2005 and its 1929 price survives on Wikipedia.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose plate carries it; no Piedmont tray does.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the eastern plate's second side, with slaw, at Melton's in 1929 and at B's now.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): the other eastern side on Melton's and Clyde Cooper's lists.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): where a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents in 1929.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans, and the potatoes are what a Piedmont visitor remarks on.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): on the buffet with collards, cabbage pastry and black-eyed peas.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): which sells potatoes by the bulk order; its stewed version is the one a recipe writer rebuilt with hot sauce, paprika and red sauce.
- kin → clyde-coopers (place): on the 1938 opening menu with fries, slaw and Brunswick stew.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): what the stewed broth is built to taste like, and what goes over them at the table.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): the hot sauce in Tad Everett's pot and in the Parker's-style broth.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the bread beside them on the eastern plate; at B's the corn stick.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the other bread; Melton's served both.
- kin → fixins (term): the eastern fixin the word covers, with slaw and bread.
- kin → bob-garner (person): who printed Tad Everett's barbecue potatoes in Flavored by Time.

## Brunswick stew (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/brunswick-stew/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/brunswick-stew.json
id: brunswick-stew
aliases: stew · barbecue stew
said: On an eastern North Carolina menu it is 'Brunswick stew' or just 'stew'; a cup or a bowl beside the plate.
facets: course=side · meat=mixed · styles=eastern-nc, lexington
region: North Carolina, Eastern North Carolina, The North Carolina Piedmont, The American South
what: A thick tomato stew of chicken or pork with corn, butter beans (lima beans), onion and, in the east, potatoes, cooked in big pots and served in a cup beside the barbecue. Virginia and Georgia both claim it; North Carolina makes it without argument at barbecue houses, church suppers and fundraisers, where it holds the place that hash holds in South Carolina. The name is a county in Virginia or a city in Georgia, both named for the German duchy of Brunswick. The squirrel of the first recipes has given way to chicken, and at a barbecue house some of the chopped pork goes into the pot.
story: Two states keep the argument. In Brunswick, Georgia, a twenty-five-gallon iron pot on a plaque is called the vessel in which the stew was first cooked, in 1898, on St. Simons Island; the Virginia General Assembly answered in 1988 with a proclamation that Jimmy Matthews, a Black cook, made a squirrel stew for Creed Haskins in Brunswick County in 1828 and gave it the county's name. The Virginia Writers' Project guide of 1941 tells it as a hunting-camp story — the cook left behind throws everything into the pot — and Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings passed on the tale in 1942 that it was a favourite of Queen Victoria and came from Braunschweig. None of the claims traces to the ground. North Carolina stays out of the fight and eats the stew. Kennedy's Barbecue in Greensboro was advertising 'Barbecue, Brunswick stew, slaw and hush puppies' in 1949, the plate that became the state's standard. Our State printed Mary Scott's recipe on November 10, 1951: the governor's wife's pot held a five-pound chicken, corn, lima beans, tomatoes, onion, potato, okra and chopped barbecue. At Melton's in Rocky Mount the stew sat beside boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks and hushpuppies until the house closed in 2005. *Tradition holds —* the eastern stew has potatoes in it and the Piedmont's may not, and church stew-masters cook it overnight in iron pots for the fall fundraisers, with a paddle and a crowd.
how: A whole chicken, or chicken and pork, boiled until it falls apart and picked from the bone; the stock takes tomatoes, corn cut from the cob, butter beans, onion and, in the east, potatoes, and simmers for hours with a long paddle going round until the meat has shredded into the vegetables and a spoon stands up in it. Salt, black and red pepper; at a barbecue house a ladle of chopped pork and its sauce. Served hot in a cup or bowl beside the tray, or by the quart to take home.
today: A standing side at eastern barbecue houses and at the Greensboro-line pits of the Piedmont; Melton's priced a plate with slaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew in 1988. *Tradition holds —* churches and fire departments across the Piedmont sell it by the quart at fall stews.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the eastern plate's stew, with potatoes in it.
- kin → lexington (style): on the Piedmont plate since Kennedy's advertised it with slaw and hushpuppies in 1949.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the South Carolina dish that takes its place on the plate.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): where it sat beside boiled potatoes and corn sticks from 1924 to 2005.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): its partner on the 1949 Greensboro plate.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the other eastern side in the same cup-and-plate arrangement at Melton's.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the plate it comes beside, in a cup.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the church and fire-department stew pots.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): sometimes served at the pickin with hushpuppies, slaw and beans.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the barbecue whose chopped meat goes into the pot at an eastern house.
- not to be confused with hash-and-rice: Hash is a smooth meat gravy over rice; Brunswick stew is chunky with corn and beans and red with tomato, and rice is not under it.

## Cheerwine (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/cheerwine/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/cheerwine.json
id: cheerwine
aliases: Cheerwine soda · Retro Cheerwine · Original 1917 Formula · Diet Cheerwine
said: One word, capital C. It is a soda with no wine in it; the name is for the burgundy colour and the cheer.
root: cheer + wine: named, the company says, for its burgundy-red colour and cheery disposition — wine for the colour, cheer for the taste; it contains no alcohol · first seen: 1917, Salisbury, North Carolina; registered as a trademark in 1926 (Wikipedia) · The company's own line, as Wikipedia quotes it: 'it made sense to name a burgundy-red, bubbly, cherry concoction — Cheerwine.'
facets: course=drink · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina, The Carolinas, The American South
what: A cherry-flavoured soft drink — burgundy-red, sweet, with a strong black-cherry note and more carbonation than most sodas — made in Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina by the Carolina Beverage Corporation since 1917, and run by founder L.D. Peeler's family throughout. On a Piedmont barbecue counter it is the soda beside the tea: Lexington Barbecue lists Cheerwine and Diet Cheerwine with the Cokes, and the Barbecue Center sells it by the 10-, 16- and 32-ounce cup. It is bottled in glass with cane sugar as Retro or 'Original 1917 Formula' Cheerwine, comes as ice cream and sherbet in Food Lion, and has had its own festival in Salisbury each year since its centennial in 2017.
story: Two accounts of 1917 survive, and they agree on the man and the town. Wikipedia's: when the Maysville Syrup Company of Maysville, Kentucky went bankrupt that year, L. D. Peeler, Hughston Kirby, Kurt Weinmann and other investors bought its assets, moved them to North Carolina as the Carolina Syrup Company, and the same year bought a cherry-soda recipe from a St. Louis flavor salesman and sold it as Cheerwine. The company's own: Peeler made it during the wartime sugar shortage from a wild-cherry flavour a St. Louis salesman brought him, and named it for its burgundy-red colour and cheery disposition. The trademark was registered in 1926. Peeler's son Clifford took over in 1931 and kept the company profitable through the Depression; the plant moved to its present Salisbury site in July 1967; Clifford's grandsons Cliff and Mark Ritchie joined in the late 1970s, and Cliff Ritchie has headed the parent company since 1992 by Wikipedia's account, since 2007 by the company's — which makes it, by its own claim, the oldest soft-drink company still run by its founding family. The rest is reach: Pepsi distributors bottling it outside the Carolinas from 2005, a Krispy Kreme Cheerwine doughnut in July 2010, a New York Times piece on 'The Expanding Cult of Cheerwine' in 2011 with a plan the same year to be nationwide by the centennial, and a festival in downtown Salisbury from 2017 that drew over 100,000 people in 2025 and, the Salisbury Post says, $5.9 million to Rowan County.
how: Carbonated water, high-fructose corn syrup (cane sugar in the glass-bottle Retro line), caramel colour, phosphoric acid, natural and artificial flavours, caffeine, citric acid, sodium benzoate and Red 40, as the label read in 2021; the flavour is cherry with a black-cherry edge and the fizz is high. It is sold in glass bottles, cans, 12-packs and two-litre bottles, and as a fountain drink at some restaurants and convenience stores, Cook Out and Bojangles among them. At the barbecue counter it comes in a cup over ice with the tray; at home it goes into a Cheerwine cake — a commercial one has been baked in Salisbury since 2008 — and into a float, and with Captain Morgan rum it is a 'Captain Cheerwine'.
today: Lexington Barbecue: Cheerwine or Diet Cheerwine $2.90 cash, $3.00 card (September 2026); the Barbecue Center: 10 oz $2.50, 16 oz $2.90, 32 oz $3.75. Sold from Maryland to Florida and in specialty-soda shops beyond. The 2026 Cheerwine Festival was Saturday, May 16, in downtown Salisbury; Cheerwine Zero Sugar arrived in 2021 and a Cheerwine Ale with NoDa Brewing in 2023.
- kin → lexington (style): the Piedmont style whose counters list it with the tea.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): on the drinks list with Coke and Diet Coke, $2.90 cash in September 2026.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): among the soft drinks, by the 10-, 16- and 32-ounce cup.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): the other glass on the counter; the tea is the older drink and the default.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): the state's other bottled name on the barbecue table, from Winston-Salem, twelve years younger.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/cheerwine/cheerwine-cheerwine-01.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · F Delventhal · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACheerwine-01.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/cheerwine/cheerwine-cheerwine-bottle.jpg · CC BY-SA 3.0 · RadioFan · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACheerwine_bottle.jpg
sources: s:wp-cheerwine — Cheerwine — Wikipedia; s:web-cheerwine-about — About — company history timeline; s:web-cheerwinefest-history — Cheerwine Festival History; s:web-salisburypost-cheerwine-festival-2026 — Cheerwine Festival pops back into Salisbury on May 16: 2025 Festival drew 100,000+ guests and generated $5.9 million for Rowan County (2026-01-18); s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:web-barbecue-center-menu — Barbecue Center — online menu (prices as posted); s:wp-texas-pete — Texas Pete — Wikipedia; s:book-virginia-house-wife — The Virginia House-Wife, or Methodical Cook; s:book-kentucky-housewife — The Kentucky Housewife, Containing Nearly Thirteen Hundred Full Receipts

## chicken bog (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/chicken-bog/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/chicken-bog.json
id: chicken-bog
aliases: bog · chicken perlo
said: 'Bog' to the people who cook it; 'chicken bog' on the sign at the Loris Bog-Off.
root: English bog 'wet, soft, spongy ground', c. 1500, from Gaelic and Irish bogach 'bog', from bog 'soft, moist'; applied to the dish for its wet rice · first seen: The Loris historical marker (2022) says the dish fed crowds by the 1920s. No source this project has read gives a first print date for the name; Stan Woodward, who filmed the dish in 2002, found it 'never well documented by its users'. · Two accounts, both reported in the South Carolina Encyclopedia. The documented one: James Villas writes that a bog, unlike a pilau, is any stew with wet, soggy rice, and Karen Hess that a pilau cooked in a big batch always ends up wet. The folk one: that the dish is named for the boggy ground of the Pee Dee where it is cooked. Wikipedia calls the wetness the likelier reading.
facets: course=main · meat=chicken · styles=sc-pee-dee
region: The Pee Dee, The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: Chicken, rice and smoked sausage cooked together in the chicken's own broth until the rice has taken up the liquid and sits wet and plump — a pilau (rice cooked in stock) that is deliberately wetter than a pilau. It belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina from Horry County west to Florence, and to the Lowcountry beyond it; Loris, a town of about two thousand north of Myrtle Beach, has held a Bog-Off cook-off every October since 1979. The pot is a fifty-gallon wash pot and the dish is cooked for crowds: tobacco crews, church suppers, the stump meeting at Galivants Ferry.
story: The rice came first. South Carolina grew more rice than any other state from the 1700s until the Civil War — Carolina Gold, planted and worked by enslaved people in the Lowcountry — and the culinary historian Damon Lee Fowler reads chicken bog as a localized pilau, 'probably of African provenance', found nowhere else in the country. The name was never written down by the people who used it; Stan Woodward, who made a documentary on the dish in 2002, concluded it went unrecorded because it was a commonplace high-protein meal that fed a lot of people in a poor place. The marker that Loris put up in 2022 says the dish fed crowds by the 1920s and was eaten after gathering tobacco in the northeast of the state: the crew that had primed and strung the leaves all day sat down to a wash pot of bog. The Democratic stump meeting at Galivants Ferry, on the Little Pee Dee, serves it with snap beans, white rolls and Pepsi, and Loris, which calls itself the chicken bog capital of the world, made it the theme of an October festival in 1979; by 2001 the Bog-Off drew about twenty thousand people. To the south, in Georgetown County, the same pot is cooked drier and called chicken pilau.
how: An old hen past laying is the first choice, a fat rooster the second. The bird is poached whole with onion, salt and plenty of black pepper; the meat is pulled from the bone, not chopped, the fat is skimmed from the broth, and the rice, chicken, smoked sausage and onion go back in to simmer until the rice is done and still wet. Woodward's bogmaster's test: the rice is plump and moist, holds together, sits up above a little gravy in the bottom, and does not cling to the chicken. Fork or spoon depends on the cook. Green peppers and other vegetables appear in some recipes; the Loris standard is chicken, sausage, rice, salt, pepper and perhaps onion.
today: The Loris Bog-Off runs every October; the town's marker, put up by the William G. Pomeroy Foundation in 2022, stands on Main Street outside the library. Bog is a church-supper and fundraiser dish across Horry County and the Pee Dee, and the Galivants Ferry stump meeting still serves it.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the region's own pot, cooked for the tobacco crew where the pit cooks the whole hog.
- kin → pee-dee (term): the river and the country the dish belongs to.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the rice South Carolina grew, whose descendant is under the chicken.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the other rice dish of the South Carolina table, at the barbecue rather than the tobacco barn.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): cooked in fifty-gallon wash pots for the same crowds.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the Galivants Ferry stump meeting serves it with snap beans, rolls and Pepsi.
- not to be confused with hash-and-rice: Hash is a gravy ladled over rice; in bog the rice is cooked in the pot with the chicken and the sausage, and there is no barbecue in it.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/chicken-bog/chicken-bog-bowl-of-chicken-bog.jpg · CC BY 4.0 · DogsRNice · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABowl_of_Chicken_Bog.jpg
sources: s:web-scencyclopedia-chicken-bog — Chicken bog; s:wp-chicken-bog — Chicken bog — Wikipedia; s:web-hmdb-chicken-bog-marker — Chicken Bog Historical Marker, Loris SC (erected 2022 by the William G. Pomeroy Foundation); s:web-discoversc-chicken-bog — A Taste of South Carolina: Just What Is Chicken Bog? (Gwen Fowler); s:wp-carolina-gold — Carolina Gold — Wikipedia; s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wikibooks-chicken-bog-i — Cookbook:Chicken Bog I — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-chicken-bog-grand-strand — Cookbook:Chicken Bog (Grand Strand) — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-chicken-bog-ii — Cookbook:Chicken Bog II — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:book-aunt-carolines-dixieland-recipes — Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes: A Rare Collection of Choice Southern Dishes; s:book-kentucky-housewife — The Kentucky Housewife, Containing Nearly Thirteen Hundred Full Receipts
