## collards (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/collards/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/collards.json
id: collards
aliases: collard greens · greens · mixed greens
said: 'Greens' on a Carolina buffet usually means these; when a house cooks turnip or mustard greens in with them it says mixed greens.
facets: course=side · styles=eastern-nc, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, lexington
region: The Carolinas, Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Broad flat leaves of a loose-headed cabbage, stripped from the stem, cut in ribbons and stewed a long time with a piece of smoked pork until they are dark and soft, in a salty broth the South calls pot liquor. They are a staple of Southern cooking and one of the vegetables a Carolina barbecue buffet is judged by; cornbread is used to soak up what is left in the bowl. Eaten with black-eyed peas and cornbread on New Year's Day for wealth in the year to come.
story: The collard is an old non-heading cabbage, and the varieties grown in the United States thinned out after the Second World War as people left the land — five kinds in common cultivation by the end of it, with the rest kept alive by individual growers and seed savers and, since the early 2000s, by projects set up to bring them back. In the Appalachian counties the cabbage collard, yellow-green and part-heading, is the one grown; the coastal South grows the dark non-heading kind. The green carries meaning past the plate: Thelonious Monk wore a collard leaf in his lapel, Alice Walker wrote with collards, the first Obama state dinner had them on the menu, and the Latibah Collard Greens Museum opened in Charlotte in 2010. In eastern North Carolina the barbecue connection runs through the garden rather than the market — Bum's in Ayden cooks collards grown by the family and keeps a vegetable table few other eastern pits keep, and Grady's in Dudley stews them for a plate whose vegetables are peeled and chopped by hand that morning.
how: The leaves are washed several times to get the grit out, the thick centre rib is pulled or cut away, and the leaves are rolled and sliced into ribbons. They go into a pot with smoked or salted pork — ham hock, smoked turkey neck, pork neckbones, fatback — with diced onion, vinegar, salt and black, white or crushed red pepper, and some cooks add a little sugar. They cook down for an hour or more until soft. The broth left in the pot is the pot liquor and is served with them. The leaves may also be sliced thin and fermented into a collard sauerkraut, which is then cooked with flat dumplings.
today: On the buffet at Bum's in Ayden from the family garden; stewed at Grady's in Dudley; on the line at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg; at Jackie Hite's in Leesville they were remembered as sweet and smoky; among the sides at Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville and at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, which is a Texas house that lists collards as the local one.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): grown by the family and cooked that day, on the vegetable table few eastern pits keep.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): stewed, on a plate whose vegetables are chopped by hand that morning.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): on the buffet line with the butter beans and the mac and cheese.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): remembered sweet and smoky on the buffet, beside hash and rice.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): one of the vegetables on the Batesburg-Leesville line.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): the Carolina side on a Texas menu, listed beside the pinto beans.
- kin → mccabes-bar-b-q (place): as turnip greens, cooked by Mrs. McCabe with the rest of the buffet.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the bread that takes up the pot liquor.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the green vegetable in a tray or on a buffet plate.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose vegetable buffets it anchors.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): on the Orangeburg buffets beside hash and rice.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins on a buffet plate.
- not to be confused with cornbread: They arrive together and the bread is there to mop the pot liquor; the greens are the wet dark thing in the bowl.
sources: s:wp-collard-greens — Collard (plant) — Wikipedia; s:sfa-bums-restaurant — Bum's Restaurant — Latham 'Bum' Dennis and Larry Dennis, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 5 Dec 2011; s:web-ourstate-bums — Bum's Restaurant — Our State (April 2014); s:web-ourstate-gradys — Grady's Barbecue — Our State (2013); s:sfa-gradys-barbecue — Grady's Barbecue — Stephen and Gerri Grady, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 7 Dec 2011; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:web-sfa-jackie-hites-bar-b-q — Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q — James Lee 'Jackie' Hite, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 13, 2012; s:web-shealys-home — Shealy's BBQ — official site; s:web-lewis-charleston — Lewis Barbecue Charleston — Hours + Location; s:web-discoversc-mccabes — 100-Mile Barbecue: McCabe's Bar-B-Que in Manning — Gwen Fowler

## cornbread (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/cornbread/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/cornbread.json
id: cornbread
aliases: corn bread · corn sticks · cornsticks · bread
said: 'Bread' on an eastern menu board means the corn stick or the cornbread square; the sandwich roll is light bread.
root: corn (American English for maize) + bread. The bread is Native American in origin — the Hidatsa call baked cornbread naktsi, the Choctaw bvnaha — and the English name is the settlers' description of it · Corn pone, the egg-less and milk-less dough baked in an iron pan, keeps the older name; in the Appalachians a round of cornbread baked in a skillet is still a 'pone'.
facets: course=bread · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina, The Carolinas, The American South
what: A quick bread of cornmeal — meal, water or buttermilk, salt, fat, often egg and soda — baked in a pan, a skillet or a stick mould. It comes with eastern North Carolina barbecue in two forms. At the Skylight Inn in Ayden it is a flat, dense cake of stone-ground cornmeal, water, salt and the day's hog drippings, spread thin on a sheet pan, baked and cut in squares; Our State calls it more grit cake than bread. At Parker's, B's, Bum's and a third of the pits in six Coastal Plain counties it is the corn stick, an eight-inch baton of meal, fat and boiling water, baked, then deep-fried. West of the Coastal Plain the bread is hushpuppies.
story: Cornbread is the older bread of the South. Wheat withered and turned rancid in the heat and humidity, so the colonies baked ground corn and water over the fire or in the hearth, a bread learned from Native cooks; buttermilk, eggs, soda and pork fat came into it in the 1700s and 1800s, and sugar and wheat flour mostly in the 1900s, when steel roller mills replaced stone ones and the meal lost sweetness and turned from white to yellow. The Skylight Inn's cornbread stays on the old side of that line: cornmeal, water, salt and pork drippings, made the same way since Pete Jones opened in 1947, and served at his grandson Sam Jones's restaurants as 'Skylight Inn-style cornbread'. The corn stick is younger than it looks. Bob Melton's Rocky Mount restaurant, the state's first sit-down barbecue house, served cornsticks beside boiled potatoes and hushpuppies from 1924 until it closed in 2005, and NCpedia lists baked corn sticks first among the Coastal Plain's sides; but nearly every corn stick sold in the region now comes from Atkinson's Mills in Selma, which began making them in the mid-to-late 1970s. In the six counties around Wilson and Greenville about one pit in three serves them and the rest serve hushpuppies, and on B's menu board in Greenville they are simply 'bread'.
how: The Skylight cake is stone-ground cornmeal stirred with water and salt to a pourable batter, enriched with drippings from the pit, spread on a sheet pan and baked until it sets and browns; it comes out coarse, heavy and chewy, and is cut in squares for the tray. A corn stick is meal, fat and boiling water with a little soda, baked in an eight-inch stick and then dropped in the fryer, so that most of it is crisp and the middle soft; the grease keeps it from drying out the way a hushpuppy does, and it reheats. At B's the corn sticks are the plate's bread; at Bum's cornbread sits on the buffet with the vegetables. Skillet cornbread — batter poured into hot fat in a cast-iron pan — is the home form.
today: Skylight Inn serves it on every tray and sells it by the slice, a dollar each in September 2025; Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville and Raleigh lists 'Skylight Inn-style cornbread' with the Jones Family Original tray (2026). Parker's in Wilson sells cornsticks and hushpuppies both by the bulk order and puts hushpuppies on every plate. Corn sticks hold in six counties; the rest of the state fries hushpuppies.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose tray it belongs to; in the Piedmont the bread is hushpuppies.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where it is a flat cake of meal, water, salt and hog drippings, cut in squares for the tray.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): whose menu names it 'Skylight Inn-style cornbread' with the family tray.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): where the corn stick is 'bread' on the menu board.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): on the buffet with the collards and the cabbage pastry; the mill's corn sticks too.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): which lists cornsticks beside hushpuppies in its bulk orders.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): which served corn sticks and hushpuppies on one table, beside boiled potatoes.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the fried bread that displaced it from the 1940s; in the east two pits in three give hushpuppies.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the bread in the eastern tray, a square or a stick beside the slaw.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): its partner on the Skylight tray: barbecue, slaw, cornbread.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the other eastern side on the same plate at B's and Melton's.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): crackling bread is this bread with cracklings baked in.
- kin → light-bread (term): the yeast loaf it is named against; the sandwich is on light bread, the tray gets cornbread.
- kin → fixins (term): the eastern fixin that is not slaw.
- kin → pete-jones (person): whose 1947 recipe — meal, water, salt, drippings — the Skylight still bakes.
- kin → sam-jones (person): who carries the Skylight cake to his own restaurants.
- not to be confused with hushpuppies: A hushpuppy is a fried ball or finger of batter, light inside. A corn stick is a baked-then-fried baton the length of a hand; Skylight's cornbread is a flat baked square. Fried and round means hushpuppy.
- not to be confused with light-bread: Light bread is the soft white roll under the sandwich; cornbread is cornmeal and comes with the tray.

## Duke's mayonnaise (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/dukes-mayonnaise/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/dukes-mayonnaise.json
id: dukes-mayonnaise
aliases: Duke's · Duke's Mayonnaise
said: Said as the brand, not the ingredient: a Carolina cook asks for Duke's the way another asks for mayonnaise.
root: the founder's married surname: Eugenia Thomas Slade Duke of Greenville, South Carolina, who put her own name on the sandwiches she sold from 1917 · first seen: 1917 for the sandwiches; about 1923 for the bottled mayonnaise (Wikipedia) · No connection to Duke University, to Dukes Bar-B-Que of Orangeburg, or to the Duke family of Durham tobacco.
facets: course=condiment · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee, sc-mustard, lexington
region: The Carolinas, South Carolina, North Carolina, The American South
what: A bottled mayonnaise made in Mauldin, South Carolina, outside Greenville: egg yolks, oil and cider vinegar, with more yolk than most brands and no added sugar, which is where the tang comes from that the company sells it on. In the Carolinas it is the jar a white slaw, a potato salad, a deviled egg, a pimento cheese and a tomato sandwich are made with, and it is the third-largest mayonnaise brand in the United States, behind Hellmann's and Kraft, after a long stretch when it was sold mostly in the South.
story: Eugenia Thomas Slade Duke was born in Columbus, Georgia in October 1881, married Harry Cuthbert Duke at eighteen and moved to Greenville. In August 1917 she and her daughter Martha began selling sandwiches at Army canteens run by the YMCA, to bring money into the family; the soldiers at Camp Sevier, a National Guard training camp nearby, and her other customers kept asking about the mayonnaise, and by about 1923 she was bottling it on its own. She spoke at the Mayonnaise Manufacturers' Convention in Boston in November 1928. Demand outran her, and in 1929 she sold the business to the C. F. Sauer Company of Richmond, Virginia, where it became the flagship product; she followed Martha to California and opened the Duchess Sandwich Company and a catering company there. She worked for the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave women the vote. She died in 1968. The South Carolina legislature marked the brand's centenary in 2017. Falfurrias Capital Partners bought C. F. Sauer and the brand in 2019 and sold Sauer Brands, Duke's with it, to Advent International in 2025.
how: It is bought, not made, and the household use is as a binder: folded into shredded cabbage for a white slaw, into diced boiled potato and egg for potato salad, into mashed yolk for deviled eggs, into grated cheddar and pimento for pimento cheese. Made by hand, a mayonnaise is egg yolk with oil beaten in a drop at a time until it thickens, then faster, with vinegar or lemon juice and salt; mustard whisked into the yolk first makes it hold together more readily.
today: The plant is at Mauldin, southeast of Greenville, and was filmed for a How It's Made episode about mayonnaise in 2011. The brand is sold across the United States and in New Zealand, Australia and the Middle East, with Latin American sales announced in 2017.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the jar the pale slaw of the east and of most of South Carolina is bound with.
- kin → potato-salad (dish): the dressing that makes a Carolina potato salad the mayonnaise kind.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the thing the Piedmont slaw is defined by leaving out.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): in the slaw on the meat, everywhere the slaw is white.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): a South Carolina product, made outside Greenville since 1917.
- kin → fixins (term): not a fixin itself, but in two of them.
- not to be confused with white-slaw: One is the jar, the other is what comes out of it mixed with cabbage.
sources: s:wp-dukes-mayonnaise — Duke's Mayonnaise — Wikipedia; s:wp-coleslaw — Coleslaw — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## fried okra (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/fried-okra/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/fried-okra.json
id: fried-okra
aliases: okra
said: Taken by the scoop; a plate of it eats like a snack, which is why it gets called Southern popcorn.
facets: course=side · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, eastern-nc
region: The Carolinas, South Carolina, North Carolina, The American South
what: Okra pods sliced into rounds, rolled in cornmeal and fried until the outside is crisp. It is the commonest way okra is cooked in the South and a standing side at barbecue houses and meat-and-three counters, eaten most in summer when the pods are in. Cutting the pods small keeps the outside crisp and leaves the inside slippery; whole pods can be fried too.
story: Okra came to the Americas on slave ships, and the method of frying it is thought to have roots in the Congo or West Africa before it arrived here. Fried vegetables and fritters spread through Southern cooking in the middle of the nineteenth century, and fried okra spread with them; the dish belongs to soul food, to Cajun cooking and to Gullah Geechee cooking, and is part of the Oklahoma state meal. In the Carolinas the barbecue connection is a farm one as much as a kitchen one: Brown's Bar-B-Que in Kingstree grows the okra it serves, along with corn, squash, butter beans, collards and cabbage, and McCabe's in Manning puts it on a buffet beside the hash and rice. Older Southern cookbooks cook it wet rather than dry — boiled and finished with cream and butter, or cut into a soup — and the frying is the newer habit.
how: The pods are topped and cut into rounds about half an inch thick. They are tossed or dredged in cornmeal, or dipped first in beaten egg or buttermilk and then in cornmeal, or cornmeal and flour, and fried in butter or vegetable oil, deep or in a pan, until browned. The batter may be seasoned with black pepper and cayenne. Drained and salted, and sometimes given a dipping sauce.
today: On the buffet line at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg with the collards and corn nuggets; at McCabe's in Manning with the tomatoes and butter beans; at Brown's in Kingstree, grown on the family's own farm.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): on the line with the collards, the corn nuggets and the mac and cheese.
- kin → mccabes-bar-b-q (place): on the buffet with the tomatoes, butter beans and perloo.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): grown on the Browns' own farm and cooked for the buffet.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the other cornmeal thing out of the same fryer.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): a scoop of it in the tray.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): a standing side on the Orangeburg buffets.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins on a South Carolina line.
sources: s:wp-fried-okra — Fried okra — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:web-discoversc-mccabes — 100-Mile Barbecue: McCabe's Bar-B-Que in Manning — Gwen Fowler; s:web-sfa-browns-bar-b-q — Brown's Bar-B-Q — Thomas M. Brown Jr. and Angela Brown, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 17, 2012; s:web-destination-bbq-browns — Brown's Bar-B-Q Restaurant in Kingstree, SC
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## green beans (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/green-beans/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/green-beans.json
id: green-beans
aliases: string beans · snaps · snap beans · simmered green beans
said: 'Beans' on an eastern plate means these when the board also lists baked beans; Parker's in Wilson prints them as string beans.
root: green + bean; the older Southern names are string beans, for the fibre pulled off the pod before cooking, and snaps, for the sound the pod makes when broken · first seen: 'snaps, string beans' as a recipe heading in Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife, 1824 · Modern varieties are bred stringless, so the first name describes a job the cook no longer has.
facets: course=side · styles=eastern-nc, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, lexington
region: The Carolinas, Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Whole or broken pods of the common bean, stewed slow with a piece of pork until they give up their squeak and take on the meat's salt, and served in a cup or a compartment beside the barbecue. They are the plain vegetable on a Carolina barbecue plate — a house that keeps one vegetable and no buffet usually keeps these — and the Southern way with them is long cooking rather than short, so the pod goes soft and olive rather than staying bright.
story: The pod bean has been in Southern cookbooks as long as there have been Southern cookbooks, under the names the field gave it. Mary Randolph heads the receipt 'Ragout of French Beans, Snaps, String Beans' in 1824 and boils them fifteen minutes before finishing them in brown gravy — the short French method. Maria Massey Barringer, writing at Concord, North Carolina in 1867, gives an hour and a half in salt water and then butter and cream, and adds that the more common way is to boil them with a piece of thin middling, the side of the hog. That second sentence is the Southern one, and the one the barbecue plate inherited. On barbecue menus the bean is the mark of a short kitchen: when Beau Hammond opened Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, the whole side list was coleslaw and simmered green beans.
how: The pods are snapped or cut into lengths and the strings pulled off, where there are any. They go into a pot with a piece of streak-of-lean, fatback, ham hock or bacon and enough water to cover, and simmer an hour or more until soft; new potatoes are often dropped in with them for the last stretch. Salt, black pepper, sometimes a little sugar or a splash of the pot's own vinegar. The pot liquor goes into the bowl with them. A shorter method — fifteen or twenty minutes, then butter and cream — is in the old books and is not what a pit serves.
today: On the plate at B's Barbecue in Greenville, North Carolina, where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans; the whole side list at Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, with the coleslaw; on the buffets at McCabe's in Manning and Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville; printed as string beans on the menu at Parker's in Wilson.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): one of the three sides: slaw, potatoes or green beans.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): half the original side list, with the coleslaw.
- kin → mccabes-bar-b-q (place): on the Manning buffet with the greens and the butter beans.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): green and butter beans both, on the Batesburg-Leesville line.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): printed as string beans on the Wilson menu.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the other plain eastern vegetable, often cooked in the same pot.
- kin → collards (dish): the other pork-cooked green; a buffet with room keeps both.
- kin → baked-beans (dish): the sweet bean on the same board, which is why a menu distinguishes them.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the vegetable compartment, where a house keeps one.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins on an eastern plate.
- not to be confused with baked-beans: Green beans are the pod, cooked with pork and served in their own liquor; baked beans are dried white beans in a sweet brown sauce.
sources: s:web-ourstate-a-day-at-bs — A Day at B's Barbecue — Our State (2016); s:sfa-bs-barbecue — B's Barbecue — Judy Drach, interviewed by Alan G. Pike, 10 Jun 2009; s:web-henrys-home — Henry's Smokehouse — official site; s:web-destination-bbq-henrys — Henry's Smokehouse on Wade Hampton in Greenville; s:web-discoversc-mccabes — 100-Mile Barbecue: McCabe's Bar-B-Que in Manning — Gwen Fowler; s:web-shealys-home — Shealy's BBQ — official site; s:web-ourstate-parkers — Parker's Barbecue in Wilson, NC — Our State (2013); s:book-virginia-house-wife — The Virginia House-Wife, or Methodical Cook; s:book-dixie-cookery — Dixie Cookery; or, How I Managed My Table for Twelve Years. A Practical Cook-Book for Southern Housekeepers
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## hash and rice (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/hash-and-rice/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/hash-and-rice.json
id: hash-and-rice
aliases: hash · barbecue hash · South Carolina hash · pork hash · liver hash · liver and lights hash · hash on rice
said: Just 'hash'. The rice is understood; 'hash and rice' is how the menu writes it.
root: French hacher 'to chop up' (from Old French hache 'axe') → English hash, verb, 1650s, 'to hack, chop into small pieces' → hash, noun, 1660s, 'a stew of meat cut into small pieces' · first seen: English verb 1650s, noun 1660s (Online Etymology Dictionary). The South Carolina dish is in print by 1854, when the Abbeville Press and Banner reported 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring (Moss, 2020). · Robert Moss traces the dish's name to 'haslet', an old English word for the viscera of a butchered animal — the head, liver and lights that went into the first hash pots. That is a claim about the dish; the dictionary word is the French chopping verb, and the two may have met in the pot. Folk — a Huguenot 'hachis' brought to Charleston is proposed on Destination BBQ without a citation.
facets: course=side · meat=mixed · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, sc-light-tomato, sc-heavy-tomato
region: South Carolina, The South Carolina Midlands, The Upstate, The Lowcountry, The Pee Dee, The American South
what: A thick stew, or gravy, of pork cooked down with onions until it can be eaten with a spoon, ladled over white rice beside the barbecue. It is South Carolina's side the way Brunswick stew is Georgia's, Virginia's and North Carolina's, and it is barely known outside the state. The old hash was made from what the whole hog left after the barbecue — the head, the liver and the lights (the lungs) — simmered for a day in an iron pot; most restaurants now use shoulder or ham. Three loose regions: mustard in the Midlands, vinegar and liver in the Lowcountry, beef and onions in the Upstate.
story: Hash was on the table before the Civil War in the counties along the Savannah River. Robert Moss found it in the Abbeville Press and Banner — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring in 1854, 'smoking hash' at Robinson's Spring in 1858 — and at an 1861 barbecue for the Edgefield Riflemen, and Estella Jones, who had been enslaved on plantations near Augusta, remembered the men cooking hash and rice there. The cooks were Black, the pots were iron, the fire was wood and the cooking took a day; what went in was the head, the liver and the lights that the whole hog left behind, which Moss reads in the name itself, haslet, the old word for the viscera. Howard Conyers, who grew up with it in the Black churches of the Midlands, calls it liver-and-lights hash and says it is now nearly impossible to get unless you kill your own hog, because federal rules keep lungs out of commercial processing. Hash houses stood across the Upstate, some set up by textile-mill owners to draw farmers to town. The Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading from the state's restaurants; Moss answered in Southern Living that new places were adding it to their menus. *Tradition holds —* the pot is stirred all night, and some say it must be cooked by the light of the moon; Lake High of the South Carolina Barbeque Association calls the finished thing 'liquid sausage'.
how: The meat — shoulder, ham, or the head and liver where a pit still uses them — is boiled until it falls from the bone, picked, then ground through a hand-crank grinder or chopped, and returned to the pot with onions and its own stock to simmer until it thickens to gravy. The seasoning marks the region: mustard in the Midlands and the Dutch Fork, vinegar and ketchup in the Lowcountry, beef with onions and butter and no dominant base in the Upstate (called white hash), a red hash around Sumter. Potatoes go in at some pits and never at others. Served by the ladle over white rice, beside the pork, on a buffet plate or in a styrofoam bowl.
today: Hash is on the buffet at Dukes in Orangeburg and Walterboro, at Sweatman's in Holly Hill, at Midway in Buffalo and at True BBQ in West Columbia; Big T in Gadsden and Brown's in Kingstree still put hog's head and liver in the pot (Moss, 2020). A survey found it most common around Columbia. Fire departments and civic clubs cook it in big pots for fundraisers.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style whose plate it sits on, over rice, beside mustard-sauced pork; in the Midlands the mustard is in the hash too.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): where liver hash holds on, around Florence, Latta and Hemingway.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the hog whose head and organs made the first hash.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the source of the head, liver and lights, and of the wash pot it was cooked in.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): the stew that holds hash's place in Georgia, Virginia and North Carolina: tomato, corn and beans, and no rice under it.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): the other rice pot of South Carolina, cooked for the tobacco crew where hash is cooked for the barbecue.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the word for both the Lowcountry rice the dish sits on and the mustard sauce beside it.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): in the Midlands pot as well as on the meat.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German-settled fork of the rivers where mustard goes into the hash.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): where hash and rice has been on the buffet since Earl Dukes opened in Orangeburg in 1955.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): where hash sits beside whole hog and mustard sauce in Holly Hill.
- kin → midway-bbq (place): the Upstate's hash, in Buffalo.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): one of the pits that still cooks hash from hog's head and liver.
- kin → lake-high (person): who calls it liquid sausage.
- kin → robert-moss (person): who found it in the 1854 newspapers and traced the name to haslet.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): Lake High's association, which judges hash with the barbecue.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): in South Carolina the pickin's side is hash or pilau over rice.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the fire-department and club hash pots.
- not to be confused with brunswick-stew: Brunswick stew is red with tomato and full of corn and butter beans; hash is brown or mustard-yellow, smooth enough to spoon, and comes over rice.
- not to be confused with chicken-bog: In bog the rice is cooked in the pot with the chicken; hash is a gravy ladled over rice cooked apart.

Moss, 2020-07-11); s:web-scencyclopedia-hash — Hash (Saddler Taylor); s:web-discoversc-hash — Enjoy SC Barbecue with a Side of Hash (Libby Wiersema); s:web-conyers-liver-lights-hash — True South Carolina Hash is Liver & Lights Hogs Head Hash (Howard Conyers, 2020-04-05); s:web-destination-bbq-sc-hash — South Carolina Barbecue Hash: History, BBQ Hash Recipes, Map (James Roller, 2019-11-02); s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:book-housekeeping-in-old-virginia — Housekeeping in Old Virginia: Containing Contributions from Two Hundred and Fifty Ladies in Virginia and Her Sister States; s:book-aunt-carolines-dixieland-recipes — Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes: A Rare Collection of Choice Southern Dishes; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. ## hushpuppies (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/hushpuppies/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/hushpuppies.json
id: hushpuppies
aliases: hush puppies · hush-puppies · red horse bread
said: One word on the Carolina menu; the pit fries them to order and puts a handful in the tray.
root: hush + puppy. 'Hush puppy' was slang for something that keeps a thing quiet — hush money in a 1738 British account of smuggling, and from 1879 the gravy or pot liquor that kept the hounds from growling, meaning a growling stomach — and was applied to deep-fried cornmeal by 1899; current in Georgia by 1927 (Moss) · first seen: 1899 for the fried cornmeal sense (Online Etymology Dictionary; Wikipedia). Moss's earliest Georgia example is the Macon Telegraph, 1927, a Methodist church fish fry; the South Carolina forerunner, 'red horse bread', is in the Augusta Chronicle in 1903. · Folk, all of them: that hunters and fishermen tossed fried batter to their dogs to hush them; that Confederate soldiers silenced camp dogs with it; that escaping enslaved people threw it to tracking hounds; that Ursuline nuns brought croquettes de maïs to New Orleans in the 1720s. Robert Moss finds no nineteenth-century source calling fried cornbread hushpuppies and reads the name as a joke about stopping a growling stomach. The shoe brand is a 1961 trademark.
facets: course=bread · styles=lexington, eastern-nc, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, The North Carolina Piedmont, Eastern North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Balls or fingers of cornmeal batter — meal, a little flour, egg, buttermilk or water, salt, soda, often onion — dropped by the spoonful into hot oil and fried until the outside is crisp and dark gold and the inside soft and steaming. In the Carolinas they are the bread of the fish fry and, since the 1940s, of the barbecue tray: Lexington pits serve them with the shoulder and red slaw in place of rolls, and most eastern pits give them with whole hog, though a third of the pits in the Wilson–Greenville counties give corn sticks instead. Sweeter and lighter than a corn stick, and fried, not baked.
story: The first of them had a fish in the name. Romeo Govan, born into slavery in the 1840s, settled after Emancipation near Cannon's Bridge on the Edisto River, five miles from Bamberg, South Carolina, and by the early 1900s ran a club house where the state's political and civic clubs came for his fish fries; the Augusta Chronicle wrote in 1903 of his never-to-be-forgotten 'red horse bread' — cornmeal, water, salt and egg dropped by spoonfuls into the lard the fish had fried in, named for the red horse, a river fish. Govan died in 1915; red horse bread lived on at fish fries in Bamberg, Orangeburg and Dorchester counties through the 1920s. Across the Savannah the same fritter was picking up another name: the Macon Telegraph in 1927 has a church fish-fry chairman cooking 'the hushpuppies', in quotation marks, a word still strange, and by 1940 a Chronicle fishing columnist could write that red horse cornbread is often called hush puppies on the Georgia side. Florida fishing camps fed them to Northern visitors and the name won. In North Carolina the hushpuppy walked from the fish camps of the Piedmont rivers into the barbecue houses in the 1940s: Kennedy's in Greensboro advertised barbecue, Brunswick stew, slaw and hushpuppies in 1949, and Warner Stamey — whose son Keith says he picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro — made them the bread of Lexington-style barbecue.
how: Self-rising cornmeal, or meal with soda and a little flour, salt, an egg, buttermilk or water, and chopped onion for the savoury kind; some pits sweeten the batter and some add beer or jalapeño. The batter rests thick enough to hold a spoon, is dropped into oil at frying heat — in the old way, the oil the fish came out of — and fried until it floats and browns. Lexington houses fry them to order and shape them round, oblong or as fingers, dense or light, house by house. Served hot in the tray or in a paper bag as a side.
today: Lexington Barbecue: hushpuppies small $3.10, large $3.90 cash (September 2026); the Barbecue Center gives a choice of hushpuppies or a potato bun with every plate. House-Autry Mills of Four Oaks still sells the Original Recipe Hushpuppy Mix descended from Walter Thompson's post-war Swansboro business.
- kin → lexington (style): the style that made them barbecue bread, from the 1940s, in place of rolls.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the bread at two eastern pits in three; the third gives corn sticks.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the baked or stick-shaped bread it displaced across most of the state.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the handful in the corner of the tray.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): its partner in a Lexington tray.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): on Kennedy's 1949 Greensboro plate together.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): who carried them from a Greensboro fish camp to the barbecue tray.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): which calls hushpuppies with barbecue a Stamey's invention.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): sells them by the small or large order.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): hushpuppies or a potato bun with every plate.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): eaten at the pickin with slaw and beans.
- kin → fixins (term): the tray's fixins, in the eastern word: hushpuppies, slaw, potatoes.
- not to be confused with cornbread: A hushpuppy is fried, round or finger-shaped and light inside; a corn stick is a dense eight-inch baton; Skylight's cornbread is a flat baked cake. If it came out of a fryer and is not a stick, it is a hushpuppy.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/hushpuppies/hushpuppies-north-carolina-barbecue-hushpuppies-baked-beans-red-cole-sla.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Jeffery Loo · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ANorth_Carolina_barbecue_hushpuppies_baked_beans_red_cole_slaw.jpg
sources: s:web-moss-hushpuppies — The True Story of Hushpuppies, a Genuine Carolina Treat (Robert F. Moss, 2023-06-25); s:wp-hushpuppy — Hushpuppy — Wikipedia; s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:web-stameys-history — History; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-cornbread — Cornbread — Wikipedia; s:web-thefoodsection-corn-stick — Beating uniformity with a corn stick (S. Farhan Mustafa, 2025-03-24); s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:web-bbq-center-menu — The Barbecue Center — online ordering menu; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:web-carolinacountry-lexington — Lexington: More than Great Barbecue (Renee Gannon, May 2018); s:wikibooks-hush-puppies — Cookbook:Hush Puppies — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:book-kentucky-housewife — The Kentucky Housewife, Containing Nearly Thirteen Hundred Full Receipts; s:book-aunt-carolines-dixieland-recipes — Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes: A Rare Collection of Choice Southern Dishes

## mac and cheese (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/mac-and-cheese/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/mac-and-cheese.json
id: mac-and-cheese
aliases: macaroni and cheese · macaroni pie · baked macaroni
said: Said as one word on a menu board — 'mac and cheese' — and counted as a vegetable on a meat-and-three line.
facets: course=side · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, eastern-nc, lexington
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Macaroni in a cheese sauce, most often cheddar, baked in a dish until the top browns. On a Carolina barbecue buffet it sits with the vegetables and is taken as one, cut in squares from a hotel pan rather than spooned; a stovetop version bound with a white sauce is the other common form. In the Lowcountry and in Black Southern kitchens the baked, custard-set kind is often called macaroni pie.
story: The dish reaches the South through the first cookbook written here. Elizabeth Raffald printed a baked macaroni with cream, butter and Parmesan in England in 1769; one account has James Hemings, enslaved by Thomas Jefferson and trained as a cook in France, bringing the method to the United States, and Jefferson served 'a pie called macaroni' at a state dinner in 1802. Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife of 1824 carries a recipe under the name macaroni and cheese: three things, macaroni, cheese and butter, layered and baked in a hot oven. Mrs. A. P. Hill's Southern cookbook of 1867 gives the same layering and then a custard version with three beaten eggs poured over. Factory macaroni and factory cheese put it within reach of every household, and by then it had stopped being a rich person's dish. On a Carolina barbecue menu it is a late arrival and a well-established one: at Luella's in Asheville it is on the board because the daughter the restaurant is half named for likes it.
how: Macaroni is boiled in salted water until just tender and drained. For the baked kind it is layered in a dish with grated cheddar, salt and pieces of butter, covered with milk or cream, and baked until the top browns; for the custard kind beaten eggs and evaporated or whole milk are poured over the layers so the dish sets and can be cut. A stovetop version makes a Mornay — a white sauce with cheese melted into it — and stirs the macaroni through. At a pit it is baked in a hotel pan in the morning and held warm on the line.
today: On the buffet at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg, at Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville, at Brown's in Kingstree, and at Jackie Hite's in Leesville while it ran. Among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston. At Luella's in Asheville it is the daughter's recipe. Barack Obama ate it at 12 Bones in Asheville on April 23, 2010, with ribs, corn pudding and sweet tea.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): on the buffet line with the collards and the fried okra.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): one of the vegetables on the Batesburg-Leesville line.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): 'macaroni' on the Kingstree buffet, between the liver hash and the sweet potatoes.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): on the buffet beside the hash and rice.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): among the Charleston sides.
- kin → luellas-bar-b-que (place): the daughter's recipe, and half the reason her name is on the sign.
- kin → 12-bones-smokehouse (place): what Barack Obama ate there on April 23, 2010, with ribs and corn pudding.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the other starch on a South Carolina buffet; a plate often takes both.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): a square of it in the tray, counted as a vegetable.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins on a Dukes buffet.
sources: s:wp-macaroni-and-cheese — Macaroni and cheese — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:web-shealys-home — Shealy's BBQ — official site; s:web-sfa-browns-bar-b-q — Brown's Bar-B-Q — Thomas M. Brown Jr. and Angela Brown, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 17, 2012; s:web-sfa-jackie-hites-bar-b-q — Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q — James Lee 'Jackie' Hite, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 13, 2012; s:web-lewis-charleston — Lewis Barbecue Charleston — Hours + Location; s:web-ourstate-luellas-2011 — Bending Barbecue Tradition: Luella's; s:web-mountainx-obama-2010 — Obamas visit Asheville

## outside brown (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/outside-brown/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/outside-brown.json
id: outside-brown
aliases: brown · outside brown meat · chopped brown · brownies · bark
said: Ask for it 'brown', or for 'extra outside brown'; some counters chop it in, some set it aside for the order.
facets: course=main · meat=shoulder · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: The dark crust from the outside of a pork shoulder — the bark, where ten hours of smoke and dip have cooked into the surface — ordered by name at Lexington pits. Regulars ask for extra outside brown on a tray or sandwich; ordered 'brown', the meat comes chopped from that crust rather than from the pale inside. The word marks the Piedmont. Eastern pits chop the whole hog together, skin and all, and have no order for it, though NCpedia notes that some North Carolinians follow South Carolina in separating skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat'.
story: Bob Garner, writing about Lexington Barbecue in 2012, watched the shoulders roast ten hours over oak coals, hickory when it could be had, the attendants shovelling fresh coals from the fireboxes under the dripping meat every half hour; when the shoulders came off, that outside 'brown', as it is called, was lifted off the meat and saved for special orders. A regular quoted by Carolina Country in 2018 counted 'chopped brown' among the ten ways to order. When Southern Living's readers named Lexington Barbecue the best in the state in 2026, the News & Observer explained the house words to newcomers: regulars ask for extra outside brown, the caramelized, heavily smoked end bits, and the pork comes dressed in a thin vinegar-and-ketchup dip. Barbecue Bros, in 2019, corrected a New York pitmaster who had called it an off-menu item: it is the bark from the shoulders, which locals know to ask for. *Tradition holds —* the crust is prized because it carries the most smoke and dip, and because a shoulder yields little of it; one shoulder feeds many trays and the brown runs out first. *Inference —* the word does for the Piedmont what the chopped skin does for the east: it puts the pit's crust, not only its meat, into the order.
how: Order the tray or sandwich and add the word: 'brown', 'outside brown' or 'extra brown'. The counter takes the crust set aside from the morning's shoulders and chops it in, or chops the whole order from it. It is darker and drier than the inside meat and has taken more of the dip. Coarse chopped shows it best; fine chopping hides it. *Tradition holds —* the supply is finite and late in the day the answer is often no.
today: Lexington Barbecue's menu (September 2026) lists chopped, sliced and coarse chop trays and sandwiches and no brown; the order is spoken at the counter. The News & Observer's 2026 guide to the house treats it as the thing regulars ask for.
- kin → lexington (style): the style whose word this is; nowhere else in the Carolinas is the crust ordered by name.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut whose outside it is.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): cooked into the crust over the fire and added again on the block.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the coals whose smoke makes the crust; Lexington Barbecue burns mostly oak, hickory when it can get it.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the order it modifies.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the other order it modifies.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): where the brown is lifted off the shoulders and saved for special orders.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): the other Lexington counter where the word is understood.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): whose pit Garner described, shoulders and coals and the brown set aside.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the eastern crust: chopped hog skin, where the Piedmont has bark.
- kin → chopped (term): the cut it is usually served in; 'chopped brown' is one of the ten ways to order.
- kin → bob-garner (person): who wrote down how the brown is set aside at Lexington Barbecue.
- not to be confused with pork-skins: Outside brown is meat, the dark outer layer of a shoulder; pork skins are the pig's hide, blistered or fried. Brown is a Lexington order; skins are an eastern chop or a side.
sources: s:web-ourstate-lexington-barbecue — Lexington Barbecue (Bob Garner, 2012-08-31); s:web-carolinacountry-lexington — Lexington: More than Great Barbecue (Renee Gannon, May 2018); s:web-newsobserver-lexington-2026 — This barbecue joint was named the best in NC — again. Here's what to know (Drew Jackson, 2026-04-14); s:web-barbecuebros-outside-brown — Posts tagged 'outside brown' (2013–2019); s:web-leisuregrouptravel-lexington — Lexington, North Carolina Barbecue is All About the Pork (Randy Mink); s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue; s:wikibooks-eastern-north-carolina-barbecued-pig — Cookbook:Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. A Practical System for Private Families, in Town and Country, Especially Adapted to the Southern States; s:book-kentucky-housewife — The Kentucky Housewife, Containing Nearly Thirteen Hundred Full Receipts

## peach cobbler (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/peach-cobbler/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/peach-cobbler.json
id: peach-cobbler
aliases: cobbler · peach pot-pie · sonker
said: 'Cobbler' on a Carolina dessert board usually means peach in summer and whatever fruit was put up the rest of the year.
facets: course=sweet · styles=lexington, eastern-nc, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Sliced peaches sweetened and thickened in a deep dish and covered with a crust — pastry, biscuit dough or a batter — then baked until the top browns and the fruit bubbles at the edge. It is a barbecue dessert of the same family as banana pudding, ordered by the cup or the square after the tray, and served warm, often with ice cream. The Southern kind is frequently closer to a deep-dish pie, with a bottom crust as well as a top.
story: Cobbler is what English settlers made when they could not make a suet pudding: with Dutch ovens, they covered a stewed filling with a layer of pastry, and later with plain biscuits, scone batter or dumplings fitted together. The first recorded recipe may be in The Kentucky Housewife, Lettice Bryan's book of 1839, where it is 'A Peach Pot-Pie' and the text says cobler is what it is often termed. Abby Fisher, born into slavery in South Carolina and dictating her book in San Francisco in 1881, gives it with two layers of pastry, peaches cut to the size of a plum, and cinnamon. The name's origin is not settled — it may come from the archaic cobeler, a wooden bowl, or from the cobbled look of the crust. North Carolina has its own deep-dish version under its own name, the sonker, made in and around Surry County. At Allen & Son outside Chapel Hill, Keith Allen rolled the cobbler crusts from his grandmother's recipe and the desserts were the second reason people came.
how: Peaches are peeled and sliced, tossed with sugar and a thickener — cornstarch or flour — and sometimes lemon juice and cinnamon, and either put straight into a buttered baking dish or brought to a boil in a pan first so the syrup thickens. The topping is rolled pastry, spoonfuls of biscuit dough, or a batter poured over; a Southern deep-dish version lines the bottom of the dish as well, cuts air-holes in the top and bakes it brown. Forty to fifty minutes in a hot oven. Served warm, with cold sweet milk in the old books and with vanilla ice cream now.
today: On the dessert board at Lexington Barbecue, whose list is pies and cobbler with no pudding on it; at Allen & Son in Chapel Hill it was made in the house from a family recipe, with ice cream churned daily.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): on a dessert list of pies and cobbler, with no banana pudding.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): rolled from Keith Allen's grandmother's recipe, with ice cream made daily.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): the other barbecue dessert; a house tends to lead with one or the other.
- kin → pig-pickin-cake (dish): the third of the desserts a Carolina pit is likely to have.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): what comes after it, not with it.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): what it is eaten with.
- not to be confused with banana-pudding: Cobbler is baked, hot, and has a crust; banana pudding is cold, built in layers, and has no oven in it after the custard.
sources: s:wp-cobbler-food — Cobbler (food) — Wikipedia; s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:web-ourstate-allen-son — Allen & Son in Chapel Hill — Our State (Jason Zengerle, 6 Aug 2017); s:web-uncpress-keith-allen — Interview with Keith Allen, owner of Allen & Son Barbecue Restaurant in Chapel Hill, on the occasion of its closing — UNC Press Blog (19 Dec 2018); s:book-kentucky-housewife — The Kentucky Housewife, Containing Nearly Thirteen Hundred Full Receipts
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## pickles (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/pickles/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/pickles.json
id: pickles
aliases: sweet pickles · dill pickles · chow-chow · cucumber pickle
said: 'Pickle' on a Carolina plate means cucumber unless the board says chow-chow.
facets: course=condiment · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, eastern-nc, lexington
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Cucumbers held in brine or vinegar until they sour, sliced into rounds or spears and put on the plate beside the meat, with the sandwich, or loose in a dish on the table. Sweet pickle — cucumbers in a vinegar-and-sugar syrup with spices — is the common Carolina one; chow-chow, a chopped relish of cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper, does the same job in a spoonful. The point of them on a barbecue plate is acid and salt against fat.
story: The pickled cucumber is old and worldwide, and the sweet Southern one is a strand of it: cucumbers marinated in vinegar, sugar and spices rather than left to sour in salt. The bread-and-butter pickle — sweeter than most, spiced with coriander — is credited to Omar and Cora Fanning, Illinois cucumber farmers who trademarked the name in 1923 after bartering pickles made from their undersized cucumbers with their grocer for staples. North Carolina's pickle industry started the same way, out of a surplus. In the mid-1920s Shikrey Baddour, a Lebanese immigrant from Goldsboro, saw farmers around Mount Olive wasting cucumber crops and began buying them, brining them in tanks and offering the brine stock to pickle firms; nobody bought it. In 1926 the Mount Olive business leader I. F. Witherington relaunched the idea as a company that would pack and sell the pickles itself, and thirty-seven shareholders put in $19,500 — a community proposition, they called it. The plant stands where the board bought an acre from the farmer J. A. Westbrook for $1,000, at the corner of Cucumber Boulevard and Vine Street. Mt. Olive now sells more than 230 million jars a year and employs more than 1,200 people in North Carolina. In 1999 the Farm Labor Organizing Committee called a boycott over the pay and conditions of cucumber pickers; it ended in 2004 when the company agreed to raise what it paid for cucumbers and growers pledged higher wages.
how: For a sweet pickle the cucumbers are cut, soaked, and cooked or steeped in vinegar with sugar, turmeric, celery seed, mustard seed and whole spices, then sealed in jars; for a sour or dill pickle they are packed in a crock or barrel with garlic, dill heads, mustard seed, leaves and salt, covered with cooled boiled water, weighted under the brine and left to ferment for weeks. Chow-chow is chopped cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper salted overnight, drained, then simmered in vinegar with sugar, mustard seed and celery seed. On the plate they are cut in rounds or spears; on a chopped sandwich they go under the slaw or on top of it, by the house's habit.
today: Pickles are part of the standing list of fixins in both states, and the South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries them by default. Mt. Olive, in Wayne County, was the top-selling pickle brand in the South in an analysis of 2024 nationwide consumption by the delivery service Instacart.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the sour thing on the tray, against the fat of the meat.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): laid on the meat or eaten alongside, by the house's habit.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): on the same South Carolina plate: pork, rice, hash, slaw, sweet pickles, white bread.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): what the pickle cuts through on a South Carolina plate.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): part of the Midlands plate as it is usually set out.
- kin → fixins (term): named in the list of fixins on both states' plates.
- not to be confused with red-slaw: Both are chopped, sour and red-flecked in a dish on the table. Chow-chow is a preserve put up in jars, mostly green tomato and cabbage; red slaw is made fresh from cabbage and dressed with the pit's dip.
sources: s:wp-pickled-cucumber — Pickled cucumber — Wikipedia; s:wp-mt-olive-pickle-company — Mt. Olive Pickle Company — Wikipedia; s:wp-mount-olive-north-carolina — Mount Olive, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## pig pickin' cake (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/pig-pickin-cake/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/pig-pickin-cake.json
id: pig-pickin-cake
aliases: pig pickin cake · pig picking cake · pineapple pig pickin' cake · pea pickin' cake · sunshine cake · mandarin orange cake
said: Named for the party, not an ingredient: a pig pickin' is the whole-hog gathering where guests pick the meat off the pig, and this is the cake that comes after.
root: pig pickin' (the whole-hog party, named for picking the meat off the cooked pig) + cake · first seen: 1975, a recipe in the Raleigh News & Observer, the oldest KC Hysmith could name (2024); a 1980 reference in the Boca Raton News · Folk: that the orange and pineapple are there to cool the mouth after vinegar barbecue (Coastal Review, 2017). 'Pea pickin' cake' is a reshaping by ear; Coastal Review calls it a mistake, Chowhound records it as a second name. John Shelton Reed, quoted by Hysmith, says North Carolinians did not say 'pig-picking' before the 1970s. *Inference —* the name is no older than the expression.
facets: course=sweet · styles=eastern-nc
region: North Carolina, Eastern North Carolina, The Carolinas
what: A layer cake of convenience-food parts: yellow or butter-golden cake mix beaten with eggs, oil and a can of mandarin oranges, juice and all, baked in three eight-inch pans and frosted with a can of crushed pineapple folded into instant vanilla pudding and whipped topping, sometimes with pecans or coconut on top, and served cold. It is North Carolina's barbecue dessert by name — the pig pickin' being the whole-hog party where guests pick the meat off the pig — and it is carried to those parties; Hysmith places it at barbecue restaurants too, though it is a home cake first. Our State calls it an essential companion to any good barbecue, noun not verb.
story: The cake has no founding story that anyone has documented, and two writers have looked. KC Hysmith, tracing it in 2024, found the oldest recipe she could name in the Raleigh News & Observer in 1975 and a reference in the Boca Raton News in 1980; every ingredient but the eggs comes from a can or a box, which reads like a brand's test kitchen, but she could not find which brand, and the 'Nancy Ware's cake' some sources credit stays a mystery. She reads it as a variation of the Pineapple Dream Cake of the convenience-food years. John Shelton Reed told her North Carolinians did not say 'pig-picking' until the 1970s, so the name is a child of that decade; *Inference —* the cake is older than its name, renamed for the party it was carried to. Liz Biro, in Coastal Review in 2017, gives the folk reason the state claims it — the name, and the way orange and pineapple cool the mouth after tangy pork — and notes that when Google sorted Thanksgiving searches by state in 2014, the New York Times reported pig pickin' cake as North Carolina's first. Our State printed Mavis Brannon of Mooresville's version the same year, sent in by her daughter, who remembered her yeast rolls as well. Chowhound records pea pickin' cake and sunshine cake as other names; Biro calls the first a mistake.
how: One box of yellow or butter-golden cake mix, four eggs, a quarter to three-quarters cup of oil and an 11-ounce can of mandarin oranges, chopped and undrained, beaten together and divided among three greased and floured 8-inch pans; 350 degrees for 15 to 20 minutes, then cooled through. The frosting is a 16- or 20-ounce can of crushed pineapple, drained, stirred into a small box of instant vanilla pudding, with two 8-ounce tubs of whipped topping folded in and, in Biro's version, a cup of chopped pecans. The layers are stacked and covered, top and sides, and the cake goes into the refrigerator; it is served cold and keeps there, loosely covered, a few hours by Our State's count. Some cooks bake it as a single layer or as cupcakes and finish it with orange segments, coconut or toasted pecans.
today: A home cake, carried to pig pickins and Thanksgiving tables: the dish North Carolinians searched for most in November 2014, by Google's count as the New York Times reported it. Recipes in Our State (2017) and Coastal Review (2017); Hysmith (2024) and Chowhound (2025) on the name. The barbecue-house menus read for this record — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Sam Jones, Parker's — do not list it.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the party it is named for and carried to; the name is no older than the 1970s, when the party got its name.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): whole hog is what a pickin cooks, and vinegar pork is what the orange and pineapple are said to cool.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the pig that gets picked before the cake is cut.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): the other barbecue dessert; the pudding is on the restaurant menu, the cake on the picnic table.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): poured with it at the pickin.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): who dates the expression 'pig-picking' to the 1970s, and with it the cake's name.
- not to be confused with banana-pudding: The cake is sliced; the pudding is spooned. Orange and pineapple in a frosted layer cake, against bananas and wafers in custard.
sources: s:web-hysmith-pig-pickin-cake — The Chilling Legend of the Pig Pickin' Cake (KC Hysmith, 2024-10-18); s:web-chowhound-pig-pickin-cake — How The Southern Pig Pickin Cake Got Its Quirky Name (Ashlen Wilder, 2025-05-22); s:web-coastalreview-pig-pickin-cake — Our Coast's Food: Pig Pickin' Cake (Liz Biro, 2017-08-14); s:web-ourstate-pig-pickin-cake — Mom's Prized Pineapple Pig Pickin' Cake (2017-05-05; the recipe of Mavis Brannon of Mooresville, sent by Donna Troutman); s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:web-barbecue-center-menu — Barbecue Center — online menu (prices as posted); s:web-samjones-menu — Menu; s:web-parkers-bbq-wilson-menu — Menu (no prices posted)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-15

## pork skins (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/pork-skins/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/pork-skins.json
id: pork-skins
aliases: skins · cracklins · cracklings · crackling · pork rinds · fried skins
said: 'Skins' at the eastern counter; 'cracklins' when they come off a whole hog at a pig pickin or out of the lard pot at a hog killing.
facets: course=side · meat=whole hog · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee, lexington
region: The Carolinas, Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, North Carolina, South Carolina
what: The pig's hide, cooked until it blisters and cracks. On an eastern whole hog the skin faces up through the night and is turned to the coals at the end to crisp; at Skylight Inn it is chopped into the meat, where the crunch and the salt are part of what 'barbecue' means. Sold on their own, skins are a side or a snack: fresh fried squares with pimento cheese at Sam Jones BBQ, a pork skin sandwich with slaw at Lexington Barbecue. In the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried on its own. A crackling keeps a little fat and meat under the skin; a rind is skin alone.
story: The skin is the pit's own by-product. At a hog killing the fat is rendered for lard and the cracklings are what is left in the pot, and *tradition holds —* crackling bread, cornbread with cracklings baked in, was the winter bread of the farm. On the eastern pit the same crust comes off the barbecue: the small hogs of the Carolinas are cooked hot enough for the skin to crisp, and the skin takes up more of the smoke than the meat does, so the chopped skin carries the flavor of the fire into every bite. At a pig pickin some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the hog is turned, to keep the cracklings clean. Tennessee cooks larger hogs at lower heat and the skin never crisps — one of the marks that separate the Carolina hog from the Memphis one. At Skylight Inn the chop takes in tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together, which NCpedia records as the eastern habit: in some areas bits of skin are integral to the finished product. South of the line the Pee Dee sometimes strips the hide before the pig goes on and fries it apart, and NCpedia notes North Carolinians who follow that lead, sorting skin from outside meat from inside meat.
how: On the pit: the hog cooks skin-up, is turned skin-down at the end, and the blistered skin is chopped with cleavers into the meat, or lifted, salted and broken into pieces. Fried: the skin is cut into squares, rendered slowly, then fried hot so it puffs. Commercial rinds are dried pellets rehydrated and fried in pork fat at 200–210 °C, which swells them to five times their size; the pink or purple spot on a bagged rind is a USDA inspection stamp. Eaten with the fingers, salted, with hot sauce, or with pimento cheese.
today: Sam Jones BBQ lists fresh fried pork skins with housemade pimento cheese (September 2026). Lexington Barbecue sells a pork skin sandwich with slaw at $4.50 cash, $4.65 card (September 2026). Bagged rinds from the gas station are the same thing at a distance.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style that chops the skin into the meat instead of setting it aside.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the hog they come off; in the Carolinas the skin is crisped on purpose.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the crisped skin goes through the chop with the tenderloin and inner meat.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): where fresh fried skins come with pimento cheese.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): where skins are sold as a sandwich with slaw.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): where the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried separately.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the Piedmont's crust: bark from a shoulder, where the east has skin.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): where cracklings began, as the residue of the lard pot.
- kin → cornbread (dish): crackling bread is cornbread with these baked in.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): where the skin is wiped clean of ash before the hog is turned, for the cracklings.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): where the skin goes into the meat under the cleavers.
- kin → hog (term): the animal whose hide this is.
- not to be confused with outside-brown: Skin is glassy and blistered and shatters; outside brown is dark meat from the outside of a shoulder and chews. If it came off a whole hog in the east it is skin.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/pork-skins/pork-skins-2020-09-05-19-03-38-a-sample-of-smithfield-farms-ori-0bcca5e.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Famartin · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3A2020-09-05_19_03_38_A_sample_of_Smithfield_Farms_Original_Pork_Rinds_Chicharrones_in_the_Franklin_Farm_section_of_Oak_Hill%2C_Fairfax_County%2C_Virginia.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/pork-skins/pork-skins-2020-09-05-19-04-25-a-single-smithfield-farms-origin-e9890de.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Famartin · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3A2020-09-05_19_04_25_A_single_Smithfield_Farms_Original_Pork_Rinds_Chicharrones_in_the_Franklin_Farm_section_of_Oak_Hill%2C_Fairfax_County%2C_Virginia.jpg
sources: s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-pork-rind — Pork rind — Wikipedia; s:wp-cracklings — Cracklings — Wikipedia; s:wp-cornbread — Cornbread — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:web-samjones-menu — Menu; s:web-lexbbq-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:book-mrs-hills-new-cook-book — Mrs. Hill's New Cook-Book; or, Housekeeping Made Easy. ## potato salad (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/potato-salad/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/potato-salad.json
id: potato-salad
aliases: tater salad
said: Ordered as a side at the counter; in the east it is the cold one, against the hot boiled potatoes on the same plate.
facets: course=side · styles=eastern-nc, lexington, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: Boiled potatoes cut up cold and dressed with mayonnaise, with hard-boiled egg, onion, celery, sweet pickle or relish and often a spoon of yellow mustard that colours the whole bowl. It is served cold beside the barbecue, and in the Carolinas it is the mayonnaise side that answers to the vinegar of the meat. Mustard in the dressing is common enough in South Carolina that a bowl of it can read as the same yellow as the sauce.
story: American potato salad came in with German immigrants in the nineteenth century, and the earliest American recipes are the German kind: cooked potatoes dressed with oil, vinegar and herbs, served warm. The north German version — cold, with mayonnaise, hard-boiled egg and sweet or sour pickle — is the one the American bowl most resembles. Mayonnaise made the change possible on this scale, and in the Carolinas that means Eugenia Duke, who began bottling hers in Greenville, South Carolina around 1923. Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes, printed in Chicago in 1922, already gives the Southern shape of it: five cold boiled Irish potatoes diced, three hard-boiled eggs, parsley, celery, salt and both peppers, bound with an oil dressing made at home. *Inference —* the sweet pickle and the mustard that distinguish a Carolina bowl from a German one are the same two things that distinguish the region's slaw and its sauce.
how: Potatoes are boiled in their skins, peeled and diced while still warm so they take the dressing, then cooled. Hard-boiled eggs are chopped in, with onion, celery and sweet pickle relish; the dressing is mayonnaise, sometimes cut with a little of the pickle liquor, and yellow mustard to taste. Salt, black pepper and paprika finish it. It is made in the morning and kept cold, and at a pit it is dished with an ice-cream scoop.
today: On the plate at Grady's in Dudley, where the day's vegetables are peeled and chopped by hand that morning; on the buffet at Brown's in Kingstree; among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, which lists it as creamy potato salad; on the Dukes buffets in the Orangeburg family of houses.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): one of the day's vegetables, peeled and chopped by hand that morning.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): on the buffet with the macaroni and the farm's vegetables.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): listed as creamy potato salad among the Charleston sides.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): on the buffet line with the collards and the mac and cheese.
- kin → dukes-mayonnaise (dish): the mayonnaise most Carolina kitchens bind it with.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the same potato, hot and undressed, on the eastern plate.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the other cold mayonnaise side; a plate often carries both.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): a scoop in the tray, cold against the hot meat.
- kin → fixins (term): one of the fixins on a South Carolina buffet.
- not to be confused with boiled-potatoes: Boiled potatoes come hot, whole or halved, with no dressing but butter or the pork's sauce. Potato salad is cold, cut small and bound with mayonnaise.
sources: s:wp-potato-salad — Potato salad — Wikipedia; s:web-ourstate-gradys — Grady's Barbecue — Our State (2013); s:sfa-gradys-barbecue — Grady's Barbecue — Stephen and Gerri Grady, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 7 Dec 2011; s:web-sfa-browns-bar-b-q — Brown's Bar-B-Q — Thomas M. Brown Jr. and Angela Brown, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 17, 2012; s:web-lewis-charleston — Lewis Barbecue Charleston — Hours + Location; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-mayonnaise — Duke's Mayonnaise — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## red slaw (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/red-slaw/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/red-slaw.json
id: red-slaw
aliases: barbecue slaw · Lexington slaw · red coleslaw · BBQ slaw
said: 'Slaw' in Lexington means this one; you ask for white slaw if you want the other.
root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' (kool 'cabbage', from Latin caulis, + sla 'salad') → American English coleslaw, 1794 → slaw, the American clipping; 'red' is the Lexington marker for the ketchup or dip in the dressing, against 'white' for mayonnaise · first seen: coleslaw 1794 in American English (Online Etymology Dictionary); the 1667 Dutch cookbook De Verstandige Kock already has cabbage strips dressed with melted butter, vinegar and oil (Wikipedia, Coleslaw) · Folk: 'cold slaw', a reshaping by ear, was the common spelling until about the 1860s, when cole was restored.
facets: course=side · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Finely chopped green cabbage dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper — or with the pit's own dip — and no mayonnaise. It is the slaw of Lexington and the Piedmont, red-pink in the boat beside the chopped shoulder, on the sandwich under the meat, and on hot dogs as a relish; it is what the counter means by 'slaw' from Lexington to Shelby. Because it carries no mayonnaise it keeps without refrigeration, which suits an outdoor pit. Across the rest of the state the pale mayonnaise slaw is the default and this one is called barbecue slaw.
story: The dressing is the dip. In Lexington the thin sauce of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper that dresses the shoulder also goes into the cabbage, so the slaw is coloured by the same bottle as the meat; NCpedia records it as red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip. The Lexington sandwich is defined by it — the town's own account calls red slaw the sandwich's most distinguishing feature — and it goes on hot dogs as a relish, where the Carolina hot dog's chili, slaw and onions are the same three things in a bun. *Tradition holds —* the slaw went red because the first pits were tents and curb stands without ice, and a vinegar dressing holds where mayonnaise will not; it was also the dressing a pit already had on the block. In the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger with chili, onions and American cheese and trademarked the name, which is as far as the slaw has travelled under its own. At Keaton's in Rowan County the house slaw is the same idea run hot: cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed.
how: Green cabbage chopped fine — finer than a Northern slaw, close to minced — and dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper, or with a ladle of the house dip; some pits add hot sauce, mustard seed or onion. It is made ahead and kept cold, and the vinegar keeps it. Served in the second half of the tray, on the sandwich under the meat, and on a hot dog with chili and onions; the Barbecue Center and Lexington Barbecue both put it on the sandwich unless you ask for none.
today: Every Lexington pit serves it and most keep a mayonnaise white slaw for the asking. It rides in the boat with a chopped tray at $8.00 cash at Lexington Barbecue and on the $5.70 chopped sandwich (September 2026). Outside the Piedmont, red slaw on the tray is the sign of a pit cooking in the Lexington manner.
- kin → lexington (style): the style it marks: the slaw is red because the pit's dip is in it.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its dressing, or the model for it: vinegar, ketchup, salt, pepper, sugar.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the other slaw, mayonnaise-dressed and pale, which the east and South Carolina eat.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style that dresses its slaw white; the two slaws divide the state with the two sauces.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): goes on it, under the meat, and defines the Lexington sandwich.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): fills the other half of the boat.
- kin → slaw (term): the word, Dutch koolsla clipped to one syllable.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): where it is on every sandwich and in every tray.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): the other Lexington counter that puts it on the sandwich by default.
- kin → keatons-barbecue (place): whose hot vinegar slaw is red slaw with cayenne.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): at Keaton's the hot slaw sits beside dipped chicken.
- not to be confused with white-slaw: Colour. Red slaw is pink to red from ketchup or dip and tastes of vinegar; white slaw is pale, creamy and sweet with mayonnaise. Red means Piedmont.

- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/red-slaw/red-slaw-red-slaw.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Jeffery Loo · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ARed_slaw.jpg
