## sweet tea (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/sweet-tea/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/sweet-tea.json
id: sweet-tea
aliases: tea · sweet iced tea · iced tea
said: 'Tea' on a Carolina barbecue menu means this: iced, and sweetened while hot. Lexington Barbecue prints it as 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)'; the unsweetened glass is the one you ask for.
facets: course=drink · styles=eastern-nc, lexington, sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, sc-light-tomato, sc-heavy-tomato
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: Black tea brewed strong, sweetened with sugar while hot — so it dissolves, rather than being stirred into a cold glass — and poured over ice. It is the drink of the Carolina barbecue house in both states and every sauce region: sold by the glass, the quart and the gallon, brewed on the stove at Grady's in Dudley, named by Dukes in Orangeburg among the five things people come for, and served, Wikipedia says, wherever whole hog is. Some cooks temper it with a pinch of baking soda against bitterness; lemon is the usual addition. Its presence on a menu is one sign used to tell whether a place counts as the South.
story: Sweet tea began as a luxury of three shipped-in things — tea, sugar and ice, the ice the dearest — and became cheap when all three did. The oldest known recipe for it is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, a community cookbook compiled by Marion Cabell Tyree (copyright 1878, and dated 1879 by the historian Robert Moss): ice, sugar, hot green tea, lemon. Green tea was the tea of the 19th-century South; the Second World War cut off its sources and black tea from British India took its place, and by the war's end black tea was the American tea. Moss, checking Summerville, South Carolina's 2013 claim to be 'The Birthplace of Sweet Tea' — a trademarked tagline, a Sweet Tea Trail and billboards on I-26 and I-95, resting on Dr. Charles Shepard's Pinehurst Tea Plantation of 1888–1915, the first successful tea farm in the country — found the Boston Journal recommending iced tea in July 1868, twenty years before Shepard planted, and Fannie Farmer's 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book telling readers to pour tea over cracked ice and sweeten to taste. Summerville answered with a jar: 'Mason', fifteen feet tall, filled on National Tea Day 2016 with 2,524 gallons of sweet tea, the world's largest, a record traded since 2010 among Chick-fil-A, Summerville and Lipton. In 2003 a Georgia House bill, apparently an April Fool's joke, would have made selling iced tea without offering sweet tea a misdemeanor; it never came to a vote.
how: Tea bags or loose black tea steep in a pot of boiling water — some cooks add a pinch of baking soda — and the sugar goes in while the tea is hot; cold water and ice bring it down. At Grady's, Gerri Grady brews it on the stovetop for the day's service; at Allen & Son Keith Allen brewed it himself and sold it by the litre. It is served in a tall glass over ice, with lemon if you want it. Pits sell it to go by the pint, quart, half gallon and gallon — Parker's in Wilson lists all four — and the Barbecue Center in Lexington prices it from a 10-ounce cup to the gallon jug. The sugar can run to 22 degrees Brix, twice a Coca-Cola.
today: Lexington Barbecue: 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)', $2.90 cash, $3.00 card (September 2026). The Barbecue Center: 10 oz $2.50, 16 oz $2.90, 32 oz $3.75, half gallon $6.00, gallon $8.50. Summerville holds a Sweet Tea Festival each September and keeps the record jar.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the drink Wikipedia names as whole hog's accompaniment; Grady's brews it on the stove.
- kin → lexington (style): 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)' at Lexington Barbecue: sweet is the default.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): one of the five things Dukes in Orangeburg says people come for.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): $2.90 cash in September 2026, unsweet on request.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): priced from the 10-ounce cup to the gallon jug.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): brewed on the stovetop by Gerri Grady.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): named by Tony Kittrell with the barbecue, hash and rice, the sauce and the sliced bread.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): sold by the pint, quart, half gallon and gallon.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): by the litre, brewed by Keith Allen himself.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): homemade, with the lemonade.
- kin → buxton-hall-barbecue (place): 'steeped, sweetened, iced', beside the cocktails.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): poured at the pickin with beer and soft drinks.
- kin → cheerwine (dish): the other glass on a Piedmont counter; both sweet, one carbonated.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): the dessert on the same table.
- kin → fixins (term): the drink counted among the fixins.
- kin → robert-moss (person): who tested Summerville's birthplace claim against the 1868 Boston Journal and the 1879 Tyree recipe.

## white slaw (dish)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/dish/white-slaw/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/dish/white-slaw.json
id: white-slaw
aliases: coleslaw · slaw · cole slaw · mayonnaise slaw · eastern slaw · sweet slaw
said: In the east it is just 'slaw'; 'white slaw' is what a Lexington counter calls it when it offers both.
facets: course=side · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee, sc-mustard
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina, South Carolina, The Carolinas
what: Finely chopped cabbage in a dressing of mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sweet and pale: the slaw of eastern North Carolina and of most of South Carolina. It goes on the tray beside the chopped whole hog and on the bun of the sandwich, where its sweetness sets off the vinegar and pepper of the meat. Eastern pits use mayonnaise almost universally; NCpedia lists white or yellow coleslaw among the eastern sides, the yellow taking mustard. The name exists only where the red slaw does. Everywhere else in the state this is coleslaw, from the Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad.
story: Coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch — the 1667 cookbook De Verstandige Kock gives a landlady's recipe of cabbage strips in melted butter, vinegar and oil — and the word is Dutch too, koolsla, cabbage salad, in American English by 1794 and spelled 'cold slaw' by ear until the 1860s. The mayonnaise version is younger than the word, since mayonnaise itself dates from the mid-eighteenth century, and it is the version the South took up, with buttermilk slaw a Southern variant. In North Carolina the coleslaw is fine-chopped and vinegary and served with barbecue; in the east it is dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing almost without exception and put on the bun of the sandwich, the way Memphis puts slaw on its pork sandwich. The South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries the same slaw beside mustard-sauced pork. *Tradition holds —* the sweetness is the point: against a whole hog dressed with vinegar and pepper, the slaw is the sweet thing on the tray.
how: Cabbage chopped fine, often with a little carrot or onion, dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sugar, vinegar, salt and pepper, and chilled until it weeps a little. Eastern pits chop it nearly as fine as the meat so the two mix on the bun. A yellow slaw takes mustard in the dressing. Served cold beside the hot pork on the tray, spooned on the sandwich, and on hot dogs across the Coastal Plain.
today: Sam Jones BBQ lists a sweet slaw (2026); Skylight Inn serves its tray with slaw and cornbread; the Lexington pits keep a white slaw for those who ask. South Carolina buffets put it beside hash and rice.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose slaw this is, mayonnaise-dressed against the vinegar of the meat.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): on the South Carolina plate beside hash, rice, pickles and white bread.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the Piedmont's slaw, dressed with dip instead of mayonnaise; the word 'white' exists to tell them apart.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): goes on the bun over the meat in the east.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): fills the other side of an eastern tray.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): on the tray with barbecue and cornbread.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): listed as sweet slaw.
- kin → slaw (term): the word, Dutch koolsla clipped.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sharpness the slaw's sweetness answers on the same tray.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): its neighbour on a South Carolina buffet plate.
- not to be confused with red-slaw: White slaw is pale and creamy with mayonnaise; red slaw is pink with ketchup or dip and has none. White is the east and South Carolina; red is Lexington.
sources: s:wp-coleslaw — Coleslaw — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-red-slaw — Red slaw — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-barbecue-sandwich — Barbecue sandwich — Wikipedia; s:web-scencyclopedia-hash — Hash (Saddler Taylor); s:web-samjones-menu — Menu; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:web-leisuregrouptravel-lexington — Lexington, North Carolina Barbecue is All About the Pork (Randy Mink); s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wikibooks-coleslaw-i — Cookbook:Coleslaw I — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:wikibooks-coleslaw-ii — Cookbook:Coleslaw II — Wikibooks Cookbook; s:book-housekeeping-in-old-virginia — Housekeeping in Old Virginia: Containing Contributions from Two Hundred and Fifty Ladies in Virginia and Her Sister States; s:book-dixie-cookery — Dixie Cookery; or, How I Managed My Table for Twelve Years. A Practical Cook-Book for Southern Housekeepers

## block pit (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/block-pit/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/block-pit.json
id: block-pit
aliases: cinder-block pit · concrete-block pit · open pit · pig pit
facets: kind=pit
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, The Carolinas
what: An open pit built above ground of cinder blocks — concrete blocks — wide and shallow, a little longer than a split hog, with a rack across the top on which the pig lies and a bed of charcoal below; brick or steel are the alternatives, and the charcoal is made in a fireplace or a burn barrel beside it. It is the whole-hog pit of the Carolinas, the one a farm, a fire department or a family can lay in an afternoon. *Tradition holds —* the blocks go up dry, without mortar, two or three courses high, a gap is left for the shovel, and a sheet of tin or plywood closes the top.
story: The trench came first. *Tradition holds —* the farm barbecue of the Carolinas was cooked over a pit dug in the ground, and Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its 1929 barbecue that way, hickory coals shoved under whole hogs in ditches; by the 1980s metal cookers had replaced the church's dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. NCpedia records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground. The cinder block — cheap, fireproof, stackable — is what the open pit became when it climbed out of the ditch. It is the pit of the pig pickin' and the cook-off, and the pit the whole-hog restaurants of the east grew from: the Skylight Inn's hogs cook over charcoal made in fireplaces beside the pits, and Rodney Scott's over hardwood charcoal shoveled from a burn barrel. The Cuban roasting box, by contrast, is a closed box of concrete blocks and steel mesh with the coals on top.
how: Blocks are laid in a rectangle a little longer and wider than the split hog; a rack spans the top, the hog goes on skin-side up, and a lid holds the heat. Coals from the burn barrel are shoveled in and spread beneath the carcass on a regular round through the night — *Tradition holds —* heavier under the hams and shoulders, thinner under the loin. The fat that drips hisses on the coals, and a flare-up is the danger the cook watches for; an uncontrolled pit fire can take the pit and the building. After eight to twenty-four hours the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp.
today: The block pit is the pit of the yard, the church lot, the fire station and the competition; restaurants that cook whole hog mostly cook in masonry or steel pits under a roof, and the form — a bed of coals, a rack, a hog, a lid — is the same.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut it is sized to: a split carcass on a rack over coals.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the coal-maker beside it.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): coals spread directly beneath the carcass.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the wood burned down for its coals.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the closed, chimneyed Piedmont pit for shoulders; the block pit is open and for hogs.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the steel, wheeled version on gas or charcoal.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the party cooked on it.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the fire department's Saturday pig is cooked on one, or on a cooker.
- kin → mallard-creek-barbecue (event): began in dirt ditches in 1929 and moved to metal cookers in the 1980s.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): its hogs cook over charcoal made in fireplaces beside the pits.
- kin → pit (term): the word, which in the east means this open bed of coals.
- not to be confused with brick-pit: A block pit is open, unmortared and sized to a whole hog; a brick pit is a closed chamber with a door and a chimney, built for shoulders.
- not to be confused with pig-cooker: A block pit is stacked masonry on the ground; a pig cooker is a steel box on a trailer.
sources: s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-roast — Pig roast — Wikipedia; s:web-mallard-creek-history — History of the Annual Barbecue; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq — Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ — Wikipedia; s:web-npr-scott-pit-burned — When His Pit Burned Down, A Southern BBQ Master Took Hogs On Tour (Debbie Elliott, February 4, 2014); s:jones-whole-hog-bbq — Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue; s:scott-world-of-bbq — Rodney Scott's World of BBQ: Every Day Is a Good Day
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## brick pit (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/brick-pit/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/brick-pit.json
id: brick-pit
aliases: Lexington pit · closed pit · pit house · the pits
said: In Lexington the pits are 'the pits', and the hand on them is 'firing the pits'.
facets: kind=pit
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: The masonry pit of the Piedmont: a closed brick chamber with a rack for the shoulders and a chimney through the roof to carry off the smoke. Coals made from oak and hickory go in through the door and are spread on the floor under the meat; the door shuts and the shoulders cook nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees. The Barbecue Center in Lexington describes its pit as a brick oven with three chambers, 'comparable to an oversized smoker', and Lexington Barbecue's roof carries a row of smoking stacks. The line of chimneys on a Lexington roof is how you know a wood pit from the road.
story: The closed pit is the restaurant's answer to the trench. *Tradition holds —* the Lexington style began under tents on the courthouse square in the 1910s and moved indoors as its cooks built permanent pits, and the pits they built were brick because brick holds heat and a chimney takes the smoke out of a dining room. NCpedia's entry records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground, and that economy, fastidiousness and health rules keep most Piedmont pits from basting with the ketchup-and-vinegar sauce, which flares; it goes on at the table instead, hence its name, dip. The Barbecue Center has cooked in its pit since 1955 under the Conrad family, and Lexington Barbecue, founded in 1962, cooks 'with wood, not gas' over oak and hickory coals only; a new pit hand there trains for a year before working the pits alone, and the heat from the fires, one visitor wrote, is overwhelming as the coals are turned. The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail admits only pits that cook on grates over wood or charcoal, so its Piedmont stops — Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center, Red Bridges in Shelby — are brick pits by definition.
how: Oak and hickory logs burn to coals in a fireplace or burner at the end of the pit house; a crew member shovels the coals through the pit door and spreads them evenly under the shoulders — the round Lexington calls 'firing the pits' — then shuts the door. The shoulders sit on the rack, salted but not basted or marinated, for nine to twelve hours at 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its three chambers. The smoke leaves by the chimney. Finished shoulders come off to the block to be chopped, coarse chopped or sliced.
today: The brick pit is still the plant of the Lexington restaurants — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center — and of the Piedmont stops on the Historic Barbecue Trail. Lexington Barbecue's site says it cooks with wood, not gas.
- kin → lexington (style): the style cooked in it: shoulders only, over hickory and oak coals, under a chimney.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut sized to its rack.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the coals on its floor.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the fireplace or burner beside it does the barrel's job.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): coals on the floor directly beneath the rack.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open, unmortared whole-hog pit of the east; the brick pit is closed and chimneyed.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): what replaced the brick pit at many restaurants.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): not basted in a closed pit because it flares; served at the table instead, which is why it is called dip.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): cooks over oak and hickory coals under a roof of smoking stacks; a new hand trains a year.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): a three-chamber brick oven cooking three hundred shoulders a week since 1955.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): the Greensboro pit house on the Historic Barbecue Trail.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): founded Lexington Barbecue in 1962; his sons Rick and Wayne run it.
- kin → pit (term): the word, which in the Piedmont means this brick chamber.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): its Trail's rule — wood or charcoal on grates — makes the Piedmont stops brick pits.
- not to be confused with block-pit: A brick pit is closed, with a door and a chimney, and cooks shoulders; a block pit is open, stacked from cinder blocks, and is sized to a split whole hog. Both are called 'the pit'.
- not to be confused with pig-cooker: A brick pit is masonry and stays put; a pig cooker is steel on wheels.

## burn barrel (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/burn-barrel/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/burn-barrel.json
id: burn-barrel
aliases: burn-barrel · coal barrel · fire barrel · the barrel · burner
facets: kind=tool
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, The Carolinas
what: A repurposed steel drum — or, at Scott's in Hemingway, two 55-gallon drums welded together — in which logs are burned down to coals: the wood goes in at the top, the coals are pulled out from below and carried by shovel to the pit. It is the coal-maker of the wood pit, the reason a whole hog can sit over a steady bed of coals for twelve hours with no flame under it. Older pit houses use a fireplace for the same job — the Skylight Inn burns its oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits — and the barrel is the version anyone can weld.
story: The barrel is the modern form of an older arrangement. *Tradition holds —* the trench pit of the farm barbecue had a fire burning at one end and coals raked down its length under the meat; when the pit climbed above ground into blocks and brick, the fire moved into a fireplace or a drum beside it. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its first barbecues, from 1929, in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath the whole hogs. At Scott's Bar-B-Que in Hemingway, Rodney Scott feeds hunks of hickory, oak and pecan through the top of the welded drums and pulls hot coals from below to stoke the pit. In November 2013 the family's wooden cookhouse caught fire — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and Scott took his hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000, part to rebuild and part for a fund to preserve the region's food traditions.
how: Split logs go in at the top and burn with the draft from the bottom; as they collapse into coals the cook rakes them out with a flat shovel and spreads them in the pit under the meat. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders and thinner under the loin, and a hog cooked through a night takes a fresh shovelful on a regular round, so the barrel is kept fed the whole time. Lexington crews call the same round, in a brick pit, 'firing the pits'.
today: Every wood-fired whole-hog pit keeps a barrel, a fireplace or a burner going through the night; the drum is the standard beside a block pit and at Scott's. Gas and electric cookers do without it, and the labor it stands for is the reason owners give for switching.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the wood it turns into coals.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): its coals go straight under the meat.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open pit it feeds, a shovel's walk away.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the closed Piedmont pit fed the same way, from a fireplace or burner at the end of the pit house.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): what its coals cook through the night.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): two 55-gallon drums welded together, fed with hickory, oak and pecan.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): the pitmaster whose barrel and pit fire NPR described in 2014.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): uses fireplaces beside the pits instead of a drum.
- kin → mallard-creek-barbecue (event): began in 1929 with hickory coals shoved under hogs in ditches.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the cookers that need no barrel and no one to tend it.
- kin → pitmaster (term): the person who tends it through the night.
- not to be confused with pig-cooker: A burn barrel makes coals; nothing is cooked in it. A pig cooker holds the pig.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/burn-barrel/burn-barrel-barbecue-pit.jpg · CC BY 2.0 · Southern Foodways Alliance · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABarbecue_pit.jpg

## chopping block (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/chopping-block/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/chopping-block.json
id: chopping-block
aliases: the block · cleavers · chop
said: 'Chopped', 'coarse chopped' and 'sliced' are the three words on a Lexington menu; in the east the only word is 'barbecue', and it comes chopped.
facets: kind=tool
region: The Carolinas
what: A thick wooden block and a pair of cleavers, on which cooked pork is turned into barbecue. The whole hog is pulled from the bones onto the block and chopped, skin and all, until the meat is fine enough to hold a thin vinegar sauce; the salt and the sauce go on at the block — at the Skylight Inn, vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. A Lexington shoulder is chopped fine, chopped coarse into small chunks, or sliced, and at Lexington Barbecue never pulled. Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on the block one of the most alluring aspects of whole hog barbecue in the Carolinas.
story: The chop is the Carolinas' answer to a question other regions answer with a knife or a fork. *Tradition holds —* the eastern chop comes from the whole hog itself: light meat, dark meat, fat and skin from one animal are one dish only once they are chopped together, and the chop is what lets the crisp skin be eaten in every bite. Eastern-style meat is chopped after it is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture and so that it holds the thin vinegar sauce; Lexington-style is served pulled or lightly chopped, with larger strands of muscle, and the Lexington restaurants add the sliced tray. NCpedia records a South Carolina habit that has crossed the state line: separating the skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat', so the customer chooses; some whole-hog restaurants let the customer choose white meat, dark meat or both, and prize the 'middlin' from the belly and the 'catfish' from under the tenderloin. The three cuts of the Piedmont are a price list. At Lexington Barbecue in September 2026 a chopped tray was $8.00 cash, a sliced tray $8.20 and a coarse-chop tray $8.60, with slaw and rolls or hush puppies; at the Barbecue Center a chopped tray was $9 small and $12 large, sliced or coarse chopped $10 and $13, dip on the meat, slaw included, hush puppies or a potato bun.
how: The cooked meat is pulled from the bones by hand and heaped on the block; the cook works the cleavers across the heap, folding the pile back on itself, adding the crisp skin in pieces once the meat is broken down, and seasoning on the block. For a Lexington shoulder the meat is chopped fine, chopped coarse for 'chunks', or sliced, and the dip goes on before it is trayed. A sandwich takes the chop and slaw on a soft bun.
today: The block and cleavers are in use at the Skylight Inn and in most whole-hog kitchens; Lexington menus carry the three cuts, and 'chopped' is the ordinary order on both sides of the state.
- kin → chopped (term): the word for what happens here, and for the result.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the carcass that becomes one dish on the block.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): chopped fine, chopped coarse or sliced on the same block.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the crisp skin chopped through the eastern barbecue.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): goes on at the block, with salt.
- kin → texas-pete (sauce): part of the Skylight Inn's seasoning at the block.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): goes on the chopped shoulder before it is trayed.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): what the chop is served as, with slaw.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the chop and slaw on a soft bun.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): the preparation that skips the block; Lexington Barbecue never pulls.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the Piedmont's word for the shoulder's dry outer meat, which the Carolinas separate from the inside meat.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): chops tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together at the block.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): chopped, coarse chop or sliced; never pulled.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): chopped, sliced or coarse chopped 'chunks', dip on the meat.
- not to be confused with chopped: The block is the tool and the place; 'chopped' is the word for the result and the order.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/chopping-block/chopping-block-cooked-and-chopped-hogs-at-b-s-barbecue.jpg · Public domain · City of Greenville, North Carolina · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ACooked_and_chopped_hogs_at_B%27s_Barbecue.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/chopping-block/chopping-block-northcarolinabarbecuebanner.jpg · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Rastapopulous · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ANorthCarolinaBarbecueBanner.JPG

## direct heat (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/direct-heat/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/direct-heat.json
id: direct-heat
aliases: coals under the meat · open-pit · pit-cooked · cooking on coals
facets: kind=method
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The Carolina way of putting fire to meat: a bed of hardwood coals directly beneath the hog or the shoulders, with no flame and no separate firebox. The coals are made elsewhere — in a burn barrel or a fireplace — and shoveled in, so the meat sits over glowing charcoal and its own dripping fat rather than in a stream of smoke. The contrast is the offset smoker of Central Texas: a cylinder with a smaller firebox attached at one end, whose burning post-oak fire sends heat and smoke sideways through the chamber past the meat — indirect heat. The whole-hog article, the Mallard Creek church and the Barbecue Center all describe the coals going under the meat.
story: The word carries the method. The Wikipedia article on barbecue draws its line between the indirect barbecues of the United States — meat roasted or smoked over wood or charcoal at low temperature for hours — and the direct grilling of most of the world, done over hot coals for minutes; in a typical American home barbecue the coals are dispersed to the sides. The Carolina pit sits across that line: the coals are directly under the meat, as on a grill, but far enough below and slow enough that the cook is barbecuing, not grilling. True 'Cue quotes a federal meat-labeling rule that defines barbecued meat as 'cooked by the direct action of dry heat resulting from the burning of hard wood'. Texas divides the same way: Central Texas cooks with indirect heat from a pecan, post-oak or mesquite fire, and West Texas over direct mesquite heat 'in a method very similar to grilling'. *Inference —* in geometry the Carolina pit is closer to the West Texas cowboy fire than to the Austin smoker, and the reason both Carolina styles burn their wood to coals first is that flame under a fat hog is a fire. Ed Mitchell in Wilson cooks 'hot and fast' with a bank of coals surrounding the hog, starting at 500 degrees and letting it fall to 250; Rodney Scott shovels coals under a hog lying belly-down for eight to twelve hours; the Barbecue Center in Lexington 'fires the pits' by distributing coals evenly beneath the shoulders.
how: Coals go in under the meat in a thin, even bed and are renewed from the burn barrel through the cook; the meat is never over flame. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders of a whole hog and thinner under the loin. Fat drips onto the coals and vaporizes — *Inference —* the source of much of what the Carolinas call wood flavor — and a flare-up from that fat is the whole-hog cook's constant danger. The pit is closed with a lid or a door to hold the heat, and a hog is flipped once near the end.
today: Every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate cooks this way by definition — on grates over pits with wood or charcoal. *Tradition holds —* the offset smoker has arrived too: Lewis Barbecue in Charleston cooks Central Texas brisket in offset smokers, and is described here the same way as a wood pit.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): makes the coals that go under the meat.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the wood burned down for the bed.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open pit built for it.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the closed pit built for it: coals on the floor, rack above, chimney over.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut cooked over a bed of coals for a night.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the Piedmont's cut, over the same coals in a brick pit.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): on charcoal it works the same way; on gas the burner stands in for the coals.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): heat from a burner or an element, smoke from a chip box: neither coals nor firebox.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): cooks hot and fast with a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): shovels burn-barrel coals under a belly-down hog for eight to twelve hours.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): quotes the federal definition — direct dry heat from burning hardwood — on its wood page.
- kin → pit (term): the word for the hole, then the box, that holds the coals under the meat.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): the Charleston restaurant that, tradition holds, cooks Texas brisket the other way, in offset smokers.
- not to be confused with hickory-and-oak: Direct heat is where the fuel sits; hickory and oak are the fuel. A Texas firebox burns the same woods beside the meat instead of beneath it.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/direct-heat/direct-heat-cooking-over-an-open-trench.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · Albert Barden; State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/32810373053/
sources: s:wp-barbecue — Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-smoker-cooking — Smoker (cooking) — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-texas — Barbecue in Texas — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-mallard-creek-history — History of the Annual Barbecue; s:web-leisuregrouptravel-lexington — Lexington, North Carolina Barbecue is All About the Pork (Randy Mink); s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:web-npr-scott-pit-burned — When His Pit Burned Down, A Southern BBQ Master Took Hogs On Tour (Debbie Elliott, February 4, 2014); s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:web-ourstate-historic-barbecue-trail — Running on Full: The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail (Bryan Mims, January 29, 2016); s:web-barbecuebible-campaign — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (John Shelton Reed, January 23, 2018); s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-barden — Albert Barden Collection, State Archives of North Carolina
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-15

## gas and electric cookers (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/gas-and-electric-cookers/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/gas-and-electric-cookers.json
id: gas-and-electric-cookers
aliases: gas pit · gas cooker · electric cooker · gas-fired pit · smoker oven
facets: kind=cooker
region: The Carolinas
what: The cookers most Carolina barbecue is cooked in: steel ovens fired by propane, natural gas or an electric element, with a thermostat and racks, and often a box for wood chips or a log to put smoke on the meat. A gas smoker lights a burner directly under a box of wood or charcoal; an electric one runs a heating element that holds any temperature from a cold smoke to about 275 degrees. New barbecue restaurants mostly open on them and many older ones switched. They cook overnight unattended, hold a set temperature, make no soot and need no one to shovel coals at three in the morning, and they are the machine behind a great deal of what both states call barbecue, sauce and slaw included.
story: The argument has two sides and each states its reasons. The cooks who switched say it plainly: gas and electricity are cheaper and easier and the product is more consistent — John Shelton Reed grants all three — and a wood pit needs someone awake through the night, produces soot, and burns more fuel and labor for the same meat. Many owners also say the health department made them do it. Reed and the True 'Cue campaign he co-founded put a Challenge in the Raleigh News & Observer on April 23, 2014, offering a prize to anyone who could name the regulation; two years on no one had, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had reported the same from their states. Reed writes that one state official mentioned environmental concerns and that the actual motives remain unclear. On the other side stands the billboard at the Skylight Inn, whose four tenets include that barbecue must be cooked with wood, and the True 'Cue Pledge for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue; the campaign's wood page calls smoke 'the umami of barbecue', quotes Pete Jones, Rodney Scott and Wilber Shirley among its witnesses, and Alton Brown's joke that with gas 'you can control the heat. But you're going to go to hell.' Reed draws the line with care: the campaign has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. The pig pickin' article records the same split at the backyard: propane for a steady temperature, charcoal 'touted as producing better-tasting meat'. Jim Early, searching a hundred counties for pits still cooking over wood coals, found fewer than thirty.
how: Shoulders or a split hog go on the racks in the evening with the smoke box loaded, the thermostat holds the temperature overnight, and in the morning the meat comes off to the block. There is no burn barrel, no shoveling round and no chimney; the cook's labor is loading, unloading and chopping. The sauce, the slaw and the chop are the same as at a wood pit, which is why the customer often cannot tell and the campaigns exist to tell them.
today: Wood pits are a counted minority: about seventy North Carolina restaurants held True 'Cue certificates in January 2018, and the Historic Barbecue Trail listed about two dozen. *Inference —* the rest of the barbecue sold in both states comes off gas or electricity.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): the campaign that certifies the pits that do not use them, and challenged the claim that health rules require them.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): its Historic Barbecue Trail excludes them.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): grants that gas is cheaper, easier and more consistent, and offered a prize to anyone who could name the regulation requiring it.
- kin → jim-early (person): found fewer than thirty wood pits in a hundred counties; the rest cook this way.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the trailer version of the same choice, gas or charcoal.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the Piedmont wood pit these replaced at many restaurants.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open whole-hog pit these replaced.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the coal-maker they do without.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the wood that goes in the chip box.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): gas-fired whole-hog pits are the common choice of new restaurants.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): many eastern pits cook shoulders or hogs on gas and are eastern by their sauce.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): its billboard says barbecue must be cooked with wood.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the same propane-versus-charcoal argument at the backyard cooker.
- not to be confused with pig-cooker: A restaurant's gas or electric cooker is fixed, thermostated and indoors; a pig cooker is the wheeled steel box of the pig pickin', gas or charcoal.
sources: s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-smoker-cooking — Smoker (cooking) — Wikipedia; s:web-uncpress-reed-myth — John Shelton Reed: Busting a Barbecue Myth (April 6, 2016); s:web-barbecuebible-campaign — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (John Shelton Reed, January 23, 2018); s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:web-wral-jim-early-dies — North Carolina Barbecue Society founder Jim Early dies (August 26, 2021); s:web-ourstate-historic-barbecue-trail — Running on Full: The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail (Bryan Mims, January 29, 2016); s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## hickory and oak (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/hickory-and-oak/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/hickory-and-oak.json
id: hickory-and-oak
aliases: hickory · oak · hardwood · pecan · wood
said: 'Hickory-smoked' is the sign's word; on the pit it is 'wood' or 'coals'.
facets: kind=fuel
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The hardwoods of the Carolina pit. Hickory and oak are the woods a Carolina cook burns, usually together and usually burned down to coals before they go under the meat: Lexington pits cook over oak and hickory coals, the Skylight Inn burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits, and Scott's in Hemingway feeds hickory, oak and pecan through the top of a burn barrel. South Carolina's barbecue is smoked over hickory or oak; Lexington's over a hardwood fire, usually hickory. Both are dense, slow-burning and abundant in the eastern forest, and both give the strong smoke that pork carries. Pecan is itself a hickory — Carya illinoinensis — with a sweeter, milder smoke.
story: Wood smoke flavors the meat, so the woods a region has decide how its barbecue tastes; hickory, oak and mesquite give a strong smoke, and pecan, maple, alder and the fruit woods a milder, sweeter one, which is why the strong woods go with pork and beef. Pecan, a hickory native to the south-central United States, is sold as a smoking wood for a 'sweet and nutty flavor stronger than many fruit woods'; Rodney Scott burns it with hickory and oak. Skin takes up more of the smoke than meat does, which is one reason the eastern chop keeps its skin. Ed Mitchell in Wilson burns oak and hickory logs and adds charcoal briquettes. *Inference —* in a Carolina pit the wood is burned to coals before it reaches the meat, so most of the flame's smoke is spent; what the meat then breathes is largely its own fat and juices vaporizing on the coals, and that is the flavor Carolina cooks call 'wood' rather than 'smoke' — the same log gives a different result in a Texas offset smoker, where the meat sits in the smoke of a burning fire. True 'Cue, the campaign that certifies wood-cooked pits, calls wood smoke 'the umami of barbecue' and 'barbecue's soul'.
how: Logs burn down to coals in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the coals are shoveled into the pit under the meat, and Lexington crews 'fire the pits' by spreading them evenly beneath the shoulders. At a pig pickin' the fuel is often bagged charcoal with chunks of blackjack oak or hickory added for flavor, or a separate stove of hardwood whose coals are shoveled under the grate; Ed Mitchell adds charcoal briquettes to his oak and hickory.
today: Hickory is the sign-painter's word across both states and oak the workhorse beside it; every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate is a wood fire of one or both. Scott's in Hemingway burns pecan with the other two.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): where these woods become coals.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): the way the coals are used: spread under the meat.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the Piedmont pit these coals are shoveled into.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open whole-hog pit these coals are shoveled into.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut whose skin takes the most smoke.
- kin → lexington (style): cooked over hickory and oak coals; the shoulder's crust is the wood's work.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the Skylight Inn's oak and hickory fireplaces are the east's version.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): feeds hickory, oak and pecan through the top of a burn barrel.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): burns oak and hickory logs with charcoal briquettes.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the fuels that replaced these woods at many pits, for cost and labor.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): certifies pits that use only wood for heat.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): its Historic Barbecue Trail admits only pits cooking over wood or charcoal.
- not to be confused with direct-heat: Hickory and oak are the fuel; direct heat is where the fuel sits. The same woods burn in a Texas firebox beside the meat and in a Carolina pit beneath it.
sources: s:wp-barbecue-in-the-united-states — Barbecue in the United States — Wikipedia; s:wp-pecan — Pecan — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:web-npr-scott-pit-burned — When His Pit Burned Down, A Southern BBQ Master Took Hogs On Tour (Debbie Elliott, February 4, 2014); s:web-lexbbq — Lexington Barbecue — official site; s:web-leisuregrouptravel-lexington — Lexington, North Carolina Barbecue is All About the Pork (Randy Mink); s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:web-ourstate-historic-barbecue-trail — Running on Full: The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail (Bryan Mims, January 29, 2016); s:web-barbecuebible-campaign — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (John Shelton Reed, January 23, 2018)
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## hog killing (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/hog-killing/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/hog-killing.json
id: hog-killing
aliases: hog killin' · hog-killing day · killing hogs · pig slaughter
said: 'Hog killin'' in speech. A hard frost is still 'hog-killing weather'.
facets: kind=prep
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The winter slaughter of the farm's hogs, done on the first cold day of autumn or winter, when the meat would keep. In rural North Carolina neighbors gathered before dawn; water was heated with fire-hot stones dropped into barrels; the penned and fattened hogs were killed with knives, bled, scalded, hung on a gambrel — a spreader bar through the hind legs — and scraped clean of hair; the carcasses cooled overnight and were cut up the next day, the hams, sides, shoulders, jowls and heads salted down in the smokehouse. Lard was rendered, the fat cooked down to cracklings, the trim ground for sausage. It is the farm year's pork day, and the social form the pit barbecue grew up beside.
story: William S. Powell's entry in the Encyclopedia of North Carolina (2006) describes the day as farms kept it: as many as a hundred hogs penned and fattened on peas, potatoes, corn gleaned from the harvested fields or mast from the woods; workers from the neighborhood gathered well before dawn; stones heated in an open fire and dropped into barrels to heat the scalding water; the hogs killed with large knives, bled, scalded, hung and scraped; cooled overnight, cut up and salted the next day on a tilted platform in the smokehouse, the dripping brine caught in troughs and boiled down to save the salt for the stock. The weeks after were spare ribs, liver and sausage; the hams came a month or two later. Carolina Country followed the Jackson family of Hopkins through a January hog killing in 2019: Terry Jackson directing, his son in training, neighbors and friends at the scalding vat; sausage seasoned with salt, red pepper and sage and a patty fried over the wood fire for approval; lard rendered and cracklings saved; hams and shoulders carried to the salt room; chitterlings, feet and bones for broth; a pot of homemade soup at midday for everyone who came. The pit's relation to the day is old: George Washington raised pigs for slaughter in November at Mount Vernon and, once the enslaved people had cured the hams and bacon, whole pigs were pit-roasted over coals 'as a treat'. John Shelton Reed writes that barbecue was never home cooking, and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies. *Tradition holds —* the hog killing and the pit shared a season and a crowd, and a pig set aside from the killing was the cheapest way to feed the neighbors who came to help.
how: Cold weather first. The hog is stuck and bled, scalded in a vat or barrel of water just under the boil and scraped clean of hair, then hung head-down from a gambrel, gutted, and left overnight to cool and firm. Next day it is cut into hams, shoulders, sides for bacon, loins and ribs; the trim is ground and seasoned for sausage, the fat rendered in a kettle for lard with the crisp bits kept as cracklings, the intestines cleaned for chitterlings, and the feet and bones boiled for broth. Hams and shoulders are salted or smoked to keep.
today: The community hog killing survives on some farms — Carolina Country followed one in 2019 — and the pig for a pit comes from a processor: the Skylight Inn buys most of its hogs from meat processors in Ayden. *Tradition holds —* the word survives in the weather: a hard frost is hog-killing weather.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the pig that, tradition holds, came off the killing and onto the pit.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the feast; the killing is the work. One is winter labor, the other a party.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): cracklings, the fat's crisp remainder, are the killing's snack; pork skins are the pit's.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the head and liver South Carolina stewed into hash came from a day like this.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open pit that, tradition holds, was dug beside the killing.
- kin → hog (term): the animal, penned and fattened for this day.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the other occasion for a whole pig before the twentieth century, per Reed.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): buys its hogs from processors in Ayden; nobody kills them on the farm any more.
- not to be confused with pig-pickin: A hog killing is butchering for the year's meat; a pig pickin' is cooking one pig for one crowd.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/hog-killing/hog-killing-hog-killing-in-rutherford-tennessee-ca-1914.jpg · Public domain · Unknown authorUnknown author · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AHog_killing_in_Rutherford%2C_Tennessee%2C_ca_1914.jpg

## pig cooker (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/pig-cooker/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/pig-cooker.json
id: pig-cooker
aliases: pig roaster · hog cooker · trailer cooker · cooker
said: 'Cooker' alone, in the east, means this; a 'pit' is masonry.
facets: kind=cooker
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Carolinas
what: A steel box on a trailer chassis, long enough for a split hog, with a hinged lid, a grate, and either a row of propane burners underneath or a bed for charcoal: the cooker of the pig pickin', towed to the church lot, the tailgate or the fire station and home again. Carolina Cooker of Micro, North Carolina, builds one of 12-gauge steel with four propane burners on a leaf-spring trailer, listed at $2,599.99 in September 2026; BQ Grills of Elm City builds towable charcoal-and-wood cookers of eighth-inch steel in five- and six-foot lengths at $7,200 to $9,800. The article on the pig pickin' calls the grills 'as varied as the methods of producing them', some homemade, some custom-made.
story: The pig pickin' moved the whole hog off the farm pit and onto wheels. *Tradition holds —* welded cookers appeared in eastern North Carolina after the Second World War, when propane and a cutting torch put a pit within reach of anyone with a trailer hitch, and the rental cooker followed. What the article on the pig pickin' records is the argument the cooker started: propane 'is said to maintain a consistent temperature, whereas charcoal or charwood are often touted as producing better-tasting meat', and the cooks who run charcoal add chunks of blackjack oak or hickory for the smoke, or keep a separate stove of hardwood to make coals and shovel them under the grate. The cooking is communal and 'usually directed by an authority figure' — the host, helped by friends and family — and the pig goes on meat-side down for four to eight hours and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat. Ed Mitchell learned on a family cooker in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him his first glass.
how: The split hog goes on the grate meat-side down; on gas the burners run low, on charcoal the coals are lit in the bed or shoveled in from a hardwood stove; the lid comes down for four to eight hours until the dripping slows, and the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp. Some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. Off the cooker the meat is chopped, pulled, or picked straight off the bones by the guests.
today: Cookers are built and sold across the Coastal Plain — Micro and Elm City among the makers — and every pig pickin', tailgate and fire-department plate sale runs on one. Gas is the ordinary choice and charcoal the argued-for one.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the party it exists for.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut it is built around: a split carcass on a six-foot grate.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): its restaurant-size relatives, fixed and thermostated.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the masonry pit it replaced on wheels.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the hardwood stove some cooks keep beside a charcoal cooker.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): on charcoal it works the Carolina way, coals under the meat; on gas the burner stands in for the coals.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the chunks added to the charcoal for smoke.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the Saturday plate sale is cooked on one.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the cooker behind the candidate's free plate.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): the other meat on the same grate at a fire-department plate sale.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): cooked his first pig, unbidden, on the family cooker in Wilson.
- not to be confused with gas-and-electric-cookers: A pig cooker is the wheeled steel box of the yard and the plate sale; the gas or electric cooker of a restaurant is fixed, thermostated and indoors.
- not to be confused with burn-barrel: A pig cooker holds the pig; a burn barrel only makes the coals.
sources: s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-roast — Pig roast — Wikipedia; s:web-carolina-cooker — Large Portable BBQ Cooker (product page, price as posted); s:web-bq-grills — Commercial Charcoal/Wood Whole Hog BBQ Pits (prices as posted); s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:web-wcti-back-swamp-vfd — Back Swamp Volunteer Fire Department to host annual BBQ fundraiser and raffle (April 15, 2026)

## pork shoulder (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/pork-shoulder/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/pork-shoulder.json
id: pork-shoulder
aliases: shoulder · Boston butt · butt · pork butt · picnic · picnic shoulder · picnic ham
said: Lexington menus say 'pork shoulders'; 'butt' means the upper shoulder, not the rear of the animal.
root: Boston + butt, a barrel: in colonial and Revolutionary-era New England butchers stored and shipped this shoulder cut in barrels called butts, and the Boston-area method of cutting it gave the cut its name. Picnic (the lower shoulder): cured on the bone it is a 'picnic ham'; no origin for the name is cited here. · first seen: 'Boston butt' in print, 1915, in Hotel Monthly; a 1912 University of Illinois Agricultural Experiment Station bulletin records the barrels still in use for export to Germany and Denmark · Folk: that the butt is the animal's hindquarter. It is not; the cut is the upper shoulder, above the picnic, and may contain the blade bone.
facets: kind=cut
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, The Carolinas
what: The front leg and shoulder of the pig, sold as one primal — a primal being one of the large first divisions of a carcass — or split in two: the butt, the upper half with the blade bone, and the picnic, the lower arm half, which cured on the bone is a 'picnic ham'. The butt's name is a barrel, not an anatomy. In the North Carolina Piedmont, shoulder is the only cut that counts as barbecue: Lexington pits salt it, lay it over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours, and serve it chopped, coarse chopped or sliced under a red dip. It is darker meat than the loin and stays moist through a long cook, and it is what packers ship when they will not ship a carcass.
story: New England butchers of the colonial and Revolutionary era stored and shipped pork in barrels called butts, and the shoulder cut they packed that way took the name of the port; a 1912 University of Illinois bulletin notes the barrels still going to Germany and Denmark, and 'Boston butt' first appears in print in 1915. In the Carolinas the cut's rise is the whole hog's decline. The Piedmont settled on shoulders early — *Tradition holds —* because a shoulder fit a small brick pit and a lunch counter's day in a way a carcass did not. By the 1980s the corporate farms replacing independent hog farms shipped butchered shoulders and hams rather than whole pigs, which pushed restaurants elsewhere the same way. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte, which began in 1929 by cooking three or four pigs and a goat, told Our State in 2016: 'Now we just use the butt.' South Carolina hash, once made from heads and liver, is now mostly made from leftover shoulder.
how: Lexington pits cook shoulders only, salted but not basted or marinated, on racks over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its pit. Elsewhere a butt is rubbed, smoked until it reaches 195 to 205 degrees inside, and shredded. Off the pit the Piedmont serves it three ways — chopped fine, coarse chopped in small chunks, or sliced; never pulled, at Lexington Barbecue — and dresses it with dip. *Tradition holds —* the crusted outer meat is sold apart as outside brown.
today: Shoulder is the cut of the Piedmont's pits — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Stamey's, Red Bridges, Short Sugar's — and of most new restaurants in both states, because it arrives boxed from the packer; a pulled-pork menu anywhere in the country means this cut. At Lexington Barbecue a chopped tray was $8.00 cash and $8.25 by card in September 2026.
- kin → lexington (style): the style that uses only this cut, darker and moister than the loin, under a red dip.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the older cut it displaced wherever packers stopped shipping carcasses.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): where it is chopped fine, chopped coarse or sliced.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the closed Piedmont pit a rack of shoulders fits.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): the national name for this cut smoked and shredded; Lexington chops or slices it and does not pull.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce the Piedmont puts on the chopped shoulder.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): modern South Carolina hash is mostly made from leftover shoulder.
- kin → mallard-creek-barbecue (event): cooked whole pigs in 1929 and pork butts by 2016.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): cooks shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them chopped, coarse chopped or sliced, never pulled.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): cooks three hundred shoulders a week in a three-chamber brick pit.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): founded Lexington Barbecue in 1962 on this cut.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): a Greensboro shoulder pit interviewed for the Southern Foodways Alliance's North Carolina project.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): a Shelby shoulder pit on the Historic Barbecue Trail.
- kin → short-sugars (place): a Reidsville shoulder pit on the Historic Barbecue Trail.
- not to be confused with pulled-pork: 'Pulled pork' names a preparation of this cut; on a Lexington menu the same shoulder is 'barbecue', and it comes chopped or sliced.
- not to be confused with whole-hog: Shoulder meat is all dark and has no crisp skin; a whole-hog chop mixes light meat, dark meat and skin.

## whole hog (pit)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/pit/whole-hog/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/pit/whole-hog.json
id: whole-hog
aliases: whole-hog barbecue · whole hog · a pig · the hog
said: Eastern cooks 'cook a pig' or 'put on a hog'; what comes off the block is just 'barbecue'.
facets: kind=cut, method
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, The Carolinas
what: The entire dressed pig — dressed meaning gutted and scraped of hair, the head sometimes left on — split open along the backbone, laid flat over coals and cooked as one piece, then pulled from the bones and chopped together: ham, shoulder, loin, belly and, in the Carolinas, the crisped skin. It is the oldest form of open-pit barbecue in the United States and the cut that defines eastern North Carolina and the Pee Dee of South Carolina. A hog of 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is the usual size for a pig pickin'; restaurants choose small hogs and cook them hot so the skin crisps, and a whole animal can run to 300 pounds.
story: Robert Moss finds the ritual barbecue of whole hogs established in the British colonies by the eighteenth century; the communal feast of whole pigs or sheep spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies. The Oxford Encyclopedia of Food and Drink in America calls whole hog the oldest style of open-pit barbecue in the country. The first sit-down restaurant built on it was Bob Melton's, opened at Rocky Mount in 1924; for most of the twentieth century such places had white owners and Black cooks, and new pits were founded by cooks trained at older ones. In Hemingway, South Carolina, the Scott family's variety store cooked one hog a week when Rodney Scott started at eleven and grew to seven or eight a day. The hazards are in the method: fat renders and pools in the cavity, so the meat cooks in its own fat, and a lean 'bacon hog' such as the American Yorkshire is chosen because a fat one feeds the fire. Pit fires are the common disaster; Scott's wooden cookhouse burned in November 2013 — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and the family took its hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000 to rebuild. In 2017 Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly counted the whole-hog restaurants of the country and found them falling: packers ship shoulders and hams, not carcasses; a whole hog costs more labor, fuel and soot than a shoulder; and much of its weight is bone and fat that cannot be sold.
how: The carcass is split so it lies flat; the backbone may be cracked and the head split. It goes on the rack skin-side up — meat-side down, in the east's phrase — over a bed of coals and cooks for eight to twenty-four hours, most of that time unturned, before one flip to crisp the skin; at Scott's the flip comes at the eight-to-twelve-hour mark and a full-size mop bathes the meat in the family's vinegar-and-pepper sauce. The meat is not basted before the flip, though some cooks season it with a dry rub. Turning a heavy carcass takes several hands. Off the pit the meat is picked from the bones and chopped fine or pulled into threads; the eastern chop takes the crisp skin in, and the Pee Dee sometimes skins the pig first and fries the skin separately.
today: Whole hog is the restaurant cut of the Coastal Plain and the Pee Dee — the Skylight Inn, B's, Grady's, Parker's and Wilber's in North Carolina; Scott's in Hemingway and Rodney Scott's in Charleston in South Carolina — and the cooking of most pig pickin's. Vaughn's 2017 count found fewer whole-hog restaurants each year; cooks who keep it say their customers come for the ritual.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose name it is: the east cooks the entire pig and chops it, skin and all.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the South Carolina region that keeps the whole hog under a vinegar-pepper sauce; the pig is sometimes skinned first and the skin fried.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the gathering built on it: a whole hog cooked for a crowd and picked off the bones by hand.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the open cinder-block pit sized to a split carcass.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): where the coals come from on a wood pit: logs burned down in a barrel or fireplace and shoveled under the hog.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the trailer cooker that takes a whole hog on gas or charcoal at a pig pickin'.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): the heat under it: coals directly beneath the carcass, not smoke drawn from a firebox.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): where the whole hog becomes barbecue: cleavers on a block, skin chopped through the meat.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the crisp skin the eastern chop is judged on, chopped into the meat.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): what South Carolina made of the head, liver and trimmings left after the chop.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut that replaced it in the Piedmont and at most new restaurants, because packers ship shoulders, not carcasses.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the winter slaughter that, tradition holds, once supplied the pig for the pit.
- kin → hog (term): the animal, and the east's word for the carcass on the pit.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): cooks its hogs heads-on over oak and hickory coals in Ayden.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): the Hemingway store that went from one hog a week to seven or eight a day.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): the Pee Dee pitmaster whose whole hog won a James Beard chef award in 2018.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): the Wilson pitmaster who cooks whole hog because, he says, a sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together.
- kin → bob-melton (person): opened the first sit-down whole-hog restaurant, at Rocky Mount in 1924.
- not to be confused with pork-shoulder: A chop with crisp skin and both light and dark meat through it is whole hog; a uniformly dark, moist chop with no skin is shoulder.
- not to be confused with pig-pickin: Whole hog is the cut and the method; a pig pickin' is the party at which it is eaten off the bones.

## 12 Bones Smokehouse (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/12-bones-smokehouse/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/12-bones-smokehouse.json
id: 12-bones-smokehouse
aliases: 12 Bones · 12 Bones South
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=2005 · fuel=unknown · styles=
region: The North Carolina mountains
what: A mountain barbecue house now trading from Hendersonville Road in Arden, south of Asheville, after Hurricane Helene took its River Arts District room in September 2024. Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley opened the first one in 2005 in a cinder-block shack on an Asheville floodplain; Bryan and Angela King have owned it since about 2012. Ribs are the signature — blueberry-chipotle and other glazes that are not Carolina orthodoxy — with pulled pork alongside. Barack Obama ate here in April 2010, which is the thing most often said about it.
story: The first 12 Bones was a cinder-block shack in a floodplain in the River Arts District, opened in 2005 by Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley. Bryan and Angela King bought it — 2012 by two 2024 accounts, 2011 by a 2017 one — and Explore Asheville's profile puts the ownership plainly in Bryan King's own words, that he owns 12 Bones with his wife Angela. On April 23, 2010 Barack Obama came in and ate ribs, mac and cheese, corn pudding and sweet tea; accounts differ on whether he visited twice or three times. In January 2017 the original Riverside Drive building was closed and demolished for a road project and a roundabout, and the business moved to Foundy Street beside Wedge Brewing. Then on September 27, 2024 Helene put the floodplain under water. Bryan King described going inside to find mud in the attic and the building almost completely submerged, and called it a very long recovery. By April 2025 the business had told Blue Ridge Public Radio it would not rebuild on Foundy Street. Arden is what is left, open seven days now rather than the weekday lunches the Asheville room kept.
how: Ribs are the thing: a dry rub and a run of glazes, the blueberry-chipotle the one people name, which is not how a Piedmont or a Coastal Plain pit finishes pork. Pulled pork, sides and a brewing operation fill the rest. An Explore Asheville listing says the meats are smoked long and slow over oak and cherry; that reads as the restaurant's own copy and could not be confirmed on the company's site, which is why the fuel here is left unknown.
today: Open seven days, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 2350 Hendersonville Road, Arden — the only location the company lists. The Foundy Street room in Asheville's River Arts District closed with Helene in September 2024 and will not be rebuilt.
address: 2350 Hendersonville Rd, Arden, NC, 28704
geo: 35.46609, -82.51633 (street)
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut behind its pulled pork, beside the ribs it is better known for.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the plate in the mountains, where the glazed rib rather than the chopped shoulder is the order.
- kin → buxton-hall-barbecue (place): the other Asheville barbecue name of the same decade; Buxton Hall closed in 2023, 12 Bones lost its river room to Helene in 2024.
sources: s:web-exploreasheville-12-bones — Bryan & Angela King — 12 Bones Smokehouse; s:web-ourstate-12-bones-2024 — 12 Bones Smokehouse; s:web-bpr-rad-2025 — Businesses spring back to life in flood-ravaged parts of Asheville's River Arts District; s:web-mountainx-obama-2010 — Obamas visit Asheville; s:web-12bones-news — 12 Bones Smokehouse — in the news; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-16

## Allen & Son Barbeque (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/allen-and-son/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/allen-and-son.json
id: allen-and-son
aliases: Allen & Son · Allen and Son Bar-B-Que · Allen & Son Barbecue
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1971 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington, eastern-nc
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The hickory-fired pork-shoulder restaurant on Millhouse Road at N.C. 86 north of Chapel Hill that Keith Allen opened in 1971 at nineteen and closed in the first week of December 2018, quietly, to avoid a long goodbye. Allen split the hickory himself, fired the pit every half hour for nine hours, and dressed the chopped shoulder with the hot vinegar sauce he had from his father — an eastern sauce on Piedmont meat. His wife Tammy waited tables for thirty years and made the ice cream; the pies, cobblers and banana pudding were the second reason to come. A separate Allen & Son in Pittsboro, under a licensing agreement, stayed open.
story: Keith Allen's father James ran an Allen & Son in Chatham County, and Keith was cooking at twelve or thirteen after his father bought the business; his father died at 51 or 52. In 1971 Keith opened the Chapel Hill restaurant with $3,000, Our State reported in 2017. He started work at 2:30 in the morning five days a week, split hickory logs by hand for the heat and the flavor — 'I keep cooking with wood because I'm chasing that flavor' — and cooked sixteen-pound shoulders down to nine or eleven over nine hours. 'Nobody's hands but mine touch my barbecue, until the customer's do.' The authors of Holy Smoke interviewed him at length; the Southern Foodways Alliance gave him its Guardian of the Tradition award in 2007. He had no son to take it on; his daughter went to graduate school in geospatial science. In early December 2018 he closed without notice, and Chapelboro reported on December 6 that the Pittsboro Allen & Son on U.S. 15-501 would continue under a separate licensing agreement. UNC Press published a closing interview with him two weeks later.
how: Sixteen-pound shoulders over hickory Allen split himself, the pit fired every thirty minutes for nine hours, the meat chopped and dressed with a vinegar sauce he called hot and spicy. Chicken, catfish and cheeseburgers filled out the menu, and the desserts — ice cream made daily, cobblers from his grandmother's recipe, coconut chess and peanut butter pies, pecan pie, banana pudding — were made in the house, with sweet tea.
today: Closed since December 2018. The building at 6203 Millhouse Road, Chapel Hill, is not the Pittsboro Allen & Son, which continued separately; this record is the Chapel Hill restaurant only.
address: 6203 Millhouse Rd, Chapel Hill, NC, 27516
geo: 35.9919056, -79.0716999 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the cut and the wood are the Piedmont's: shoulders over hickory.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the sauce was the east's, hot vinegar from his father, on Piedmont meat.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): sixteen pounds going in, nine to eleven coming out.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory, split by hand by the owner for the heat and the flavor.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): his sauce, inherited, hot and spicy.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): on the dessert board with the pies and cobblers.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): on every table.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): interviewed Allen at length for Holy Smoke.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): gave Allen its Guardian of the Tradition award in 2007.
