## Hite's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/hites-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/hites-bar-b-q.json
id: hites-bar-b-q
aliases: Hite's BBQ · Hite's Bar-B-Q · Hite's
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1957 · fuel=wood · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: A take-out barbecue stand on Dreher Road in West Columbia, open only on Friday and Saturday, where the Hite family has cooked whole hogs and hams over oak and hickory coals since 1957. It sells chopped pork, ham, ribs, pork skins, chicken, hash and rice and slaw by the plate and the pound, with a yellow mustard sauce applied lightly; there is no dining room, only picnic tables by a pond. The hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — is made in cast-iron kettles over wood embers. It is not Jackie Hite's of Batesburg-Leesville, some twenty-five miles west, which closed in 2018.
story: John D. Hite farmed on Dreher Road — minnows, hogs, corn and sweet potatoes — and in 1957 began selling barbecue as a side project, a farmer looking for extra income. The stand stayed a two-day business beside the farm and passed to his grandson David Hite, who runs it with the family recipes and, in the words of the restaurant's site, 'the age-old process for cooking barbeque'. Destination BBQ describes that process: coals rendered in a modified campfire fashion, then shoveled, 'payload after smoky payload', under whole hogs and hams until the meat is lacquered with smoke. The hash is cooked the old way in cast-iron kettles over wood embers, and the stand makes an onion sausage that Destination BBQ calls unique to the Midlands. *Inference —* the Dreher Road Hites and Jackie Hite of Leesville share a Lexington County surname and a mustard sauce; no source in this project links the two businesses.
how: Whole hogs and hams cook on a pit over oak and hickory coals. The meat is chopped and lightly dressed with a mustard sauce whose base is a strong yellow mustard. Orders are plates — pork, rib or chicken with hash, rice, slaw and rolls — or sandwiches, or meat by the pound, all to go; picnic tables by the pond are the only seating. Hash simmers in cast-iron kettles over wood embers; pork skins and onion sausage are the extras.
today: Open Friday and Saturday only. The restaurant's site gives 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. both days; Destination BBQ recorded 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. Friday and 8 to 6 Saturday. Take-out only. 240 Dreher Road, West Columbia. Checked September 15, 2026.
address: 240 Dreher Rd, West Columbia, SC, 29169
geo: 33.978304, -81.0928311 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style: a Lexington County farm stand with a strong yellow mustard sauce.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): its sauce, applied lightly — the base is a strong yellow mustard.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): whole hogs and hams together on the same pit.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): kettle hash over wood embers, the old way, on every plate.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its wood, burned to coals campfire-fashion and shoveled under the meat.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): sold from the same hogs.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): the other Hite's, in Leesville, closed in 2018; same surname, same county, no business link shown.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the other West Columbia mustard house: a chain of eight beside this two-day stand.
- not to be confused with jackie-hites-bar-b-q: Hite's is the Dreher Road stand in West Columbia, open Friday and Saturday since 1957. Jackie Hite's was James 'Jackie' Hite's whole-hog buffet house in Leesville, 1979 to 2018.

## Home Team BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/home-team-bbq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/home-team-bbq.json
id: home-team-bbq
aliases: Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ · Home Team
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=2006 · styles=
region: The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: A Charleston barbecue company that began in November 2006 when Aaron Siegel, a Culinary Institute-trained cook from Atlanta, turned Bunch's, a mid-century gas station at 1205 Ashley River Road in West Ashley, into Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ. It cooks pulled pork, ribs, brisket and smoked chicken wings with an Alabama white sauce, runs a bar known for American whiskey and frozen drinks — the Game Changer is its signature — and books live Americana, blues and bluegrass. Seven locations by 2026: West Ashley, Sullivan's Island (2009), downtown Charleston (2016), Aspen (2016), Columbia (2019), Greenville (2021) and north Mount Pleasant (2022), with more than six hundred employees.
story: Aaron Siegel grew up in Atlanta without barbecue, went to the University of Georgia and then, in January 1997, to the Culinary Institute of America at Hyde Park; he interned at Nava in Atlanta under Kevin Rathbun, cooked in Aspen at a white-tablecloth restaurant and a burrito shop, and moved to Charleston in 2002. In 2006, with little money and much help from friends and family, he and his partners Taylor Garrigan, Tony McKie and Madison Ruckel opened in the old gas station on Ashley River Road; Garrigan was the opening sous chef and is an operating partner now. Sullivan's Island came in 2009; downtown at 126 Williman Street and Aspen, Colorado, in 2016; Columbia in 2019, Greenville in 2021, north Mount Pleasant in 2022. McKie curates the music. The company gives to Hogs for a Cause, has run the Rock the Block fundraiser since 2017 and started the Holy Smokes festival in 2021. 'There wasn't a place where you could go have a good time and hang out for a few hours, watch a game, catch a music show' with the family, Siegel told the City Paper before the twentieth anniversary in July 2026.
how: Low and slow, in the company's phrase, on smokers at each store: pulled pork, ribs, brisket, smoked wings tossed in Alabama white sauce — *Tradition holds —* a mayonnaise-based sauce from north Alabama — pulled-pork sandwiches, barbecue tacos, tots and queso, a kids' menu. The bar carries a wide American whiskey list, frozen cocktails and craft beer; live Americana, blues and bluegrass play at several stores.
today: Open at seven locations: the original at 1205 Ashley River Road, Charleston (West Ashley); Sullivan's Island; 126 Williman Street downtown; north Mount Pleasant; Columbia; Greenville; and Aspen, Colorado — per the company's site and the City Paper in July 2026. Checked September 15, 2026.
address: 1205 Ashley River Rd, Charleston, SC, 29407
geo: 32.7969462, -79.9978283 (street)
- kin → pulled-pork (term): its pork is pulled, and called so on the menu.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the pulled-pork sandwich is the company's named staple.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): the older West Ashley barbecue, on Savannah Highway since 1961, about a mile from the original Home Team.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): the Texas-style house on the peninsula since 2016; Home Team's downtown store opened the same year.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): the whole-hog house on King Street, 2017 to 2026.

- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): its Rock the Block (since 2017) and Holy Smokes festival (since 2021) are the modern fundraiser barbecue.

## Hursey's Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/hurseys-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/hurseys-bar-b-q.json
id: hurseys-bar-b-q
aliases: Hursey's · Hursey's Pig Pickin' Bar-B-Q · Hursey's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1945 · fuel=unknown · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The Burlington, Alamance County, barbecue business of the Hursey family: Sylvester and Daisy Hursey began smoking pork over a backyard pit in 1945 with a sauce of their own, moved to a cafe in Gibsonville with two big pits behind it, and built a Burlington restaurant on Rauhut Street in 1957; their son Charles took over the Burlington trade in 1966, and his sons Chuck and Chris manage it now, a fourth generation coming on. It smokes more than 1,200 pork shoulders a week over hickory, plus hams, for five restaurants, a catering house and a wholesale trade; broasted chicken and hot apple turnovers are the other things it is known for.
story: The family's telling starts in the mid-1940s with Sylvester Hursey and a friend cooking their first pig after a night out; in 1945 he and Daisy set up a homemade pit in the yard and sold to neighbors, using his father's way with hickory-smoked pork and a sauce they kept to themselves. When the yard was too small they bought a cafe on Piedmont Street in Gibsonville and built two large pits behind it. The family says the state issued them its first license to wholesale barbecue — in 1949 by the company's history, in 1945 by Our State's 2014 account. Sylvester built the Rauhut Street restaurant in Burlington in 1957; Charles Hursey went full-time in 1960 out of high school and took over Rauhut Street in mid-1966, expanding the wholesale plant on Highway 87 North. Our State in 2014 found Charles, about seventy, and his wife Ellen at the register, and counted five addresses in Burlington, Graham and Mebane. The company lists a win at a North and South Carolina cook-off held in Washington, D.C., and a National Golden Chicken Award among its credentials.
how: Pork shoulders, more than 1,200 a week, and hams are hickory-smoked and served chopped or sliced with the family's Old-Fashioned Barbecue Sauce and hushpuppies; broasted chicken — pressure-fried — and hot apple turnovers are the other things people drive for. The wholesale kitchen also makes hot-dog chili by the ton: Our State reckoned 200,000 hot dogs' worth in ten days.
today: Open daily 11 to 9 at 1834 South Church Street, Burlington, per OpenStreetMap (2026); four more Hursey's stand in Burlington, Graham and Mebane (Our State, 2014).
address: 1834 S Church St, Burlington, NC, 27215
geo: 36.08222, -79.46281 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style, on shoulders with a Piedmont sauce, at wholesale scale.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut, 1,200 a week and more.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on the plate.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the phrase on the South Church Street sign, 'Pig Pickin' Bar-B-Q'.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory smoke; the cooker type is not described in the sources read.

## Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/jack-cobb-and-son/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/jack-cobb-and-son.json
id: jack-cobb-and-son
aliases: Jack Cobb & Son · Jack Cobb and Son Barbecue
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1971 · fuel=wood · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A Black-owned whole-hog counter on South Main Street in Farmville, Pitt County, that Jack Cobb and his son Rudy built as a cinder-block storefront in 1971 and closed in the autumn of 2018. Hogs cooked all night over oak, pecan and hickory coals banked around them; Rudy Cobb shovelled glowing coals in from the hearth and would not use gas. There were no chairs and no tables, only a counter, three days a week. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey shared the board with the pork.
story: Jack Cobb made tobacco hogsheads for A.C. Monk & Co. for about fifty years and cooked barbecue on Saturdays. When his son Rudy came home from Vietnam in 1966 — North Carolina A&T, then combat — the business faced the plain arithmetic of a segregated town. Our State put it in 2013: white customers wanted Jack's barbecue but would not walk into a Black-owned business. So Jack and Rudy carried it out to the cars. A hundred plates a trip, barbecue and cornbread and slaw, sixty-five cents each. Rudy dated the turn to 1966 or 1967 and remembered how he ended the deliveries: he used to carry it to their houses, and when there got to be too many he told them they had to come get it — nobody would bother them, he would be there. He told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance on November 30, 2011 that he was the principal owner, born September 1941, and that he still cooked with wood and did not use gas. Jack died in September 1989, having blessed his son's decision to stop turning the hogs overnight. Rudy's own sons did not want it and no buyer came. He closed in 2018: it was like losing a wife or a son, he told WRAL.
how: Whole hogs — always whole hogs — cooked overnight on oak, pecan and hickory, the wood banked around the pit so it lit through the night, the coals shovelled in from the hearth. Decades of it stained the white walls grey. The pork came chopped with a vinegar sauce, and the hushpuppies were made to Rudy's stepmother Lillian Blunt Cobb's recipe. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey were the other meats. There was nowhere to sit: you took your food and went.
today: Closed. The last service was in the autumn of 2018 — WNCT reported in August that the closing had been put off to October 18 while buyers were sought, and WRAL confirmed the closure the following July. The building stands at 3883 South Main Street, Farmville.
address: 3883 S Main St, Farmville, NC, 27828
geo: 35.59375, -77.58887 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it cooked: whole hog over wood coals, chopped, with vinegar.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, and the only one — always whole hogs, in the owner's words.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its wood: oak, pecan and hickory, banked around the pit to burn through the night.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): made to Lillian Blunt Cobb's recipe, the one part of the board that came from the stepmother.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Rudy Cobb here on November 30, 2011 for its North Carolina barbecue project.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): the interviewer who took Rudy Cobb's oral history in 2011.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): carried it on the Historic Barbecue Trail, third of the twenty-three stops.
- kin → jim-early (person): wrote it up in The Best Tar Heel Barbecue, the book behind the Society's trail.
sources: s:sfa-jack-cobb-and-son — Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place — Rudy Cobb, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, November 30, 2011; s:web-ourstate-jack-cobb — Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place; s:web-wnct-jack-cobb-2018 — Jack Cobb & Son closing postponed while buyers are sought; s:web-wral-jack-cobb-2019 — Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place has closed; s:web-barbecuebros-nc-trail — NC Historic Barbecue Trail; s:early-best-tar-heel-barbecue — The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/jackie-hites-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/jackie-hites-bar-b-q.json
id: jackie-hites-bar-b-q
aliases: Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Que · Jackie Hite's BBQ · Jackie Hite's
facets: state=SC · status=closed · founded=1979 · fuel=wood · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: A whole-hog buffet house on East Railroad Avenue in Leesville, across the tracks from the town, that James Lee 'Jackie' Hite opened in May 1979 and ran until his death in September 2016; his family closed it in 2018. Hogs cooked whole over hickory coals, the coals made in a burn barrel — a steel drum in which the logs burn down — and the chopped meat was dressed with a mustard, vinegar and pepper sauce and set on a buffet with fried chicken, hash and rice, collards, field peas and creamed corn, paid for on the way out. Hite was also Leesville's mayor and fire chief.
story: Jackie Hite's father was a plumber, a fisherman and a part-time barbecue man, and the son learned the pit helping him cook for the annual Firemen's Ball. Hite went into Leesville's public life from 1966 — fire chief, water commissioner, councilman, magistrate, and three terms as mayor — and in May 1979 opened the restaurant across the railroad tracks. He cooked hogs whole over hickory as his father had, and told Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, five years after open-heart surgery and with constituents asking him to run for mayor again: 'Once you been there, you can't get it out of your blood', and 'We just never done nothing but what we're doing and that's why it's so hard.' He died in September 2016 after weeks of failing health; WIS called him a Midlands barbecue legend, and the restaurant had then been open more than thirty-five years. *Tradition holds —* his family kept the pits going two more years and closed the doors on September 23, 2018, the anniversary of his burial, saying it was what Jackie Hite himself would have wanted.
how: Whole hogs over hickory coals, the wood burned down in a burn barrel and shoveled under the meat — *Tradition holds —* on pits of concrete block. The chopped pork got a sauce a visitor called 'like straight mustard': mustard seed and vinegar. Service was a buffet: fried chicken, hash and rice, coleslaw, collards sweet and smoky, salad, creamed corn, mac and cheese, field peas. Guests ate first and paid on the way out. The last listed hours were Wednesday and Thursday 9 to 2, Friday and Saturday 9 to 3, Sunday 9 to 2, cash or card.
today: Closed since 2018. The building stands at 460 East Railroad Avenue, Leesville (Batesburg-Leesville); Destination BBQ marks it permanently closed. Nothing continues under the name as of September 15, 2026, so far as this project's sources show.
address: 460 E Railroad Ave, Batesburg-Leesville, SC, 29070
geo: 33.9173595, -81.5130142 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): its style: whole hog under a mustard-vinegar sauce, in Lexington County.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): mustard cut with vinegar and pepper — 'like straight mustard' to one visitor.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, cooked whole over hickory as Jackie Hite's father had.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): where its hickory burned down to coals before the shovel.
- kin → block-pit (pit): its pits, by the tradition's account: concrete block, hickory coals shoveled in.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory, burned to coals in the barrel.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): on the buffet beside the fried chicken.
- kin → hites-bar-b-q (place): the other Hite's — the West Columbia stand, still open; no business link shown.
- kin → shealys-bar-b-que (place): the town's other barbecue house, a quarter mile across the tracks, still open.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Jackie Hite here in June 2012.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed Jackie Hite here in June 2012.
- not to be confused with hites-bar-b-q: Jackie Hite's was the Leesville buffet house, 1979 to 2018, now closed. Hite's is the Dreher Road take-out stand in West Columbia, open Friday and Saturday since 1957.

## Keaton's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/keatons-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/keatons-barbecue.json
id: keatons-barbecue
aliases: Keaton's · Keaton's Original BBQ · Keaton's Barbecue, Inc.
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1953 · fuel=unknown · styles=
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A chicken house in the crossroads community of Cleveland, Rowan County, west of Salisbury, where since 1953 the chicken has been fried (or baked) and then dipped whole in a hot vinegar-and-tomato barbecue sauce — 'dipped chicken', a North Carolina barbecue of its own kind. Burette Walker 'B.W.' Keaton, a Black railroad man laid off in 1953, started it in a shack and turned down moves to Statesville and Charlotte; he died in 1989, and his niece Kathleen Murray has run it since 1991. Half or whole, white or dark, hot or mild, with a slice of white bread and a hot vinegar slaw.
story: B.W. Keaton lost his railroad job in 1953 and started selling chicken from a shack on Cool Springs Road. The lore, as Our State tells it: the Schlitz Brewing Company offered $10,000 for the sauce recipe and Keaton countered at $100,000; a shotgun lived under the checkout counter; no weapons, no swearing, no photographing the staff; no utensils, because he did not believe in them. He refused offers to relocate to bigger towns. David Cecelski wrote it up for the North Carolina Folklife Institute in December 2010 as a place found on the back roads between Statesville and Winston-Salem, the chicken fried or baked and then dipped in the hot vinegar-tomato sauce, with a slaw of cabbage in a spicy red dressing of vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed. Keaton died in 1989; Kathleen Murray, his niece, took over in 1991. Cash orders want exact change in small bills; cards are taken over five dollars.
how: Chicken is fried or baked, then dipped in the hot vinegar-tomato sauce and served with a white-bread bun — half or whole bird, white or dark meat, hot or mild sauce. The sides are secondary; the slaw is cabbage in a spicy red vinegar-tomato dressing. Plastic forks are now available; the founder did not provide them.
today: Open Tuesday 11 to 2 and Wednesday to Saturday 11 to 2 and 5 to 8, closed Sunday and Monday, at 17365 Cool Springs Road, Cleveland — hours as the restaurant's site listing and Our State give them, with the warning that they vary. Cash preferred.
address: 17365 Cool Springs Rd, Cleveland, NC, 27013
geo: 35.8340052, -80.7093506 (street)
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): the dish turned inside out: the bird is fried, then dipped in the barbecue sauce, and the town calls the result barbecue.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): its slaw is cabbage in a spicy red vinegar-tomato dressing, the Piedmont's red slaw with cayenne.
- kin → dip (term): the word means the act here: the chicken is dipped, whole, in the sauce.
- kin → lexington (style): the sauce is the Piedmont's, vinegar and tomato; the meat is not.

## Kepley's Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/kepleys-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/kepleys-barbecue.json
id: kepleys-barbecue
aliases: Kepley's Barbecue · Kepley's
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1948 · fuel=unknown · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A High Point, Guilford County, barbecue stand in a surplus World War II Quonset hut — a half-cylinder of corrugated steel — opened in June 1948 by Hayden Kepley on North Main Street and closed on February 8, 2025 after 77 years. Bob Burleson came to work there as a sixteen-year-old curb boy the year it opened, bought it with Charlie Johnson when Kepley retired in 1962, and ran it until his death in May 2022 at ninety; his daughter Susan Burleson closed it when she could not staff the hours. It served chopped, vinegary pork with tangy red slaw on a bun, hushpuppies, and 85-cent coffee with refills.
story: Hayden Kepley bought an Army Quonset hut in 1948 and started selling barbecue from it; Bob Burleson, newly motherless at sixteen, arrived that summer as a curb boy. In 1962 Kepley sold to Burleson and his son-in-law Charlie Johnson; Johnson retired in 2001 and Susan Burleson became her father's co-owner, then sole owner after he died in May 2022. The menu board was hand-painted wood and did not change for decades; the hut got green awnings outside and wood paneling within. The High Point Enterprise reported in January 2025 that after four longtime waitresses retired Susan Burleson could not find people willing to work the hours — 'I would have to work up here all day and night, and I'm just too old to do that' — and would not sell, because new owners 'would run it the way they want to run it, and it just wouldn't be Kepley's anymore.' The last day was February 8, 2025. Stephanie Hunt, who grew up nearby, wrote its farewell in Garden & Gun two days before.
how: Pigs roasted slowly — the sources read do not say over what fuel — and the pork chopped and dressed vinegary, served on a bun under red slaw with hushpuppies on the side; coffee 85 cents with free refills, in 2025. Kepley's shipped barbecue nationwide from the hut.
today: Closed since February 8, 2025. The Quonset hut stands at 1304 North Main Street, High Point; OpenStreetMap still carried the listing, with a 1948 start date, in February 2026.
address: 1304 N Main St, High Point, NC, 27262
geo: 35.97231, -80.01672 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style, in the High Point form: chopped pork, red slaw, a bun.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): on the sandwich, tangy.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the signature: chopped pork and red slaw on a bun.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on the side.
- kin → chopped (term): the pork came chopped, vinegary.
- kin → short-sugars (place): the Reidsville drive-in of the same era, closed three weeks earlier in the same winter.
sources: s:web-hpe-kepleys-closing — Kepley's, city's iconic barbecue restaurant, to close next month — High Point Enterprise (24 Jan 2025, via Yahoo News); s:web-gardenandgun-kepleys — An Ode to Kepley's Barbecue, a North Carolina Institution — Garden & Gun (Stephanie Hunt, 6 Feb 2025); s:web-kepleysbarbecue-history — History — Kepley's Bar-B-Q; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Lewis Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/lewis-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/lewis-barbecue.json
id: lewis-barbecue
aliases: Lewis BBQ · Lewis Barbecue Charleston
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=2016 · styles=
region: The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: A Central Texas-style barbecue restaurant at 464 North Nassau Street on the upper peninsula of Charleston, opened in June 2016 by John Lewis, a pitmaster from El Paso who cooked in Austin with Franklin Barbecue and then as a partner in La Barbecue, welding his own smokers along the way. The meat is sold by the pound from a counter: prime brisket, beef ribs, pork spare ribs, turkey breast, pulled pork, 'Texas hot guts' sausage and a green-chile cheddar sausage, with sides from Texas — pinto beans, green chile corn pudding — and from here, collards. A second Lewis opened in Greenville in August 2022 and a third in Atlanta in December 2025.
story: John Lewis grew up in El Paso and moved to Austin at eighteen; a New Braunfels smoker, a birthday present, started the habit. He competed on the barbecue circuit in Denver, came back to Austin to cook with Franklin Barbecue, and partnered with LeAnn Mueller to open La Barbecue, where the brisket made his name. He moved to Charleston in 2015 and opened Lewis Barbecue in June 2016; Rodney Scott's whole hog arrived on King Street eight months later. Lewis welds his own custom smokers. The Greenville store followed at 214 Rutherford Street in August 2022; in December 2025, after six years of looking, he opened at Ansley Mall in Atlanta with six smokers on the roof, an open-air smokehouse above the Beltline. The Charleston house holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Lewis's own line, to Rough Draft Atlanta: 'I think beef is better than pork.'
how: Everything is sold by weight or the link, cut to order at the counter: USDA prime brisket at $35 a pound, pulled pork $19, turkey breast $22, spare ribs $24, hot-guts sausage $8 a link and green-chile cheddar $7 — the Charleston menu as posted on September 15, 2026. Sides are creamy potato salad, tangy coleslaw, cowboy pinto beans, green chile corn pudding, collard greens, mac and cheese and fries. Beef ribs and oxtail come off the smokers too.
today: Open Tuesday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., Sunday and Monday 11 to 9, at 464 North Nassau Street, Charleston, per the restaurant's site on September 15, 2026. Greenville (214 Rutherford Street) and Atlanta (1544 Piedmont Avenue) are open as well.
address: 464 N Nassau St, Charleston, SC, 29403
geo: 32.80872, -79.94661 (street)
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): its neighbour up the peninsula from February 2017 to May 2026, cooking the Carolina hog where Lewis cooks Texas beef.
- kin → home-team-bbq (place): the older Charleston company, from 2006, with a Greenville store in the same city as Lewis's.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): Greenville's older barbecue house; Lewis's 2022 store is the Texas newcomer.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): the one Carolina word on a Texas menu; sold by the pound beside the brisket.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word, meaning beef on this menu.

## Lexington Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/lexington-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/lexington-barbecue.json
id: lexington-barbecue
aliases: Lexington Barbecue #1 · The Honeymonk · Honey Monk's · The Monk
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1962 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The pork-shoulder pit on Smokehouse Lane in Lexington, Davidson County, that Wayne Monk opened in 1962 at 26 after working under Warner Stamey, and that he owns with his son Rick. Shoulders cook nearly half a day over oak and hickory coals under four brick chimneys whose white smoke shows from the road; the meat is served chopped or sliced with the 'dip', the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the Piedmont, and with red slaw dressed with the same. Locals call it the Honeymonk, after Monk and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2003.
story: Wayne Monk worked under Warner Stamey, the man who carried the Lexington method out of the Weaver and Swicegood stands of the 1920s, and in 1962, at 26, opened his own place with Sonny Hunneycutt. The partner left; the joined name, Honeymonk, stayed on the town's tongue, and DavidsonLocal, reporting Monk's induction into the NC Bar-B-Q Hall of Fame on March 1, 2024, tied the name to the two surnames. Wikipedia records the 1962 founding and the James Beard Foundation's America's Classic award of 2003, the same year the Skylight Inn in Ayden got one — the two North Carolinas honored together. Our State counts about a thousand customers a day. Wayne and Rick Monk own it together, and the restaurant's own page lists Rick as owner.
how: Pork shoulders cook nearly half a day over oak and hickory coals. The plate is barbecue — chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced — with red slaw, hushpuppies and fries; a tray drops the bread. The dip is thin, vinegar with ketchup, spices and sugar, and the slaw is dressed with it, which is why it is red. Onion rings and barbecue beans are on the board.
today: Open Tuesday to Saturday 10 to 9, closed Sunday and Monday, at 100 Smokehouse Lane, Lexington, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. OpenStreetMap lists Monday hours as well; the restaurant's own page is followed here.
address: 100 Smokehouse Ln, Lexington, NC, 27295
geo: 35.8341, -80.26746 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style, in the restaurant most often named as its standing example.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut, half a day over coals.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its sauce, thin and reddened with ketchup, served at the table.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): on the plate, dressed with the dip.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on the plate.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its fuel, burned to coals in the fireplaces under four brick chimneys.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): its founder, at the pit since 1962 and in the state's barbecue hall of fame since 2024.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): the man Monk trained under, which makes this pit a grandchild of the Swicegood stand.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): the Greensboro house of Monk's teacher.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): the other Lexington pit on Main Street, ice cream and all.
- kin → cooks-barbecue (place): the small brick-pit house south of town, closed since 2022.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the eastern pit that received the same James Beard America's Classic award in 2003.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the October street festival uptown that shares its name and cooks its style.
- not to be confused with lexington-barbecue-festival: The restaurant is a pit on Smokehouse Lane open six days a week; the festival is a one-day October street fair uptown, held since 1984, with many restaurants cooking.
- not to be confused with lexington: Lower-case, 'Lexington barbecue' is the style — shoulders, dip, red slaw — cooked at some twenty places in town; capitalized, it is this one restaurant.

## Luella's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/luellas-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/luellas-bar-b-que.json
id: luellas-bar-b-que
aliases: Luella's · Luella's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=2007 · fuel=wood · styles=eastern-nc
region: The North Carolina mountains
what: An Asheville barbecue house on Merrimon Avenue with a second room at Biltmore Park, opened in 2007 by Jeff Miller and named for his grandmother and his daughter. Jeff and Ashley Miller own it. Pork butts, ribs, whole chickens, brisket and turkey come off a smoker that a 2011 account had running hickory coals around the clock; the sauce is the Coastal Plain's vinegar rather than a mountain sweet one. Macaroni and cheese is on the board because the daughter it is half named for likes it.
story: Jeff Miller opened Luella's in 2007, naming it for his grandmother and for his six-year-old daughter. The first room was in south Asheville by two 2017 accounts, and Merrimon Avenue came in 2009, mid-recession; he later bought the Merrimon property. Explore Asheville's profile of him says he owns the business with his wife Ashley Miller, and a 2017 piece has the two of them beginning a hunt for a second site in 2014; the Biltmore Park room opened in spring 2016 and the business marked ten years in 2017. The restaurant's own pages name only Jeff, as owner and pit boss, which is the asymmetry a reader should know about before deciding what the ownership line means. The fire is the other open question. The only description of it found anywhere is from Our State in August 2011, which watched the kitchen manager open the heavy doors of a smoker cycling meat over hickory coals twenty-four hours a day. Every page since — the restaurant's own, the tourism listings, the 2017 features — is silent on fuel, and none says gas or electric either. *Inference —* silence across fifteen years of copy is not a change of method; it is copy that stopped mentioning the method.
how: Pork butts, racks of ribs, whole chickens, beef brisket and turkey go through the smoker; the chopped pork comes with an eastern vinegar-based sauce, which is a Coastal Plain sauce carried into the mountains. Ribs are cut St. Louis style. The sides are the reason the daughter's name is on the sign: the macaroni and cheese is hers. Both rooms run eleven to nine, seven days.
today: Open at 501 Merrimon Avenue and at 33 Town Square Boulevard in Biltmore Park, both eleven to nine daily, per the restaurant's own pages read on September 16, 2026. No independent report from 2026 confirms trading, and nothing on this disk records how Hurricane Helene touched either room.
address: 501 Merrimon Ave, Asheville, NC, 28804
geo: 35.61528, -82.55463 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the sauce it uses — Coastal Plain vinegar, three hundred miles west of the Coastal Plain.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut behind its chopped pork: butts rather than whole hog.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce, the eastern one, carried into the mountains.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the wood a 2011 account watched cycling under the meat around the clock.
- kin → 12-bones-smokehouse (place): the other Asheville barbecue name of the same years, two miles south.

## Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/maurices-piggie-park/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/maurices-piggie-park.json
id: maurices-piggie-park
aliases: Maurice's Piggie Park · Maurice's BBQ · Maurice's Gourmet Barbeque · Piggie Park · Maurice's
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1953 · fuel=wood · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: A chain of eight barbecue restaurants around Columbia run from the original drive-in at 1600 Charleston Highway, West Columbia, where Maurice Bessinger and his brother Joe Jr. opened in 1953. Pork hams cook twenty-four hours over hickory coals at the West Columbia pits and go out daily to the 'Pit-Stop' locations; the meat is served chopped, in sandwiches and plates, with the yellow mustard sauce the company bottles as Southern Gold — sold for decades as Carolina Gold. Maurice's sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run it. The name also carries a 1968 Supreme Court case and the flag fight of 2000.
story: Joe Bessinger opened his first restaurant in Holly Hill in 1939 with a mustard sauce of his own. His son Maurice, born in Orangeburg County in 1930, came home from the Korean War in 1952 and with his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953; by 1964 there were four. That year Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry, and Matthew J. Perry filed a class action under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Bessinger answered that his religion compelled him to oppose integration. The district court held the Act reached his sandwich shop but not the drive-ins; the Fourth Circuit reversed; and in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, 390 U.S. 400 (1968), the Supreme Court held 8–0 that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. Bessinger ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974; by 1999 his was the largest barbecue business in the country, with Carolina Gold in some 3,000 groceries. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came off the State House dome, he raised it over his restaurants. Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce; he sued them for $50 million and lost at the state Supreme Court in 2007. His brothers' Charleston restaurants were reported as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'. His children took the company, took the last flags down in 2013, and sell the sauce as Southern Gold. Maurice died on February 22, 2014. On October 26, 2024 a three-alarm fire destroyed the pits, kitchen and offices beside the West Columbia restaurant; the restaurant and its sign survived, three locations reopened within a week on rented smokers, and Lloyd Bessinger said: 'we want to be positive, we want to help people.'
how: Pork hams — not whole hogs — cook twenty-four hours over hickory wood coals at the original West Columbia pits, the company says, and the barbecue is delivered daily to the other locations, the 'Pit-Stops' where customers drive in. The meat is chopped for sandwiches and plates and dressed with the family's yellow mustard sauce, whose bottled recipe lists mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar. The company sells the sauce by the bottle, the half gallon and the gift box.
today: Open: eight locations — West Columbia (Charleston Highway), Irmo, downtown Columbia on Elmwood Avenue, Devine Street, Clemson Road, O'Neil Court and two in Lexington — per the company's site on September 15, 2026. The West Columbia restaurant reopened within a week of the October 2024 fire; the pit house and offices behind it are being rebuilt.
address: 1600 Charleston Hwy, West Columbia, SC, 29169
geo: 33.97086, -81.077535 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style it made national: the Midlands mustard sauce, bottled and shipped.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): its Southern Gold, formerly Carolina Gold — the bottled mustard sauce of the 1990s supermarkets.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name it sold the sauce under until the family renamed it Southern Gold.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): its founder, 1953 to his death in 2014, and the reason the name carries a court case and a flag.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): Maurice's father, whose 1939 Holly Hill sauce is the recipe on the label.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): the Charleston brothers' house: the same sauce lineage, a separate business.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory coals under the hams, twenty-four hours, at the West Columbia pits.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): its founder stood for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and flew the Confederate flag over the restaurants from 2000 to 2013.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the other Orangeburg County mustard family; the Dukes stayed on the buffet line while the Bessingers bottled.
- kin → hites-bar-b-q (place): the other West Columbia mustard house — a two-day farm stand beside this chain.
- not to be confused with bessingers-bar-b-q: Both are Bessinger houses with Joe's mustard sauce. Maurice's is the West Columbia chain from 1953, with the court case and the flags; Bessinger's is Thomas Bessinger's Charleston house from 1960, run separately.

## McCabe's Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/mccabes-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/mccabes-bar-b-q.json
id: mccabes-bar-b-q
aliases: McCabe's Bar-B-Que · McCabe's BBQ · McCabe's
facets: state=SC · status=open · fuel=wood · styles=sc-pee-dee
region: The Pee Dee, South Carolina
what: A family buffet house on North Brooks Street in Manning, Clarendon County, where the McCabes cook whole hogs, shoulders and hams together for ten to twelve hours over wood coals, on pits David McCabe built in a screened room off the back porch. The pulled meat is mixed and dressed with a vinegar-and-pepper sauce, slightly sweet with a little heat — the Pee Dee's sauce, not the Midlands' mustard — and set out with hash and rice, perloo, fried chicken and a table of vegetables. Open Friday and Saturday middays, cash only, closed for January. Southern Living has listed it among the South's top fifty barbecue houses.
story: Two sons of Jessie McCabe opened the restaurant some thirty years before Gwen Fowler wrote it up for the state tourism office, and almost everyone working in the small place was a McCabe. Mrs. McCabe, ninety at the time, still cooked the sides — rice and hash, perlo, green beans, turnip greens, cabbage, sweet potatoes, peas, coleslaw, hushpuppies — and her fried chicken went faster than it could be fried. The pork cooked on pits in a screened room in the back, and there was one sauce, vinegar and pepper, slightly sweet. Garden & Gun wrote the place up in its June/July 2010 issue; the South Carolina Barbeque Association put it on its 100-Mile list, the houses worth a hundred-mile drive; Southern Living named it among the South's top fifty. David McCabe, who runs it now, cooks whole hog, shoulders and hams together for ten to twelve hours on pits he built himself over coals he makes himself, and keeps the sauce as 'the big secret': 'vinegar-based with salt, pepper, and ketchup... and our secret ingredient.'
how: Whole hogs, shoulders and hams share the pits for ten to twelve hours; the meat is picked and mixed, then dressed with the vinegar-pepper sauce — vinegar, salt, pepper, ketchup and the secret. The buffet: hash and rice, perloo (rice cooked with chicken, the Pee Dee's chicken bog under its other name), fried chicken, green beans, greens, cabbage, sweet potatoes, peas, okra, tomatoes, butter beans, coleslaw and hushpuppies. Cash only.
today: Open Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., closed the month of January; the state tourism office's older listing gave Thursday to Saturday. 480 North Brooks Street, Manning. Cash only. Checked September 15, 2026 against Destination BBQ's page, which carries a March 2026 menu.
address: 480 N Brooks St, Manning, SC, 29102
geo: 33.7050719, -80.2090309 (street)
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): its style: whole hog and vinegar-pepper, at the Pee Dee's inland edge.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce — vinegar, salt, pepper and a little ketchup — the Pee Dee's, not the mustard of the Midlands an hour west.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the neighbouring style: Manning's sauce is vinegar, the Midlands' is mustard.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): whole hogs on the pit with shoulders and hams, all mixed in the pull.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): on the buffet, with Mrs. McCabe's rice.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): its perloo is the Pee Dee's chicken-and-rice, the same dish under the coast's other name.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on the buffet.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): the Kingstree buffet forty minutes east, the same whole-hog-and-vegetables form.

## Melton's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/meltons-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/meltons-barbecue.json
id: meltons-barbecue
aliases: Bob Melton's · Bob Melton's Barbecue · Melton's
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1924 · fuel=mixed · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: The Rocky Mount whole-hog house that Wikipedia records as North Carolina's first sit-down barbecue restaurant. Bob Melton, a horse trader, cooked hogs for friends in an open pit by the Tar River, sold meat by the pound, and in 1924 (some accounts say 1922) opened a shed of a restaurant that grew room by room. It served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue out by bus to parties across the state. Floods from Hurricanes Fran and Floyd drove it out of the river bottom, and it closed in 2005.
story: Robert Benjamin Melton traded horses in Rocky Mount and cooked whole hogs on the banks of the Tar River for his friends; by 1922 he was selling barbecue there, and in 1924 he built the shed that Wikipedia and UNC's North Carolina Miscellany call the state's first indoor, sit-down barbecue restaurant. In 1929 a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents and a sandwich 15. Food writer Beth Tartan recorded that a Raleigh hostess with company coming would call and say 'Ride me a party,' and Melton's would put barbecue and fixings on the bus. Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue in 1958, the year he died; his partners W.B. Melton, T.O. Fulghum and Add Smith carried on. By the time John Egerton visited for Southern Food (1993) the pits had gone from charcoal to gas with wood chips, a change he judged for the worse. The low ground flooded: after Hurricane Fran the restaurant reopened in ten days and customers came by boat for a stretch, and a plaque later marked the high-water line. Hurricane Floyd in 1999, the 75th-anniversary year, put water over the ceiling and silt through the building. The restaurant moved to a strip mall, could not make the numbers in a shrinking local economy, and closed in 2005.
how: Small hogs of 80 to 90 pounds, cooked whole over charcoal in the early decades and over gas with wood chips by the 1990s, chopped fine — 'the consistency of chopped peanut butter,' a 1988 Boating writer said — and seasoned with a vinegar sauce. The sides were boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, the plate of the Coastal Plain.
today: Closed since 2005. The original site was in the Tar River bottom at Rocky Mount; the map point marks the town, not the building.
address: Rocky Mount, NC
geo: 35.9423833, -77.7956949 (town)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style's first restaurant, which put the vinegar-sauced whole hog on a menu in 1924.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, small hogs of 80 to 90 pounds chopped fine.
- kin → bob-melton (person): its founder, the horse trader Life magazine crowned in 1958.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): on the 45-cent plate of 1929 and on every plate after.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): a side here, as at the other eastern houses of its generation.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): served with corn sticks, both breads on one table.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the switch it made from charcoal to gas and wood chips, which Egerton noted in 1993.
sources: s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-ncm-bob-melton — bob melton — North Carolina Miscellany (UNC Libraries), post of 5 Jun 2023; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-16

## Melvin's Legendary Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/melvins-legendary-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/melvins-legendary-bar-b-que.json
id: melvins-legendary-bar-b-que
aliases: Melvin's · Melvin's BBQ · Melvin's Legendary Barbecue
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1982 · fuel=wood · styles=sc-mustard
region: The Lowcountry
what: A Charleston mustard-sauce house with rooms on Folly Road on James Island and on Houston Northcutt Boulevard in Mount Pleasant, opened in 1982 by Melvin Bessinger with his son David after Melvin left the partnership with his brother Thomas at Bessinger's. David Bessinger runs it now, and the thing that distinguishes it is a reversal: in 2015 he took out the gas-assisted pits and went back to cooking over wood alone. Pork shoulders go twenty-four hours at about two hundred degrees over smouldering hickory.
story: The line starts at the Holly Hill Cafe, where Joseph Bessinger — Big Joe — was cooking in 1939, and it runs out through his sons into four or five Lowcountry and Midlands businesses that share a mustard sauce and not much else. Melvin left the partnership with his brother Thomas at Bessinger's on Savannah Highway and opened his own on Houston Northcutt Boulevard in 1982, with James Island following in 1984. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded David Bessinger on June 26, 2012, and he put the family plainly: as far as why they all got into the restaurant business, he thought it trickled down from one generation to another — it was in the blood. The turn came in 2015. Southern Living reported on October 1 of that year that David had made a weighty decision, installed new pits and gone back to the family's wood-cooking roots; the company's own history says he discontinued the gas-assisted pits and brought back smoking over all wood. *Inference —* that is a rare direction of travel. Most of the Carolinas' movement over seventy years has run from wood to gas, one pit at a time, and it is nearly always one-way. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified both houses afterwards.
how: Pork shoulders, not whole hogs, cook about twenty-four hours at two hundred degrees in metal boxes the size of a pair of refrigerators, over smouldering wet hickory logs. Since 2015 the fire is wood alone; before that the pits were gas-assisted. The sauce is the Midlands mustard, which the Alliance's oral history records the Bessinger and Sweatman families as having worked out between them. Hash is not on the menu in any source read.
today: Open Monday to Saturday, 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m., closed Sunday, at 538 Folly Road on James Island and at 925 Houston Northcutt Boulevard, Mount Pleasant. The map point here is the James Island house.
address: 538 Folly Rd, Charleston, SC, 29412
geo: 32.75317, -79.97224 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the sauce family it belongs to, carried from Holly Hill down to the coast.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): its sauce, which the oral history credits to the Bessinger and Sweatman families together.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut — shoulders, twenty-four hours over hickory, not whole hog.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): the grandfather at the Holly Hill Cafe in 1939, where the family's barbecue starts.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): his brother Thomas's Charleston house, the partnership Melvin left in 1982.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the Columbia branch of the same family, from the same Holly Hill kitchen.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): the Holly Hill family the oral history names as co-authors of the mustard sauce.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): what it took out in 2015, going back to wood alone — the reverse of the usual direction.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): certified both houses after the return to wood.
- not to be confused with bessingers-bar-b-q: Brothers, two businesses, one highway apart. Bessinger's is Thomas Bessinger's, on Savannah Highway in West Ashley, run by his sons Tommy and Michael. Melvin's is Thomas's brother Melvin's, on Folly Road and in Mount Pleasant, run by David. Melvin left the shared partnership in 1982.
- not to be confused with maurices-piggie-park: Same grandfather, different branch and different state of mind. Maurice's is Maurice Bessinger's Columbia chain, whose name also carries a 1968 Supreme Court case and the flag fight of 2000. Melvin's is his brother Melvin's Charleston business, which has no part in that history.
sources: s:web-melvins-story — Our Story — Melvin's BBQ; s:web-sfa-melvins-legendary-bar-b-q — Melvin's Legendary Bar-B-Q — David Bessinger, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 26, 2012; s:web-melvins-press — Press — Melvin's BBQ; s:web-truecue-sc — True 'Cue SC — certified pits; s:sfa-oral-histories — Southern Foodways Alliance oral history collection — barbecue projects (North Carolina, South Carolina); s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Midway BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/midway-bbq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/midway-bbq.json
id: midway-bbq
aliases: Midway Barbecue · Midway
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1941 · fuel=wood · styles=
region: The Upstate, South Carolina
what: A hash house and meat market on Main Street in Buffalo, a mill village in Union County in the Upstate, in business since about 1941 and the last of the nearly fifty hash houses the county once had. Hash here is the Upstate's kind: beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper cooked down slowly in three hundred-gallon pots, sold over rice and by the quart, and it outsells the barbecue three or four to one. The barbecue is hickory-smoked shoulder and ham, chopped; a creamy, spicy chicken stew goes out by the hundred gallons a day; and the front of the building is a butcher's counter with sawdust on the floor.
story: Jack O'Dell opened Midway some time around 1941 — 'the date is sketchy', the family says. Union County was hash-eating country and O'Dell's was one of nearly fifty hash houses; the others closed and Midway stayed. His daughter Amy Allen owns it; her husband Jay Allen has managed it since 1994, and it was Jay whom Rien Fertel recorded for the Southern Foodways Alliance on June 12, 2012, at what the interview page lists as 811 Hash Boulevard. Jay's arithmetic: catering, three parts hash to one of barbecue; in the store, four to one. 'Without hash, we're done. We're closed.' The slogan calls Buffalo the hash and chicken stew capital of the world.
how: Hash: beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper, slow-cooked in three 100-gallon pots into a thick stew and ladled over white rice — no pork, no mustard, the Upstate's version. Chicken stew, creamy and spicy, a hundred gallons a day. Barbecue: shoulder and ham smoked over hickory, chopped or pulled, and chopped barbecue chicken. A full-service meat counter sells across the front of the store.
today: Open Tuesday to Friday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday 10 to 4, closed Sunday and Monday, per the company's site on September 15, 2026. 811 Main Street, Buffalo, Union County.
address: 811 Main St, Buffalo, SC, 29321
geo: 34.72383, -81.65961 (street)
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the reason the place exists: beef hash, the Upstate's kind, three or four to one against the barbecue.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): shoulder and ham, hickory-smoked and chopped, are the barbecue.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory, for the shoulders and hams.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): the Carolinas' other stew; Midway cooks a chicken stew of its own by the hundred gallons.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): chopped barbecue chicken is on the daily menu.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): the Upstate's other old name, forty miles west in Greenville, where the hash is pork.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Jay Allen here in June 2012.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed Jay Allen here on June 12, 2012.

## Morris Barbeque (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/morris-barbeque/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/morris-barbeque.json
id: morris-barbeque
aliases: Morris Barbecue · Morris BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=unknown · founded=1956 · fuel=gas · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A Saturday-only whole-hog house on Morris BBQ Road outside Hookerton, in Greene County, in business since 1956; the county named the road for it. William Morris Jr., grandson of the founder Willie McKinley Morris, cooks the hogs, chops the meat and works the counter. The pig goes on a gas machine built in Wilson in the early 1970s, its burners set off to one side rather than under the meat. Doors open at eight for take-out and half past nine for the dining room, and the barbecue is usually gone by one.
story: Willie McKinley Morris — Pop — peddled barbecue through Hookerton from a cart as early as 1931, in what the family's history page calls the Hoover days; that page says a mule, the Southern Foodways Alliance transcript says a horse and buggy. A country store came first, the kind of place for a Coca-Cola and a pack of Nabs, and the barbecue business dates itself from 1956. Frances Morris, called Nannie, died in 1974. Pop died in 1991 and left the business to his grandson William Morris Jr., born in March 1956, the year it opened. Rien Fertel recorded Morris for the Alliance on November 26, 2011, and Morris described the cooker himself: gas, built in Wilson by a company no longer in business, bought around the early seventies, the burners offset from the hog. His own history page does not say that. It describes his grandfather's pit of charcoal, corncobs and oak wood and then says the tradition continues with very little change. On July 10, 2026 a storm dropped a large tree on the back of the building. The pit was undamaged. Repairs pushed past a Labor Day reopening, and no date had been set when WCTI reported on September 2, 2026 — the first run of consecutive missed Saturdays in some seventy years.
how: Whole hogs — hams and shoulders chopped together — cook about six and a half hours, and the chop is judged by a committee of six, with Morris's daughter Ashley Morris Godley taking the final say. Orders go up on a board: telephone ahead and the name is written down, first come first served, and paying in advance holds the tray. Skins, ribs and bone trays have to be ordered ahead; the skins are the first thing gone each week.
today: Closed since the storm of July 10, 2026, with no reopening date in the reports read through September 2, 2026. The restaurant's own site still advertises its usual Saturday hours, which is stale copy rather than news. 891 Morris BBQ Road, Hookerton. Check before driving.
address: 891 Morris BBQ Rd, Hookerton, NC, 28538
geo: 35.41813, -77.57354 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style of its plate: whole hog chopped, vinegar and pepper, in the Coastal Plain.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut — hams and shoulders from the same pig, chopped together.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the cooker its owner describes: a one-off gas machine out of Wilson with the burners offset from the meat.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the first thing it sells out of every Saturday; they have to be ordered ahead.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded William Morris Jr. here on November 26, 2011 for its North Carolina barbecue project.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): the interviewer who took the oral history in 2011, and to whom Morris described the gas cooker.
sources: s:sfa-morris-barbeque — Morris Barbeque — William Morris Jr., interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, November 26, 2011; s:web-morris-barbeque — Morris Barbeque — history; s:web-witn-morris-storm-2026 — Storm damages Morris BBQ in Hookerton, forcing rare Saturday closure; s:web-wcti-morris-repairs-2026 — Storm damage repairs and added improvements push back Morris Barbeque return; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Parker's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/parkers-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/parkers-barbecue.json
id: parkers-barbecue
aliases: The Original Parker's Barbecue · Parker's · Parker's BBQ of Wilson
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1946 · fuel=gas · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A large eastern barbecue house on U.S. 301 south of Wilson, opened in August 1946 by brothers Graham and Ralph Parker and their cousin Henry Parker Brewer, and owned since 1987 by Donald Williams, who started there in 1963, with partners Eric Lippard and Kevin Lamm. It cooks about 150 whole hogs and fries about 8,000 chickens a week for some 20,000 customers, on gas cookers the founders installed in the 1950s. The barbecue is chopped fine and dressed with vinegar and red pepper; young staff in white paper caps seat the room; cash or check only.
story: The restaurant opened in August 1946 just off Highway 301 as a family destination for pit-cooked barbecue and fried chicken, the owners' history says. The day that set it on its feet came in 1954, when the Ralston Purina plant opened in Wilson and Parker's served 17,000 plates at 75 cents each in four hours. In the 1950s the cookers went from wood coals to gas, for a temperature that could be regulated. Donald Williams came to work in 1963 and bought the business when Graham and Ralph Parker retired in 1987. June Brunson worked there more than 62 years, until her death in 2020; Richard Ward, who came on opening day, was still a customer at 100 in 2013. Ralph Parker, the last of the founders, died on July 4, 2013 at 89. Williams and Kevin Lamm gave the Southern Foodways Alliance an oral history in November 2011, in which Lamm said the owners knew they were consistent because customers told them the place had not changed across decades. Three or four employees have been there more than forty years. On Mother's Day the kitchen uses 45 pigs and 26 chicken fryers.
how: Hogs are dressed and cooked whole in a cinder-block building behind the restaurant, on gas cookers, and the meat is chopped fine and seasoned with a vinegar-and-red-pepper sauce. Barbecue is served from nine in the morning. Plates come with hushpuppies and slaw, and the menu runs to fried chicken, fish, string beans and, in season, oysters battered or stewed. Waiters in white caps seat and serve; the owners greet at the door.
today: Open seven days, 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. for dine-in and to 7:30 for take-out, at 2514 U.S. Highway 301 South, Wilson, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. Cash or check; an ATM is on site. A separate Parker's operates in Greenville; the relationship is not documented here.
address: 2514 US Highway 301 S, Wilson, NC, 27893
geo: 35.6974271, -77.9369771 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style at industrial scale: 150 whole hogs a week, chopped fine, vinegar and red pepper.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, though the pits are gas; Parker's shows the two are not the same question.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): its cookers since the 1950s, chosen because the temperature could be held.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on every plate with the slaw.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): Wilson's other barbecue name, a whole-hog cook who sold from his family's grocery in the same town.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded the owners' oral history in 2011.

## Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/red-bridges-barbecue-lodge/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/red-bridges-barbecue-lodge.json
id: red-bridges-barbecue-lodge
aliases: Bridges Barbecue Lodge · Bridges BBQ Lodge · Red Bridges
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1946 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The Shelby, Cleveland County, pork-shoulder house of the Bridges family, begun in 1946 by Red Bridges, an Army cook home from the war, and his wife Lyttle, and run by their daughter Debbie Bridges-Webb with her children Natalie Ramsey, who runs the front, and Chase Webb, who tends the pits overnight. Shoulders cook seven to eight hours a side over hickory and oak — no gas, no electric, the family told WBTV in 2026 — and the recipes are the ones the Bridges started with. The lodge on U.S. 74, across from the Cleveland Mall, marked eighty years in June 2026.
story: Red Bridges came home from the Army, where he had cooked, and in 1946 began selling barbecue sandwiches from a livestock yard, the family told the Southern Foodways Alliance; the restaurant's own history calls that first venture Dedmond's Barbecue. In 1949 it became Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge, and the lodge building dates from 1953. Red died in 1966 and Lyttle ran the business after him — 'probably the first female barbecue entrepreneur in North Carolina,' her grandchildren said in 2011. Debbie, their daughter, owns it now; Natalie Ramsey and Chase Webb told the Alliance's Rien Fertel that nothing would change, 'because you don't find pit-cooked barbecue hardly anymore.' WBTV, marking the eightieth year in June 2026, found server Wanda Montgomery in her 44th year and the family planning to put the sauce in grocery stores.
how: Pork shoulders smoke seven to eight hours on each side over hickory and oak coals, Chase Webb at the pits through the night. The barbecue is chopped or sliced and dressed with the family's sauce, unchanged since 1946 by the family's account; the plate is the Piedmont plate, red slaw and hushpuppies beside the meat.
today: Open Wednesday to Sunday at 2000 East Dixon Boulevard (U.S. 74), Shelby, across from the Cleveland Mall, per WBTV in June 2026.
address: 2000 E Dixon Blvd, Shelby, NC, 28152
geo: 35.265807, -81.480884 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style at its western edge, in Shelby, where the dip runs a little sweeter than in Lexington.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut, seven to eight hours a side.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its fuel; the family says no gas and no electric.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): on the plate.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): on the plate.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): took the Lexington method to Shelby in the 1930s, the decade before the Bridges began.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded the third generation in 2011.

## Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq.json
id: rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq
aliases: Rodney Scott's BBQ · Rodney Scott's
facets: state=SC · status=closed · founded=2017 · fuel=charcoal · styles=sc-pee-dee
region: The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: A whole-hog restaurant at 1011 King Street on the Charleston peninsula, opened in February 2017 by Rodney Scott of Hemingway and the restaurateur Nick Pihakis in a former fried-chicken house, with seats for about 128, a drive-through and delivery. It cooked whole hogs over hardwood coals and served the pulled pork with a hot vinegar sauce beside spare ribs, fried catfish, a rib-eye sandwich and banana pudding. Sister restaurants followed in Birmingham in 2019 and in Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021. Every location closed in May 2026 amid lawsuits and liens against Pihakis's restaurant group, and the King Street doors have stayed shut since.
story: Rodney Scott was born in Philadelphia in 1971 and raised at his parents' store and pits in Hemingway, where he cooked his first hog at eleven. A customer, Nick Pihakis of the Jim 'N Nick's chain, told him he was undercharging; after the Hemingway cookhouse burned in November 2013 it was Pihakis's Fatback Collective that staged the Bar-B-Que in Exile dinners to rebuild it. The two opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in February 2017 in the old Chick's Fry House on upper King Street. In May 2018 the James Beard Foundation gave Scott its chef award for the Southeast, the second pitmaster to win one; the Chef's Table: BBQ episode about him in 2020 set sales records three days running, with hour-long lines; Food & Wine put the restaurant among the forty most important of the past forty years. Birmingham opened in 2019, Atlanta and a fourth Alabama site in 2021, and a cookbook with Lolis Eric Elie came out the same year. On May 3, 2026 the King Street restaurant closed at 5 p.m. 'until further notice', in general manager Sam Ayala's words, days after a meat supplier sued Pihakis Restaurant Group for $394,238.74 and a landlord filed more than $12 million in liens; every Rodney Scott's closed with it. In June Scott cooked a pop-up at Munkle Brewing under the name Pitmaster Scott and said reopening in Charleston was his first priority.
how: Whole hogs cooked over hardwood charcoal, pulled, and seasoned with a spice rub that includes MSG — Scott calls it a 'flavor maker' — and a hot vinegar sauce. Past the hog: spare ribs, fried catfish, a rib-eye steak sandwich, banana pudding. The room seated about 128, with a drive-through window and delivery.
today: Closed. The King Street restaurant shut at 5 p.m. on May 3, 2026 'until further notice' and had not reopened when this record was written on September 15, 2026; the Birmingham, Atlanta and other Alabama locations closed the same week. Rodney Scott has said he means to reopen in Charleston. Address of record: 1011 King Street.
address: 1011 King St, Charleston, SC, 29403
geo: 32.80344, -79.95121 (street)
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): the Hemingway store and pits where the method and the sauce come from.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): its namesake and pitmaster, given the James Beard chef award for the Southeast in 2018.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut in the name, cooked whole over coals as at Hemingway.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce, the Pee Dee's vinegar and pepper, carried to the coast.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the style: Pee Dee whole hog in a Lowcountry city.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): on the dessert list from the opening menu.
- kin → lewis-barbecue (place): its neighbour on the peninsula, opened eight months earlier, cooking Texas beef where this house cooked the Carolina hog.
- kin → home-team-bbq (place): the older Charleston barbecue company, from 2006.
- kin → pitmaster (term): the word Rodney Scott chose for his pop-up name in 2026: Pitmaster Scott.
- not to be confused with scotts-bar-b-que: Scott's Bar-B-Que is the family store in Hemingway, open, run by Rodney's uncle and son. Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ was the King Street restaurant in Charleston, 2017 to May 2026.

## Sam Jones BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/sam-jones-bbq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/sam-jones-bbq.json
id: sam-jones-bbq
aliases: Sam Jones Barbecue · Sam Jones BBQ Winterville · Sam Jones BBQ Raleigh
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=2015 · fuel=wood · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A whole-hog restaurant in Winterville, Pitt County, opened on November 10, 2015 by Sam Jones, grandson of the Skylight Inn's founder Pete Jones, with his partner Michael Letchworth, and a second house in downtown Raleigh since February 2021. Whole hogs are smoked on site over wood, chopped and served daily; the menu runs longer than the Skylight's, with ribs, smoked chicken and turkey, cornbread, slaw and collards, banana pudding, and in Raleigh a full bar. Winterville is seven miles from the Skylight Inn in Ayden; Raleigh is the family's first restaurant outside Pitt County.
story: Sam Jones grew up in the Skylight Inn, which his grandfather Pete Jones opened in Ayden in 1947; he left the family business as a teenager and came back, telling the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that returning was like a flag-bearer keeping the standard up on the field. In 2014 he and Michael Letchworth, who had worked at the Skylight since 2004, signed for a loan and began building in Winterville; Sam Jones BBQ opened on November 10, 2015. The restaurant's own history counts Southern Living's 2012 list of ten Southern pitmasters among its credentials. In 2019 Jones and Daniel Vaughn published Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue, which writes the family method down. The Raleigh restaurant at 502 West Lenoir Street opened softly in February 2021 in a building that had been Dusty's Garage, keeping the old floor and hanging family photographs; it seats about 140 inside and out, with a private room upstairs and a bar. INDY Week reported in May 2021 that three hogs a day went on at about one in the afternoon, cooked at 250 degrees until ten, were held overnight, and had their skin crisped the next morning.
how: Whole hogs of about 180 pounds cook some sixteen hours in wood-fired pits; the meat is chopped with the crisp skin through it and dressed in the eastern way, with vinegar, salt and pepper. A tray — the eastern plate, barbecue with slaw and bread and no plate under it — comes with cornbread. Beyond the hog there are ribs, smoked turkey and chicken, collards, a sweet slaw and banana pudding, and in Raleigh a bourbon old-fashioned infused with pig fat and named Jay the Butcher.
today: Open, both houses. Winterville: 715 West Fire Tower Road, Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, Sunday 11 to 8:30. Raleigh: 502 West Lenoir Street, the same hours. Hours as posted on the restaurant's site in September 2026.
address: 715 W Fire Tower Rd, Winterville, NC, 28590
geo: 35.5476993, -77.4021514 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it cooks, whole hog over wood with a vinegar dressing, carried from Ayden to Raleigh.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut: hogs of about 180 pounds, sixteen hours in the pit, skin chopped into the meat.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the family pit it grew out of, seven miles away in Ayden, where Sam Jones and Michael Letchworth both worked.
- kin → sam-jones (person): its founder, who wrote the family method down in 2019.
- kin → pete-jones (person): the grandfather whose 1947 pit is the reason this one exists.
- kin → cornbread (dish): on the tray here as at the Skylight.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): the other Pitt County whole-hog pit, on the far side of Greenville, cash only and closed when sold out.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): the other Ayden pit, run by the Dennis family the Joneses count as their own root.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Sam Jones's oral history in 2011, before he had a restaurant of his own.
