## Scott's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/scotts-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/scotts-bar-b-que.json
id: scotts-bar-b-que
aliases: Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q · Scott's Variety Store · Scott's BBQ · Scott's of Hemingway
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1972 · fuel=wood · styles=sc-pee-dee
region: The Pee Dee, South Carolina
what: A whole-hog pit behind a country store on the Hemingway Highway in Williamsburg County, in the Pee Dee. Roosevelt and Ella Scott opened the store in 1972 and the barbecue began as a weekend sideline; it grew into the business, and into the pit where their son Rodney Scott learned the trade before he opened his own restaurant in Charleston in 2017. Whole hogs cook eight to twelve hours over coals burned down from hickory, oak and pecan, and the meat is pulled and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar and pepper. It sells by the plate and the sandwich, cash only, four days a week.
story: Roosevelt and Ella Scott came from Philadelphia to the Pee Dee in 1972 with their infant son, farmed tobacco and raised hogs near Nesmith, and opened a variety store and gas station on the Hemingway highway. Ella and the family smoked a hog on weekends; demand climbed from one or two a week to four or six, and Rodney cooked his first pig at eleven and joined full time at seventeen. John T. Edge profiled the store in 2009, and when Rien Fertel recorded Rodney for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 the pits were turning eight to ten hogs a night. On November 27, 2013, at 4 a.m., a pit flared while two employees roasted fourteen pigs in the wooden cookhouse beside the store; the cookhouse burned, no one was hurt, and the store kept cooking on other pits. Rodney answered with the Bar-B-Que in Exile Tour: fundraising dinners in Birmingham, Charleston and elsewhere, staged with the Fatback Collective — the chefs and restaurateurs around Nick Pihakis of Jim 'N Nick's — to raise $100,000 and rebuild in metal, so the pits could be insured. Rodney had taken the business over in 2011; in 2017 he left to open Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Pihakis. Roosevelt Scott died on December 10, 2020. Ella Scott died in 2023, the store closed for five months, and in May 2024 her brother Sam Wilson and Rodney's son Dominic Scott reopened it.
how: Hogs are split and cooked eight to twelve hours at around 250 degrees over coals of hickory, oak and pecan, shoveled under the meat through the night; *Tradition holds —* the coals come from a burn barrel, a steel drum in which the logs burn down. The cooked meat is pulled from the bones and seasoned with the family's sauce, which Rodney Scott gives as 'vinegar, pepper, some more pepper, some love'. Orders are a whole-hog plate or a sandwich; the SCETV crew in 2021 filmed the same wood-burning pit and the same counter. The rebuilt pit house is metal.
today: Open at 2734 Hemingway Highway, Hemingway. Destination BBQ lists Wednesday to Saturday from 9:30 a.m., closing between 5 and 7 p.m., cash only. Run since May 2024 by Sam Wilson and Dominic Scott. Checked September 15, 2026 against the sources named; check before driving.
address: 2734 Hemingway Hwy, Hemingway, SC, 29554
geo: 33.7433, -79.47498 (street)
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the style it stands for: whole hog over wood coals, vinegar and pepper, in the Pee Dee.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut — the entire pig, split, cooked through the night and pulled.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): its sauce: vinegar, black and red pepper, nothing thicker.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): its wood — hickory, oak and pecan — burned to coals for the pit.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): the son who cooked his first hog here at eleven, ran the business from 2011 and left in 2017 for Charleston.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): the Charleston restaurant Rodney opened in 2017 with the same hogs and the same sauce.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Rodney Scott here in June 2012 for its South Carolina barbecue project.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed Rodney Scott here in June 2012.
- kin → browns-bar-b-que (place): the Kingstree buffet house twenty miles west; the two are Williamsburg County's whole-hog names.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): Hemingway's spring Bar-B-Q Shag Festival is the town's version: a cookoff of pork barbecue and the state dance.
- not to be confused with scotts-famous-barbecue: Two Scott's, two states. Adam Scott's is Goldsboro, North Carolina, from 1917, with a bottled sauce; this Scott's is Roosevelt and Ella Scott's Hemingway store from 1972, whole hog behind the counter. The two histories in this project's sources never meet.
- not to be confused with rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq: Rodney Scott's is the Charleston restaurant opened in 2017 and closed since May 2026; Scott's Bar-B-Que is the family store in Hemingway where he learned, now run by his uncle and his son.
sources: s:wp-scotts-variety-store-and-bar-b-q — Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q — Wikipedia; s:wp-rodney-scott-pitmaster — Rodney Scott (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:web-sfa-scotts-bar-b-que — Scott's Bar-B-Que — Rodney Scott, interviewed by Rien Fertel, June 21, 2012; s:sfa-oral-histories — Southern Foodways Alliance oral history collection — barbecue projects (North Carolina, South Carolina); s:web-live5-scotts-fire-2013 — Scott's BBQ damaged in early morning fire (November 27, 2013); s:web-npr-pit-burned-down-2014 — When His Pit Burned Down, Southern BBQ Master Took Hogs On Tour — Debbie Elliott, The Salt, February 4, 2014; s:web-carolina-trust-roosevelt-scott-2020 — In Memory of Roosevelt Scott (December 17, 2020); s:web-scetv-scotts-backroad-bites-2021 — Scott's Bar-B-Que — Backroad Bites (August 31, 2021); s:web-destination-bbq-scotts — The Scott's Bar-B-Que in Hemingway, SC; s:wp-hemingway-south-carolina — Hemingway, South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina; s:web-truecue-sc — True 'Cue SC — certified pits

## Scott's Famous Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/scotts-famous-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/scotts-famous-barbecue.json
id: scotts-famous-barbecue
aliases: Scott's Barbecue · Scott's Cafe · Adam Scott's · Scott's Sauce Company
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1917 · fuel=unknown · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: The Goldsboro barbecue of the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black cook and preacher who catered barbecues from the 1910s, sold from the back door of his house on Brazil Street from the early 1930s, and whose son A. Martel Scott patented the family's vinegar sauce as Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946. The company dates the sauce to 1917 and sells about a million bottles a year. The restaurants — three around Goldsboro by 1950 — are closed: after a first closure in 2001 the family ran on Thursday and Friday lunches for a while, then stopped to make sauce.
story: Adam Scott was born in 1890 and took his first cooking job in 1911 at the Elberon Hotel in Atlantic City; back in Goldsboro he catered barbecues from about the mid-1910s, and between 1931 and 1933 opened a back-door restaurant at his home on Brazil Street — two hogs a week on Saturdays at first, later four to seven a day, with an enclosed porch for a dining room. His first customers were mostly white. In 1933 he cooked barbecue for Franklin Roosevelt in the White House Rose Garden. He said the final recipe for the sauce came to him in a vision. In the 1940s he moved to Winston-Salem to cook for R.J. Reynolds, and his son Alvin Martel Scott, born 1913, patented Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946 and put it in stores. By 1950 there were three Scott's around Goldsboro — Martel's on the Mount Olive highway, Ed Scott's on the Wilson highway, Adam's on the Raleigh road — and the Green Book, the travel guide for Black motorists, listed a Scott's at 404 Gulley Street from 1950 to 1955. Martel ran the business until his death in 1992; his wife Ann chaired the company until hers in 2009. Adam Scott died in 1983 at 93. The restaurant closed in 2001, reopened on Thursday and Friday lunches when customers kept calling, then closed for good; the Scotts' children and grandchildren make the sauce. The National Barbecue Hall of Fame inducted Adam Scott in 2022.
how: Hogs cooked at the house, two a week and then several a day, chopped and dressed with the vinegar sauce; the later restaurants served chopped pork with hushpuppies and fried chicken. What survives is the sauce: vinegar, salt and spices, no tomato, fat-free and sugar-free, sold in grocery stores across the east and by the case online.
today: Closed. The Scott family's sauce company continues in Goldsboro; the restaurant's last address is not confirmed on this disk, so the map point marks the town.
address: Goldsboro, NC
geo: 35.3848841, -77.9927651 (town)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose sauce it put in a bottle before anyone else did.
- kin → adam-scott (person): its founder, cook, preacher and the man who cooked for Roosevelt in 1933.
- kin → scotts-barbecue-sauce (sauce): the product that outlived the restaurant; patented by Martel Scott in 1946.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the family sauce is the eastern sauce: vinegar, salt, spices, no tomato.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): Goldsboro's other barbecue name, on U.S. 70, still cooking.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): the Black-owned whole-hog pit south of Goldsboro that carries the county's tradition on.
- not to be confused with scotts-bar-b-que: That Scott's is in Hemingway, South Carolina, opened as a store and gas station by Roosevelt and Ella Scott in 1972 and known for whole hog; this one is Adam Scott's in Goldsboro, a generation older, and closed. No relation is recorded.
- not to be confused with rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq: Rodney Scott is the Hemingway family's pitmaster, with restaurants since 2017 starting in Charleston; the Goldsboro Scotts bottle a sauce and no longer cook.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/scotts-famous-barbecue/scotts-famous-barbecue-adam-scotts-place-goldsboro-1944.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · Bill Sharpe; State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/47848599202/
sources: s:web-aahc-scotts-cafe — Scott's Cafe — The Green Book in North Carolina (essay by Brandie K. Ragghianti, 2022); s:web-cecelski-adam-scott — Remembering a Barbecue Legend: The Rev. Adam Scott of Goldsboro, N.C. — David Cecelski (21 Nov 2025); s:web-scottsbarbecuesauce — Scott's Barbecue Sauce — official site; s:web-ncarts-goldsboro — Let's Eat: Goldsboro — African American Music Trails; s:wp-scotts-variety-store-and-bar-b-q — Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q — Wikipedia; s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-condev — Department of Conservation and Development, Travel Information Division Photograph Collection

## Shealy's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/shealys-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/shealys-bar-b-que.json
id: shealys-bar-b-que
aliases: Shealy's Bar-B-Que House · Shealy's BBQ · Shealy's
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1969 · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: A buffet house on East Columbia Avenue in Batesburg-Leesville, Lexington County, opened in June 1969 by Victor and Sara Shealy with their teenage children Tommy and Nancy, and family-run since. It is the barbecue buffet in its fullest form: pork shoulders smoked by the thousand each week and served chopped with mustard sauce — vinegar and tomato sauces alongside — hash over rice, fried chicken, ribs, country-fried steak and more than forty home-cooked sides, with a salad bar and a dessert bar, all you can eat. The South Carolina House marked its fiftieth anniversary with a resolution in 2019.
story: Victor and Sara Shealy barbecued whole hogs in their back yard on weekends in the early 1950s, and word of Victor's sauce spread until they were cooking four or five hogs a week. They quit their jobs, borrowed about $20,000 to buy a building, and in June 1969 opened Shealy's Bar-B-Que House with Tommy and Nancy, then teenagers, working beside them. *Tradition holds —* Sara put the food on a buffet from the first year, and the family counts it among the first barbecue buffets in the state. On April 30, 2019 the South Carolina House of Representatives adopted a resolution for the fiftieth anniversary, naming the 'all-you-can-eat buffet' of 'renowned barbeque and over forty home-cooked sides'. The house stands at the western edge of the Midlands mustard belt; *Inference —* by the map, a quarter mile across the railroad from where Jackie Hite's cooked whole hogs until 2018.
how: Everything is on the line: chopped pork and ribs with a choice of mustard, vinegar or tomato sauce; hash — the thick pork gravy of the Midlands — over white rice; fried chicken by the heap, and off the menu the pulley bone, the wishbone piece; country-fried steak with milk gravy, lima beans, creamed corn, collards, mac and cheese, green and butter beans, mashed potatoes, a salad bar and a dessert bar. A 2015 review put the buffet under $15 a head with a drink. Carry-out plates go from 10 a.m.
today: Open Monday, Tuesday and Thursday to Saturday, buffet 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., carry-out 10 to 8:30; closed Wednesday and Sunday. 340 East Columbia Avenue, Batesburg-Leesville — OpenStreetMap records the building at number 240. Checked September 15, 2026.
address: 340 E Columbia Ave, Batesburg-Leesville, SC, 29070
geo: 33.91475, -81.51528 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): its style, at the western edge of the mustard belt; vinegar and tomato sauces stand beside the mustard.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce it is known for, from Victor Shealy's back-yard recipe.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the thick pork gravy over white rice on its line.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut: shoulders by the thousand each week, smoked and chopped, not whole hogs.
- kin → jackie-hites-bar-b-q (place): the town's other barbecue house, across the tracks, closed in 2018.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the Orangeburg buffet lineage; Shealy's is the Lexington County answer, forty sides long.
- kin → hites-bar-b-q (place): the West Columbia stand twenty-five miles east; another Lexington County mustard house.
sources: s:web-sc-house-h4503-shealys-2019 — H. 4503, Session 123 (2019–2020): a House resolution honoring Shealy's Bar-B-Que House on its fiftieth anniversary (April 30, 2019); s:web-shealys-home — Shealy's BBQ — official site; s:web-lake-murray-country-shealys — Shealy's Bar-B-Que; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/short-sugars/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/short-sugars.json
id: short-sugars
aliases: Short Sugar's · Short Sugars BBQ · Short Sugar's Drive-In
facets: state=NC · status=closed · founded=1949 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A drive-in barbecue on South Scales Street in Reidsville, Rockingham County, opened in June 1949 by the Overby brothers and named for the one who died two days before the opening, and closed in January 2025 after 75 years. It cooked over hickory coals in two small pits visible from the counter — hams for sliced barbecue, shoulders for chopped — and dressed the meat with a thin dark sauce built on Worcestershire and sugar rather than the ketchup of the Piedmont dips, a sauce that fit neither of North Carolina's camps. Curb service ran to the end.
story: Johnny, Clyde and Eldridge Overby meant to open the Overby Brothers Drive-In in June 1949; two days before opening Eldridge was killed in a car crash, and his brothers named the place for him alone, by his nickname, Short Sugar — a small man, whether friendly or fetching Our State leaves open. In 1982 Short Sugar's won the Barbecue Bowl, the first restaurant from either Carolina to do so. The Wilson family ran it in its later decades: David Wilson, whose wife was an Overby daughter, and his son John David, who told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that a barbecue place with no pit in sight was 'an insult to those families who still do it the way it's supposed to be done.' A dining room was added about the 1980s to the 1950s drive-in. Hobbled by the pandemic closures and then by the economy, it served its last plates in mid-January 2025; a Reidsville writer who went by on January 16 found it shut, and The State You're In wrote the farewell the next day.
how: Two small hickory-coal pits behind the counter; hams for the sliced, shoulders for the chopped, cooked fresh to order rather than held. The sauce was thin and dark, sugar and Worcestershire, runny and salty-sweet, with less ketchup or tomato paste than the Piedmont dips; it went on sandwiches sliced or chopped, and the kitchen sold it by the gallon.
today: Closed since mid-January 2025. The building stands at 1328 South Scales Street, Reidsville; no successor is recorded on this disk.
address: 1328 S Scales St, Reidsville, NC, 27320
geo: 36.34422, -79.66475 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style's shoulders and its region, with a sauce that belonged to neither North Carolina camp.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): for the chopped; hams were for the sliced.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): what its sauce was not: Worcestershire and sugar in place of the ketchup.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory coals in two pits in sight of the counter.
- kin → chopped (term): chopped from shoulders, sliced from hams — the two words meant two cuts here.
- kin → kepleys-barbecue (place): the other Piedmont drive-in of the same generation, closed the same winter, February 2025.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded the Wilsons in 2011.
sources: s:web-ourstate-short-sugars — Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q — Our State; s:sfa-short-sugars-pit-bar-b-q — Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q — David Wilson and John David Wilson, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 21 Nov 2011; s:web-stateyourein-short-sugars — Short Sugars BBQ, closed after 75 years — The State You're In (17 Jan 2025); s:web-knightshift-short-sugars — Dateline: Reidsville, North Carolina: Short Sugar's is no more — The Knight Shift (16 Jan 2025); s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina; s:web-barbecuebros-nc-trail — NC Historic Barbecue Trail

## Shuler's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/shulers-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/shulers-bar-b-que.json
id: shulers-bar-b-que
aliases: Shuler's BBQ · Shuler's Barbecue
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1996 · fuel=wood · styles=
region: The Pee Dee
what: An all-you-can-eat barbecue house on Highway 38 between Latta and Sellers, in Dillon County in the Pee Dee, opened in 1996 by Norton and Lynn Hughes and named for Norton's father Shuler Hughes, who made the sauce in 1956, and for their grandson of the same name. Pork cooks over wood coals; the buffet runs to more than twenty items and includes liver hash over rice. It is open Thursday to Saturday. The Barbeque Association gives it the hundred-mile designation.
story: Shuler Hughes made the sauce in 1956. His son Norton learned the method from him and put it plainly to a visiting writer in February 2016: low and slow, and cook on wood — that was what his father taught him. Lynn Hughes traded a master's degree in education and teaching to start the restaurant with her husband in 1996, which is the sentence the business's own page uses and the reason a woman is named as an owner here rather than as a helper. The name skips a generation twice: it is the founder's father's given name and their grandson's. In 2014 the business appeared on CNBC's The Profit, and it has taken the Dillon Herald's readers' award for barbecue every year since 2008 by its own account. Payment is where the sources disagree — a visiting writer in 2016 recorded cash only and no credit cards, and Destination BBQ's page says cards and cash — so nothing is tagged here either way. A separate Shuler's Barbecue at Lake City is permanently closed and is not this business.
how: Pork cooks low and slow over wood; chicken and ribs share the pits. The buffet is all you can eat and runs past twenty items, and the liver hash — hash made with the liver in it, as the Pee Dee makes it — goes over white rice. The house phrase for the buffet is to eat until it hurts. Whole hog is not claimed by any source read; the pit is described as shoulder-based.
today: Open Thursday to Saturday, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 419 Highway 38 West, between Latta and Sellers. The map point is the town of Latta, not the building: no street-level coordinate for the highway address came back from the geocoder.
address: 419 Highway 38 W, Latta, SC, 29565
geo: 34.3371, -79.43116 (town)
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the region it cooks in, and the vinegar-leaning country north of the Midlands mustard belt.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut the sources describe; no whole hog is claimed here.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the plate beside the barbecue, made here with the liver in it.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): certified the pit as cooking on wood or charcoal alone.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): gives it the hundred-mile designation, the association's highest.

## Skylight Inn BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/skylight-inn/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/skylight-inn.json
id: skylight-inn
aliases: Skylight Inn · Pete Jones' Skylight Inn · the Skylight
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1947 · fuel=wood · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A whole-hog pit in Ayden, Pitt County, opened by Walter B. 'Pete' Jones on July 8, 1947 and run by his family since. Hogs cook, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory logs; the meat is chopped on a block with the crisp skin chopped through it, dressed with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete, and served on a tray with slaw and a square of dense cornbread. A wood-and-aluminum copy of the U.S. Capitol dome sits on the roof.
story: The Jones family counts its barbecue back to 1830 and Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds* sold barbecue from a covered wagon near Ayden — a claim painted on the billboard outside and repeated by the press, with no document behind it that this project has seen. Pete Jones opened the Skylight at eighteen, in 1947, having learned whole hog at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe; he gave the place beer and a jukebox, it ran late with rowdy crowds, and the late nights ended when the town set a 7 pm curfew. In 1979 a National Geographic article called the restaurant 'the barbecue capital of the world'; the dome went up in 1984 as the family's answer, and 'Capital of 'Cue' has been on the sign since. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2003. Pete Jones died in 2006; the family kept the pits. *Tradition holds —* his son Bruce and nephew Jeff Jones run the Skylight, and grandson Samuel Jones opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville in 2015, then a second in Raleigh, cooking the same whole hog with a longer menu.
how: Whole hogs, heads still on, cook over charcoal the pit crew makes by burning oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. The chop takes in tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together. The plate is a tray: barbecue, slaw, cornbread; the sandwich is the same on a white roll. The cornbread is stone-ground cornmeal, water and pork drippings baked flat — denser and chewier than a skillet cornbread. Barbecue chicken is the one other meat.
today: Open Monday to Saturday, lunch through early evening, at 4618 S Lee Street, Ayden. Cash and cards. The dome, the block and the cleavers are all still in use.
address: 4618 S Lee St, Ayden, NC, 28513
geo: 35.4635, -77.4177 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style it is the standing example of: whole hog, wood coals, vinegar and pepper, white slaw.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut it has never departed from; the skin goes into the chop.
- kin → cornbread (dish): its cornbread is its own — a dense pork-fat cake, the one side that visitors argue about.
- kin → pete-jones (person): its founder, who cooked here from 1947 until his death in 2006.
- kin → sam-jones (person): the grandson who carried the method to his own restaurants and wrote it down in a book.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): the family's second pit, in Winterville, opened 2015.
sources: s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:jones-whole-hog-bbq — Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue; s:fertel-one-true-barbecue — The One True Barbecue: Fire, Smoke, and the Pitmasters Who Cook the Whole Hog; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina; s:web-truecue-nc — True 'Cue NC — certified pits; s:wp-james-beard-americas-classics — List of James Beard America's Classics; s:web-barbecuebros-nc-trail — NC Historic Barbecue Trail; s:sfa-skylight-inn — Skylight Inn — Samuel Jones, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 29 Nov 2011

## Smithfield's Chicken 'N Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/smithfields-chicken-n-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/smithfields-chicken-n-bar-b-q.json
id: smithfields-chicken-n-bar-b-q
aliases: Smithfield's · SCNB · Smithfield Bar-B-Q · Smithfield's Chicken and Barbeque · Smithfield Chicken & BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1977 · fuel=unknown · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: A quick-service chain of eastern North Carolina barbecue and fried chicken — 41 restaurants across the state as of March 2024, and an online store — begun by Junius and Maggie Moore in downtown Smithfield, Johnston County, in 1977 as Smithfield Bar-B-Q. It sells the eastern pairing over a counter, chopped pork and fried chicken, from the coast to the Triangle, and it stands in Wikipedia's list of the state's notable barbecue restaurants beside Melton's and the Skylight Inn. It is the chain form of the tradition, described here the same way as a wood pit.
story: Junius and Maggie Moore opened Smithfield Bar-B-Q in downtown Smithfield in 1977 and soon a second in Clayton, the next town toward Raleigh; a third followed at Salter Path on the Bogue Banks in 1979. Through the early 1980s the company opened across eastern North Carolina, and in the 1990s it reached the Raleigh-Durham area. By March 2024 Wikipedia counted 41 locations statewide. OpenStreetMap in 2026 carries a dozen of its restaurants from Leland to Rocky Mount, tagged for barbecue and chicken, with a brand entry on Wikidata (Q7545474); its mappers have spelled the name three ways — Bar-B-Q, Barbeque, BBQ — as the signs themselves have. The chain's own site did not render for this project, so what it says of its cooking is not on disk.
how: Counter service: chopped eastern barbecue and fried chicken, alone or together on a plate, to eat in or take out, with an online store for shipping. The cooker and the sauce are not described in the sources read for this record; a customer should look at the plate and the map, not this page, for either.
today: Open; 41 restaurants in North Carolina as of March 2024 (Wikipedia). The map point marks Smithfield, the town of the first restaurant, and not a headquarters.
address: Smithfield, NC, 27577
geo: 35.5111996, -78.346102 (town)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style in its chain form: chopped pork, fried chicken, a counter, 41 doors.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word on 41 signs, spelled three ways.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): the older eastern house that pairs barbecue with fried chicken at scale under one roof, in Wilson.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the wood pit beside which Wikipedia lists it.

## Speedy Lohr's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/speedy-lohrs-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/speedy-lohrs-barbecue.json
id: speedy-lohrs-barbecue
aliases: Speedy Lohr's · Speedy Lohr's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=2013 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A wood-burning pork house on NC 8 south of Lexington, Davidson County, run by Randy and Amy Lohr, who bought the building in June 2013 from Whitley's Barbecue and carried the family name onto it. Randy's father was Sherman Paul 'Speedy' Lohr, who started the first Speedy's on Highway 52 and learned under Warner Stamey. The pits burn wood and the family says plainly that they always will. The tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip and red slaw; pork-skin sandwiches come out on Thursdays.
story: There are three businesses in the Carolinas carrying the Lohr name and they do not cook alike, which is the first thing to settle. This is the NC 8 house. Amy Lohr set out the line herself, in a comment on a visiting writer's post on February 2, 2023: her father-in-law founded the original Speedy's on Highway 52, and Randy bought this building in 2013. She wrote, of the pits, that they still cook over them with wood, have never stopped and never will, Lord willing — which is as direct a statement of method as a pit gives, and it comes from an owner rather than from a listing. Highway work had already cost the family twice: Randy's father's place went in an earlier expansion of Highway 8, and a Speedy Lohr's at Southmont closed in 2005 for the same reason. Then in 2015 this building caught fire and closed. It reopened in August 2016, thirteen months and about $200,000 later, with the pits rebuilt to code. Randy and Amy's son Luke is the named successor, and a visiting writer recorded in 2018 that he means to keep cooking with wood. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified the pit.
how: Pork cooks over wood in pits behind the building, rebuilt after the 2015 fire. The meat is chopped and served the Piedmont way, with the dip — thin vinegar reddened with ketchup — and red slaw dressed from the same jug. Pork-skin sandwiches are a Thursday item rather than an everyday one.
today: Open at 3664 NC Highway 8 South, Lexington, and carried on Visit Lexington's current barbecue list. The map point here is the town, not the building: no street-level coordinate for the address came back from the geocoder. Hours are not on this disk. Check before driving.
address: 3664 NC Highway 8 S, Lexington, NC, 27292
geo: 35.82403, -80.25338 (town)
- kin → lexington (style): the style of its tray: shoulder over wood, the dip, red slaw.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut of the Piedmont houses, chopped from the pit.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its sauce, and the dressing that makes its slaw red.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): a Thursday sandwich here rather than a daily side.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): taught Randy Lohr's father, Sherman Paul 'Speedy' Lohr, whose name the business carries.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): certified the pit as cooking on wood or charcoal alone.
- not to be confused with speedys-barbecue: Two Speedys, four miles apart, cooking differently. Speedy's Barbecue on Piedmont Drive is Roy and Ella Dunn's, bought from Paul Lohr in the early 1970s, and cooks on electric cookers. Speedy Lohr's on NC 8 is Randy and Amy Lohr's, bought in 2013, and burns wood.

## Speedy's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/speedys-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/speedys-barbecue.json
id: speedys-barbecue
aliases: Speedy's · Speedy's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1963 · fuel=electric · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A Lexington pork-shoulder house that Paul 'Speedy' Lohr opened as a drive-in in 1963 and the Dunn family has run since the early 1970s. Roy and Ella Dunn hold it now. The pork cooks in five electric cookers that look like large rotisserie ovens — not over wood, which is why the house appears on no wood list and on no trail, and which makes it a plain case of how much of the Piedmont cooks. The tray is the Piedmont tray: chopped shoulder, the dip, red slaw, hushpuppies.
story: Roy Dunn started at Speedy's as a curb boy. In the early 1970s Paul Lohr sold the business to Roy and a cousin, and the Dunn brothers have run it together since 1978; a local paper gives the purchase year as 1970 and Our State as the early seventies, a small gap left open here. What the Dunns bought included the name, which is why a Lexington driver can pass two Speedys in twenty minutes and find two different fires. Our State's writer stood in the kitchen in September 2013 and described what is actually there: the pork cooking slowly inside five electric cookers that look like giant rotisserie ovens. A visiting writer put it flatly in July 2016 — Speedy's of Lexington cooks over electricity, not wood. Neither the Historic Barbecue Trail, which requires wood or charcoal, nor the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which requires the same, lists the house, and both absences follow from the cookers rather than from anything about the food. In about 2023 the restaurant left Winston Road after some sixty years and moved to Piedmont Drive, pushed out by the state highway widening that also took Smiley's down the road.
how: Shoulders — a short shank is the cut the kitchen prefers — cook slowly in five electric cookers. The meat is chopped and served with the dip, the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the Piedmont, with red slaw dressed from the same jug and hushpuppies on the tray. The room runs eleven to eight, six days a week.
today: Open Monday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 408 Piedmont Drive, Lexington, the address it moved to after roughly sixty years on Winston Road. OpenStreetMap last checked the listing on August 10, 2025.
address: 408 Piedmont Dr, Lexington, NC, 27295
geo: 35.83524, -80.24499 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style of its tray, cooked on electric rather than over coals.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut — a short shank shoulder, bought from a Gastonia distributor.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): what is behind the counter: five electric cookers like large rotisserie ovens.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its sauce, and the dressing on its slaw.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the slaw on its tray, dressed with the dip.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): taught Paul 'Speedy' Lohr, who opened this drive-in in 1963 and sold it to the Dunns.
- not to be confused with speedy-lohrs-barbecue: The name went with the business. Speedy's Barbecue is the Dunns' house on Piedmont Drive, cooking on electric; Speedy Lohr's on NC 8 is Randy and Amy Lohr's, cooking over wood. The founder, Paul Lohr, is behind both names and neither fire.

## Stamey's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/stameys-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/stameys-barbecue.json
id: stameys-barbecue
aliases: Stamey's · Stamey's Old Fashioned Barbecue
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1953 · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The Greensboro pork-shoulder house of the Stamey family, opened by Warner Stamey in 1953 as a drive-in on High Point Road (now West Gate City Boulevard) and run by his grandson Chip since 1993, with a second restaurant on Battleground Avenue. Fifteen-pound shoulders cook eight to ten hours over hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped or sliced and served with the dip, the thin red vinegar sauce of the Piedmont, red slaw and hushpuppies — which the family says Warner Stamey was the first to put beside barbecue in North Carolina. The name reaches back to a Lexington stand of 1938.
story: Charles Warner Stamey, born in 1911, the youngest of eleven, learned pit-cooking in Lexington under Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver, the men who set up the town's first stands, and took the method home to Shelby in the 1930s. In 1938 he came back to Lexington and bought Swicegood's stand, renaming it Stamey's; Wayne Monk trained under him there before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962. In 1953 Stamey moved to Greensboro and opened a drive-in on High Point Road; the present building replaced it in 1979. He handed the business to his son Charles in 1957, and Charles's brother Keith joined in 1970; the second generation opened the Battleground Avenue restaurant, which burned in 2016 and reopened with a drive-through in July 2017. Chip Stamey left another career to take over in 1993 and told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that the shoulders still cook over hickory and the barbecue is still served with dip rather than squirted with sauce. The American Royal put Warner Stamey in its barbecue hall of fame in 2020.
how: Shoulders of about fifteen pounds cook eight to ten hours over hickory coals. The meat is chopped or sliced and served on a tray or a bun with red slaw and hushpuppies; the dip goes on at the table, not in the kitchen. Warner Stamey's hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — became the bread of the Piedmont plate.
today: Open. Battleground Avenue: 2812 Battleground Avenue, Greensboro, Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, per OpenStreetMap (checked August 2026). The 1953 site on West Gate City Boulevard is the other restaurant.
address: 2812 Battleground Ave, Greensboro, NC, 27408
geo: 36.11161, -79.83095 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style, carried from Lexington to Greensboro in 1953 by the man who taught half its cooks.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut, fifteen pounds, eight to ten hours.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce, served at the table; 'dip' is the family's word.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the family says Warner Stamey was the first to serve them with barbecue in the state.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): on the tray.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory coals, still.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): its founder, who bought his teacher's stand in 1938 and moved the name to Greensboro in 1953.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): the Lexington man whose stand Stamey bought and renamed in 1938.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): the other Lexington pioneer Stamey learned from.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): trained under Stamey in Lexington before opening his own pit in 1962.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): the pit of Stamey's pupil, still cooking in Lexington.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded Chip Stamey in 2011.

## Stephenson's Bar-B-Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/stephensons-bar-b-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/stephensons-bar-b-q.json
id: stephensons-bar-b-q
aliases: Stephenson's Barbecue · Stephenson's · Stephenson's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1958 · fuel=charcoal · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A family barbecue house on N.C. 50 at Willow Spring, in western Johnston County south of Raleigh, opened in July 1958 by hog farmer Paul Stephenson and run since his death by his son Andy. It cooks pork shoulders over hardwood charcoal — whole hogs at the start, shoulders later for leaner meat — and barbecue chicken with a tangy sauce, with hushpuppies and collards from the recipes of Paul's wife Jean, a home-economics teacher. It serves about 600 meals a day and closes on Sundays.
story: Paul Stephenson raised shoats — young pigs — on a Depression-era farm. A man bought fourteen of them one day, and when Stephenson asked what for, he said the barbecue man wanted them. Stephenson did the arithmetic: a hundred-pound pig sold for $11.50, and cut into three-ounce sandwiches at 35 cents each it was worth a good deal more. He taught himself to cook a pig, put up a building on his own land, and sold his first barbecue in July 1958. He cooked over hardwood until the energy crisis of the mid-1970s, when the family switched to hardwood charcoal; Andy Stephenson, who took over after his father died about 2008, told Our State in 2014 that charcoal cooks slower and needs checking less often than wood. The whole hog gave way to shoulders for the reason customers everywhere gave, leaner meat. Jean Stephenson worked out the collards and the hushpuppies.
how: Shoulders cook over hardwood charcoal; the barbecue is chopped and sauced in the eastern way, and the barbecue chicken gets a tangy sauce of its own. Plates carry hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — and collards, both to Jean Stephenson's recipes. The kitchen turns out about 600 meals a day (Our State, 2014).
today: Open, closed Sundays, at 11964 N.C. Highway 50 North, Willow Spring, per Our State (2014). The map point marks the community, not the building.
address: 11964 NC Highway 50 N, Willow Spring, NC, 27592
geo: 35.5957129, -78.7313999 (town)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style, on shoulders now rather than the whole hog it began with.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut since the switch from whole hog, made for leaner meat.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): what Paul Stephenson cooked first, in 1958, before shoulders took over.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): the second meat, with its own tangy sauce.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): Jean Stephenson's recipe.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the road it did not take: the family chose hardwood charcoal in the 1970s energy crisis.
sources: s:web-ourstate-stephensons — Stephenson's Barbecue — Our State (2014); s:web-truecue-nc — True 'Cue NC — certified pits; s:web-barbecuebros-nc-trail — NC Historic Barbecue Trail

## Sweatman's Bar-B-Que (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/sweatmans-bar-b-que/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/sweatmans-bar-b-que.json
id: sweatmans-bar-b-que
aliases: Sweatman's BBQ · Sweatman's
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=1977 · fuel=mixed · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: A whole-hog barbecue house in an old farmhouse on Eutaw Road outside Holly Hill, in Orangeburg County, the mustard belt of the Midlands. Harold 'Bub' Sweatman and his wife Margie opened it in 1977 and it has served two days a week since: Friday and Saturday, pulled pork from whole hogs, ribs, hash over rice — hash being the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — and a spicy-sweet mustard sauce, with pork skins when the hogs give them. The open block pits became gas-and-wood smokers; the buffet that made the name ended after the pandemic; the family sold in 2011, and new owners took over in 2026.
story: Bub and Margie Sweatman first opened a small barbecue restaurant in Holly Hill in 1959. It did not last, and for years they cooked hogs only for friends and family. In 1977 they bought an old farmhouse in Eutawville, a rural community close to Holly Hill, and opened Sweatman's Bar-B-Que in its rooms; it has not closed since. The sauce belongs to a shared story: Joseph 'Big Joe' Bessinger, who opened the Holly Hill Café in 1939, worked out a mustard-based sauce with the Sweatman family — both families of German descent — and the Bessingers came to call theirs the Golden Secret. When Rien Fertel came for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 he recorded the cook Douglas Oliver, who said that whatever the economy did, 'everybody going to eat barbecue, especially if it's good; they're going to eat what we got, they'll be back.' Margie Sweatman died in 2003 and Bub in 2005; the family ran the house until 2011, when close family friends Lynn and Mark Behr bought it. In the Behr years the open concrete-block whole-hog pits gave way to Southern Pride smokers, and after COVID-19 the buffet ended. In 2026 the Patel family took over.
how: Whole hogs, oak- and hickory-smoked, pulled and dressed with the house mustard sauce, with vinegar and red sauces alongside. The plate is pork or ribs with hash and rice and sides; pork skins are fried when there are skins; banana pudding ends it. The old pits were open beds of concrete block over wood coals; the hogs now cook in Southern Pride smokers — *Tradition holds —* cabinet cookers fired by gas with wood for smoke.
today: Open Friday and Saturday, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 1427 Eutaw Road, Holly Hill, per the restaurant's site on September 15, 2026; Destination BBQ's 2026 page lists Thursday to Sunday instead. New owners since 2026. Check before driving.
address: 1427 Eutaw Rd, Holly Hill, SC, 29059
geo: 33.3618738, -80.3820857 (street)
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style it belongs to: whole hog under a sweet mustard sauce, in Orangeburg County.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): its sauce, worked out between the Sweatman and Bessinger families in Holly Hill.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut: whole hogs, pulled, since 1977.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): on every plate; the Midlands' pork stew over rice.
- kin → block-pit (pit): its original pits — open beds of concrete block over wood coals — since replaced.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the Southern Pride smokers that cook the hogs now.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): fried when the hogs yield them.
- kin → banana-pudding (dish): the dessert.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): worked out the mustard sauce with the Sweatmans at Holly Hill after 1939.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): the Bessinger brothers' Charleston house, cousin to this one by sauce.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the other Orangeburg County buffet lineage.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded its cook Douglas Oliver in June 2012.

## Tarheel Q (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/tarheel-q/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/tarheel-q.json
id: tarheel-q
aliases: TarHeel Q · Tarheel Q BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · fuel=wood · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: A pork-shoulder pit on US 64 west of Lexington, Davidson County, cooking on brick masonry pits behind the building. Leon and Becky Simmons have owned it since December 2017. Smoke shows from the stacks when wood and pork go on together; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip, red slaw and hushpuppies, and a weekend pork-and-chicken special ran at $11.95 in April 2026. It carries True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat. It is not a stop on the Historic Barbecue Trail.
story: The founding year and the first owner are not on this disk; the business is older than the current owners, who took it over in December 2017. Leon and Becky Simmons had worked for the Lohrs about twenty-five years before that, a visiting writer recorded in 2019 — and Paul 'Speedy' Lohr had learned under Warner Stamey, so the line back to Lexington's teaching pit runs through two hands rather than one, and no source read states a Stamey line for Tarheel Q itself. In December 2018 the Simmonses opened a second house, Arcadia Q, on NC 150, taking over from Roger and Lisa Lohr; it closed in late August, and the manager Toni London reopened the room days later under her own name for it, Southern Fire Pit Barbecue and Home Cooking. The hardest thing in the record is older. In the summer of 2015 a Salmonella Typhimurium outbreak traced to Tarheel Q sickened 280 people across twenty-one North Carolina counties and six states and killed one; state health officials declared it over on July 8, 2015, and a wrongful death suit followed that August. The restaurant is open, and John Tanner ate there and wrote it up on April 18, 2026.
how: Pork shoulders cook on brick masonry pits out back, wood and meat going on together through the day; the smokestacks run hard in the afternoon. The meat is chopped and served the Piedmont way, with the dip — thin vinegar reddened with ketchup — and red slaw dressed from the same jug. Barbecue chicken shares the weekend special with the pork.
today: Open Monday to Saturday, closed Sunday, at 6835 West US Highway 64, Lexington. Last confirmed by a visiting writer's meal on April 18, 2026. The restaurant's own site refused the fetch, so the hours here come from a listing rather than from the house.
address: 6835 W US Highway 64, Lexington, NC, 27295
geo: 35.85743, -80.3821 (street)

- kin → brick-pit (pit): its pits — brick masonry, out behind the building, with the stacks showing.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): its sauce, and the dressing on its slaw.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): two hands back: the Simmonses worked for the Lohrs, and Paul Lohr learned under Stamey.

## The Fiction Kitchen (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/the-fiction-kitchen/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/the-fiction-kitchen.json
id: the-fiction-kitchen
aliases: Fiction Kitchen
said: The barbecue here has never been near a hog, and the menu says so first.
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=2012 · fuel=unknown
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: A vegetarian and vegan restaurant in Raleigh whose menu carries a Southern-style pulled barbecue made without pork, served with the slaw and the sides a Carolina plate expects. Carolina Morrison opened it in 2012 on money raised through Kickstarter, ran it downtown for a decade, and reopened it at Gateway Plaza after a move in 2023. It is in this catalogue because it is one of the ways barbecue is cooked and eaten in North Carolina now, and because it is one of the few places in either state a published list names as LGBTQ-owned.
story: Morrison crowdfunded the restaurant in 2012 and built it into a fixture of the state capital over more than a decade. When the downtown lease ended early in 2023 the restaurant ran as a pop-up while the new room was fitted, and reopened at Gateway Plaza alongside two other tenants. Cardinal & Pine named it in a list of eight LGBTQ-owned North Carolina businesses, introduced as 'the LGBTQ-owned bars and restaurants that deserve your patronage in June and beyond', and pointed readers at the pulled barbecue.

*Inference —* a vegan pulled barbecue in Raleigh is not a pit and does not claim to be one. It sits here for the same reason a gas cooker and a bottled dip sit here: this catalogue describes what is cooked and sold under the word, and lets the reader decide what to drive to.
how: The barbecue is the kitchen's own preparation rather than a pit product; the plate is built the way a Carolina plate is built, with slaw and sides. Check the menu before going, as it changes.
today: Open at Gateway Plaza, Raleigh. Hours are on the restaurant's own site; check before driving.
address: Raleigh, NC
geo: 35.7785, -78.6415 (town)
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): what its pulled barbecue is served as, slaw and all, without the hog.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): the outsider's word this kitchen uses deliberately, since there is no pork in it.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word, stretched to cover a dish cooked without an animal — which is a thing the word is doing in the Carolinas now.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the slaw on its plate, the eastern kind.

## True BBQ (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/true-bbq/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/true-bbq.json
id: true-bbq
aliases: True BBQ of West Columbia
facets: state=SC · status=open · founded=2010 · fuel=wood · styles=
region: The South Carolina Midlands
what: A Black-owned pit on D Avenue in West Columbia, opened in 2010 by the brothers Ernest and Milton Zanders after years of selling from street corners and events. The wood-fired pits are visible from the front parking lot. Hash and rice is what the place is known for and what it sells by the pint and the quart alongside pulled pork, ribs, pork chops, brisket and chicken. It is open four days, Thursday to Saturday and no more. A second True BBQ trades in Myrtle Beach.
story: Ernest Zanders started the business and Milton, his brother, took over as head cook. They built it up selling barbecue on street corners and at events before they took a building in West Columbia in 2010; a 2026 local piece says fifteen years rather than sixteen, which is the sort of drift an anniversary line picks up. The hardest stretch is recent and it is in the record because Hannah Wade put it there for the Post and Courier's Free Times on June 25, 2022: a relative, Bryan Williams, died of a heart attack in early October 2021, and just before Christmas that year Milton's wife had her fourth stroke. The restaurant kept its doors. Wade also reported that national attention came when Eater named the hash the best in the state — the original Eater piece and its year are not on this disk, so that reaches this record at one remove. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified the pits for burning wood rather than gas, and the directory EatOkra lists the business as Black-owned. The Free Times profile itself, which names both brothers and the head cook, never uses the phrase.
how: Wood-fired pits sit where a customer can see them from the parking lot. Pulled pork, ribs, pork chops, brisket and chicken come by the plate; the hash — the Midlands stew of pork cooked down — goes over white rice and also sells by the pint and the quart to take home. Cards and cash are both taken. There is no buffet.
today: Open Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., closed Sunday to Wednesday, at 1237 D Avenue, West Columbia. A second True BBQ trades in Myrtle Beach and is also on the wood-certified list.
address: 1237 D Ave, West Columbia, SC, 29169
geo: 33.9842, -81.07217 (street)
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the dish it is known for, sold by the plate and by the quart.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut behind its pulled pork; no whole hog is described in any source read.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): certified the pits for burning wood rather than gas.
- kin → adrian-miller (person): wrote the history of African American barbecue that the Black-owned directories sit downstream of.
sources: s:web-pc-free-times-true-bbq-2022 — How a little faith and good barbecue got West Columbia's True BBQ through tragedy; s:web-destination-bbq-true-bbq — True BBQ in West Columbia; s:web-eatokra-true-bbq — True BBQ — EatOkra listing; s:web-eatokra — EatOkra — a directory of Black-owned restaurants; s:web-truecue-sc — True 'Cue SC — certified pits; s:web-destination-bbq-hash-map — The South Carolina BBQ Hash Map; s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Wilber's Barbecue (place)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/place/wilbers-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/place/wilbers-barbecue.json
id: wilbers-barbecue
aliases: Wilber's · Wilbers BBQ · Wilber's BBQ
facets: state=NC · status=open · founded=1962 · fuel=wood · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: A whole-hog pit on U.S. 70 east of Goldsboro, Wayne County, opened in 1962 by Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley and cooked the same way since: split hogs over oak coals in open pits in a cinder-block cookhouse behind a red-brick restaurant with knotty-pine walls and red-checked tablecloths. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes and reopened in July 2020 under Goldpit Partners, a group of Goldsboro natives who bought it and restored the building. The pork is hand-chopped on oak blocks and seasoned with vinegar and spices; fried chicken, collards, fried okra and hushpuppies come alongside.
story: Wilber Shirley learned the trade at Griffin's Barbecue in Goldsboro and in 1962 bought the former Hill's Barbecue on Highway 70 and put his name on it. He told the authors of Holy Smoke that he cooked 'split halves of whole hogs over oak coals in closed pits,' and that the grease hitting the coals made the smoke flavor. Staff split and cut oak all year; on a Labor Day weekend the pits held up to 130 pigs, and the dining rooms seated more than 300. Shirley worked twelve or thirteen hours a day, six days a week, for more than forty years, with some ninety employees. In March 2019 the restaurant was shut for nonpayment of taxes. Willis B. Underwood III, an insurance salesman and lifelong regular, gathered other customers into Goldpit Partners, bought the place, kept the paneling and the tablecloths, and reopened it in July 2020 — curbside only at first, Wednesday to Sunday, with a shortened menu. 'I just didn't want to see the smoke die,' he told Our State. Shirley's son-in-law Dennis Monk took a management role, and Shirley, who turned ninety in June 2020, advised. He died in April 2021. Pitmaster Jackie Martin, at the pits nearly forty years, works from two in the afternoon to five or six in the morning.
how: Whole hogs cook all night over oak embers on open pits — nine hours by one account, twelve or more by another — then are hand-chopped on oak blocks and seasoned with vinegar and spices. The plate is barbecue with fried okra and slaw; the sandwich is barbecue and slaw; the 'Bone Box' is a tray-sized pig pickin', the meat left on the bone for pulling by hand. Sides run to hushpuppies, collards, cabbage, macaroni and cheese and fried chicken; the desserts — pecan pie, coconut and carrot cake, banana pudding, Wilber's cookies — are made in the house.
today: Open Wednesday to Saturday 11 to 7 and Sunday 11 to 3, at 4172 U.S. Highway 70 East, Goldsboro, per the restaurant's site in September 2026. Goldpit Partners own it.
address: 4172 US Highway 70 E, Goldsboro, NC, 27534
geo: 35.35061, -77.9224636 (street)
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style; Wilber's is one of the pits the press names first when it names the east.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, split and cooked over oak coals through the night.
- kin → wilber-shirley (person): its founder, at the pits from 1962 until the 2019 closure; he died in April 2021.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): oak here, split and cut by the staff all year round.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): the oak blocks the pork is chopped on by hand.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the 'Bone Box' on the menu is a pig pickin' in a tray: meat on the bone, pulled by hand.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): interviewed Shirley for Holy Smoke; the closed-pit quotation comes from that book.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): the other Wayne County whole-hog pit, at a crossroads south of town.
- kin → scotts-famous-barbecue (place): Goldsboro's earlier barbecue name, closed now, whose sauce is still sold.

## Adam Scott (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/adam-scott/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/adam-scott.json
id: adam-scott
aliases: Rev. Adam Scott · Elder Adam Scott
facets: role=cook, founder, sauce-maker · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: The Rev. Adam Scott (1890–1983) was a Black cook and Holiness minister in Goldsboro who by his company's date went into the barbecue business in 1917, cooking whole hogs in his back yard and selling chopped pork with a vinegar sauce through the back door; between 1931 and 1933 the house on Brazil Street became a restaurant. He said the sauce came to him in a dream; his son A. Martel Scott patented it in 1946, and the family still bottles it. David Cecelski's account has him catering a barbecue for President Franklin Roosevelt at the White House in 1933.
story: Adam Scott was born in Goldsboro in 1890, the son of Joseph Scott, who was born in Oberlin, Ohio, and the grandson of Charles and Mary Scott, who had likely been enslaved in Johnston County. His first cooking job was at the Elberon Hotel in Atlantic City in 1911. Back home he catered barbecues from about the mid-1910s — 1917 is the company's founding date — and between 1931 and 1933 opened a restaurant at his home on Brazil Street: two hogs a week at first, cooked Friday night and sold Saturday through the back door, then four to seven hogs a day, with an enclosed porch for a dining room. His first customers were mostly white; he ran a separate cafe for Black customers elsewhere in town. The sauce, sugar-free and fat-free, took him three years to settle, and he said the precise ingredients were revealed to him in a dream. *Tradition holds —* in 1933 he catered barbecue in the White House Rose Garden for President Franklin Roosevelt; Cecelski tells it as fact, without a document behind it, and this record has seen none. He was a minister of the United Holy Church of America, by 1938 pastor of three churches and its general treasurer, and he closed on Sundays. In the 1940s he moved to Winston-Salem to cook for R.J. Reynolds and other private clients; his son Alvin Martel Scott, born 1913, took the Goldsboro business, patented Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946, and by 1950 there were three Scott's around town, one run by Adam on the Raleigh road. He died in 1983 at ninety-three and is buried in Elmwood Cemetery under the word 'Elder'. The American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022.
today: Dead: 1983, at ninety-three, in Goldsboro. The restaurants closed after 2001; the sauce is made by his descendants and sold in eastern North Carolina groceries and online, and the American Royal's Barbecue Hall of Fame lists him as a 2022 legacy inductee.
- kin → scotts-famous-barbecue (place): the business he began at his back door and his son grew to three restaurants by 1950.
- kin → scotts-barbecue-sauce (sauce): the sauce he said came to him in a dream, patented by his son in 1946 and still bottled by the family.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): his sauce is the eastern sauce: vinegar and spices, no tomato, no sugar.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style he cooked and bottled: whole hog and vinegar in Goldsboro from 1917.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, two a week in the back yard and later seven a day.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): Goldsboro's later barbecue name, opened in 1962 on U.S. 70, still cooking.
- kin → bob-melton (person): the other founding name of the east's first generation: Melton's shed at Rocky Mount in 1924, Scott's back door in Goldsboro from 1917.
- kin → adrian-miller (person): whose Black Smoke tells the history of Black cooks like Scott, whose customers were white and whose name went on the bottle.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/adam-scott/adam-scott-adam-scotts-place-goldsboro-1944.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · Bill Sharpe; State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/47848599202/

Adam Scott of Goldsboro, N.C. — David Cecelski (21 Nov 2025); s:web-aahc-scotts-cafe — Scott's Cafe — The Green Book in North Carolina (essay by Brandie K. Ragghianti, 2022); s:web-scotts-history — Our History; s:web-ncarts-goldsboro — Let's Eat: Goldsboro — African American Music Trails; s:web-moss-bbq-hof-2022 — BBQ Hall of Fame Inductees Announced — Robert F. Moss (25 May 2022); s:miller-black-smoke — Black Smoke: African Americans and the United States of Barbecue; s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-condev — Department of Conservation and Development, Travel Information Division Photograph Collection

## Adrian Miller (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/adrian-miller/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/adrian-miller.json
id: adrian-miller
aliases: Adrian E. Miller · the Soul Food Scholar
facets: role=writer, scholar
region: The American South
what: A Denver writer and lawyer, the 'Soul Food Scholar' of his own site, whose Black Smoke: African Americans and the United States of Barbecue (UNC Press, 2021) is the history of the Black cooks, pitmasters and restaurant owners behind American barbecue and of their absence from its legends. It won the James Beard Foundation's 2022 Media Award for Reference, History, and Scholarship, his second after Soul Food (2013; award 2014). A former special assistant to President Clinton, he directs the Colorado Council of Churches and is a certified barbecue judge.
story: Miller left the White House when the Clinton administration ended — he had been special assistant to the president and deputy director of the President's Initiative for One America — and between jobs took up food writing after reading John Egerton's Southern Food. Soul Food: The Surprising Story of an American Cuisine, One Plate at a Time (UNC Press, 2013) took him to 150 restaurants in 35 cities and won the 2014 Beard award for reference and scholarship; The President's Kitchen Cabinet (2017) named 150 African Americans who had cooked in the White House. Black Smoke came out in April 2021: essays on how barbecue was built on Black labor, enslaved cooks and then paid ones, and on how the menus, the television and the legends that followed left them out, with profiles of forgotten cooks and twenty-two recipes. The Beard Foundation gave it the Media Award for Reference, History, and Scholarship in Chicago on May 12, 2022. Miller sat on the board of the Southern Foodways Alliance from 2004 to 2010 and received its Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award in 2018; he is a certified Kansas City Barbeque Society judge and was a consultant on Netflix's Chef's Table: BBQ. *Tradition holds —* the cooks at the eastern Carolina trenches were Black men for most of two centuries, enslaved and then paid; Black Smoke is the book this catalogue cites for that labor and its erasure.
today: Executive director of the Colorado Council of Churches since June 2013, in Denver. His 2025 book with Deborah Chang, Cooking to the President's Taste: Asian Heritage Chefs in White House History (White House Historical Association), followed Black Smoke; in 2026 he earned a James Beard Media Award nomination for feature reporting.
- kin → pitmaster (term): Black Smoke tells the history of the Black pitmasters the word was late to name.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): his book is the record this catalogue cites for the Black cooks at the eastern pits and their erasure from the menus and legends.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the oldest cooking, whose labor — Black and mostly unnamed — Black Smoke traces.
- kin → backyard-bbq-pit (place): the Durham pit the press framed with his book: a Black-owned pit and what it takes to keep one.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): he sat on its board from 2004 to 2010 and received its Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award in 2018.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/adrian-miller/adrian-miller-adrian-miller-1.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Aemlegal · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAdrian_Miller_1.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/adrian-miller/adrian-miller-adrian-miller-the-soul-food-scholar.jpg · CC0 1.0 · Aemlegal · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAdrian_Miller_the_Soul_Food_Scholar.jpg

## Bob Garner (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/bob-garner/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/bob-garner.json
id: bob-garner
aliases: the barbecue man · Robert Garner
facets: state=NC · role=writer · styles=eastern-nc, lexington
region: North Carolina
what: A North Carolina television reporter and writer who has covered the state's barbecue since 1994, when he began short features on it for UNC-TV's magazine program North Carolina Now. His first book, North Carolina Barbecue: Flavored by Time (John F. Blair, 1996), toured the state's pits; a one-hour television special followed, and with it the name 'the barbecue man'. Bob Garner's Guide to North Carolina Barbecue (2002) and Bob Garner's Book of Barbecue (2012) came after. He writes restaurant pieces for Our State magazine and divides his time between Burlington and Raleigh.
story: Garner learned to cook over a fire in the Boy Scouts and, as a young married man, learned whole pigs from his wife's brothers — she was a farm girl from northeastern North Carolina — and he dates his conversion to the smell of the juices dripping onto the coals. The UNC-TV features began in 1994; the 1996 book went across the state pit by pit, and after the special based on it he was 'the barbecue man' on the state's public television. He was executive producer and host of the UNC-TV series Carolina Countryside, appeared on Food Network, the Travel Channel and Good Morning America, and made a special, A North Carolina Pig Pickin', with his youngest son, Everett. The 2002 Guide described a hundred restaurants from the mountains to the coast; the 2012 Book of Barbecue folded both earlier books into one, with recipes, tips and profiles of pitmasters — a pitmaster being the person who tends the pit. For Our State he wrote up Lexington Barbecue, Stamey's, B's, Wilber's, Short Sugar's and the Skylight Inn, among others; his 2012 Lexington Barbecue piece records the shoulders roasting ten hours over oak coals, fresh coals shovelled under the meat every half hour, and the crust, the 'brown', lifted off and saved for special orders. Asked by the blog BBQ Jew in 2011 whether wood was required, he answered that he preferred live coals but had eaten too much good barbecue cooked otherwise to be dogmatic, and named Smithfield's Chicken 'N Bar-B-Q and Ken's Grill in LaGrange among the gas-and-electric places he eats at. His five favourites that year were The Pit in Raleigh, Lexington Barbecue, Bridges in Shelby, Grady's in Dudley and B's in Greenville.
today: Still on the state's public television: he visited Sam Jones BBQ in Raleigh for North Carolina Weekend in August 2021 and named his places in a 2023 NC Weekend segment. Our State keeps his restaurant pieces online. No 2025 or 2026 activity was found for this record (checked September 15, 2026).
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): Wayne Monk's pit, which he wrote up for Our State in 2012: ten hours over oak coals, the brown set aside for special orders.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the crust of the shoulder; his 2012 piece records it being lifted off and saved at Lexington Barbecue.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): written up by him for Our State in 2012.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): his 2012 Our State piece: red picnic tables, counter service, no promise the food lasts till noon; one of the five he named to BBQ Jew in 2011.
- kin → gradys-barbecue (place): one of the five places he named to BBQ Jew in 2011.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): one of the five places he named to BBQ Jew in 2011.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): an Our State piece of his, and on the list he gave NC Weekend in 2023.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): an Our State piece of his, on Pete Jones's line that a place like this needs no sign.
- kin → short-sugars (place): an Our State piece of his, on David Wilson's sauce.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): the Raleigh restaurant he visited for North Carolina Weekend in August 2021.
- kin → smithfields-chicken-n-bar-b-q (place): named by him in 2011 as a place cooking without live coals whose barbecue he still eats.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style his wife's brothers taught him: whole pigs, in the northeast of the state.
- kin → lexington (style): the Piedmont half of his state-wide books and segments.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the subject of his television special A North Carolina Pig Pickin', made with his son Everett.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): he prefers live coals but told BBQ Jew in 2011 he has eaten too much good barbecue off them to be dogmatic.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): he has spoken at its annual symposium in Oxford, Mississippi.

## Bob Melton (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/bob-melton/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/bob-melton.json
id: bob-melton
aliases: R. B. Melton · Robert Melton
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: R. B. 'Bob' Melton (died 1958), a horse trader raised on a Nash County farm, cooked whole hogs for friends in an open pit on the Tar River at Rocky Mount, began selling barbecue there in 1922, and in 1924 built the shed that Wikipedia and UNC's North Carolina Miscellany call the state's first indoor, sit-down barbecue restaurant. He served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue across the state by bus. Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue in 1958, the year he died.
story: Melton had been cooking since he was twelve, the Miscellany says, and traded horses for a living. By 1922 he was selling barbecue from pits on the Tar River bank; two years later he built the restaurant, a large shed that grew room by room, and Rocky Mount took to it. In 1929 a plate with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents and a sandwich 15. The food writer Beth Tartan recorded the catering: 'When a woman who lives in Raleigh is having company, she calls up Bob Melton's and says: "Ride me a party."' The bus carried the barbecue and fixings. In later years he retired from the pits and greeted at the door; in 1958 Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue, and he died that year. His partners W.B. Melton, T.O. Fulghum and Add Smith carried the restaurant on — by 1993 on gas and wood chips rather than charcoal, a change John Egerton noted with regret in Southern Food — until the Tar River put it under: Hurricane Fran's flood, then Hurricane Floyd in 1999, the seventy-fifth anniversary year, with water above the ceiling. The restaurant moved to a strip mall and closed in 2005. *Inference —* the vinegar-sauced whole hog on Melton's menu is the eastern style as it is still described, which is why the tradition dates its restaurant history from his shed.
today: Dead: 1958, at Rocky Mount. The restaurant outlived him by forty-seven years and closed in 2005; the riverside building is gone.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): the shed he built by the Tar River in 1924, the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style's first restaurant menu was his: whole hog, vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, corn sticks.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, small hogs of 80 to 90 pounds chopped fine, 'the consistency of chopped peanut butter'.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): on his 45-cent plate of 1929.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): on his table beside the barbecue.
- kin → down-east (term): he cooked whole hog in an open pit by the Tar River before he sold it.
- kin → adam-scott (person): his contemporary in Goldsboro: Scott sold from a back door from 1917, Melton from a shed from 1924.
sources: s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-ncm-bob-melton — bob melton — North Carolina Miscellany (UNC Libraries), post of 5 Jun 2023; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## Bum Dennis (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/bum-dennis/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/bum-dennis.json
id: bum-dennis
aliases: Latham Dennis · Latham Wade 'Bum' Dennis
facets: role=pitmaster, founder, family · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Latham Wade 'Bum' Dennis (June 12, 1937 – December 9, 2022) opened Bum's Restaurant in downtown Ayden in 1963 with his wife Shirley and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for the rest of his working life, with a table of vegetables beside the barbecue that few eastern pits keep. He was of the Dennis family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of the trade, and a kinsman of Pete Jones of the Skylight Inn. His son Larry, at the pit since he was nine, runs the restaurant.
story: His mother could not settle on a name for weeks, and people said a man without a name would grow up to be a bum; she named him Latham, and Bum stuck. He was born in Pitt County on June 12, 1937, finished Ayden High School in 1956 and joined the Navy that year. In 1963 he and Shirley opened the restaurant that carries his nickname; he cut the wood for the pits, opened for breakfast at 5:30 and closed at nine every day but Sunday. The family's barbecue, he and Larry told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011, runs back through six generations of Dennises to the wagon of 1830. 'People have been cooking with wood for 500,000 years,' Larry told Our State. 'We just never stopped.' Bum's own account of the trade, as he gave it to Fertel: 'In this type restaurant business, what you got to do you got to love it and it's a way of life. You get up every morning and that's what you do.' When Daniel Wallace visited for Our State in 2014 Bum had retired but came in to serve breakfast around five, silver handlebar moustache and all, and Shirley sat at her table with her friend Hilda Worthington; Larry arrived at four to burn oak and pecan down to coals and did everything but kill the pig. Bum died at his home, Raven Hall, on December 9, 2022, at eighty-five.
today: Dead: December 9, 2022, at home in Ayden, aged eighty-five. Larry Dennis runs Bum's Restaurant at 566 East Third Street; the Dennis family's whole hog and vegetable table continue there.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): the restaurant he and Shirley opened in 1963; his son Larry runs it.
- kin → skilton-dennis (person): the ancestor whose 1830 wagon he counted his barbecue back to when the Alliance asked.
- kin → pete-jones (person): his kinsman of the same Dennis line, who opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, sixteen years before Bum's.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the other Ayden pit, a few blocks away, claiming the same root; Larry says his chop is coarser.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style, with a vegetable table beside it.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, over oak and pecan coals his son burns down before dawn.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded him and Larry together at the restaurant on December 5, 2011.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed him for the Alliance in 2011.
sources: s:sfa-bums-restaurant — Bum's Restaurant — Latham 'Bum' Dennis and Larry Dennis, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 5 Dec 2011; s:web-ourstate-bums — Bum's Restaurant — Our State (April 2014); s:web-legacy-latham-dennis-obituary — Latham Dennis Obituary (1937–2022) — The Standard (Ayden), via Legacy.com; s:web-tanner-bum-dennis-2022 — Rest in Peace, Latham 'Bum' Dennis — John Tanner's Barbecue Blog (10 Dec 2022)
