## Dennis Rogers (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/dennis-rogers/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/dennis-rogers.json
id: dennis-rogers
aliases: the oracle of the holy grub
facets: state=NC · role=writer · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Dennis Rogers (October 10, 1942 – August 8, 2020), a News & Observer columnist for more than thirty years, raised in Wilson and an Army veteran, who wrote about small-town eastern North Carolina and its soldiers and, in barbecue, spoke for the east: whole hog with vinegar and pepper and nothing else. He called himself the 'oracle of the holy grub' in a long mock war of columns with Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro over ketchup in the sauce. His columns were collected in Home Grown (1979), Second Harvest (1981), Crossroads (1984) and It's Bad News When the Bartender Cries (1988).
story: The war ran in print for decades, Rogers from Raleigh for the whole hog of Wilson, Greenville and Goldsboro, Bledsoe from Greensboro for the Piedmont's shoulder and red dip, each with a self-conferred title. Rogers's line, in one column, was that people who would put ketchup in the sauce they feed to innocent children are capable of most anything, and that the eastern purveyors of pure barbecue would not be roadkill for their western kin. When the 2005 bills over the Lexington Barbecue Festival's title brought the argument to the General Assembly, ABC's World News Tonight put the two men on air: Rogers said of the eastern sauce, 'It doesn't need anything else', and that somebody who would put ketchup on barbecue and give it to a child was capable of pretty much anything; Bledsoe answered that America loves ketchup and that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue. In January 2007, after thirty years as a columnist, Rogers gave up the column at 64 for a new beat — the home front and the war's weight on eastern North Carolina, reported from Sanford — telling WRAL, 'I'm not dead yet!' and that he could not walk away with the soldiers' stories untold. He retired later that year, kept a website of his and his wife's RV travels, wrote a novel, acted in local theatre and rode motorcycles. He died in his sleep on August 8, 2020, at 77, after a long illness.
today: Died August 8, 2020, at 77. His column collections, published by the News & Observer between 1979 and 1988, survive in libraries and used bookshops; his family promised a barbecue in his memory once the pandemic allowed.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style he spoke for: the whole hog of Wilson, Greenville and Goldsboro.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): 'It doesn't need anything else': his verdict on it, to ABC in 2005.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children — his charge against it.
- kin → lexington (style): the style his columns needled for decades.
- kin → jerry-bledsoe (person): his opponent from Greensboro, the self-styled world's leading, foremost barbecue authority.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): whose 2005–07 bills brought the war back onto the air.
- kin → down-east (term): the country he came from, Wilson, and wrote about.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the eastern cut, 'with vinegar and pepper sauce only', as he put his side.
sources: s:web-wral-dennis-rogers-dies — Former WRAL contributor, N&O columnist Dennis Rogers dies at 77 (August 8, 2020); s:web-bryan-lee-dennis-rogers-obituary — Dennis Rogers obituary (August 8, 2020); s:web-wral-rogers-new-beat-2007 — Longtime N&O Columnist Begins New Beat (January 29, 2007); s:web-openlibrary-dennis-rogers — Dennis Rogers — author page; s:web-abc-barbecue-feud — Smoke, Fire as BBQ Bigshots Battle Over Ketchup (John Berman, World News Tonight, 2 Jun 2005); s:web-bbqjew-defining-styles — Defining the Styles (30 Nov 2009); s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-barbecue-festival — Lexington Barbecue Festival — Wikipedia

## Ed Mitchell (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/ed-mitchell/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/ed-mitchell.json
id: ed-mitchell
aliases: The Pitmaster · Pitmaster Ed Mitchell
facets: role=pitmaster, founder, writer · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Ed Mitchell (born 1948 or 1949) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Wilson who began cooking pigs behind his family's grocery store in the early 1990s, turned the store into Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q, co-founded The Pit in Raleigh in 2007, and has argued for pasture-raised heritage hogs since the 2000s. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded him in 2007; the American Royal put him in its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022. His book, Ed Mitchell's Barbeque, written with his son Ryan Mitchell and Zella Palmer, came out from Ecco in 2023.
story: He cooked his first pig at fourteen or fifteen, at a family gathering in Wilson where the men had passed the moonshine and fallen asleep; his grandfather woke to a cooked hog, asked who had done it, and poured him a glass. 'Growing up, all our lives on any celebration... it had to be accompanied by barbecue,' he told Amy Evans of the Southern Foodways Alliance in September 2007. After his father died — in 1991, by his own account in WALTER magazine; 1990 by the Alliance's — his mother asked for barbecue, he cooked a pig behind Mitchell's Grocery, customers asked for it, and by 1992 the store was Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q. From 2002 he headlined New York's Big Apple Barbecue Block Party each year; in 2003 he began cooking free-range pigs. The Wilson restaurant closed in 2004 or 2005 amid a state tax case. In 2007 he opened The Pit in Raleigh with a real-estate developer and left it in May 2011; Que, in Durham's American Tobacco campus, ran less than a year from 2014. He cooks hot and fast, a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250, with a rub of salt, black and red pepper and onion powder and a sauce of cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper; he wants the whole hog because a sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together. With Ryan he has worked with True Made Foods on sauces since 2018 and announced The Preserve, a Raleigh restaurant with LM Restaurants, in 2019. 'I barbeque not because I love hoisting 150-pound hogs over my shoulders, but because I want to keep the tradition of my African American ancestors alive,' he wrote in 2023.
today: Living. He has not run a restaurant since Que closed in 2015; he ships barbecue from a smokehouse in Micro, Johnston County, through Goldbelly, sells sauces with True Made Foods, and works with his son Ryan. The Preserve, announced for Raleigh in 2019, had not opened as of July 2024.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style he cooks and speaks for: whole hog over wood, a vinegar-and-pepper sauce, from Wilson.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut he insists on, because a pulled-pork sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): his sauce: cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the family gathering where he cooked his first pig at fourteen or fifteen while the men slept.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the family cooker in Wilson on which that first pig was cooked.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): his method: a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250, vents closed overnight.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): his fuel, oak and hickory logs with charcoal briquettes.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded him in Wilson on September 5, 2007, and made him the subject of a Gravy episode.
- kin → pitmaster (term): the word in his Wikipedia title and his company's name, Ed Mitchell & Sons, 'The Pitmaster'.
- kin → pit (term): The Pit, the Raleigh restaurant he co-founded in 2007 and left in 2011, took the word for its name.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): he builds the sandwich from a whole hog rather than a shoulder.
- kin → parkers-barbecue (place): Wilson's other barbecue name, on the highway; Mitchell's was a converted grocery in the same town.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): quotes him on its wood page on places that cook over gas or on a rotisserie.

## Elliott Moss (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/elliott-moss/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/elliott-moss.json
id: elliott-moss
facets: role=pitmaster, chef, founder · state=both · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee
region: The North Carolina mountains, The Pee Dee, North Carolina, South Carolina
what: Elliott Moss is a chef and whole-hog pitmaster from Florence, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who grew up watching his grandfather smoke hogs, moved to Asheville in 2007 to open The Admiral, and in August 2015 opened Buxton Hall Barbecue there with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani group, bringing wood-cooked whole hog and South Carolina hash to the mountains. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022; it closed in November 2023. In 2025 he and his wife Jennifer opened Elliott's Barbecue Lounge inside Seminar Brewing in Florence, which Southern Living named the South's best new barbecue restaurant for 2026.
story: Moss, 'a son of the low country of Florence, S.C.' in the Asheville chamber's words, learned smoke from his grandfather's whole hogs. He came to Asheville in 2007 to help open The Admiral, whose cooking put him on the James Beard Foundation's semifinalist list for Best Chef: Southeast in 2013. A first deal for a barbecue place fell through; Meherwan Irani of Chai Pani reached out within forty-eight hours, and Buxton Hall Barbecue opened in August 2015 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue on the South Slope: pasture-raised hogs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning, hash and rice made from the pig's organs and trimmings, a fried chicken sandwich, pies on lard crusts. 'When I'm in here, I cut all the lights off except this little lamp,' he told Our State in 2016, 'and it's just like I'm outside, cooking a pig, standing in front of the burn barrel.' Bon Appétit put the restaurant ninth among the country's new restaurants in 2016 and named the sandwich its fried chicken sandwich of the year; the Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist again in 2017. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022, opened two West Asheville restaurants, Regina's and Little Louie's, in the summer of 2023 and left them within six weeks, and in March 2024 announced on Instagram that after seventeen years he and Jennifer were leaving Asheville to keep cooking whole hog somewhere else. The somewhere was home: Elliott's Barbecue Lounge opened inside Seminar Brewing at 551 West Lucas Street, Florence, in the spring of 2025 — pasture-raised whole hog 'cooked Pee Dee burn barrel-style', in Robert Moss's words for Southern Living, with collards, hash and rice and a buttered, grilled bun.
today: Living. He and Jennifer Moss run Elliott's Barbecue Lounge in Florence, South Carolina, open since spring 2025; Southern Living ranked it 36th among the South's fifty barbecue restaurants in 2025 and its best new barbecue restaurant in 2026.
- kin → buxton-hall-barbecue (place): the Asheville restaurant he opened in 2015 and left in July 2022, fifteen months before it closed.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut he has cooked from Asheville to Florence: pasture-raised, overnight, over wood.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): his home style — Florence is in the Pee Dee — and the burn-barrel method his Florence pit is described by.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the chopped whole hog at Buxton Hall was cooked the eastern way, in a city that had not had one.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): he put South Carolina hash on an Asheville plate and asked what other pits did with those parts of the pig.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the barrel he described standing in front of in the dark at Buxton Hall, and the method named for his Florence hog.
sources: s:web-ourstate-buxton-hall — Buxton Hall Barbecue Brings Whole-Hog Tradition and Hash to Asheville — Our State; s:web-ashevillechamber-moss-2017 — Chef Elliott Moss named semifinalist for 2017 James Beard Foundation Awards — Asheville Area Chamber of Commerce (Feb 2017); s:web-chswf-elliott-moss — Elliott Moss — Charleston Wine + Food participant biography; s:web-barbecuebros-buxton-hall-2024 — Buxton Hall Barbecue's 2023 closure was the latest blow for NC whole hog barbecue — Barbecue Bros (25 Mar 2024); s:web-ashevegas-moss-shakeup-2023 — Asheville restaurant shake-up: Elliott Moss — Ashevegas Hot Sheet (8 Jul 2023); s:web-smokesheet-buxton-hall-closes — Buxton Hall Barbecue closes — The Smoke Sheet (8 Nov 2023); s:web-wmbf-elliotts-southern-living-2026 — Southern Living ranks Florence's Elliott's BBQ Lounge best new BBQ spot in the South — WMBF News (10 Sep 2026); s:web-smokesheet-elliotts-2026 — Elliott's Barbecue Lounge Makes Florence Proud — The Smoke Sheet (14 Jan 2026)

## Jerry Bledsoe (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/jerry-bledsoe/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/jerry-bledsoe.json
id: jerry-bledsoe
aliases: Jerry Carroll Bledsoe · the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority
facets: state=NC · role=writer · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Jerry Carroll Bledsoe (July 14, 1941 – December 31, 2025), a Greensboro newspaper columnist and author, born in Danville, Virginia and raised in Thomasville, who wrote for the Greensboro Daily News, later the News & Record, for twenty-three years and became a true-crime writer with Bitter Blood (1988), a number-one New York Times bestseller. In barbecue he was Lexington's man: the self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' in a decades-long mock war of columns with Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer over ketchup in the sauce.
story: Bledsoe delivered the Thomasville Tribune at nine, served three years in the Army after high school, and worked at papers in Kannapolis and Charlotte before the Greensboro Daily News, where his columns of the 1970s and 1980s made his name; he was later a contributing editor at Esquire. The barbecue war was one of those columns' running jokes: Bledsoe for the Piedmont's chopped shoulder with its red dip, Rogers for the east's whole hog and clear vinegar, each claiming a title — Bledsoe the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority, Rogers the oracle of the holy grub. Bledsoe wrote that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue; Rogers wrote that people who would put ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children were capable of most anything. The joke outlived the columns. When bills to make the Lexington Barbecue Festival the state's official barbecue festival divided the General Assembly in 2005, ABC's World News Tonight came to Greensboro, and Bledsoe gave them 'America loves ketchup' and called vinegar an astringent thing that ruins the taste buds. In 1996 he wrote 'Slaw Crazy', an essay holding that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. Bitter Blood, on the Lynch–Newsom–Klenner murders of 1984–85, was followed by Blood Games (1991), Before He Wakes (1994) and Death Sentence (1998); he founded Down Home Press to publish books about North Carolina, and in later years wrote for the Rhino Times, including a long series on the Greensboro police. He died on December 31, 2025, at 84.
today: Died December 31, 2025, at 84. The Rhino Times, where he last wrote, marked his death the next day; The Assembly's tribute, 'A Hell of a Writer', ran on January 12, 2026.
- kin → lexington (style): the style he championed in print from Greensboro.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): 'America loves ketchup': his defence of the red sauce, to ABC in 2005.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): 'an astringent thing', in his words to ABC in 2005.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the other side; he wrote that Rogers had ruined the state's chances of distinction in barbecue.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): his opponent for decades, the Raleigh columnist and 'oracle of the holy grub'.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): whose fight over an official title in 2005–07 brought the columnists' war back into the news.
- kin → slaw (term): his 1996 essay 'Slaw Crazy': barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina, and always has been.
sources: s:wp-jerry-bledsoe — Jerry Bledsoe — Wikipedia; s:web-assembly-bledsoe-obituary — 'A Hell of a Writer' (Joe Killian, January 12, 2026); s:web-rhinotimes-bledsoe-dies — Jerry Bledsoe Passes At Age 84 (January 1, 2026); s:web-abc-barbecue-feud — Smoke, Fire as BBQ Bigshots Battle Over Ketchup (John Berman, World News Tonight, 2 Jun 2005); s:web-bbqjew-defining-styles — Defining the Styles (30 Nov 2009); s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-barbecue-festival — Lexington Barbecue Festival — Wikipedia; s:wiktionary-slaw — slaw — Wiktionary; s:wp-bitter-blood — Bitter Blood — Wikipedia

## Jess Swicegood (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/jess-swicegood/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/jess-swicegood.json
id: jess-swicegood
aliases: Jesse Swicegood
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Jess Swicegood ran a barbecue stand a few yards from Sid Weaver's tent by the Lexington courthouse in the 1920s, taught Warner Stamey pit cooking alongside Weaver, and sold Stamey the business in 1938 — for $300, by Robert Moss's account — when Stamey came back from Shelby and renamed it Stamey's. Through that sale the Swicegood stand is the ancestor of Stamey's in Greensboro and, through Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk, of Lexington Barbecue. He is spelled Jess and Jesse in the sources, and no dates of birth or death are on record here.
story: The sources agree on the order: Weaver's tent in 1919, Swicegood's stand beside it within the decade, then the two of them together. Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros relay it, says Weaver 'later teamed up with Jess Swicegood and those two men perfected Lexington-style barbecue and helped spread the technique across the Piedmont of North Carolina'. Stamey's history and the American Royal's 2020 bio put Swicegood first in the pair that taught Warner Stamey when he was a high-school boy boarding with his sister, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's note on Stamey's calls the two 'pit-cooking pioneers'. In 1938 Stamey moved back to Lexington, bought out his mentor and renamed the operation Stamey's; Wayne Monk worked under Stamey in downtown Lexington for several years before he opened Lexington Barbecue in 1962. *Inference —* a stand that changed hands for $300 was a tent or a shed, not a building; the first permanent barbecue restaurant in town was Alton Beck's, in 1938, the same year.
today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The Lexington stand he sold in 1938 carried the Stamey name into the 1950s; the Stamey family's restaurants are in Greensboro, and Lexington Barbecue, opened by Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk in 1962, cooks a mile or two from where his stand stood.
- kin → lexington (style): the style's second name after Weaver's: his stand and Weaver's tent are where it was worked out.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): the tent his stand stood beside; Weaver was first, by a few years.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): his pupil, who bought him out in 1938 and put his own name over the door.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): the name on his old stand from 1938, carried to Greensboro in 1953.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): Wayne Monk trained at the stand Stamey bought from him; the pit is his grandchild.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce came out of his stand and Weaver's tent.

Moss, Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:moss-barbecue-history — Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:sfa-stameys-barbecue — Stamey's Barbecue — Chip Stamey, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 18 Nov 2011; s:web-ourstate-lexington-barbecue — Lexington Barbecue (Bob Garner, 2012-08-31); s:web-ourstate-lexington-cover-up — The Great Lexington Barbecue Cover-Up (Jeremy Markovich, 31 Mar 2015); s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue

## Jim Early (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/jim-early/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/jim-early.json
id: jim-early
aliases: James Howard Early Jr. · Chef Early
facets: state=NC · role=founder, organizer, writer, cook · styles=eastern-nc, lexington
region: North Carolina
what: James Howard Early Jr. (1939–2021), a Winston-Salem lawyer and cook who founded the North Carolina Barbecue Society in 2006 and led it until his death. His self-published guide, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy (2002), came out of a search through all hundred counties for pits still cooking pork over wood coals; the society's Historic Barbecue Trail is that list under rules he wrote — wood or charcoal on grates, a house sauce, fifteen years' cooking, no more than two stops in a town.
story: Early was born in Henderson, grew up in Winston-Salem, took his bachelor's and law degrees at Wake Forest, and practiced law for years before barbecue took over. The search behind the book covered 22,000 miles and about 4,000 hours across the state's hundred counties; he found fewer than thirty restaurants still cooking over wood coals, six of them Black-owned and three owned by women. The society he founded in 2006 set itself to preserve the state's barbecue history and, in its own words, to secure North Carolina's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World; the less formal motto was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends. It ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year — Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July, Castle Hayne in September — teaching whole hog, pork butt, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. He published a monthly magazine, Pigtails, and a second book, Jim Early's Reflections: The Memories and Recipes of a Southern Cook. In September 2017 he closed his law office to run the society full time. He took no side in the east–west argument, and told Our State in 2016 that '99.99 percent of places' now cooked with gas or electricity; the Trail bypasses all of them. He died on June 21, 2021, at 82, weeks after a stroke.
today: Died June 21, 2021. The society's two web addresses did not resolve when this project checked on September 15, 2026; its Facebook page carries on as a forum, and the Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others. His 2002 guidebook is held by libraries and sold used.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): founded it in 2006, was its president, and ran it full time from September 2017 until his death.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): what he found at almost every pit in a hundred counties; fewer than thirty cooked over wood coals.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the fuel his Trail requires: wood or charcoal, on grates.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): what the Trail's Piedmont stops cook in.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): taught at his boot camps, beside butts, ribs, chicken and brisket.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): a stop on the Trail he drew; WRAL named it in his obituary.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): a stop on the Trail he drew; WRAL named it in his obituary.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): a stop on the Trail he drew; WRAL named it in his obituary.
- kin → stephensons-bar-b-q (place): a stop on the Trail he drew; WRAL named it in his obituary.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → short-sugars (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): a stop on the Trail he drew.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): one of the events his society existed to promote.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the eastern half of a Trail that runs Manteo to Murphy; he took no side.
- kin → lexington (style): the western half of the same Trail.

## Joe Bessinger (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/joe-bessinger/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/joe-bessinger.json
id: joe-bessinger
aliases: Joseph Jacob Bessinger · Big Joe Bessinger · Joseph Bessinger Sr.
facets: role=founder, sauce-maker, family · state=SC · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger, a farmer from Orangeburg County, traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for a cafe in Holly Hill and opened it in 1939 serving pork with a mustard-based sauce — the Golden Secret, his family calls it, worked out with the Sweatman family on shared German roots. Five of his sons opened barbecue restaurants on it: Maurice and Joe Jr. at West Columbia in 1953, Melvin and Thomas in Charleston from 1955, and, by two accounts, Robert. Some name him the inventor of South Carolina's mustard sauce; the evidence names no one.
story: Big Joe was one of fourteen children of Mack Bessinger and raised eleven of his own — Maurice was the eighth — on a farm near Orangeburg with his wife Genora. In 1939 he gave up farming, sold a cow, and opened the Holly Hill Café; Melvin, ten, was taught to make the sauce, and Maurice, nine, went to work in the restaurant. Robert Moss's 2011 history in the Charleston City Paper puts the move to Holly Hill in the 1940s; the family's own dates say 1939. After the war Melvin's Army pay went into a second Holly Hill restaurant, Eat At Joe's, in 1946, where Thomas started cooking at fourteen. Then the sons scattered with the recipe. Maurice and Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; Melvin closed Eat At Joe's in 1955 and moved to Charleston with Thomas, where Thomas opened his own place in 1960 and the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on Savannah Highway in 1961, renamed Bessinger's in 1971; Melvin crossed the Cooper River to Mount Pleasant in 1982. Moss writes that three sons — Melvin, Thomas and J.D. — opened Piggy Park drive-ins around Charleston; West Of lists Thomas, Melvin, Maurice, J.D., Woodrow and Robert as owners of competing restaurants, with Robert's Bar B Que in North Charleston. The businesses were separate: when Maurice raised Confederate flags in 2000 the Charleston brothers were reported as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'. His grandson David Bessinger told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2012: 'It's just in our blood.' *Inference —* the 'Joe Jr.' of Wikipedia and Maurice's obituary and the 'Joe David' or 'J.D.' of the Charleston writers are one son.
today: Dead; no source read for this record gives the year. The sauce he served in 1939 is on the tables of Maurice's Piggie Park, Bessinger's and Melvin's, and bottled by Maurice's heirs as Southern Gold.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): his eighth child, who started in the Holly Hill kitchen at nine and took the sauce to the supermarkets.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the West Columbia chain of his sons Maurice and Joe Jr., from 1953; his recipe is on its label.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): the Charleston house of his sons Melvin and Thomas, from 1961.
- kin → sweatmans-bar-b-que (place): the Holly Hill family he worked the mustard sauce out with; their pit opened in 1977.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): his Golden Secret of 1939, the earliest name attached to the Midlands sauce.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style his sons carried from Orangeburg County to Columbia and the coast.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name his son Maurice sold the family sauce under.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German-settled country whose roots the family and the Sweatmans credit the sauce to.

## John Shelton Reed (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/john-shelton-reed/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/john-shelton-reed.json
id: john-shelton-reed
aliases: Éminence Grease · Eminence Grease · J. S. Reed
facets: state=NC · role=scholar, writer, organizer · styles=eastern-nc, lexington
region: North Carolina
what: A sociologist of the American South, born 1942, who taught at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill from 1969 until 2000 and retired as William Rand Kenan Jr. Professor. With his wife Dale Volberg Reed and William McKinney he wrote Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue (UNC Press, 2008); alone, Barbecue: A Savor the South Cookbook (2016) and On Barbecue (2021). In 2013 he and Dan Levine founded the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which certifies restaurants that cook their local style over wood alone. He lives in Chapel Hill.
story: Reed came to barbecue after a career on the South itself: MIT, a Columbia doctorate in 1971, the Center for the Study of the American South, which he helped found, and the quarterly Southern Cultures, which he co-edited. Holy Smoke, written with Dale and William McKinney, gives North Carolina's two styles their history, their recipes and their people, and in it the Reeds lamented how much of the state's barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2011 he wrote the introduction to the Southern Foodways Alliance's North Carolina barbecue oral histories, opening with George Washington's diary for May 27, 1769 — a barbecue in Alexandria and a night away — and the point that until the early twentieth century barbecue was for harvests, fundraisers and rallies, never home cooking. The campaign came two years later: a retired professor 'with time on my hands', in his words, and Dan Levine, 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, set out to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood, Levine as Chief Smoke Detector, Reed as Éminence Grease. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they offered a prize — an apron, later a cap as well — to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch; two years on nobody had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states. Reed allows that gas is cheaper, easier and more consistent. Dale Volberg Reed died in 2018. On Barbecue (University of Tennessee Press, 2021) collects his essays, reviews and op-eds on the subject, and in 2023 the governor gave him the Order of the Long Leaf Pine.
today: Retired, in Chapel Hill; co-founder and Éminence Grease of the campaign, whose site listed about seventy North Carolina restaurants in January 2018 and remains active in 2026. His own site lists The Ramos Gin Fizz (LSU Press, 2025) and a revised 1001 Things Everyone Should Know About the South, due in 2027.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): co-founded it in 2013 with Dan Levine; Éminence Grease on its masthead; wrote the True 'Cue Challenge of April 23, 2014.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): wrote the introduction to its North Carolina barbecue oral-history project, posted April 25, 2011.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): grants that they are cheaper, easier and more consistent, and put up a prize for anyone who could name the regulation said to require them.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the only heat the campaign he co-founded certifies.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): the Reeds interviewed Wilber Shirley for Holy Smoke; UNC Press reprinted the interview when he died in 2021.
- kin → wilber-shirley (person): interviewed by the Reeds for Holy Smoke.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): Keith Allen, interviewed at length for Holy Smoke.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): one of the two styles Holy Smoke sets out, history and recipes together.
- kin → lexington (style): the other style Holy Smoke sets out.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): his line — that until the early twentieth century barbecue was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies — opens the Alliance's North Carolina project.
- kin → robert-moss (person): found in South Carolina, as Reed's challenge had in North Carolina, that no rule forbids cooking with wood.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): Reed's blurb on The One True Barbecue: it 'should be read by anyone who thinks barbecue is about sticky red sauce'.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word his 2016 Savor the South book takes as its whole title.
sources: s:wp-john-shelton-reed — John Shelton Reed — Wikipedia; s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue; s:reed-savor-the-south — Barbecue: A Savor the South Cookbook; s:reed-on-barbecue — On Barbecue; s:web-truecue-about — About — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:web-barbecuebible-campaign — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (John Shelton Reed, January 23, 2018); s:web-uncpress-reed-myth — John Shelton Reed: Busting a Barbecue Myth (April 6, 2016); s:web-sfa-north-carolina-bbq — North Carolina BBQ (oral history project, posted April 25, 2011; introduction by John Shelton Reed); s:web-uncpress-wilber-shirley — Celebrating the Life of North Carolina's Barbecue Legend Wilber Shirley — UNC Press Blog (16 Apr 2021); s:web-uncpress-keith-allen — Interview with Keith Allen, owner of Allen & Son Barbecue Restaurant in Chapel Hill, on the occasion of its closing — UNC Press Blog (19 Dec 2018); s:web-johnshelton-books — Books — John Shelton Reed (personal site); s:web-rienfertel-onetruebarbecue — The One True Barbecue — the author's book page; s:true-cue — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (True 'Cue)

## Lake High (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/lake-high/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/lake-high.json
id: lake-high
aliases: Lake E. High Jr. · Lake Edward High Jr.
facets: state=SC · role=founder, organizer, writer · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee, sc-light-tomato, sc-heavy-tomato
region: South Carolina, The South Carolina Midlands
what: Lake E. High Jr. of Columbia, a wine judge and, in his own account, a born critic, who founded the South Carolina Barbeque Association with the psychologist Walter Rolandi in 2004 to train judges and promote the state's barbecue, and wrote its history: A History of South Carolina Barbeque (The History Press, 2013). His account gives South Carolina all four of the barbecue sauces he counts — vinegar-and-pepper, mustard, light tomato and heavy tomato — each with a region and a date, and the association publishes them as a map.
story: High was 74 when South Carolina Living profiled him in September 2015 as 'the guru of 'que': a master judge of the association he founded, certified as well by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the Memphis Barbecue Network and the American Wine Society, who said he had probably eaten more barbeque than anyone in the state. When he and Rolandi founded the association the state had two cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association had certified more than 800 judges. His book, published in June 2013 while he was the association's president, runs from the 1500s — Native Americans cooking pork on frames after the Spanish brought the pig, and, in his telling, Europeans learning barbecue at the sixteenth-century colony of Santa Elena at what is now Port Royal — through the 1920s, when the craft settled into restaurants, to the cook-off era. The sauce account, posted on the association's site over his name as founder, runs in order of age: vinegar-and-pepper first, hundreds of years old; mustard from the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s, distinct to South Carolina; light tomato, vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900; heavy tomato, the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, he holds, has all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two: sweet mustard and spicy vinegar. In 2015 High told the magazine, 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the co-founders named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.
today: The association is active in 2026 with a full cook-off calendar; its site names High as founder and 'a professional wine judge' and lists no current officers. His book remains in print with The History Press. No later interview with High was found for this record (checked September 15, 2026).
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): co-founded it in 2004 with Walter Rolandi; its president when his book appeared in 2013; its historian.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): one of his four regions: the German mustard of the Midlands, which he dates to the settlers of the 1730s to 1750s.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): one of his four: vinegar-and-pepper, which he calls the oldest sauce.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): one of his four: vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): one of his four: the newest, of the last sixty years.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce his history credits to the German families — Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman among them.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the oldest sauce in his account, hundreds of years old.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900, in his account.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the newest sauce in his account.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name the mustard sauce carries on his association's map.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German-settled fork of the Midlands; his history credits those settlers with the mustard sauce.
- kin → robert-moss (person): the historian who counts two sauces where High counts four.
sources: s:web-scliving-guru-of-que — The guru of 'que (Diane Veto Parham, September 1, 2015); s:web-scba-about — About Us; s:web-scba-bbq-history — BBQ History (Lake E. High Jr.); s:web-google-books-high-sc-barbeque — A History of South Carolina Barbeque — publisher's description and author note; s:web-columbia-star-scba-leadership — S.C. ## Maurice Bessinger (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/maurice-bessinger/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/maurice-bessinger.json
id: maurice-bessinger
aliases: Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr. · L. Maurice Bessinger
facets: role=founder, sauce-maker · state=SC · styles=sc-mustard
region: The South Carolina Midlands, South Carolina
what: Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr. (July 14, 1930 – February 22, 2014) opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr., built it into a chain, and bottled his father's mustard sauce as Carolina Gold for supermarkets nationwide. He refused Black customers until the suit that became Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises (1968), ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and raised the Confederate flag over his restaurants on July 1, 2000, the day it came off the State House dome. His children took the last flags down in 2013.
story: Bessinger was born on the family farm near Orangeburg on July 14, 1930, the eighth of eleven children of Joseph Jacob and Genora Thomas Bessinger, and started cooking at nine in his father's Holly Hill restaurant in 1939. He served in the Army in the Korean War, came home in 1952, and with Joe Jr. opened the first Piggie Park drive-in in West Columbia in 1953; there were four by 1964. That year Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry, and Matthew J. Perry filed a class action under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Bessinger answered that his religious beliefs compelled him to oppose integration. The district court held the Act reached his sandwich shop but not the drive-ins; the Fourth Circuit reversed; and in 1968 the Supreme Court held 8–0 in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, 390 U.S. 400, that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. He chaired George Wallace's 1964 campaign in the state, lost a House race that year by about a hundred votes, and took 2.5 percent in the 1974 Democratic primary for governor. By 1999 the sauce — mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar, sold as Carolina Gold — had made his the largest barbecue business in the country. On July 1, 2000 he raised Confederate flags over them and called the flag a Christian symbol; his restaurants distributed a tract arguing that slavery is not inherently evil; Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce, and his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007. He published an autobiography, Defending My Heritage, in 2001. He died on February 22, 2014, at eighty-three.
today: Dead: February 22, 2014, West Columbia, aged eighty-three. His sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run Maurice's Piggie Park; the flags came down by 2013 and the sauce is sold as Southern Gold.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the drive-in he opened in 1953 and ran until his death in 2014.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): his father, in whose Holly Hill restaurant he started cooking at nine.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): he bottled it as Carolina Gold, put it in supermarkets nationwide, and lost those shelves in 2000.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): his brand name for the sauce, from the 1990s until his family renamed it Southern Gold.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style he made a national product and the name that carries its court case.
- kin → bessingers-bar-b-q (place): his brother Thomas's Charleston house, reported as a separate concern when the flags went up.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): he ran for the House in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and chaired George Wallace's state campaign.
sources: s:wp-maurice-bessinger — Maurice Bessinger — Wikipedia; s:wp-newman-v-piggie-park-enterprises-inc — Newman v. Maurice Bessinger Sr. obituary — The State, via Legacy.com (February 2014); s:web-piggiepark-history — Uncover Our Rich History — Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ; s:web-baltimore-sun-bessinger-2002 — S.C. barbecue king stands his ground (September 22, 2002); s:web-seattle-times-piggie-park-2002 — Confederate flag still flies over Piggie Park — Ariel Sabar (October 5, 2002)

## Pete Jones (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/pete-jones/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/pete-jones.json
id: pete-jones
aliases: Walter B. Jones · Walter B. 'Pete' Jones
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Walter B. 'Pete' Jones (died 2006) opened the Skylight Inn in Ayden, Pitt County, in the summer of 1947 — at seventeen by his family's count, eighteen by Wikipedia's — and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for nearly sixty years. He learned the trade at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe, counted his barbecue back to a Dennis ancestor's wagon, and put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on his roof after National Geographic called the place the barbecue capital of the world. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.
story: Pete Jones told Bob Garner that he sat in school as far back as the fifth or sixth grade and daydreamed about having his own barbecue place. He got it at seventeen: he built the Skylight while working for his uncle Emmitt Dennis at the City Cafe, where he cooked whole hog, and opened on July 8, 1947. He gave the place beer and a jukebox to set it apart from Ayden's other barbecue stands, thought about adding a dance hall, and ran late with rowdy crowds until the town's 7 pm curfew ended the late nights. The cooking did not change: whole hogs, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits, chopped with the crisp skin through the meat. He could not read or write, Kathleen Purvis records in Garden & Gun. In 1979 a National Geographic article called the restaurant the barbecue capital of the world; the dome went up in 1984, silver-painted wood, so that people could find the place — 'A place like this don't need any sign,' he told Garner. By the restaurant's own account he cooked at a congressional event attended by President Reagan and Vice President Bush in 1982, and in 2003 the James Beard Foundation named the Skylight an America's Classic. His line on fuel — 'If it's not cooked with wood, it's not barbecue' — is the one the Campaign for Real Barbecue prints on its wood page. He died in February 2006; his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam kept the pits.
today: Dead. Pete Jones died in February 2006 by the restaurant's account; Wikipedia gives the year, and Bob Garner's 2012 profile prints 2005. The Skylight Inn is run by his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam Jones.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the pit he opened in 1947 and ran until his death; the dome on its roof was his answer to National Geographic.
- kin → sam-jones (person): his grandson, who grew up in the Skylight and carried the family's whole hog to Winterville and Raleigh.
- kin → skilton-dennis (person): the ancestor whose wagon he counted his barbecue back to; the 1830 on the billboard is his family's date.
- kin → bum-dennis (person): his kinsman across town, of the same Dennis line, who opened Bum's in 1963.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style he is named for first when the east is named: whole hog over wood, vinegar and pepper, cornbread.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the only cut he cooked, heads on, the skin chopped into the meat.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): his grandson's restaurant, seven miles from his own.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): quotes him on its wood page: 'If it's not cooked with wood, it's not barbecue.'
- kin → pitmaster (term): he ran the Skylight's pits for most of sixty years before the word was in the dictionaries.
- kin → bob-garner (person): profiled him for Our State in 2012 and kept his line about the sign.
sources: s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:web-skylightinn-about — About Us — Skylight Inn BBQ; s:web-ourstate-skylight-inn — The Skylight Inn — Our State (Bob Garner, 31 Aug 2012); s:sfa-skylight-inn — Skylight Inn — Samuel Jones, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 29 Nov 2011; s:web-gardenandgun-sam-jones-2019 — Sam Jones, North Carolina's Barbecue Baron — Garden & Gun (Kathleen Purvis, April/May 2019); s:web-samjonesbbq — Sam Jones BBQ — official site (home and About pages); s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue

## Rien Fertel (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/rien-fertel/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/rien-fertel.json
id: rien-fertel
aliases: Rien T. Fertel
facets: role=writer, scholar · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee
region: The American South, The Carolinas
what: A New Orleans writer and historian — a Tulane doctorate in history, 2013 — who recorded the Southern Foodways Alliance's barbecue oral histories in North Carolina in 2011 and South Carolina in 2012, then spent five years following the whole-hog pitmasters of Tennessee and the Carolinas for The One True Barbecue (Touchstone, 2016): part travelogue, part memoir, about the cooks who fire, flip and chop 200-pound pigs in smoke-filled pit houses, from Rodney Scott of Hemingway and Sam Jones of Ayden to Ricky Parker of Lexington, Tennessee.
story: Fertel's first bite of whole hog was at Siler's Old Time BBQ in Henderson, Tennessee, in 2008, and the cook who held his attention was Ricky Parker of Scott's-Parker's in Lexington, Tennessee, who died of liver disease at fifty-one; Fertel went back to see Parker's sons at the pits. For the Southern Foodways Alliance he recorded the North Carolina set in November and December 2011 — Chip Stamey in Greensboro, Sonny Conrad at the Barbecue Center, David Wilson at Short Sugar's, Brandon Cook at Cook's, Debbie Holt at Clyde Cooper's, the Parker's crew in Wilson, Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn on November 29, Bum and Larry Dennis in Ayden, Stephen and Gerri Grady in Dudley — and the South Carolina set in June 2012: Douglas Oliver at Sweatman's, Tony Kittrell at Dukes, Jay Allen at Midway, Jackie Hite, Russell Cooper at Cooper's Country Store, the Browns in Kingstree, David Bessinger at Melvin's, and Rodney Scott in Hemingway, where the pits were turning eight to ten hogs a night. The One True Barbecue follows the whole-hog line from those pits: Scott, who went on to a Charleston restaurant and a James Beard award; Jones, the Skylight's grandson; Keith 'Pop' Ward, who tends Wilber's pits through the night in Goldsboro; Oliver at Sweatman's; three places named Scott's; and a new generation, Tyson Ho at Arrogant Swine in Brooklyn and Elliott Moss at Buxton Hall in Asheville. Robert Moss reviewed it for Southern Living, and John Shelton Reed wrote that it 'should be read by anyone who thinks barbecue is about sticky red sauce'. Fertel holds that most barbecue writing is hyperbole.
today: Visiting professor of history at Tulane and book critic for the Times-Picayune/Advocate; his fourth book, Brown Pelican (LSU Press, 2022), left barbecue behind. He calls New Orleans home and lives part of the time in a century-old church in St. Martinville, Louisiana.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded its North Carolina barbecue interviews in November and December 2011 and its South Carolina set in June 2012, before writing The One True Barbecue.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cooking The One True Barbecue is about: the pitmasters who cook the whole animal, in Tennessee and the Carolinas.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): interviewed Samuel Jones there on November 29, 2011; one of the pits his book follows.
- kin → sam-jones (person): the Skylight's grandson, one of the pitmasters his book follows.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): interviewed Rodney Scott there in June 2012; one of three places named Scott's in his book.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): followed from the Hemingway pits onto the national scene in his book.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): where Keith 'Pop' Ward, who tends the pits through the night, is one of his subjects.

## Robert F. Moss (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/robert-moss/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/robert-moss.json
id: robert-moss
aliases: Robert Moss · Robert F. Moss
facets: state=SC · role=writer, scholar · styles=sc-mustard, sc-pee-dee
region: South Carolina, The Lowcountry
what: A food writer and historian in Charleston — a Furman graduate with a doctorate in English from the University of South Carolina — who is contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and was restaurant critic for the Post and Courier. Barbecue: The History of an American Institution (University of Alabama Press, 2010; revised and expanded 2020) is a documentary history of the subject built from newspapers, letters, diaries and travel narratives; Barbecue Lover's the Carolinas (2015) is his guide to both states. He counts South Carolina's sauces as two, mustard and vinegar, where the state's association counts four.
story: Moss's history reads the colonial and early-republic barbecue out of the record: whole hogs cooked as a ritual in the British colonies by the eighteenth century, the communal feast spreading from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s, the political barbecue as an institution of the new republic, and the restaurants of the twentieth century. The second edition, published October 6, 2020, added colonial material, profiles of early restaurateurs and African American cooks, and a final chapter, 'The Second Golden Age of Barbecue', on the wood-cooked places that opened across the country in the 2010s. On South Carolina hash he went to the newspapers — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring, in the Abbeville Press and Banner of 1854 — and traced the name to haslet, the old word for the viscera: the head, liver and lights the whole hog left behind. When the Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading, he answered in Southern Living that new places were putting it on their menus, and used the recently closed Cannon's in Little Mountain as his example of the Midlands' mustard-yellow kind. He has tested Summerville's claim to sweet tea (2013) and told the story of hushpuppies (2023). When John Shelton Reed's campaign asked in 2014 for any regulation that forbade wood cooking in North Carolina, Moss looked in South Carolina and reported in the Columbia Free Times that there was none there either. He reviewed Rien Fertel's The One True Barbecue for Southern Living in 2016. His other books are Southern Spirits (2016), The Lost Southern Chefs (University of Georgia Press, 2022) and The Roffignac (LSU Press, 2024).
today: Based in Charleston; contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and a frequent contributor to Charleston Magazine, Garden & Gun, Serious Eats and The Local Palate. His site, robertfmoss.com, carries his features on hash, hushpuppies and the revised history.
- kin → barbecue (term): his 2010 history is the source behind the colonial feast and the political barbecue in the word's story.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the institution of the early republic he documents from newspapers, letters and diaries.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): which he finds established as a ritual in the British colonies by the eighteenth century.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): found in the 1854 Abbeville newspapers; he traced the name to haslet, the old word for the viscera.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): whose story he told on his site in 2023.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): Summerville's claim to it, which he tested for the Charleston City Paper in 2013.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): one of the two sauces he counts: sweet mustard.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the other: spicy vinegar.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): a variation on vinegar sauce, in his count, not a region of its own.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): folded back into the vinegar family by his count.
- kin → cannons-bbq (place): his example of the Midlands' mustard-yellow hash, recently closed when he wrote in March 2020.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): counts four sauces where he counts two.
- kin → lake-high (person): whose four-sauce map he answers with two.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): found no South Carolina rule against wood cooking, as the campaign's 2014 challenge found none in North Carolina.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): whose True 'Cue Challenge Moss answered from South Carolina in the Columbia Free Times.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): whose The One True Barbecue Moss reviewed for Southern Living in May 2016.
- not to be confused with elliott-moss: Elliott Moss is the pitmaster who opened Buxton Hall in Asheville; Robert F. Moss is the Charleston historian. No relation is recorded.

## Rodney Scott (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/rodney-scott/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/rodney-scott.json
id: rodney-scott
aliases: Pitmaster Scott
facets: role=pitmaster, founder, chef, writer · state=SC · styles=sc-pee-dee
region: The Pee Dee, The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: Rodney Scott (born November 1, 1971) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Hemingway, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who cooked his first pig at eleven at his parents' store, took the business over in 2011, and in February 2017 opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis. In 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. His book with Lolis Eric Elie, Rodney Scott's World of BBQ, came out in 2021. Every Rodney Scott's location closed in May 2026; he cooks pop-ups as Pitmaster Scott.
story: Roosevelt and Ella Scott moved from Philadelphia to the Pee Dee in 1972 with their infant son, farmed and raised hogs near Nesmith, and opened a gas station and variety store on the Hemingway highway; the barbecue began as a weekend hog. Rodney cooked his first at eleven and was full time at seventeen, when the store cooked four to six a week. 'My whole life has been barbecue,' he told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, by which time the pits held eight to ten hogs a night. John T. Edge had profiled the store in 2009, and Nick Pihakis of the Jim 'N Nick's chain, a customer, told him he was undercharging. On November 27, 2013 the wooden cookhouse burned; Scott took his hogs on the road — the Bar-B-Que in Exile Tour, staged with Pihakis's Fatback Collective — to rebuild in metal. After a quarrel with his father in 2016 he left Hemingway, and in February 2017 he and Pihakis opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in a former fried-chicken house on upper King Street, Charleston. In May 2018 the James Beard Foundation gave him its Best Chef: Southeast award; the Chef's Table: BBQ episode about him in 2020 set the restaurant's sales records three days running. Birmingham followed in 2019, Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021, and the book with Lolis Eric Elie the same year. On May 3, 2026 the King Street restaurant closed 'until further notice' amid suits and liens against Pihakis Restaurant Group, and the other locations with it; in June he cooked at Munkle Brewing under a new name, Pitmaster Scott. Roosevelt Scott died in 2020 and Ella in 2023; the Hemingway store reopened in May 2024 under her brother Sam Wilson and Rodney's son Dominic.
today: Living. His Charleston restaurant has been closed since May 3, 2026; he cooks pop-ups in Charleston as Pitmaster Scott, has said that reopening there is his first priority, and was announced in July 2026 as a headliner of the Pair'd Margaret River Region Festival in Western Australia.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): his parents' store and pits at Hemingway, where he cooked his first hog at eleven and which he ran from 2011 to 2017.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): the Charleston restaurant that carried his name from February 2017 until it closed in May 2026.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the style he took to the coast: whole hog over hardwood coals, vinegar and pepper.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut in his restaurant's name and the one he has cooked since he was eleven.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): his sauce: 'vinegar, pepper, some more pepper, some love', as the Hemingway record gives it.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the barrel his wood burns down in before the coals go under the hog; NPR described it in 2014.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded him at Hemingway on June 21, 2012, for its South Carolina project.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed him for the Alliance in 2012.
- kin → pitmaster (term): the word in his Wikipedia title, his 2018 award's footnote — the second pitmaster with a Beard chef award — and his 2026 pop-up name.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): quotes him on its wood page: 'When I see the future of barbecue I see pits, I see fire, I see wood-burning.'

## Sam Jones (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/sam-jones/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/sam-jones.json
id: sam-jones
aliases: Samuel Jones
facets: role=pitmaster, founder, family, writer · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Samuel 'Sam' Jones is the grandson of Pete Jones and a third-generation pitmaster of the Skylight Inn in Ayden, where he sold chopped pork as a child. With Michael Letchworth he opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville on November 10, 2015, and a second restaurant in Raleigh in February 2021. His book with Daniel Vaughn, Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue (2019), writes the family method down. He was a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South (2025).
story: At four, Sam Jones told a reporter that he wanted to be a trash man and the Prince of Barbecue; his father Bruce joked about putting hog grease in his milk bottle. He grew up in the Skylight Inn, quit it at fifteen, and came back after a college paper on barbecue told him what his work was. He described the return to Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 as a flag-bearer's job, keeping the standard up on the field: 'I don't want our style of barbecue to be one of them things where you read about it in the history books. I want it to be one of them things where you can go get it and taste it and see it.' Southern Living put him among ten Southern pitmasters in 2012. A cooking event in Charleston in 2013 turned him toward a place of his own; in 2014 he and Michael Letchworth signed for a loan, and Sam Jones BBQ opened in Winterville on November 10, 2015, with a longer menu than the Skylight's — ribs, turkey, chicken, banana pudding — around the same wood-cooked hog. The James Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018; Whole Hog BBQ, written with Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly, came out from Ten Speed Press in 2019. The Raleigh restaurant opened in a former garage on West Lenoir Street in February 2021. He has served as Ayden's fire chief, lives on the farm he grew up on with his wife Sarah and two daughters, and told Garden & Gun in 2019: 'Today I'm proud to be from Ayden, North Carolina.'
today: Living. He runs Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville and Raleigh with Michael Letchworth and the Skylight Inn with his father Bruce and Jeff Jones; a stall in Raleigh's Morgan Street Food Hall is planned for the end of 2026, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South, November 2025.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): the family pit he grew up in and still helps run; his grandfather opened it in 1947.
- kin → sam-jones-bbq (place): his own restaurant, opened in Winterville in 2015 with Michael Letchworth and in Raleigh in 2021.
- kin → pete-jones (person): his grandfather, whose whole hog over wood is the method he wrote down.
- kin → skilton-dennis (person): the ancestor whose 1830 wagon his family's billboard names as the start of the trade.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style he cooks and wrote the book on: whole hog, wood coals, vinegar and pepper.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, cooked whole and chopped with the skin, at both of his restaurants.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded his oral history at the Skylight Inn on November 29, 2011, before he had a restaurant of his own.
- kin → rien-fertel (person): interviewed him for the Alliance in 2011.
- kin → pitmaster (term): Southern Living named him one of ten Southern pitmasters in 2012.

Fertel, 29 Nov 2011; s:web-samjonesbbq — Sam Jones BBQ — official site (home and About pages); s:web-southernsmoke-sam-jones — Sam Jones — chef biography, Southern Smoke Foundation; s:web-gardenandgun-sam-jones-2019 — Sam Jones, North Carolina's Barbecue Baron — Garden & Gun (Kathleen Purvis, April/May 2019); s:web-hoodline-sam-jones-morgan-street-2026 — Sam Jones BBQ plants second Raleigh flag at Morgan Street Food Hall — Hoodline (9 Sep 2026); s:web-visitraleigh-sam-jones — Sam Jones BBQ is Now Open in Raleigh, N.C.! — Visit Raleigh (10 Feb 2021); s:jones-whole-hog-bbq — Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia

## Sid Weaver (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/sid-weaver/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/sid-weaver.json
id: sid-weaver
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent across from the Davidson County courthouse in Lexington from 1919 — cooked in the alley behind, sold to people on their way to court — and is the first name in every account of Lexington-style barbecue. Jess Swicegood set up beside him within the decade; the two taught Warner Stamey, and Weaver's hand Alton Beck built the town's first permanent barbecue restaurant in 1938. What is known of him is the tent, the date, the pupils and the sauce that came out of those stands: vinegar and pepper with ketchup, the Piedmont's dip.
story: Our State's Jeremy Markovich calls him Lexington barbecue's Abraham, 'first cooking up his barbecue in the alley outside and selling it from a tent to people heading over to the old courthouse in 1919'. Robert Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros summarize it, has him first and Jess Swicegood joining him later, the two working out the shoulder-and-dip style and spreading it across the Piedmont. Stamey's own history puts both men 'selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse' when Warner Stamey, boarding with his sister for high school in the late 1920s, came to learn from them; the American Royal's 2020 citation for Stamey says they taught him everything there was to know about pit cooking. Alton Beck, who had worked for Weaver, opened the first bricks-and-mortar barbecue restaurant in town on West Center Street in 1938, rebuilt it in 1949, and retired after thirty-one years; the wood pits found behind a wall of Lexington's city hall in 2015 are thought to be his. *Tradition holds —* Weaver later built a small cafe of his own near the square. No birth date, death date or photograph of Weaver is in any source read for this record.
today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The stands are gone; Lexington counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, and the Lexington Barbecue Festival has closed Main Street each October since 1984, a few blocks from where the tent stood.
- kin → lexington (style): the style begins with his tent by the courthouse in 1919.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): the stand beside his; the two are named together as the men who taught Warner Stamey.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): his pupil, who carried the method to Shelby and Greensboro.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce came out of his tent and Swicegood's: vinegar and pepper with ketchup.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): the Greensboro house of his pupil, two steps from the tent.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): Wayne Monk learned under Stamey, who learned under Weaver; the pit is his grandchild.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): held each October since 1984 on the Main Street his tent sold to.
sources: s:web-ourstate-lexington-cover-up — The Great Lexington Barbecue Cover-Up (Jeremy Markovich, 31 Mar 2015); s:web-stameys-history — History; s:web-americanroyal-stamey-bio — Warner Stamey, Pitmaster, Restaurateur — 2020 Legacy Inductee biography, American Royal Barbecue Hall of Fame (PDF); s:web-barbecuebros-jess-swicegood — Jess Swicegood — Barbecue Bros tag page, summarizing Robert F. Moss, Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:moss-barbecue-history — Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:sfa-stameys-barbecue — Stamey's Barbecue — Chip Stamey, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 18 Nov 2011; s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-barbecue-festival — Lexington Barbecue Festival — Wikipedia; s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue

## Skilton Dennis (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/skilton-dennis/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/skilton-dennis.json
id: skilton-dennis
aliases: Skilton M. Dennis
facets: role=cook, family · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Skilton Dennis is the ancestor the Dennis and Jones families of Ayden name as the start of barbecue for sale in North Carolina: by their account he sold smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis, of the same family, founded the town. The 1830 is painted on the Skylight Inn's billboard as one of its four tenets and was recorded from Bum and Larry Dennis by the Southern Foodways Alliance; Bob Garner's 2012 profile of Pete Jones puts the covered wagon in the mid-1800s. No document has been produced.
story: The claim is the families'. Pete Jones, who opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, learned the trade from the Dennis side of his family and liked to say that barbecue ran in his blood; his great-great-grandfather, he told Bob Garner, sold barbecue from a covered wagon in Ayden in the mid-1800s. The billboard outside the Skylight sets the tradition at 1830. Bum Dennis and his son Larry gave Rien Fertel the same story for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011: Skilton Dennis selling smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis founding the 'enigmatically-named' town. John Tanner's post on Bum's death counts the wagon-seller as a great-great-great-grandfather, 'add 4 or 5 more greats' — the arithmetic of a family story, not of a record. The Alliance's page for Sam Jones says the Dennis clan's history shows them as the first in North Carolina to serve pit barbecue publicly. *Inference —* Ayden was incorporated only in 1891, around a railroad depot on William Henry Harris's farm; a wagon in 1830 would have served the farms and churches of what became southern Pitt County, not a town. *Inference —* this project has seen no census, deed or grave for a Skilton Dennis selling barbecue in 1830; the date is held here as the families' and nothing more.
today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The two families that tell his story cook whole hog in Ayden: the Joneses at the Skylight Inn, opened 1947, and the Dennises at Bum's Restaurant, opened 1963, a few blocks apart.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): its billboard names his 1830 wagon as the tradition the Jones family upholds.
- kin → bums-restaurant (place): the Dennis family's pit, whose founder told the Alliance the wagon story in 2011.
- kin → pete-jones (person): his descendant, who put the 1830 on the Skylight's sign.
- kin → bum-dennis (person): his descendant, who gave the Southern Foodways Alliance the wagon and the date.
- kin → sam-jones (person): his descendant, who wrote the family's claim into a book in 2019.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose oldest dated claim — a wagon, 1830, Ayden — is his.
sources: s:sfa-bums-restaurant — Bum's Restaurant — Latham 'Bum' Dennis and Larry Dennis, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 5 Dec 2011; s:sfa-skylight-inn — Skylight Inn — Samuel Jones, interviewed by Rien T. ## Warner Stamey (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/warner-stamey/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/warner-stamey.json
id: warner-stamey
aliases: Charles Warner Stamey · C. Warner Stamey
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Charles Warner Stamey (born 1911), the youngest of eleven children, learned pit-cooking as a high-school boarder in Lexington from Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver at their tents across from the courthouse, sold barbecue in Shelby through the 1930s, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's stand and rename it Stamey's, and in 1953 opened the Greensboro drive-in his family runs. His restaurant credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue in North Carolina. Wayne Monk, Red Bridges and his brother-in-law Alston Bridges learned under him; the American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2020.
story: Stamey was born in 1911 — in Lincoln County, by Cleveland County's local history — and moved to Lexington to live with his older sister while he attended high school. There he hooked up with Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver, who were selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse, and they taught him pit cooking. With a diploma and $350 he went to Shelby and sold barbecue to growing crowds; he married Mary Linda Bridges in 1933, and the county history has Stamey's Barbecue at 230 South Washington Street in 1937. Her brother Alston Bridges learned smoking from him and managed his Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years; Red Bridges, no relation, learned from him too and opened at the same Washington Street address about 1949. In 1938 Stamey sold the Shelby operation, went back to Lexington, bought Swicegood's and put his own name on it — for $300, Robert Moss's history says. Wayne Monk worked under him there for several years before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962. In 1953 Stamey opened a drive-in on High Point Road in Greensboro, his sixth restaurant by the American Royal's count, with call-in service; four years later he handed it to his son Charles, and Charles's brother Keith joined in 1970. The hushpuppy — the fried cornmeal fritter of the fish camps — went onto the barbecue tray under him: Keith said his father picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro, and the restaurant's history says he introduced it to North Carolina barbecue diners. Chip Stamey, his grandson, left another career to take the Greensboro house in 1993, and told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that his rule is to keep everything the same.
today: Dead; his death year is not confirmed by any source this record cites. The American Royal inducted him as a 2020 legacy member of its Barbecue Hall of Fame, and the fourth generation of Stameys runs the two Greensboro restaurants.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): the Greensboro house he opened as a drive-in in 1953, run by his grandson Chip since 1993.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): the pit of his pupil Wayne Monk, opened 1962.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): Red Bridges learned from him in Shelby and opened at Stamey's old Washington Street address about 1949.
- kin → lexington (style): the style he carried to Shelby and Greensboro and taught to the men who run its pits.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): his teacher, whose Lexington stand he bought and renamed in 1938.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): his other teacher at the courthouse tents.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): worked under him for several years in Lexington before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): he put them beside barbecue, by his family's account, after seeing them at a Greensboro fish camp.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce he learned in the courthouse tents and served in Shelby, Lexington and Greensboro.
- kin → dip (term): the family's word for the sauce, served at the table and not squirted.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut he took from the tents to Shelby: shoulders over hickory coals.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): recorded his grandson Chip at the Greensboro restaurant on November 18, 2011.
sources: s:web-stameys-history — History; s:web-americanroyal-stamey-bio — Warner Stamey, Pitmaster, Restaurateur — 2020 Legacy Inductee biography, American Royal Barbecue Hall of Fame (PDF); s:sfa-stameys-barbecue — Stamey's Barbecue — Chip Stamey, interviewed by Rien T. Fertel, 18 Nov 2011; s:web-clevelandcounty-food — Food & Eateries — Cleveland County History; s:web-ourstate-stameys — Stamey's Old Fashioned Barbecue (Bob Garner, 31 Aug 2012); s:web-ourstate-lexington-barbecue — Lexington Barbecue (Bob Garner, 2012-08-31); s:web-barbecuebros-jess-swicegood — Jess Swicegood — Barbecue Bros tag page, summarizing Robert F. Moss, Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:web-moss-hushpuppies — The True Story of Hushpuppies, a Genuine Carolina Treat (Robert F. Moss, 2023-06-25); s:moss-barbecue-history — Barbecue: The History of an American Institution
