## Wayne Monk (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/wayne-monk/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/wayne-monk.json
id: wayne-monk
aliases: Honeymonk
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: Wayne Monk opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in Lexington, Davidson County, in 1962, at twenty-six, after years as a carhop and then a pit hand under Warner Stamey, and he owns it with his son Rick. The pit cooks pork shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them with the dip, the Piedmont's thin red vinegar sauce; locals call it the Honeymonk, from his name and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt's. He cooked for the heads of government at the 1983 economic summit in Williamsburg, and the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.
story: Monk was a teenage carhop at a Lexington barbecue place, worked for Holland Tussey, and spent several years working directly under Warner Stamey at Stamey's in downtown Lexington — Stamey had bought Jess Swicegood's stand there in 1938 — so that his own pit stands two teachers from the courthouse tents of 1919. At twenty-six, in 1962, he bought a roadside parcel beside U.S. Highway 29/70 that had been Tussey's, built onto the small cafe on it, and opened Lexington Barbecue #1 with Sonny Hunneycutt; the partner left, and the joined name, Honeymonk, stayed on the town's tongue. In 1983 a politically connected local attorney asked whether he would cook for President Reagan, and he served barbecue to the heads of government at that year's economic summit in Williamsburg, Virginia, Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand among them. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003, the same year as the Skylight Inn in Ayden. Garden & Gun found three generations at the pits in 2015: Wayne; Rick, who started at thirteen and is pitmaster, bookkeeper or janitor as the day requires; and Rick's son Nathan, who began in the kitchen at about sixteen. 'It's not a job. It's a way of life,' Rick said. The American Royal inducted Wayne Monk into its Barbecue Hall of Fame on September 14, 2019 — he 'set the standard that practically defines North Carolina barbecue', the citation said — and the new North Carolina Bar-B-Q Hall of Fame inducted him at Burlington on March 1, 2024.
today: Living: no death notice was found in the sources read for this record (September 2026). The restaurant's site names him as founder and lists Rick Monk as owner; Lexington Barbecue is open Tuesday to Saturday at 100 Smokehouse Lane, Lexington.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): the pit he opened in 1962 and owns with his son Rick.
- kin → lexington (style): the style, in the restaurant most often named as its standing example.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): his teacher: he worked under Stamey for several years in downtown Lexington before opening his own place.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): his teacher's Greensboro house, opened in 1953 while Monk was still learning.
- kin → jess-swicegood (person): the stand Stamey bought in 1938 is where Monk's teacher learned; his pit is two steps from Swicegood's tent.
- kin → sid-weaver (person): the 1919 tent at the head of the line Monk stands in.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): his sauce, which went to the 1983 economic summit at Williamsburg.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut he has cooked since 1962, over oak and hickory coals.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the pits under his four chimneys, whose smoke shows from the road.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the crusty outside of his shoulders, which Bob Garner described set aside on the block.
- kin → pitmaster (term): 'serving pork barbecue since 1962' — two decades before the dictionaries record the word.
- kin → bob-garner (person): wrote his Our State profile in 2012, the source for Tussey, Stamey and the summit.

Miller (29 May 2019); s:web-gardenandgun-keepers-of-the-flame — Keepers of the Flame — Garden & Gun (Jed Portman and John T. Edge, June/July 2015); s:wp-lexington-barbecue — Lexington Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-stameys-history — History; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia

## Wilber Shirley (person)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/person/wilber-shirley/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/person/wilber-shirley.json
id: wilber-shirley
aliases: Wilberdean Shirley · Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley
facets: role=pitmaster, founder · state=NC · styles=eastern-nc
region: Eastern North Carolina, North Carolina
what: Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley (1930–2021) learned barbecue at Griffin's in Goldsboro, bought the former Hill's Barbecue on U.S. 70 east of town in 1962 and put his name on it, and cooked split whole hogs over oak coals there for more than forty years. Wilber's fed presidents, governors and senators and, on a holiday weekend, up to 130 pigs. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes; a group of customers bought it and reopened it in July 2020, while he lived. He died on April 5, 2021, at ninety.
story: 'I went to work at a place called Griffin's Barbecue... That's how I first learned to cook it,' he told John Shelton Reed and Dale Volberg Reed for Holy Smoke. In 1962 — July 24, 1961, by WRAL's obituary — he bought Hill's Barbecue on Highway 70 and renamed it. 'Split halves of whole hogs over oak coals in closed pits,' he said of his method: 'That grease hitting those coals makes the smoked flavor. You can't spray it on there, paint it on there, put it on there.' The pits ran overnight, from about ten at night to ten in the morning; in season the place cooked 100 to 125 pigs a week, and Our State counts 130 on a Labor Day weekend and dining rooms for more than 300. 'I work seven days a week,' he said. 'Some weeks I come in eight days a week.' A waitress had been there more than thirty years, a cook since before he bought the place. Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton, Governors Terry Sanford and Jim Hunt and Senator Jesse Helms ate there. The restaurant was shut in March 2019 for nonpayment of taxes. Willis B. Underwood III, an insurance salesman who had eaten there all his life, gathered other regulars into Goldpit Partners, bought it, and reopened it in July 2020 for curbside orders: 'I just didn't want to see the smoke die.' Shirley, a longtime member of First Free Will Baptist Church in Goldsboro, died at a retirement community in Kinston on April 5, 2021. The Campaign for Real Barbecue quotes him on its wood page: cooking whole hogs over hardwood coals overnight 'is not easy or cheap, but it is the right way, and something we as a community take a lot of pride in'.
today: Dead: April 5, 2021, at Kinston, aged ninety. Wilber's Barbecue is open under Goldpit Partners at 4172 U.S. Highway 70 East, Goldsboro, cooking whole hogs over oak; his portrait hangs in the dining room.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): the pit he bought and named in 1962 and ran until the 2019 closure.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style as he stated it: split whole hogs over oak coals, a thin vinegar sauce, grease on the coals for the smoke.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut, split in halves, 100 to 125 a week in season.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): oak, split and cut by his staff all year.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): interviewed him for Holy Smoke; the quotations here are from that book.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): quotes him on its wood page on the cost and the pride of overnight hardwood coals.
- kin → scotts-famous-barbecue (place): Goldsboro's earlier barbecue name, whose founder began at his back door in 1917.
- kin → adam-scott (person): the Goldsboro cook of the generation before his; Scott's sauce is still sold in the town where Wilber's still cooks.
sources: s:web-wral-wilber-shirley-dies — Wilber Shirley, original owner of Wilber's Barbecue in Goldsboro, dies at 90 — WRAL (5 Apr 2021); s:web-uncpress-wilber-shirley — Celebrating the Life of North Carolina's Barbecue Legend Wilber Shirley — UNC Press Blog (16 Apr 2021); s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue; s:web-ourstate-wilbers-way — Where There's A Wilber's, There's A Way — Our State; s:web-ourstate-wilbers — Wilber's Barbecue in Goldsboro, NC — Our State; s:web-wral-wilbers-reopens — Loyal fans restore, reopen Wilber's Barbecue in Goldsboro — WRAL (15 Jul 2020); s:web-gardenandgun-wilbers — Wilber's Barbecue Bounces Back — Garden & Gun; s:web-wilbersbbq — Wilber's Barbecue — official site; s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue

## Campaign for Real Barbecue (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/org/campaign-for-real-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/org/campaign-for-real-barbecue.json
id: campaign-for-real-barbecue
aliases: True 'Cue · True Cue · the Campaign · True 'Cue USA
said: Its members say True 'Cue; the full name is on the certificate.
facets: state=both · founded=2013 · status=open
region: North Carolina, South Carolina, The American South
what: A campaign, founded in 2013 by the sociologist and barbecue writer John Shelton Reed and the blogger Dan Levine, that certifies restaurants which cook the barbecue style traditional to their area and rely solely on wood for heat, and gives them a certificate and a decal. It began in North Carolina — about seventy places certified by January 2018 — and has regional 'smoke detectors' for South Carolina, Kentucky, Georgia, Alabama and the Virginia–Washington region under a True 'Cue USA program. Its three stated goals are to celebrate wood-cooking, to honor the places that keep it, and to teach eaters the difference between wood-cooked barbecue and what it calls 'faux 'cue'.
story: Reed and his wife Dale wrote Holy Smoke (2008) and in it lamented how much North Carolina barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2013 he and Dan Levine — 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, the campaign's 'Chief Smoke Detector' to Reed's 'Eminence Grease' — founded the campaign to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood or charcoal. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they issued the True 'Cue Challenge: a prize to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch. Two years on, Reed wrote, no one had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states; one state official mentioned environmental concerns, and Reed allows that gas and electricity are cheaper, easier and more consistent. The campaign draws its line with care: it certifies only wood-for-heat, but has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. Its Pledge is for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue. Its wood page quotes a federal meat-labeling rule defining barbecued meat as cooked by the direct action of dry heat from burning hardwood, and gathers witnesses from Pete Jones to Rodney Scott, Wilber Shirley and Aaron Franklin, with Alton Brown's joke that gas lets you control the heat, 'but you're going to go to hell'.
how: A restaurant is certified once the campaign confirms it cooks its region's style with wood as the only heat; it receives a certificate and a window decal and is listed on truecue.org by state. Eaters sign the Pledge; the site sells merchandise; regional smoke detectors handle the other states.
today: Active; the site lists certified places by state and runs the True 'Cue USA program. About seventy North Carolina restaurants held certificates in January 2018; no current count is posted.
- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): its co-founder, 'Eminence Grease', and the author of the 2014 Challenge.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): what it does not certify, and whose stated reasons it answers.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the only heat its certificate allows.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): the federal definition it quotes: direct dry heat from burning hardwood.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): the older North Carolina list of wood pits, with stricter rules and one state.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): whose billboard makes the campaign's case in four tenets.
- kin → pete-jones (person): quoted on its wood page.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): quoted on its wood page.
- kin → wilber-shirley (person): quoted on its wood page.
- kin → robert-moss (person): found no wood-banning rule in South Carolina either.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): one of the 'styles traditional in their area' its certificate requires.
- kin → lexington (style): the other North Carolina style its certificate requires a pit to cook.
- not to be confused with north-carolina-barbecue-society: True 'Cue (2013) certifies any place cooking its local style solely with wood, in several states; the society's Trail (2006) is one state, fifteen years, a house sauce and two per town.
sources: s:true-cue — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (True 'Cue); s:web-truecue-about — About — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:web-truecue-wood — Wood — The Campaign for Real Barbecue; s:web-barbecuebible-campaign — The Campaign for Real Barbecue (John Shelton Reed, January 23, 2018); s:web-uncpress-reed-myth — John Shelton Reed: Busting a Barbecue Myth (April 6, 2016); s:reed-holy-smoke — Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## North Carolina Barbecue Society (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/org/north-carolina-barbecue-society/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/org/north-carolina-barbecue-society.json
id: north-carolina-barbecue-society
aliases: NCBS · NC Barbecue Society · the Society
facets: state=NC · founded=2006 · status=unknown
region: North Carolina
what: A non-profit founded in 2006 in Winston-Salem by Jim Early, a lawyer and cook, to promote North Carolina's barbecue culture and, in its own words, to secure the state's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World. Its lasting work is the Historic Barbecue Trail: a route of about two dozen restaurants, some 700 miles end to end, admitted only if the meat cooks on grates over pits with wood or charcoal, the owners make their own sauce, the pits have run fifteen consecutive years, and no town has more than two. Early wrote the guidebook, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy, and the society ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year.
story: Jim Early had a law office in Winston-Salem and a self-published guide to every barbecue place from Manteo to Murphy when he founded the society in 2006; he closed the law office in September 2017 to run it full time. Searching the state's hundred counties for pits still cooking pork slowly over wood coals, he found fewer than thirty, and the Trail is that list under its rules — Wilber's in Goldsboro, the Skylight Inn in Ayden, B's in Greenville, Allen & Son near Chapel Hill, Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center in Lexington and Red Bridges in Shelby among them. Wikipedia's article counts twenty-five establishments in twenty-one locales; WRAL in 2021 counted twenty. The boot camps ran at Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July and Castle Hayne in September, teaching whole hog, butts, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. The society's motto, in its less formal version, was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends, and to promote the state as the Cradle of 'Cue. It took no side in the east-west argument but recorded it: the 2006 bills that would have made Lexington's festival official, and their failure. Early died on June 21, 2021, at 82, after a stroke. In March 2024 John Tanner's barbecue blog reported that the society 'appears to have withered considerably' since, with Ben Thompson keeping its Facebook page as a forum, and that a separate group of pitmasters, Chuck Hursey among them, had started a North Carolina Barbecue Hall of Fame. Neither ncbbqsociety.com nor ncbbqsociety.org resolved when this project checked on September 15, 2026.
how: Membership is by dues, and the sponsors are mostly barbecue restaurants. The Trail is followed by car with the map or Early's book; a stop earns its place by its pit, its sauce and its years, not its fame. The boot camps were two-day schools open to anyone who paid.
today: Status unknown as of September 2026: the founder is dead, both web addresses are down, and the Facebook page carries on as a forum. The Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others.
- kin → jim-early (person): its founder, president and guidebook author, 2006 until his death in 2021.
- kin → campaign-for-real-barbecue (org): the other North Carolina list of wood pits, drawn by different rules and different founders.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): one of the events the society existed to promote.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): the Trail's rule: wood or charcoal on grates, nothing else.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): excluded from the Trail by rule.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): what the Trail's Piedmont stops cook in.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): a Trail stop in Ayden.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): a Trail stop in Goldsboro.
- kin → bs-barbecue (place): a Trail stop in Greenville.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): a Trail stop in Orange County.
- kin → stameys-barbecue (place): a Trail stop in Greensboro.
- kin → short-sugars (place): a Trail stop in Reidsville.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): a Trail stop in Lexington.
- kin → red-bridges-barbecue-lodge (place): a Trail stop in Shelby.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the society's Trail runs from Manteo to Murphy without ranking east against west.
- kin → lexington (style): the other half of the Trail, and of the argument the society recorded without joining.
- not to be confused with campaign-for-real-barbecue: Both list North Carolina's wood pits. The society's Trail (2006, Jim Early) requires fifteen years, a house sauce and no more than two stops per town; True 'Cue (2013, Reed and Levine) certifies any place cooking its local style solely with wood, in several states.
sources: s:wp-north-carolina-barbecue-society — North Carolina Barbecue Society — Wikipedia; s:web-ourstate-historic-barbecue-trail — Running on Full: The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail (Bryan Mims, January 29, 2016); s:web-wral-jim-early-dies — North Carolina Barbecue Society founder Jim Early dies (August 26, 2021); s:web-legacy-jim-early-obituary — James Early Obituary (1939–2021), Winston-Salem Journal; s:web-tanner-nc-hall-of-fame — A New North Carolina Barbecue Hall of Fame (March 12, 2024); s:early-best-tar-heel-barbecue — The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy; s:ncbs — North Carolina Barbecue Society — Historic Barbecue Trail
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-15

## South Carolina Barbeque Association (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/org/south-carolina-barbeque-association/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/org/south-carolina-barbeque-association.json
id: south-carolina-barbeque-association
aliases: SCBA · SC Barbeque Association · South Carolina Barbecue Association
said: Spelled barbeque, with a q, as its founder spells it.
facets: state=SC · founded=2004 · status=open
region: South Carolina
what: A judging body and booster founded in 2004 by Lake E. High Jr., a wine judge, and Walter Rolandi, a psychologist, 'to train the best BBQ judges in the world and to preserve and promote the unique nature of South Carolina Barbecue'. It runs judging seminars in Columbia that turn eaters into certified judges — more than 800 by 2015 — sanctions cook-offs across the state, eight of them listed between September 12 and October 24, 2026, and keeps a points championship for the teams. Its account of the state's barbecue is Lake High's: South Carolina as the home of all four sauces — mustard, vinegar-pepper, light tomato and heavy tomato — mapped by region.
story: When High and Rolandi founded the association, South Carolina had two barbecue cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association's judge-training system was being copied elsewhere. High is its historian as well as its founder. His A History of South Carolina Barbeque (2013) and the association's history page hold that Europeans first learned barbecue from the Native Americans at Santa Elena, the sixteenth-century colony in what is now South Carolina; that vinegar-and-pepper is the original sauce, hundreds of years old; that mustard came with the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s; that light tomato is vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup added, from around 1900; and that heavy tomato is the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, the page says, is home to all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two — sweet mustard and spicy vinegar — and the state's Wikipedia article gives both counts, along with the four-or-five-region division first drawn by Charles Kovacik and John Winberry in South Carolina: A Geography (1987). High's line, to South Carolina Living in 2015: 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the association named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.
how: Judges train at an annual seminar in Columbia and advance through levels; a team enters a sanctioned cook-off, is scored by certified judges, and earns points toward the SCBA Championship. The cook-offs are run by towns, churches, scout troops and civic groups — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria and the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster were on the 2026 list — with the association supplying the judging.
today: Active. The 2026 calendar lists cook-offs from Mauldin to Barnwell through October 24, the judge seminars are held in Columbia each year, and the association posts from PO Box 115, Blythewood.
- kin → lake-high (person): its co-founder and historian, author of the four-sauce account.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): one of the four regions on its sauce map: the Midlands' German mustard.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): one of the four: vinegar-and-pepper, which the association calls the original sauce.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): one of the four: vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): one of the four: the newest, of the last sixty years.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce it calls distinct to South Carolina.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the sauce it dates back hundreds of years.
- kin → light-tomato-sauce (sauce): the sauce it dates to the arrival of bottled ketchup.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the sauce it calls the newest.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the name the mustard sauce carries on its map.
- kin → robert-moss (person): the South Carolina historian who counts two sauces where the association counts four.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): the North Carolina society founded two years later, a trail rather than a judging program.
- kin → festival-of-discovery (event): the Greenwood festival's cook-off is sanctioned by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, not by the SCBA.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): most of its sanctioned cook-offs are somebody's fundraiser.
- not to be confused with north-carolina-barbecue-society: The SCBA trains judges and sanctions cook-offs; the NCBS drew a restaurant trail. Different states, different founders, two years apart.

## Southern Foodways Alliance (org)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/org/southern-foodways-alliance/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/org/southern-foodways-alliance.json
id: southern-foodways-alliance
aliases: SFA
facets: founded=1999 · status=open · state=us
region: The American South, The Carolinas
what: An institute of the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi, founded in 1999 and directed since then by John T. Edge, that documents the food of the South: oral histories, films, writing, awards and events, funded by about 800 members. For the Carolinas its work is the Southern BBQ Trail, an oral-history project begun in February 2011 across nine states, whose North Carolina set includes the Skylight Inn, Parker's, Grady's, B's, Bum's, Stamey's, Short Sugar's, Red Bridges, Cook's, Clyde Cooper's, the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell, and whose South Carolina set holds eight interviews: Sweatman's, Scott's, Midway, Jackie Hite's, Dukes, Cooper's Country Store, Brown's and Melvin's. Each interview is a transcript with audio, free online.
story: The SFA came out of a 1999 meeting called by the journalist John Egerton, with John Martin Taylor among the founders, and John T. Edge has directed it since. It gives the Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award with the Fertel Foundation and the John Egerton Prize, and Corby Kummer in the Atlantic called it 'this country's most intellectually engaged (and probably most engaging) food society'. The Southern BBQ Trail went up on February 22, 2011, and the Carolina sets on April 25 of that year. The North Carolina introduction, by John Shelton Reed, opens on the point that barbecue was never home cooking — too much trouble — and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies; the South Carolina introduction opens: 'Like everything in South Carolina, we cook barbeque cantankerously.' Rien Fertel interviewed Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn for the project and went on to write The One True Barbecue (2016) about the whole-hog pitmasters; John and Dale Reed drew on the North Carolina interviews for Holy Smoke; in 2009 Edge himself profiled the Scott family of Hemingway. Rodney Scott's interview sits in the South Carolina set beside Bub Sweatman's and Jackie Hite's; Chip Stamey's, Sonny Conrad's of the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell's are in the North Carolina set.
how: Interviews are recorded by SFA oral historians, transcribed and posted with audio, a portrait and a short biography, under the project and the state; the site filters by state and by tag. Membership funds the work; the awards and events run alongside it.
today: Active at the University of Mississippi; the Carolina barbecue interviews remain online under the Southern BBQ Trail.

- kin → john-shelton-reed (person): wrote the introduction to its North Carolina barbecue project.

## fundraiser barbecue (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/fundraiser-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/fundraiser-barbecue.json
id: fundraiser-barbecue
aliases: plate sale · barbecue plate sale · church barbecue · fire department barbecue · hash sale · BBQ fundraiser
facets: state=both · when=Saturdays; spring and fall · status=open
region: The Carolinas
what: The plate sale: a church, a volunteer fire department, a Ruritan club or a scout troop cooks pork — a whole hog or a stack of butts — and sells it by the plate on a Saturday to pay for a roof, a truck or a mission. In eastern North Carolina the plate is barbecue or barbecue chicken with slaw and bread; Back Swamp Volunteer Fire Department in Richlands sold pork or chicken plates for $10 on April 18, 2026, from 11 a.m. until the food ran out. In South Carolina the same money is often raised on hash: the Highway 34 Volunteer Fire Department outside Ninety Six cooks it in cast-iron pots and sells it by the quart to neighbors who read the notice in the paper and phone in an order.
story: The fundraiser is where the whole-hog barbecue of the colonial Carolinas went when the plantation left: barbecues for fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies are on record in the Carolina colonies, and John Shelton Reed's line is that until the early twentieth century barbecue was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and rallies. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte is the form at full scale: begun in 1929 to pay $89.50 of Sunday-school debt, it grew to 14,600 pounds of pork and 20,000 eaters by 2015 and ran ninety-three years on volunteers taking a week off work. Hillsborough's Hog Day began in 1983 as a chamber-of-commerce fundraiser and since 2014 has been the Orange County Optimist Club's, its proceeds to children's programs — Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H and a church youth group in 2025. On the coast the volunteer fire departments own the Saturday calendar: Back Swamp's annual barbecue and raffle at the station on Catherine Lake Road is one of dozens. South Carolina's version is the hash sale: fire stations, churches and civic groups stew pork, liver and onions in iron kettles over a wood fire and sell hash by the quart; at Highway 34 VFD, Melvin Fouchee learned the recipe from Ike Berry and the department buys its equipment on the proceeds. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's cook-off calendar is much the same list under another name — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria, the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster.
how: A Saturday, 11 a.m. until sold out. The pigs or butts cook overnight on a rented or department-owned cooker; volunteers make slaw and stew; plates are packed to go — barbecue, slaw, bread, sometimes potatoes or beans — and sold at a window or a drive-through for a set price, with a raffle beside the table. Hash is ordered by the quart in advance and picked up; Mallard Creek sold by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart.
today: Continuous. Back Swamp VFD's plate was $10 in April 2026; Mallard Creek's was $15 in October 2024 and is no more; the SCBA calendar listed eight cook-offs for the autumn of 2026.
- kin → mallard-creek-barbecue (event): the church plate sale at its largest scale, 1929 to 2024.
- kin → hillsborough-hog-day (event): a chamber's, then a service club's, fundraiser for youth programs.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the candidates come to the fundraiser's crowd.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the same pig, sold by the plate instead of picked.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): what the pigs cook on behind the fire station.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the other thing they cook on.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the South Carolina fundraiser's product, sold by the quart.
- kin → barbecue-chicken (dish): the other plate at a fire-department sale.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): in the church's kettles beside the pork.
- kin → slaw (term): on every plate.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): sanctions the cook-off version.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the fire department's Saturday pig.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the butts that replaced the pig at many sales.
- not to be confused with political-barbecue: A fundraiser sells the plate; a political barbecue gives it away and the candidate pays.

## Hillsborough Hog Day (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/hillsborough-hog-day/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/hillsborough-hog-day.json
id: hillsborough-hog-day
aliases: Hog Day · Hog Day Festival · Hillsborough Hog Day Festival
facets: state=NC · when=a weekend in September (June until 2014) · founded=1983 · status=open
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: A two-day barbecue festival and cook-off at River Park in downtown Hillsborough, Orange County, held since 1983 — the oldest continuing barbecue festival in North Carolina, by the Daily Tar Heel's account — and run since 2014 by the Orange County Optimist Club as a fundraiser for children's programs. A Friday evening opens it; Saturday brings the cook-off, live music, a car show, a fun run and the Pigs on Parade. In 2019 the count was 27 cooking teams, more than 100 vendors and a collective three tons of barbecue; the 2025 festival, September 13 and 14, came two months after Tropical Storm Chantal flooded the Eno riverfront and lost its 5K to the water.
story: Hog Day was the Hillsborough/Orange County Chamber of Commerce's festival for thirty-one years, drawing up to 35,000 people as the county's largest festival, until the chamber's board voted in January 2014 that it was not 'an adequate use of resources' for the chamber's mission. Craig Lloyd, the chamber's former executive director and a Hog Day hand since he won a design contest more than thirty years ago, gathered the volunteers into a new Orange County Optimist Club and put the festival on that June 20 and 21 at the Efland Ruritan Club under the theme 'Bringing Home the Bacon', because it was '100% developed and produced by local volunteers'; after two years in Efland it came home to River Park in 2016, the thirty-fourth festival, now in September. Hurricane Florence pushed 2018 to a make-up weekend on November 2 and 3; the pandemic cancelled 2020 and 2021; 2022 was the return. The cook-off carries a North Carolina Pork Council contest alongside the festival's own — James Catlett and Brittany Thompson took the two first places in 2025 — and the proceeds go to youth: Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H club and a Holy Family Catholic Church youth group in 2025. Lloyd, now the club's president, is the 'Godfather of Hog Day' on the festival's site; Al Hartkopf chairs it.
how: Friday night music at River Park; Saturday from 10 to 5, the cook-off teams sell plates and sandwiches, vendors line the park, and the car show, the fun run along the Eno and the Pigs on Parade fill the day. Proceeds go to the Optimist Club's charities.
today: Open. The 2025 festival ran September 13 and 14 at River Park; the organizer is the Orange County Optimist Club, at hogday.org.
address: 144 E Margaret Ln, Hillsborough, NC, 27278
geo: 36.073, -79.0984 (exact)
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): a chamber's, then a service club's, fundraiser for youth programs.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the state's other long-running barbecue festival, a year younger: Lexington's first was 1984, Hillsborough's 1983.
- kin → allen-and-son (place): Orange County's pit on the Historic Barbecue Trail, up the road from River Park.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): what the cook-off teams bring to the park.
- not to be confused with lexington-barbecue-festival: Hog Day is a two-day cook-off in a riverside park in September; Lexington is one Saturday on Main Street in October with the town's restaurants cooking.
sources: s:web-dailytarheel-hog-day-2025 — Food, fundraising and swine-filled festivities: Hillsborough holds 'Hog Day' festival (September 22, 2025); s:web-wral-hog-day-canceled — Hillsborough Hogg Day canceled (January 12, 2014); s:web-chapelboro-hog-day-returns-2014 — Hog Day Returns (May 29, 2014); s:web-chapelboro-hog-day-2016 — Hillsborough Hog Day Kicks Off Friday Night (September 16, 2016); s:web-chapelboro-hog-day-2019 — Hillsborough's Hog Day Festival Returns to the Riverpark This Weekend (September 19, 2019); s:web-hogday-org — Hog Day — Meet the Hog Day Team; s:web-ourstate-historic-barbecue-trail — Running on Full: The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail (Bryan Mims, January 29, 2016); s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## Lexington Barbecue Festival (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/lexington-barbecue-festival/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/lexington-barbecue-festival.json
id: lexington-barbecue-festival
aliases: the Barbecue Festival · Lexington BBQ Festival
facets: state=NC · when=one Saturday in October; October 24, 2026 · founded=1984 · status=open · styles=lexington
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: A one-day street festival on Main Street in uptown Lexington, Davidson County, each October since 1984, built on the town's pork-shoulder barbecue: up to twenty area restaurants cook and sell, several blocks close to traffic, and hundreds of other vendors sell crafts and fudge around them. Wikipedia's article says it draws as many as 200,000 people; the first festival drew 30,000 and 3,000 pounds of barbecue, and by 1994 the count was over 100,000 and 11,000 pounds. Since 2007 it holds a title from the General Assembly — Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina. The 2026 festival is planned for October 24.
story: The idea came from Joe Sink Jr., publisher of Lexington's daily, The Dispatch, in 1983; the bank BB&T hired Kay Saintsing to study whether a festival could work, the study found Lexington already a weekend destination for barbecue, and the first festival was held on October 27, 1984. In 1995 the North Carolina Championship Pork Cook-Off joined it, so that Piedmont crowds could watch eastern whole-hog cooks at work in the capital of the shoulder. NC By Train sets up a temporary stop a block away for the day, served by Amtrak's Carolinian and Piedmont. The 2020 festival went virtual. The politics is the story the festival tells about itself under the heading 'Pork-Barrel Politics'. In 2006 House Bill 21 and Senate Bill 47 would have made it the official barbecue festival of North Carolina; the east read that as making Lexington the official barbecue, nearly half the state prefers the other kind, and neither bill passed. In 2007 House Bill 433 gave it the Piedmont Triad title instead — a designation that names a region and so leaves the east out of the question. Jerry Bledsoe, the 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' by his own account, said that Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, the self-styled 'oracle of the holy grub', had ruined the state's chances of distinction in barbecue. Eastern vendors turn up on Main Street each year; the article calls the controversy mild, and sometimes not so mild.
how: One Saturday in October: Main Street closes, the restaurants set up on the street, and the plate is Lexington's — chopped or sliced shoulder with red slaw and hush puppies, the dip on the meat. Around it are four hundred or more vendors, live music on up to five stages, lumberjack games and street performers. Visitors come by car and, for the day, by train.
today: Held each October; the 2026 date is October 24. It is listed in 1,000 Places to See in the USA & Canada Before You Die, and in 2012 U.S. News & World Report ranked Lexington fourth among the country's barbecue cities.
address: Main Street, Lexington, NC, 27292
geo: 35.8261, -80.251 (street)
- kin → lexington (style): the style it sells by the ton: shoulder, dip, red slaw.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): on every tray on Main Street.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the slaw of the festival plate.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the bread of the festival plate.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut: 3,000 pounds the first year, 11,000 by 1994.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the eastern cut demonstrated at the Pork Cook-Off since 1995.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the other North Carolina, whose legislators kept the festival from being the state's official one.
- kin → jerry-bledsoe (person): the Piedmont columnist whose mock war the festival's politics inherit.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): the eastern columnist on the other side of that war.
- kin → north-carolina-barbecue-society (org): one of the society's causes.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): a Main Street pit house in the festival's town.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the festival's own politics: two failed bills in 2006 and a regional title in 2007.
- kin → hillsborough-hog-day (event): the state's other long-running barbecue festival, a year older.
- not to be confused with lexington: The festival is one Saturday; the style is the town's everyday food.
- not to be confused with lexington-barbecue: Lexington Barbecue is a restaurant, founded 1962; the Festival is a street event, founded 1984.

## Mallard Creek Barbecue (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/mallard-creek-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/mallard-creek-barbecue.json
id: mallard-creek-barbecue
aliases: Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church Barbecue · the Mallard Creek BBQ · the granddaddy of barbecues
facets: state=NC · when=fourth Thursday of October · founded=1929 · status=closed · styles=eastern-nc
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, North Carolina
what: The one-day church barbecue of Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in northeast Charlotte, held on the fourth Thursday of October from 1929 to 2024 and retired in 2025 after ninety-three editions. It sold hickory-smoked chopped pork, Brunswick stew and the church's own slaw by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart — dine-in, drive-through and carry-out; a plate was $15 and a sandwich $7 in 2024 — and it was one of North Carolina's best-known political stops: a rope line in the parking field where candidates for every office from vice-president to dog catcher worked the crowd in the last weeks before an election.
story: In late 1928 or early 1929 the pastor, Dr. W. H. Frazer, and his brother Ben held a men's meeting with a barbecued pig; the church owed money on a Sunday-school building, and that October the deacons cooked three or four pigs and a goat to pay it. The first year cleared $89.50, enough to retire the debt with a little over. The fourth Thursday was chosen to keep clear of Halloween. The hogs cooked in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath; by 1979, the fiftieth year, the church cooked 4,800 pounds of meat, 2,000 pounds of slaw and 250 gallons of Brunswick stew, and in the 1980s metal cookers replaced the dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. By 2015 Our State counted 20,000 people, 14,600 pounds of pork, 2,500 gallons of stew and two tons of slaw, and Tommy Oehler told the magazine the whole hogs were gone: 'Now we just use the butt', dressed with an eastern-style vinegar sauce. The politics grew with the plates. Dan Quayle came seeking the 2000 Republican nomination; Charlotte mayors Richard Vinroot, Pat McCrory and Jennifer Roberts worked the line; Deborah Ross came running for the Senate. No speeches: candidates set up booths, hand out fliers and court voters along a rope in the parking area. On October 1, 2025, the church announced with 'heavy hearts' that the barbecue was retired. The leaders of its four main components had stepped aside, co-chair Charles Kimrey said, and the church could not find volunteers able to take eight to ten days off work for the preparation; each prep day took about a hundred volunteers and the day itself about three hundred. 'Everything seems to have a life cycle and for the Mallard Creek BBQ, that life cycle is 93 years.'
how: For a week before, volunteers cooked pork butts — hickory-smoked, then chopped, cooled and seasoned — and stewed Brunswick stew in quantity; on the Thursday the church served from morning, dine-in, drive-through and walk-up, by plate (barbecue, stew, applesauce, slaw and bread), sandwich, pound or quart. Proceeds went to the church's missions and to the building debt the barbecue was founded to retire.
today: Retired. The last barbecue was held Thursday, October 24, 2024; the church announced the end on October 1, 2025, three weeks before the date it would have kept.
address: 1600 W Mallard Creek Church Rd, Charlotte, NC, 28262
geo: 35.3345, -80.7497 (exact)
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): a church plate sale kept up for ninety-three years by volunteers.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): North Carolina's standing political stop: candidates on a rope line, no speeches.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut by 2016 — 'now we just use the butt' — after decades of whole hogs.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): three or four pigs and a goat in 1929; whole hogs in ditches for decades after.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): 2,500 gallons of it in 2015, and a quart to take home.
- kin → slaw (term): the church's own blend, two tons of it in 2015.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the eastern-style vinegar sauce on the chopped pork.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style of its sauce, in a Piedmont city.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): hickory coals in the ditches in 1929; hickory-smoked to the end.
- kin → block-pit (pit): began in dirt ditches and moved to metal cookers in the 1980s.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the metal cookers that replaced the dirt pits in the 1980s.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): $7 in 2024.
- not to be confused with fundraiser-barbecue: Mallard Creek was one church's barbecue; the fundraiser barbecue is the whole form, still running at hundreds of churches and fire stations.
- not to be confused with political-barbecue: Mallard Creek sold plates to pay a church's debts and the candidates came to the crowd; a political barbecue is put on by the candidate.
sources: s:web-mallard-creek-history — History of the Annual Barbecue; s:web-mallard-creek-annual-barbecue — Annual Barbecue (2024 event page: menu, prices, service); s:web-ourstate-mallard-creek — Pork & Politics Merge at Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church (Greg Lacour, February 2016, updated 2018); s:web-wfae-mallard-creek-ends — Mallard Creek Barbecue ends after 93 years (Kenneth Lee Jr., October 1, 2025); s:web-wbtv-mallard-creek-canceled — Nearly 100-year-old BBQ canceled in Charlotte, organizers say (October 1, 2025); s:web-spectrum-mallard-creek-ending — After 93 years, Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church ending longstanding barbecue event (October 2, 2025); s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## pig pickin' (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/pig-pickin/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/pig-pickin.json
id: pig-pickin
aliases: pig picking · pig pickin · pig pull · rolling a pig · hog roast
said: Always with the g dropped, as in the Wikipedia article's own title.
root: pig + pickin' (picking): the guests pick the meat off the cooked hog with their hands, and the gathering takes its name from the act · Pig pull and hog roast name the same event elsewhere; pig roast is the wider term, used of the Cuban, Filipino and Hawaiian roasts, which are other traditions. Kingstree, South Carolina, calls its fall cook-off the Pig Pickin' Festival.
facets: state=both · when=any month; homecomings, tailgates, weddings, rallies · status=open · styles=eastern-nc, sc-pee-dee
region: Eastern North Carolina, The Pee Dee, The Carolinas
what: A party at which a whole hog is cooked for the crowd and the crowd eats it off the pig — picked by hand from the split carcass, or chopped on a block beside it. A barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt of about 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is split and laid on a large charcoal or propane cooker for four to eight hours, under the direction of the host and whoever is helping; the meat is basted or dressed in the local sauce and served with slaw, hush puppies, baked beans, Brunswick stew or, in South Carolina, hash and rice. It is the eastern Carolinas' form of the wedding, the homecoming, the tailgate, the political rally and the fire-department fundraiser.
story: The whole-hog feast is older than the name. Communal barbecues of whole pigs spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed church gatherings, fundraisers and political rallies; George Washington wrote of attending a barbecue on August 4, 1769. The pig pickin' is that feast on a trailer cooker. Its year is the church's and the college's: 'dinner on the grounds', family reunions, Thanksgiving and Christmas, graduations and weddings, and the tailgate — East Carolina University in Greenville has run a pig pickin' contest, the Pigskin Pig-Out, since 1985. Politics keeps it: local parties and candidates still use a pig pickin' to draw a crowd, and in 1983 Rufus Edmisten, running for governor of North Carolina, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue, would eat no more, and was taking his stand. Ed Mitchell's first hog was a family pickin' in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him a glass. Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, holds a Pig Pickin' Festival each fall for the vinegar-based barbecue of Williamsburg County; seventy teams competed in 2010. The name is the one thing the article is sure of: the meat is picked off the hog by the guests, and the gathering is named for it.
how: The host borrows or rents a cooker, buys a dressed hog, and lights charcoal or gas the morning of, or the night before for a big pig. The hog goes on meat-side down and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat; some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. The baste is the region's: mustard in the South Carolina Midlands, vinegar and red pepper flakes in eastern North Carolina, a ketchup base in the west. When the meat falls from the bone the pig is carried to the table and the guests pick, or a cook chops it at the block; sweet tea, beer and soft drinks alongside.
today: Held year-round in a mild climate; cookers are rented by the weekend across the Coastal Plain, the tailgate pickin' is a college-football fixture, and Kingstree's festival and ECU's Pigskin Pig-Out put it on a calendar.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut and the method the party is built on.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the trailer cooker it is cooked on, charcoal or propane.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the stacked-block pit it is cooked on when there is no cooker.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose sauce bastes the eastern pig: vinegar and red pepper.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): Kingstree's Pig Pickin' Festival is the Pee Dee's version, vinegar-based.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the eastern baste.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the baste in the South Carolina Midlands.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the South Carolina side dish, made of the leftover pork.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): sometimes on the table beside the pig.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): fried cornmeal beside the pig.
- kin → slaw (term): the other constant beside the pig.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): poured with beer and soft drinks.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the cracklings a clean flip produces.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the same pig with a candidate attached.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the same pig sold by the plate.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the winter work; the pickin' is the party.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): cooked his first pig at a family pickin' in Wilson while the men slept.
- kin → pig-pickin-cake (dish): the sheet cake that borrows the party's name.
- kin → barbecue (term): the noun the east uses for what comes off the pig, and the word for the gathering itself.
- not to be confused with hog-killing: A pig pickin' cooks one pig for one crowd; a hog killing butchers the year's meat in winter.
- not to be confused with whole-hog: Whole hog is the cut and the method; the pig pickin' is the party.

## political barbecue (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/political-barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/political-barbecue.json
id: political-barbecue
aliases: stump meeting · campaign barbecue · rally barbecue · the candidate's pig
facets: state=both · when=election years; the weeks before a vote · status=open
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The free feed a candidate or a party puts on to draw a crowd: a whole hog, or these days a pile of pork butts, cooked for whoever comes, with speeches or a rope line attached. It is as old as the republic in the Carolinas — the communal whole-hog barbecue fed political rallies in the colonial Carolinas and Virginia — and it has two living forms. In South Carolina the Galivants Ferry Stump Meeting in Horry County has gathered Democratic candidates on the Holliday family's land every second spring since 1880, descended from Wade Hampton's 1876 appearance there. In North Carolina the Mallard Creek church barbecue in Charlotte was the candidates' October stop from 1929 to 2024.
story: Robert Moss finds the political barbecue an institution of the early republic and the whole-hog rally established in the colonies by the 1700s. In North Carolina the tradition runs through the pig pickin' — local parties and politicians still use one to draw people to meetings and rallies — and its cost is recorded in one sentence from 1983, when Rufus Edmisten, running for governor, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue and was not going to eat any more. In South Carolina the form is the stump meeting. Wade Hampton, the Confederate general running for governor, spoke at Galivants Ferry in 1876 and was elected that year; in 1880 Joseph William Holliday, merchant and tobacco farmer, invited the county's Democratic candidates to speak at his store, and the meeting has been held there in the spring of every second year since, carried on by the Hollidays and grown into a statewide event with national candidates — the longest-running Democratic campaign-speech site in the country, by the county's marker and the community's own account; by 2004 it counted 128 years. *Tradition holds —* chicken bog and barbecue are the food of the day. Mallard Creek's Presbyterians did not plan a political stop; they planned to pay off a Sunday-school building in 1929, and the candidates came to the crowd. By 2015 the crowd was 20,000 and the guests had included a former vice-president; the church retired the barbecue in 2025. The Lexington Barbecue Festival's politics — two bills in 2006 to make it the state's official festival, defeated by the east, and a regional title in 2007 — are the same appetite turned on the food itself.
how: A hog or a pile of butts is cooked by a church, a club or a hired pit; the candidate pays, or the host does; plates are free or cheap; the speaking is from a stump, a flatbed or a stage, or there is no speaking at all and the candidates walk a rope line with fliers. The date is the calendar's: spring of an election year at Galivants Ferry, the fourth Thursday of October at Mallard Creek.
today: Galivants Ferry continues on its two-year cycle; Mallard Creek ended in 2025; the pig pickin' rally goes on wherever a county party has a cooker.
geo: 34.0561, -79.2465 (town)
- kin → mallard-creek-barbecue (event): North Carolina's political stop for ninety-three Octobers.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the North Carolina rally's usual form: a pig, a cooker, a candidate.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the church that cooks the pig is usually raising money at the same time.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the politics of barbecue itself: bills, a compromise title.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the colonial rally's meat.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the modern rally's meat, by the butt.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): the Pee Dee's rally dish, tradition holds, at Galivants Ferry.
- kin → robert-moss (person): the historian of the early republic's barbecue.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word that also names the gathering.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): Galivants Ferry sits at the Pee Dee's edge, in Horry County.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the other occasion for a whole pig before the twentieth century.
- not to be confused with fundraiser-barbecue: Who pays. A political barbecue is free to the eater and paid for by the candidate or the party; a fundraiser sells the plate.
- not to be confused with mallard-creek-barbecue: Mallard Creek was a church fundraiser the candidates attended; a political barbecue is the candidate's own.

- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/political-barbecue/political-barbecue-the-political-barbecue-going-the-whole-hog-c-1832-1833-by-an.jpg · Public domain · Unknown authorUnknown author · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AThe_political_barbecue%2C_Going_the_whole_hog%2C_c._1832-1833%2C_by_an_unknown_artist%2C_from_the_Digital_Commonwealth_-_commonwealth_9880w959q.jpg

## South Carolina Festival of Discovery (event)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/event/festival-of-discovery/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/event/festival-of-discovery.json
id: festival-of-discovery
aliases: Festival of Discovery · SC Festival of Discovery · Greenwood BBQ and Blues Festival of Discovery
facets: state=SC · when=July, second weekend, Thursday to Saturday; July 9–11, 2026 · founded=2000 · status=open
region: The Upstate, South Carolina
what: A three-day barbecue-and-blues festival in Uptown Greenwood each July — Thursday to Saturday of the second weekend; July 9 to 11 in 2026 — hosted by the Uptown Greenwood Development Corporation. Its cook-off is sanctioned by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the national competition body, and is billed as a South Carolina state championship with a Black Kettle hash competition beside it; the barbecue vendors fill the Main Street parking lot between Court and Seaboard avenues, and the Blues Cruise puts bands in restaurants and venues around the uptown into the night. The organizers billed 2026 as the twenty-fifth anniversary; press accounts date the first festival to 2000.
story: Greenwood is a county seat in the Old 96 District on the Piedmont side of the state, and the festival is its downtown corporation's summer event rather than a pit's or a church's. The competition is Kansas City's — KCBS judges, KCBS categories, and a date the society sets rather than the town — laid over a South Carolina crowd, with a hash kettle competition to keep the state's own dish in view and the public sampling and voting on Carolina hash, and a blues program, the Blues Cruise, run under the artistic direction of the bluesman Shrimp City Slim. *Inference —* it is the Upstate's festival in the way Lexington's is the Piedmont's, and the sanctioned cook-off, not a local pit, is its center.
how: Thursday evening through Saturday: teams cook overnight in the Main Street lot for KCBS judging; the public samples barbecue and hash and votes; the Blues Cruise runs at venues around the uptown from late morning to midnight.
today: Held July 9–11, 2026; the 2027 dates are July 8–10. Contact is the Uptown Greenwood office at 104 Main Street.
address: Main Street, Greenwood, SC, 29646
geo: 34.1904, -82.1605 (street)
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the Black Kettle hash competition keeps the state's stew on the program.
- kin → south-carolina-barbeque-association (org): not its sanctioning body; the cook-off is KCBS.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the other Carolina street festival: Lexington's restaurants cook, Greenwood's teams compete.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): a town's event, not a plate sale; the cook-off form the SCBA's calendar is full of.
- not to be confused with lexington-barbecue-festival: Lexington is one Saturday in October with restaurants on the street; Greenwood is three days in July with competition teams and a blues program.
sources: s:web-festivalofdiscovery — City of Greenwood BBQ and Blues Festival of Discovery 2026; s:web-discovergreenwood-festival — SC Festival of Discovery; s:web-drugstoredivas-festival-of-discovery — South Carolina Festival of Discovery 2026: Details & Full Schedule (September 14, 2026); s:osm — OpenStreetMap — places tagged cuisine=barbecue in North Carolina and South Carolina

## barbecue (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/barbecue/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/barbecue.json
id: barbecue
aliases: bar-b-q · bar-b-que · barbeque · BBQ · 'cue · cue · Q
said: In the Carolinas the word is a noun for the cooked pork: you eat barbecue, you do not 'have a barbecue'. The grill in the yard is a grill; cooking on it is grilling.
root: Taíno (Arawakan) barbacoa, a framework of sticks set on posts → Spanish barbacoa (1526, Oviedo) → English barbecue (1660s: the frame and the method; the cooked animal and the gathering by the 1700s) · first seen: English 1661, Edmund Hickeringill's Jamaica Viewed ('Barbacu'd'), per the OED as quoted in the Wikipedia article; 'barbecado' in 1648; as a noun 1697, William Dampier. Spanish barbacoa printed by Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, 1526. · The folk etymology from French barbe à queue ('beard to tail', i.e. the whole animal) is a joke first printed in the eighteenth century and has no standing; the Taíno origin is the dictionary etymology. Spellings with -que and Bar-B-Q are twentieth-century sign-painting and are as common on Carolina signs as the dictionary form.
facets: letter=B · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The cooked meat itself — in the Carolinas, pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker and then chopped, pulled or sliced — and, by extension, the place that sells it and the gathering that eats it. Elsewhere in the country the same word means a grill, or a cookout of any meat; here the narrower sense is the ordinary one.
story: The word came north from the Caribbean with the Spanish and into English by way of the colonial Atlantic: a frame of sticks first, then the method, then the meat. Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 already gives the Carolina sense — 'to barbecue: a term for dressing a whole hog', and the noun, 'a hog dressed whole'. *Tradition holds —* the whole-animal feast over wood coals was the shape of the colonial Southern gathering by the eighteenth century, and the political barbecue, a free feed put on by a candidate, was an institution of the early republic. *Inference —* the Carolina insistence that barbecue is a noun for pork is a memory of that feast: what was cooked at the rally was the pig, and the pig was what you came for.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): one of the two North Carolina answers to what the word means: the whole hog, chopped, with vinegar.
- kin → lexington (style): the other North Carolina answer: pork shoulder with a red dip.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the gathering the word also names — a barbecue as an event, still a pig.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/barbecue/barbecue-crowd-braswell-1944.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · John Hemmer; State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/47111378764/
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wp-barbecue — Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:oed — Oxford English Dictionary; s:moss-barbecue-history — Barbecue: The History of an American Institution; s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-condev — Department of Conservation and Development, Travel Information Division Photograph Collection
