## Carolina Gold (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/carolina-gold/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/carolina-gold.json
id: carolina-gold
aliases: Carolina Gold rice · Carolina Gold sauce · Carolina Gold BBQ sauce
said: 'Carolina Gold' on a sauce bottle in the Midlands means mustard; on a Charleston menu it means the rice under the shrimp. Both are South Carolina's, and neither knows the other.
root: Carolina + gold. For the rice, the colour of the unhulled grain (Wikipedia); for the sauce, the colour of yellow mustard and the brand name under which Maurice Bessinger's Piggie Park sold it (Wikipedia). Two coinages, one name, no common root but the state · first seen: rice: 'first popularized in South Carolina in the 1780s' (Wikipedia); sauce: undated — Bessinger sold sauce under the Carolina Gold brand by the 1990s, and Wikipedia says the mustard sauce 'is sometimes called Carolina Gold' · A third thing wears the name: Riviana Foods sells a parboiled 'Carolina Gold' under its Carolina Rice brand with, Wikipedia says, no connection to the heirloom variety. *Inference —* the sauce borrowed a name the rice had made mean the state's own treasure, and its use for any yellow mustard sauce is a brand gone generic.
facets: letter=C · part_of_speech=noun
region: The South Carolina Midlands, The Lowcountry, South Carolina
what: Two South Carolina things with one name. The sauce: the yellow-mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands — mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices — which Wikipedia says is sometimes called Carolina Gold and which Maurice Bessinger of Piggie Park sold in supermarkets under that brand. The rice: an heirloom variety of Oryza sativa named for the gold of its unhulled grain, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people from the 1780s, the staple of Lowcountry cooking, last harvested commercially in 1927 and revived from a seed bank in the 1980s.
story: The rice came first. Carolina Gold was popularized in South Carolina in the 1780s; at the outset of the Civil War 3.5 million of the 5 million bushels of rice grown in the United States were Carolina Gold, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people. The last commercial crop was harvested in 1927. In the 1980s Richard and Patricia Schulze, restoring rice ponds at Hardeeville, found a stock in a USDA seed bank in Texas, planted 14 pounds and harvested 64; by 1988 they had 10,000 pounds a year, and Anson Mills and Carolina Plantation Rice sold it to the public from 1998. The sauce's name is younger. Mustard sauce belongs to the German-settled Midlands. Maurice Bessinger, who opened Maurice's Piggie Park in West Columbia with his brother Joe in 1953, sold a sauce of mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar under the Carolina Gold brand and by 1999 had the largest barbecue operation in the country; in 2000, when he raised Confederate flags over his restaurants, grocery chains dropped the sauce from their shelves. *Inference —* Carolina Gold for any yellow mustard sauce is the brand gone generic, wearing a name the rice made first.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce the name is used for on bottles and in the press.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style whose sauce goes by this name.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): who sold his mustard sauce under the Carolina Gold brand, and lost the shelves for it in 2000.
- kin → joe-bessinger (person): Maurice's father, to whom some accounts attribute the mustard sauce itself.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the West Columbia drive-in, opened 1953, the brand's home.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): rice is the other half of the dish, and Carolina Gold is the Lowcountry's historic variety of it.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): a Pee Dee and Lowcountry rice dish; rice is the crop the name first belonged to.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the German Midlands the mustard sauce is credited to.
- not to be confused with mustard-sauce: The bottle says Carolina Gold; the sauce is mustard sauce. The rice is on a Charleston menu, not a barbecue one.
sources: s:wp-carolina-gold — Carolina Gold — Wikipedia; s:wp-maurice-bessinger — Maurice Bessinger — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sandwich — Barbecue sandwich — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:wp-chicken-bog — Chicken bog — Wikipedia; s:wp-hash-stew — Hash (stew) — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## chopped (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/chopped/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/chopped.json
id: chopped
aliases: chopped barbecue · coarse chopped · coarse chop · chop · minced · sliced
said: 'Chopped or sliced?' is the question at a Lexington counter, and 'coarse chopped' gets it in bigger pieces. In the east nobody asks: the whole hog is chopped, and fine.
root: chop (v.), mid-14c., 'to cut with a quick blow', of uncertain origin, perhaps Old North French choper or Old French couper 'to cut'; the noun 'a slice of mutton, lamb or pork' from the 1630s. Coarse chopped: the same, in larger pieces. Minced: Old French mincier 'to chop in little pieces', in English cooking from the late 14c. Sliced: the far pole — not chopped at all · first seen: chop, verb, mid-14c. (etymonline); the counter sense is undated in the sources consulted · The three-word scale — chopped, coarse chopped, sliced — is a Lexington menu's, read on 15 September 2026 at Lexington Barbecue. NCpedia gives the eastern meat as 'boned, chopped, or shredded' and the western as 'chopped or sliced pork shoulders or butts'.
facets: letter=C · part_of_speech=adjective
region: The Carolinas
what: The way most Carolina barbecue reaches the tray: cooked meat cut across on a block with cleavers — in the east fine enough to hold the thin vinegar sauce, in the Piedmont in larger pieces. At a Lexington counter it is an ordering word with a scale, chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, and each is a different plate from the same shoulder. 'Sliced' is the far end, the shoulder cut into slabs and not chopped at all. A whole hog is chopped all together, skin included, so that every tray gets every part.
story: Chop is a Middle English verb of uncertain parentage, and by the 1630s a chop was a slice of pork. The barbecue sense grows out of the whole hog: once the meat comes off the bones it goes to the block, and the food writers Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on it among the most alluring things about Carolina whole hog. NCpedia gives the eastern meat as 'boned, chopped, or shredded' and the western as 'chopped or sliced pork shoulders or butts'; the Wikipedia article has the east chopping after the meat is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture that holds the thin sauce, and Lexington serving 'pulled' or very lightly chopped, leaving strands. Melton's in Rocky Mount chopped whole hog so fine that a 1988 magazine compared it to chopped peanut butter. At Lexington Barbecue the menu on 15 September 2026 reads Chopped BBQ, Coarse Chopped BBQ and Sliced BBQ, on plate, tray or sandwich, a chopped plate at $13.40 cash. *Tradition holds —* some eastern pits call their finest chop minced. *Inference —* the scale exists at Lexington because a shoulder can be sliced to order and a whole hog cannot.
- kin → lexington (style): the style that made chopping an ordering scale: chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, all from the shoulder.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style that chops everything — the whole hog, skin included — fine enough to hold vinegar.
- kin → chopping-block (pit): the block the chop happens on, with cleavers; the sound of it is the sound of an eastern pit.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut that is chopped whole, crisp skin and all, so every tray gets every part of the hog.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut that can also be sliced; Lexington's chopped and sliced come from the same shoulder.
- kin → pulled-pork (term): the outsider's word for meat taken apart by hand instead of cut across with a blade.
- kin → outside-brown (dish): the other counter word: the crusted outer meat, which NCpedia notes some pits keep apart as 'outside meat' from 'inside meat'.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): whose menu lists Chopped, Coarse Chopped and Sliced BBQ — the vocabulary in one line.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): which chopped whole hog so fine a 1988 writer compared it to chopped peanut butter.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the crisp skin is chopped through the meat on the block.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the tray is chopped barbecue with slaw and no bread.
- not to be confused with pulled-pork: Chopped is cut across with a blade and comes in pieces; pulled comes in strands. Sliced is neither: slabs of shoulder, a Piedmont order.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-lexington-barbecue-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## dip (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/dip/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/dip.json
id: dip
aliases: Lexington dip · barbecue dip · the dip
said: 'Dip' is what a Lexington pit calls the reddish sauce on its table; the same bottle dresses the red slaw. Say 'barbecue sauce' there and you are from somewhere else.
root: dip (v.), Old English dyppan 'to plunge, immerse', from Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'; the noun 'act of dipping' 1590s, 'liquid into which something is to be dipped' 1825; also in the 19th century 'a sweet sauce for pudding' and 'the juices and fat left after cooking meat'; the party dip of 1962 is, etymonline says, probably a re-coinage · first seen: noun, 'liquid into which something is dipped': 1825 (etymonline); the Lexington sense is undated in the sources consulted · NCpedia's explanation of the name is service: the thin tomato sauce is served at table because sauce on meat over an open fire is a hazard, so the meat is dipped after. *Inference —* the nineteenth-century sense 'juices and fat left after cooking meat' fits a sauce that began as drippings, vinegar and pepper before ketchup was cheap.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=noun
region: The North Carolina Piedmont
what: The Lexington word for its sauce: vinegar, water, ketchup or tomato, salt, black and red pepper, sugar to taste — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red. It goes on the chopped shoulder at the counter, sits on the table in a bottle, and is the dressing of the red slaw. Each pit's recipe is its own and, the town's own article says, closely guarded; the taste runs from tangy to slightly sweet or spicy. The eastern sauce is the same idea without the tomato, and is not called dip.
story: Dip is Old English dyppan, to plunge, kin to deep. The Online Etymology Dictionary dates the noun for a liquid you dip something into to 1825, and records a nineteenth-century kitchen sense: the juices and fat left in the pan after cooking meat. NCpedia explains the Lexington name by service — the thin tomato sauce is served at the table, because sauce on meat over an open fire is a hazard, so the meat is dipped after cooking. *Inference —* the pan-juice sense fits as well: the first Piedmont dips were drippings, vinegar and pepper, and the Wikipedia article on barbecue sauce has the early homemade sauces as vinegar, salt and pepper, with ketchup and sugar arriving in the 1920s. The Wikipedia article on Lexington says the shoulder is basted in a sauce 'called dip locally' of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper; the North Carolina Barbecue Society's page has red slaw made with the barbecue sauce 'locally called dip' in place of mayonnaise. *Tradition holds —* the recipe line runs from the tent pits on the Lexington courthouse square in the 1910s to Warner Stamey and the pits his cooks opened.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the sauce itself; this page is only its name.
- kin → lexington (style): the style whose sauce goes by this word; 'Piedmont' and 'Western' style mean the same dip.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the slaw is red because it is dressed with the dip instead of mayonnaise.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut the dip is made for, basted with it on the pit and dressed with it on the block.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the eastern cousin: the same vinegar and pepper without the tomato that makes a dip red, and called sauce.
- kin → heavy-tomato-sauce (sauce): the thick, sweet, molasses-and-brown-sugar sauce of the rest of the country and of western South Carolina — what a dip is not.
- kin → warner-stamey (person): the Lexington cook whose dip, *tradition holds*, is the ancestor of most of the others.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): a Lexington pit where the dip and the slaw come from the same kitchen, shoulders only, over oak and hickory coals.
- not to be confused with vinegar-pepper-sauce: Both are thin and vinegar-based. Dip has tomato or ketchup in it and is reddish; the eastern sauce has none and is clear or pepper-flecked. If the slaw beside it is red, the sauce is a dip.
- not to be confused with heavy-tomato-sauce: A dip pours and is tart; a heavy tomato sauce clings and is sweet. Dip is a Piedmont word; nobody calls the thick sauce a dip.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wiktionary-dip — dip — Wiktionary; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:wp-north-carolina-barbecue-society — North Carolina Barbecue Society — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## Down East (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/down-east/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/down-east.json
id: down-east
aliases: down east · Downeast · Down-East
said: 'Down East' in North Carolina is where the whole hog is; a Raleigh eater 'goes Down East for barbecue'. On the coast the phrase narrows to the fishing villages east of Beaufort.
root: down + east, a sailing direction. Along the New England coast the summer wind is south-westerly, so a ship bound east from Boston runs downwind, and Maine was Down East (Wiktionary; Wikipedia). In North Carolina the same phrase names the coastal communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County and, broadened, the eastern part of the state (Wikipedia) · first seen: 1817, nautical, for the New England sense (Wiktionary); 1810–20, an Americanism (dictionary.com); the North Carolina sense is undated in the sources consulted · *Inference —* the North Carolina phrase is the same logic on another coast: rivers and roads run down to the sea, and east is where the sea is. No source consulted derives it from the Maine phrase, and none needs to.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=phrase
region: Eastern North Carolina
what: In North Carolina, the coastal plain east of Raleigh — the barbecue east, where the hog is cooked whole and the sauce has no tomato; eastern North Carolina barbecue is also called Down East barbecue. The narrow sense is the string of fishing communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County — Bettie, Otway, Straits, Harkers Island, Gloucester, Marshallberg, out to Cedar Island — and Wikipedia says the phrase has broadened to mean eastern North Carolina generally, the central coastal plain of Greenville, Goldsboro, Kinston, New Bern, Rocky Mount, Tarboro, Washington and Wilson.
story: The phrase is New England's first: a ship from Boston bound for Maine ran before the south-west wind, so Maine was down east, and the term is on record from 1817. North Carolina has its own. To Carteret County, Down East is the villages east of Beaufort, where the accent is the coastal 'High Tider' brogue; to Raleigh and the Piedmont the same words cover the whole coastal plain, and the towns Wikipedia lists for that broader sense are the barbecue towns — Rocky Mount, where Bob Melton opened the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant in 1924; Wilson, where Ed Mitchell grew up; Greenville, with Ayden and the Skylight Inn just south. In the 1980s newspaper war over what barbecue meant, Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer spoke for the east and Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro for Lexington. *Tradition holds —* in barbecue talk Down East means whole hog and vinegar, and where it begins is argued; the fall line east of Raleigh is the usual answer. *Inference —* down is the way the rivers run — Neuse, Tar, Roanoke — and east is where they go; the Carolina phrase needs no ship.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style, which is also called Down East barbecue.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): what Down East cooks.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the Down East sauce: no tomato.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the Down East slaw: mayonnaise, pale, on the bun.
- kin → piedmont (term): the other direction — west of the fall line, where the shoulder and the dip begin.
- kin → pee-dee (term): South Carolina's name for the same whole-hog coastal plain, across the state line.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): in Ayden, a Down East pit in the broad sense, cooking whole hogs over wood since 1947.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): in Rocky Mount, in the broadened Down East: the first sit-down barbecue restaurant in the state, 1924.
- kin → bob-melton (person): who cooked whole hog in an open pit by the Tar River before he sold it.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): of Wilson, a Down East town in the broad sense, who learned barbecue at family gatherings there.
- kin → dennis-rogers (person): the Raleigh News & Observer columnist on the eastern side of the 1980s barbecue feud with Jerry Bledsoe.
- not to be confused with piedmont: Down East is east of the fall line — whole hog, clear sauce, white slaw. The Piedmont is west of it — shoulder, red dip, red slaw.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/down-east/down-east-cropping-tobacco-eastern-nc-1946.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/8475119249/
sources: s:wiktionary-down-east — down east — Wiktionary; s:web-dictionary-com-down-east — down east — Dictionary.com; s:wp-down-east — Down East — Wikipedia; s:wp-down-east-north-carolina — Down East (North Carolina) — Wikipedia; s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-condev — Department of Conservation and Development, Travel Information Division Photograph Collection

## Dutch Fork (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/dutch-fork/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/dutch-fork.json
id: dutch-fork
aliases: the Dutch Fork · the Fork
said: The Dutch Fork is the wedge between the Saluda and the Broad above Columbia; a mustard-sauce pit in Newberry County is in it, and the 'Dutch' are Germans.
root: Dutch, in its older English sense 'German': from the late 14th century Dutch meant German and the non-Scandinavian continental Germanic peoples generally, from Middle Dutch duutsch, cognate with German deutsch, from Proto-Germanic *theudo 'of the people'; the sense narrowed to the Netherlands around 1600 in England, but in America the older sense lasted, as in Pennsylvania Dutch (etymonline) + fork, Old English forca from Latin furca, of rivers from 1753 (etymonline): the land between the Saluda and the Broad, which join to form the Congaree at Columbia · first seen: the name is undated in the sources consulted; the settlement it names began between 1730 and 1766 (Wikipedia) or in the 1740s (South Carolina Encyclopedia) · The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the name as 'Dutch Fork for deutsch Volk (German people)'; Wikipedia gives Dutch as an anglicization of deutsch. Nobody from the Netherlands is involved — the Dutch of slaw, koolsla, is the other Dutch.
facets: letter=D · part_of_speech=noun
region: The South Carolina Midlands
what: The land between the Saluda and the Broad rivers above their meeting at Columbia, in Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties, settled by German-speaking Protestants in the middle of the eighteenth century and named for them, Dutch for deutsch. It is the upstream end of the mustard belt: the yellow mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands is linked to the German families who settled between Orangeburg County and Newberry County, and the Fork is the Newberry end of that line. Lutheran churches, place names and family names are what remains of the German; the dialect is gone.
story: The British colony offered incentives to foreign Protestants to settle its backcountry, and between 1730 and 1766 German-speaking families took up the fork of the Saluda and the Broad; the South Carolina Encyclopedia dates the first European settlement to the 1740s and says German language and culture lasted in the Fork's isolation into the early twentieth century. The name is English for what the settlers called themselves. Their mark on the plate is mustard. Wikipedia says South Carolina's mustard sauce may have originated with the French and German immigrants of the eighteenth century and is linked to a 'Mustard Belt' from Orangeburg County to Newberry County where Germans settled; the Dukes family of Orangeburg County, of German origin, is the example historians give; and mustard goes into the hash of the German Midlands. Newberry is still the only South Carolina county more than a tenth Lutheran. *Inference —* the Fork is not the whole belt but its upstream end; Orangeburg, the other end, lies south of the Congaree and outside it. *Tradition holds —* the Dutch Fork is claimed as the birthplace of mustard sauce; no document in the sources consulted places the first pot.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style the Fork's Germans are credited with.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): the sauce the German families of the Midlands are credited with.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the brand name the mustard sauce goes by on bottles.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): mustard goes into the hash in the German Midlands.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): an Orangeburg County family of German origin whose mustard sauce historians point to — the other end of the mustard belt.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): the Midlands' best-known mustard-sauce pit, in West Columbia, a few miles from the Fork.
- kin → slaw (term): the other Dutch: koolsla came from the Netherlands, the Fork's Dutch from Germany.
- kin → piedmont (term): the Fork's rivers join at Columbia on the fall line, where the Piedmont ends.
- not to be confused with slaw: Two Dutches. The Fork's Dutch is deutsch, German; slaw's Dutch is the Netherlands' koolsla. One brought mustard, the other cabbage.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wp-dutch-fork — Dutch Fork — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-encyclopedia-dutch-fork — Dutch Fork — South Carolina Encyclopedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sauce — Barbecue sauce — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:wp-hash-stew — Hash (stew) — Wikipedia; s:wp-congaree-river — Congaree River — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## fixins (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/fixins/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/fixins.json
id: fixins
aliases: fixin's · fixings · all the fixins
said: 'A plate with all the fixins' — the slaw, the hushpuppies, the potatoes, the tea. Said with no g, and spelled on Carolina menus as said.
root: fix (v.), late 14c., from Old French fixer, Latin fixus 'fastened' → fixing, verbal noun, 'act of putting in order', c. 1600 → fixings, American English, 'apparatus' 1820, 'food, garnishing' 1839 (etymonline); spelled fixin's or fixins for the g that Southern speech drops · first seen: 1839, American English, in the food sense (etymonline) · Wiktionary: the necessary ingredients for something, especially food, and the side dishes or accompaniments — 'a sandwich with all the fixings'. The apostrophe marks the missing g; the spelling without one marks that nobody misses it.
facets: letter=F · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The sides and trimmings that come with the meat: slaw, hushpuppies or cornbread, boiled potatoes in the east, hash and rice in South Carolina, pickles, sweet tea. 'Fixings' is American English of 1839 for the garnishing of a meal; fixins is how it is said and, on Carolina signs and menus, how it is spelled. Beth Tartan wrote of a Raleigh hostess telephoning Melton's — 'Ride me a party' — and Melton's putting barbecue and fixings on the bus to her.
story: Fix is a verb that does a great deal of work in the South, and its noun did the same: fixings, first the apparatus of a thing, in 1820, then by 1839 the food that goes round the main thing. The barbecue plate is the word's natural home because the meat is one thing and the rest is a list. The Skylight Inn tray is barbecue, slaw and cornbread; Melton's plate in 1929 was barbecue with boiled potatoes for 45 cents, and in 1988 came with coleslaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew; a pig pickin' is eaten with hushpuppies, coleslaw, baked beans or Brunswick stew, and in South Carolina with hash over rice or pilaf; the Dukes buffets run to collard greens, macaroni and cheese, black-eyed peas, hushpuppies, corn nuggets, potato salad, coleslaw and white bread. The spelling is the speech: a menu that prints fixin's is telling you how the owner talks. *Inference —* the word keeps the order of the plate — barbecue is the noun, and everything else is fixins.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the tray's fixins are slaw and cornbread, and nothing more.
- kin → slaw (term): the one fixin that is never missing.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): fried cornmeal, a fixin in both states.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the Skylight's fixin, a dense pork-fat cake.
- kin → boiled-potatoes (dish): the eastern fixin — at Melton's a plate came with boiled potatoes for 45 cents in 1929.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the South Carolina fixin.
- kin → brunswick-stew (dish): on the plate at Melton's and at pig pickin's.
- kin → sweet-tea (dish): the drink among the fixins.
- kin → light-bread (term): the sandwich's bread; on a plate, one more fixin.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): which put 'barbecue and fixings on the bus' for Raleigh parties.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): whose buffet is the fixins as a list.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): whose tray is the fixins at their fewest: slaw and cornbread.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): where the fixins are hushpuppies, slaw, baked beans or Brunswick stew, and in South Carolina hash and rice.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wiktionary-fixings — fixings — Wiktionary; s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## hog (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/hog/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/hog.json
id: hog
aliases: whole hog · hogg
said: A Carolina pit cooks a hog, not a pig — 'we cook whole hog', 'a hundred-and-twenty-pound hog' — and gives its size in dressed weight, the carcass with the innards out.
root: Old English hogg, implied in the late-12th-century hogaster and written hogge by the mid-14th century; origin uncertain — a Celtic source (Welsh hwch, Cornish hogh 'swine') is proposed, and the OED, quoted by etymonline, calls it improbable. The original sense was age, not species: a castrated male, or a swine reared for slaughter at about a year old; stockmen also said it of yearling sheep and horses · first seen: before 1100 (dictionary.com); hogaster late 12c., hogge mid-14c. (etymonline); 'go the whole hog' 1828, American English (etymonline) · Whole hog, 1828, is explained two ways in the Online Etymology Dictionary: the butcher's offer of the whole slaughtered animal at a discount rather than the choice bits, or — the entry leans this way — an allegory, in English from 1779 and in a poem by Cowper, of Muslim sophists who argued away the ban on pork one part at a time until the whole hog was exempt. Wiktionary's derivation from Old Norse hǫggva 'to cut', making the hog 'the cut one', is not in the Online Etymology Dictionary and is given here as folk.
facets: letter=H · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: In Carolina barbecue speech the animal is a hog. Whole hog is the eastern North Carolina and Pee Dee style; a hog killing is the winter work of the farm; a hog's size is its dressed weight. American dictionaries make a hog a domesticated swine of 120 pounds or more raised for market and a pig the younger, smaller animal; the pit's small hogs of 80 to 120 pounds dressed sit at the bottom of that range. The pig pickin' hog is a barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt, a young female — boars and sows are too big.
story: Hog is older than pig for the grown animal. Old English hogg meant a swine of a certain age — a castrated male, or one reared for slaughter at about a year; pig, until the fourteenth century, meant a young one. Dressed weight is the pit's unit: the weight after the organs, head and inedible parts are removed, about 72 per cent of live weight for a pig by Wikipedia's example. A pig pickin' hog is 80 to 120 pounds dressed; elsewhere hogs run to 300 pounds, but in the Carolinas small hogs cooked hot so the skin crisps and can be chopped in. Hog killing was the farm's winter work: NCpedia describes it beginning on the first frigid day of autumn or winter, neighbours gathering before dawn, as many as 100 hogs penned and fattened on gleaned peas, potatoes and corn, and the weeks after full of spare ribs, liver and sausage, the hams a month or two later. *Tradition holds —* the barbecue was what a hog killing or a church homecoming did with fresh meat before curing. 'Go the whole hog', American English of 1828, is the same animal as a figure of speech.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut that is the whole animal; the phrase and the style share the word.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the winter farm work the word names: neighbours before dawn, scalding water, and the first frigid day.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style whose answer to what barbecue is, is the hog, entire.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the South Carolina region where whole hog over hardwood coals is the common style.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the gathering named for pulling meat off the hog by hand; its hog is a barrow or gilt of 80 to 120 pounds dressed.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): the skin of the hog, fried; in the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): what the head and liver of the hog become in South Carolina.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut the Piedmont takes instead of the hog.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word that in the east means the hog after cooking.
- not to be confused with whole-hog: 'Hog' is the animal; 'whole hog' is the cut and the style. The pig-or-hog tell is size: a hog is the market-weight animal, a pig the young one; the pit's hog is small, 80 to 120 pounds dressed.

- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/hog/hog-razorback-hog-cape-hatteras.jpg · No known copyright restrictions · H. H. Brimley; State Archives of North Carolina · https://www.flickr.com/photos/north-carolina-state-archives/51959374242/

Powell, Encyclopedia of North Carolina, 2006); s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-hash-stew — Hash (stew) — Wikipedia; s:flickr-commons — Flickr Commons; s:flickr-ncsa — State Archives of North Carolina on Flickr Commons; s:ncsa-brimley — H. ## light bread (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/light-bread/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/light-bread.json
id: light-bread
aliases: light-bread · lightbread · white bread
said: 'Light bread' is the store loaf or the soft bun, said against cornbread and biscuits; a sandwich is barbecue and slaw on light bread.
root: light (adj.), Old English leoht 'not heavy', from Proto-Germanic *lingkhtaz — of bread, risen with yeast, against the dense pone and quick breads of cornmeal — + bread. Midland and Southern American English for white bread, or any bread leavened with yeast (dictionary.com); 'Southern US: white bread' (Wiktionary) · first seen: 1815–25 (dictionary.com) · The name is about leavening, not colour: the loaf is light because yeast lifts it. Cornbread was the South's daily bread because wheat withered and turned rancid in its heat and humidity (Wikipedia). *Inference —* wheat bread was the bought, occasional loaf, and the name marks it as the exception.
facets: letter=L · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The Southern name for white yeast bread — a store loaf or a soft bun — as against cornbread, biscuits and pone, a dense cornmeal cake. On a Carolina barbecue tray it is what the sandwich is built on: chopped barbecue and slaw on a soft white bun. At the Skylight Inn the sandwich is on a white roll; Dukes buffets in South Carolina set out white bread beside the hash. Dictionary.com labels the term Midland and Southern U.S., and defines it as white bread or any bread leavened with yeast.
story: The word is old on the farm and young on the menu. Dictionary.com dates light bread to 1815–25; it is light in the baker's sense, risen with yeast, against the heavy cornmeal breads that fed the South because wheat would not keep in its heat. The barbecue sandwich is a twentieth-century form — Wikipedia says the tradition of whole hog as a sandwich filling began in the 1900s, and Melton's in Rocky Mount sold a barbecue sandwich for 15 cents in 1929 — and the bread it needed was the soft white bun that machine-sliced loaves made ordinary from the 1920s. The bun is never the point: Wikipedia's barbecue-sandwich article says the bread keeps the meat from drying and holds its heat, and in the east the slaw goes on the bun. *Tradition holds —* the tray, barbecue and slaw without bread, is the order for people who do not want the light bread at all; hushpuppies and cornsticks are the tray's bread and light bread the sandwich's. NCpedia's sides are baked corn sticks and fried hush puppies.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the dish: barbecue and slaw on light bread.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): the order without it.
- kin → hushpuppies (dish): the tray's bread instead — fried cornmeal, not wheat.
- kin → cornbread (dish): the other bread, and the older; light bread is named against it.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): what goes on the light bread with the meat in the east.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the sandwich is on a white roll.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): whose buffets set out white bread beside the hash and rice.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): selling a barbecue sandwich for 15 cents in 1929.
- kin → fixins (term): on a plate, light bread is one more fixin.
- not to be confused with cornbread: Light bread is leavened with yeast and white; cornbread is cornmeal, quick or unleavened, yellow or white. The sandwich is on light bread; the tray comes with cornbread or hushpuppies.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:web-dictionary-com-light-bread — light bread — Dictionary.com; s:wiktionary-light-bread — light bread — Wiktionary; s:wp-cornbread — Cornbread — Wikipedia; s:wp-white-bread — White bread — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-meltons-barbecue — Melton's Barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-sandwich — Barbecue sandwich — Wikipedia; s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia

## Pee Dee (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/pee-dee/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/pee-dee.json
id: pee-dee
aliases: Pedee · Peedee · the Pee Dee · Great Pee Dee
said: 'The Pee Dee' is the river and the corner of South Carolina it drains — Florence, Marion, Kingstree, Hemingway; in barbecue it means whole hog with a thin, hot vinegar-and-pepper sauce.
root: from the Pee Dee (Pedee) people, an Indigenous nation of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley; the river took their name and the region took the river's. Their language was never recorded and the name's meaning is unknown · The anthropologist Frank Speck suggested Catawban words meaning 'something good' or 'smart, capable'; a story that a trader named Patrick Daley carved 'P.D.' on trees is folk etymology without scholarly support (Wikipedia). Spellings: Pedee, Peedee, Peadea, Pidee.
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Pee Dee
what: The river and the region. The Pee Dee rises in the North Carolina mountains as the Yadkin, takes the name Pee Dee below the mouth of the Uwharrie, crosses into South Carolina and reaches the sea at Winyah Bay. The region is the state's north-east corner — Chesterfield, Darlington, Dillon, Florence, Marlboro and Marion counties always, Horry, Georgetown and Williamsburg usually. Its barbecue is whole hog over hardwood coals, sometimes skinned first with the skin fried, and a sauce of vinegar, salt and pepper that Wikipedia calls virtually identical to eastern North Carolina's.
story: The people gave the river its name and the river gave it to the land. The Pedee were a Southeastern Woodlands people of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley, part of the South Appalachian Mississippian culture — the mound-building culture of the Southeast, about 1000 to 1500 — and numbered about 600 in 1600; their language was never written down, and the name's meaning is a guess. Four state-recognized tribes claim their descent. Its barbecue is the whole hog. The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the Pee Dee sauce as 'watery thin and fiery hot pepper and vinegar concoctions'; the Wikipedia article on South Carolina barbecue calls the vinegar sauce heavily based on Native American basting sauces, a claim it makes without a document behind it. Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q opened in Hemingway in 1972 and became known for whole-hog platters; Rodney Scott grew up at its pit and took the Pee Dee hog to Charleston in 2017. Kingstree holds a Pig Pickin' festival every fall for Williamsburg County's vinegar barbecue. *Inference —* the Pee Dee and Down East are one barbecue country cut by a state line.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the style named for the region.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the same cooking north of the line: whole hog, vinegar and pepper.
- kin → down-east (term): North Carolina's name for the same coastal-plain whole-hog country.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the Pee Dee's cut.
- kin → vinegar-pepper-sauce (sauce): the Pee Dee sauce: 'watery thin and fiery hot'.
- kin → pork-skins (dish): in the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): the Pee Dee's hash is liver hash.
- kin → chicken-bog (dish): the Pee Dee's rice dish, most common there and in the Lowcountry.
- kin → scotts-bar-b-que (place): Hemingway, 1972: the Pee Dee's best-known whole-hog pit.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): who cooked at Scott's from about age eleven and took the Pee Dee hog to Charleston.
- kin → rodney-scotts-whole-hog-bbq (place): the Charleston restaurant, opened 2017, that carried the Pee Dee hog to the coast.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): Kingstree's fall festival is a Pig Pickin', for the county's vinegar barbecue.
- kin → piedmont (term): where the Pee Dee people lived before the name moved downriver.
- not to be confused with sc-mustard: Pee Dee sauce is thin, clear and hot; Midlands sauce is yellow with mustard. If the sauce is yellow you have left the Pee Dee.
sources: s:wp-pee-dee — Pee Dee — Wikipedia; s:wp-pee-dee-river — Pee Dee River — Wikipedia; s:wp-pee-dee-people — Pee Dee people — Wikipedia; s:wiktionary-pee-dee — Pee Dee — Wiktionary; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-encyclopedia-barbecue — Barbecue — South Carolina Encyclopedia; s:wp-hemingway-south-carolina — Hemingway, South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-scotts-variety-store-and-bar-b-q — Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q — Wikipedia; s:wp-rodney-scott-pitmaster — Rodney Scott (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-kingstree-south-carolina — Kingstree, South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-chicken-bog — Chicken bog — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## Piedmont (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/piedmont/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/piedmont.json
id: piedmont
aliases: the Piedmont · Piedmont-style · Piedmont Triad · Upstate · Upcountry · Western
said: In North Carolina barbecue talk 'Piedmont style' is Lexington style — shoulders and a red dip — and a Piedmont pit is west of Raleigh. South Carolina calls its Piedmont the Upstate, and once called it the Upcountry.
root: Italian Piemonte, from medieval Latin Pedemontium, ad pedem montium, 'at the foot of the mountains' — Latin pes, pedis 'foot' + mons, montis 'mountain' — the region below the Alps, in documents from the end of the twelfth century (Wikipedia); through French Piémont; applied to the American plateau at the foot of the Appalachians as piemont in 1755, with the d by 1855, and extended to the foot of other ranges by 1860 (etymonline) · first seen: American sense 1755, as piemont (etymonline); Pedemontium, late twelfth century (Wikipedia) · The Piedmont Triad — Greensboro, Winston-Salem, High Point — is the region whose 'Official Food Festival' the legislature made the Lexington Barbecue Festival in 2007, a way of not naming a state barbecue.
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The North Carolina Piedmont, The Upstate
what: The plateau between the coastal plain and the Blue Ridge, from New York to Alabama and nearly 300 miles wide in North Carolina; its eastern edge is the fall line, where rivers drop off hard rock onto the soft plain and towns grew at the head of navigation. In North Carolina barbecue, Piedmont style is Lexington style — pork shoulder, a red vinegar-and-ketchup dip, red slaw — and 'Western' means the same. In South Carolina the Piedmont is the Upstate, Greenville, Spartanburg and Anderson, where the sauce is a thin ketchup and vinegar and the hash is pork and beef.
story: Piemonte is the foot of the Alps, named in Latin documents by 1200; English took it through French and in 1755 applied piemont to the country at the foot of the Appalachians, adding the d by 1855. The fall line is where the name earns itself: the Piedmont's rivers leave the hard rock in a line of rapids, and the Congaree forms at Columbia on it. Wikipedia calls Lexington style 'Piedmont- or Western-style', most common in the Piedmont and west, pork shoulder only, with a red dip and red slaw; the South Carolina Encyclopedia has shoulders, hams and Boston butts in the Piedmont against the whole hog of the coastal plain. Lexington, 20 miles south of Winston-Salem in the Piedmont Triad, calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World, and in 2007 the legislature made its festival the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region. South Carolina's Upstate takes a light tomato sauce that Wikipedia attributes to North Carolina's influence, and its hash is beef and pork with onions. *Inference —* the Piedmont cooks the shoulder because a shoulder is what a town butcher sells; the whole hog stayed with the farm.
- kin → lexington (style): the style the word means in North Carolina barbecue: 'Piedmont- or Western-style'.
- kin → dip (term): the Piedmont's word for its sauce.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the Piedmont's sauce.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the Piedmont's slaw, dressed with the dip.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the Piedmont's cut; the coastal plain cooks the whole hog.
- kin → sc-light-tomato (style): the South Carolina Piedmont's sauce, a thin ketchup and vinegar credited to North Carolina's influence.
- kin → sc-heavy-tomato (style): western South Carolina's sweeter, thicker sauce, also Piedmont country.
- kin → hash-and-rice (dish): in the Upstate the hash is beef and pork with onions.
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region, by act of the legislature, 2007.
- kin → down-east (term): the other side of the fall line.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the Fork lies where the Piedmont's rivers join at the fall line.
- kin → pee-dee (term): the people the river is named for lived in the South Carolina Piedmont.
- not to be confused with down-east: Piedmont means west of the fall line: shoulder, red dip, red slaw. If the tray has white slaw and chopped skin through the meat, you are east of it.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wp-piedmont — Piedmont — Wikipedia; s:wp-piedmont-united-states — Piedmont (United States) — Wikipedia; s:wiktionary-piedmont — Piedmont — Wiktionary; s:wp-upstate-south-carolina — Upstate South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-congaree-river — Congaree River — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-encyclopedia-barbecue — Barbecue — South Carolina Encyclopedia; s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-lexington-barbecue-festival — Lexington Barbecue Festival — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-south-carolina — Barbecue in South Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-hash-stew — Hash (stew) — Wikipedia

## pit (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/pit/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/pit.json
id: pit
aliases: barbecue pit · the pit · pit house · open pit
said: 'The pit' is the brick or block box the coals go in, the room it sits in, and often the whole business: 'out back at the pit', 'the pit opens at ten'.
root: Old English pytt 'a hole in the ground, water hole, well, grave', a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus 'well, pit, shaft'; the barbecue sense keeps the hole's name after the hole has become a box of brick or cinder block above ground, and then a gas cooker inside a building · first seen: Old English (etymonline); the barbecue-pit sense is undated in the dictionaries consulted — Wiktionary lists two dozen senses of pit and none for barbecue · Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue says the word is applied across the 'barbecue belt' to an enclosed, above-ground pit; NCpedia says few commercial barbecue pits today are dug in the ground.
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at many places, a gas cooker, still the pit. The word also names the room, the building — a pit house — and the restaurant, as in Backyard BBQ Pit or Dickey's Barbecue Pit. A smokehouse is a different building: a windowless outbuilding where hams and bacon are cured in cold smoke for weeks, not a place a meal is cooked.
story: Pit is a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus, a well; in Old English a hole, a well, a grave and hell. The barbecue pit was that hole: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue describes meat cooked buried below ground, an earth-oven practice of Indigenous peoples. The whole-hog article has the pit dug into the earth or built above it as a wide, shallow container, usually of cinder blocks, filled with charcoal burned down from wood in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the traditional pit as an open pit fuelled by hardwood coals in a rectangular cement-block structure, the meat suspended above. NCpedia says few commercial pits today are dug in the ground; the whole-hog article says new restaurants mostly use gas-fired pits and many older ones have switched. At the Skylight Inn the pit crew makes its charcoal from oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. Ed Mitchell co-founded a Raleigh restaurant called The Pit. *Inference —* a word that survived the loss of the hole survived the loss of the fire: the pit is wherever the barbecue is made, and the name on the sign says so.
- kin → brick-pit (pit): the masonry pit, the first form above ground.
- kin → block-pit (pit): the cinder-block pit, the common whole-hog form: a rectangular cement-block structure with the meat above the coals.
- kin → burn-barrel (pit): the drum beside the pit where logs become the coals shovelled in.
- kin → hickory-and-oak (pit): what burns beside the pit to make its coals.
- kin → direct-heat (pit): the pit's way of cooking: coals under the meat, the meat on a rack above.
- kin → gas-and-electric-cookers (pit): the cooker that replaced the coals at many pits and kept the name.
- kin → pig-cooker (pit): the pig pickin's charcoal or propane cooker, homemade or custom-built: a pit on wheels.
- kin → pitmaster (term): the person; the word is built on this one.
- kin → backyard-bbq-pit (place): a Durham restaurant named for the thing.
- kin → skylight-inn (place): where the coals for the pits are burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside them.
- kin → henrys-smokehouse (place): a Greenville, South Carolina pit that calls itself a smokehouse — the two words meet on the sign.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): who co-founded The Pit in Raleigh and left it in 2011.
- not to be confused with gas-and-electric-cookers: A cooker is an appliance; a pit is a place. When a pit switches to gas the appliance sits inside the place and the sign does not change.
- not to be confused with pig-cooker: A pig cooker is towed to the party; a pit stays where it was built.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wiktionary-pit — pit — Wiktionary; s:wp-pit-barbecue — Pit barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-sc-encyclopedia-barbecue — Barbecue — South Carolina Encyclopedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-skylight-inn-bbq — Skylight Inn BBQ — Wikipedia; s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-smokehouse — Smokehouse — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-the-united-states — Barbecue in the United States — Wikipedia; s:wp-pig-pickin — Pig pickin' — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## pitmaster (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/pitmaster/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/pitmaster.json
id: pitmaster
aliases: pit master · pit-master · pit man · pit boss
said: Press and menus say pitmaster. Older Carolina speech says the cook, or the pit man, or the man's name — a cook forty years at the pit is called by his first name before either.
root: pit (Old English pytt, the cooking pit) + master (Old English, from Latin magister 'chief, teacher'; 'a workman qualified to carry on a trade on his own account' from c. 1300), on the pattern of quartermaster and the other -master compounds for the person in charge of a thing · first seen: 'pit master', of a barbecue cook: 22 September 1939, Daily Times-News, Burlington, North Carolina — 'Jeter Crutchfield, pit master, will supervise the beginning of roasting pork for the barbecue tonight at midnight' — as quoted by Texas Monthly (2018) and Destination BBQ (2021); the one-word form 1980–85 (dictionary.com) · The compound had other lives first: an English coal-mining word in the nineteenth century, a sportswriter's word for boxing referees in the 1920s, and in the 1970s a label for snake wranglers and a cockfight ringleader (Texas Monthly). Wiktionary carries no citation; the OED was not consulted. Destination BBQ notes that Crutchfield was white and that the verb is supervise: the cooking that night was done by Black men.
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The person who runs the pit — the fire, the coals, the turning of the hog, the call that it is done. A recent word for an old job. Wiktionary defines it as one who operates a barbecue pit and adds that it is used as a term of respect; dictionary.com dates it 1980–85; Wikipedia titles its articles 'Ed Mitchell (pitmaster)' and 'Rodney Scott (pitmaster)', and BBQ Pitmasters has been on cable since 2009. In the Carolinas the older words are the cook and the pit man, and a place is known by a family's name before any title.
story: Pit is the hole and master is Latin magister, the chief; the compound follows quartermaster. Texas Monthly traced 'pit master' through unrelated trades and found the earliest barbecue use it could in a 1939 North Carolina newspaper item: 'Jeter Crutchfield, pit master, will supervise the beginning of roasting pork for the barbecue tonight at midnight.' Destination BBQ gives the paper as the Burlington Daily Times-News of 22 September 1939 and points at the verb: Crutchfield supervised, and the men at the pit that night were Black. Adrian Miller's Black Smoke traces the history of those cooks — Black barbecuers, pitmasters and restaurateurs — and their place in the tradition. Dictionary.com dates the one-word pitmaster to 1980–85; the television series BBQ Pitmasters premiered on TLC on 3 December 2009. Rodney Scott of Hemingway, named Best Chef Southeast by the James Beard Foundation in 2018, was only the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. *Inference —* the word arrived with the audience: once barbecue was written about, the cook needed a title a writer could print. *Tradition holds —* in the Carolinas he still answers to his name.
- kin → pit (term): the word it is built on.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): the Wilson pitmaster the press calls North Carolina's most famous.
- kin → rodney-scott (person): the Hemingway pitmaster who won a James Beard chef award in 2018, the second pitmaster to do so.
- kin → pete-jones (person): who ran the Skylight Inn's pits from 1947 until 2006, most of it before the word was common.
- kin → wayne-monk (person): owner of Lexington Barbecue, 'serving pork barbecue since 1962' — two decades before dictionaries record the word.
- kin → adrian-miller (person): whose Black Smoke tells the history of the Black pitmasters the word was late to name.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut whose cooking most needs one: several people to flip and tend, and a cook who becomes prominent in the community.
- kin → southern-foodways-alliance (org): whose oral histories record pitmasters in their own words.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wiktionary-pitmaster — pitmaster — Wiktionary; s:web-dictionary-com-pitmaster — pitmaster — Dictionary.com; s:web-texas-monthly-call-barbecue-greats — What Should We Call the Barbecue Greats?; s:web-destination-bbq-history-of-barbecue — Beneath Its Whitewashed Veneer: The Darker History of Barbecue; s:wp-bbq-pitmasters — BBQ Pitmasters — Wikipedia; s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-rodney-scott-pitmaster — Rodney Scott (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-adrian-miller — Adrian Miller — Wikipedia; s:miller-black-smoke — Black Smoke: African Americans and the United States of Barbecue; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:web-lexington-barbecue-menu — Lexington Barbecue — Menu; s:sfa-oral-histories — Southern Foodways Alliance oral history collection — barbecue projects (North Carolina, South Carolina)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-15

## pulled pork (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/pulled-pork/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/pulled-pork.json
id: pulled-pork
aliases: pulled-pork · pulled
said: In the Carolinas the meat is barbecue and the counter asks 'chopped or sliced?'; 'pulled pork' is what the same meat is called on a menu written for people from somewhere else, and on the Carolina menus that are.
root: pull (v.), Old English pullian 'to pluck off (wool), to draw out', of uncertain origin + pork (n.), c. 1300, Old French porc 'pig', Latin porcus; the participle names how the cooked meat leaves the bone — pulled apart, not cut · No dictionary consulted dates the compound: Wiktionary defines it without a citation, and the etymologies here are of the two words. The cut it assumes, the Boston butt, is the upper shoulder, named for the barrels, called butts, that New England butchers packed pork in; the name is in print by 1915 (Wikipedia).
facets: letter=P · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: Pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker until it comes off the bone in strands, then taken apart by hand or with forks rather than cut. Outside the Carolinas it is the name of the dish, and the dish is a shoulder — the Boston butt, the upper shoulder, is the cut it almost always means. Inside the Carolinas the meat is called barbecue, and 'pulled' is one answer, with 'chopped' and 'sliced', to how you want it: Memphis pulls by hand; the North Carolina east chops fine; Lexington serves it pulled or lightly chopped, leaving strands.
story: Pull is Old English pullian, to pluck off or draw out, and pork came in from Old French porc after 1300. Together they name a texture: meat cooked until its connective tissue gives way, which the Wikipedia article puts at an internal temperature of 195 to 205 °F, and taken apart along the grain. The cut the phrase assumes is the shoulder, and the shoulder's upper half is the Boston butt, named for the New England barrels, called butts, that pork was packed in; the name is in print by 1915. The Carolinas had the thing before the phrase. The east chopped its whole hog with cleavers; Lexington chopped or sliced its shoulders; Memphis built its sandwich on shoulder pulled by hand, not chopped with a blade. Ed Mitchell of Wilson builds a pulled pork sandwich from a whole hog, shoulder, ham and belly together; the Dukes restaurants of Orangeburg list pulled pork on the buffet; the South Carolina mustard sandwich is described as pulled pork. *Inference —* a Carolina menu that says pulled pork is speaking to the road; one that says barbecue is speaking to the county. No source consulted dates the compound.
- kin → barbecue (term): the Carolina word for the same meat; pulled pork is what it is called when the menu speaks to the rest of the country.
- kin → chopped (term): the other answer at the counter — cut with a cleaver rather than taken apart by hand; the east chops fine, Lexington coarse.
- kin → pork-shoulder (pit): the cut the phrase assumes: almost always a shoulder, and the upper half of it is the Boston butt.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cut the east pulls instead; Ed Mitchell's pulled pork sandwich is shoulder, ham and belly from one hog.
- kin → lexington (style): the North Carolina style most often served 'pulled' or very lightly chopped, leaving larger strands of muscle.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): the style that chops after pulling from the bone, so its meat is never called pulled.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): the sandwich the phrase usually sells; in South Carolina the mustard-sauce version is described as pulled pork.
- kin → sc-mustard (style): the style whose sandwich Wikipedia describes as pulled pork under a yellow sauce.
- kin → ed-mitchell (person): the Wilson pitmaster who builds a pulled pork sandwich from a whole hog rather than a shoulder.
- kin → dukes-bar-b-que (place): the Orangeburg family of restaurants whose buffets list pulled pork beside hash and rice.
- not to be confused with chopped: Pulled meat comes in strands the length of the muscle; chopped meat has been cut across with a blade into pieces. On a Carolina tray, strands mean the Piedmont or a hand-pulled kitchen; a fine, even chop means the east.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wp-pulled-pork — Pulled pork — Wikipedia; s:wp-boston-butt — Boston butt — Wikipedia; s:wiktionary-pulled-pork — pulled pork — Wiktionary; s:wp-barbecue-sandwich — Barbecue sandwich — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-the-united-states — Barbecue in the United States — Wikipedia; s:wp-whole-hog-barbecue — Whole hog barbecue — Wikipedia; s:wp-ed-mitchell-pitmaster — Ed Mitchell (pitmaster) — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina)
provenance default: cited · confidence: medium · needs_verification: True · updated: 2026-09-15

## slaw (term)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/word/slaw/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/term/slaw.json
id: slaw
aliases: cole slaw · coleslaw · cold slaw · barbecue slaw · red slaw · white slaw
said: 'Slaw', never 'coleslaw', on a Carolina tray; a Lexington sandwich comes 'with slaw', and the slaw is red.
root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' — kool 'cabbage' (from Latin caulis) + sla, clipped from salade (from French) — → American English cole slaw, 1794, heard and written as 'cold slaw' → slaw, the back half alone, by the 1860s · first seen: cole slaw 1794 — 'A piece of sliced cabbage, by Dutchmen ycleped cold slaw' (etymonline); slaw alone 1860–65 (dictionary.com), about 1861 (Wiktionary) · 'Cold slaw' is a folk etymology, Dutch kool heard as English cold; it held until the 1860s, when cole was revived (etymonline). Wiktionary's definition of coleslaw now splits it into white slaw, dressed with mayonnaise, and red slaw, dressed with vinaigrette — the Carolina split written into the dictionary.
facets: letter=S · part_of_speech=noun
region: The Carolinas
what: Shredded raw cabbage, dressed and served cold, on every Carolina barbecue tray and most sandwiches. East of Raleigh the dressing is mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing and the slaw is white or yellow; in Lexington it is vinegar, ketchup and pepper — the dip — and the slaw is red, also called barbecue slaw. South Carolina buffets list coleslaw among the sides. The word is the back half of coleslaw, and the front half is not said; coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch settlers of New York.
story: Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad, was written down in American English in 1794 as 'cold slaw', the Dutch kool heard as the English cold; the folk spelling lasted until the 1860s, when cole came back, and by then the back half had come loose and slaw stood alone. Dutch colonists brought coleslaw to the Thirteen Colonies. Jerry Bledsoe, the Greensboro columnist of the 1980s barbecue war, wrote in 1996 that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. The split is by region. The Wikipedia article on coleslaw calls North Carolina slaw fine and vinegary and says that around Lexington red slaw is made with ketchup and vinegar rather than mayonnaise and is the prevailing kind, unlike the rest of the state; NCpedia has white or yellow coleslaw in the east and red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip, in the Piedmont. The Lexington sandwich's distinguishing feature, the town's article says, is its red slaw, and in the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger. *Inference —* red slaw is the dip's second job, and a pit that makes one makes the other from the same pot.
- kin → red-slaw (dish): the Lexington slaw: cabbage, vinegar, ketchup, pepper, no mayonnaise — also called barbecue slaw.
- kin → white-slaw (dish): the eastern slaw, dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, and put on the bun of an eastern sandwich.
- kin → lexington-dip (sauce): the dressing of the red slaw; the dip's second use.
- kin → barbecue-sandwich (dish): in both halves of North Carolina the sandwich comes with slaw on it.
- kin → barbecue-tray (dish): on the tray, slaw is the one side that is always there — Bledsoe: always served with slaw, and always has been.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): white slaw there.
- kin → lexington (style): red slaw there, and no question asked.
- kin → jerry-bledsoe (person): who wrote 'Slaw Crazy' (1996): barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina.
- kin → dutch-fork (term): the other Dutch: the Fork's Dutch is deutsch, German; slaw's Dutch is the Netherlands' koolsla.
- kin → fixins (term): the first fixin on every plate.
- not to be confused with red-slaw: Red means dip-dressed and Piedmont; white means mayonnaise and east. Ask for slaw in Lexington and it comes red without a question; ask in Ayden and it comes white.
sources: s:etymonline — Online Etymology Dictionary; s:wiktionary-slaw — slaw — Wiktionary; s:wiktionary-coleslaw — coleslaw — Wiktionary; s:web-dictionary-com-slaw — slaw — Dictionary.com; s:web-dictionary-com-coleslaw — coleslaw — Dictionary.com; s:wp-coleslaw — Coleslaw — Wikipedia; s:wp-red-slaw — Red slaw — Wikipedia; s:ncpedia-barbecue — NCpedia — Barbecue (Encyclopedia of North Carolina); s:wp-lexington-north-carolina — Lexington, North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-barbecue-in-north-carolina — Barbecue in North Carolina — Wikipedia; s:wp-cuisine-of-the-southern-united-states — Cuisine of the Southern United States — Wikipedia; s:wp-dukes-bar-b-que — Dukes Bar-B-Que — Wikipedia
provenance default: cited · confidence: high · needs_verification: False · updated: 2026-09-15

## barbecue postcards (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/barbecue-postcards/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/barbecue-postcards.json
id: barbecue-postcards
aliases: linen postcards · Tichnor cards · advertising postcards
facets: kind=postcard · state=both
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina
what: Between about 1930 and 1945 an American restaurant could order its own postcards by the thousand. A printer took a photograph, had an artist colour it by hand, and ran it on paper with a woven texture — the linen card, whose surface takes bright ink and softens a plain building into something worth mailing. Roadside businesses on the highways through both Carolinas bought them and set them by the register. The caption on the back names the route number, because that is how a customer found the place again.
- kin → roadside-barbecue-signs (art): the same buildings and the same highways, photographed forty years later in colour.
- kin → pig-mascot (art): the house pig, which turns up on the card as often as on the sign.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word as a card caption, which is how a business told a stranger what it sold.
- kin → fsa-barbecue-photographs (art): the same decade, photographed by a government rather than a printer, and with nothing to sell.
- kin → meltons-barbecue (place): a Rocky Mount pit of exactly this period, when a Carolina barbecue house would order cards.

## Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/political-barbecue-prints/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/political-barbecue-prints.json
id: political-barbecue-prints
aliases: The Political Barbecue · Going the Whole Hog · Jackson-era barbecue cartoons
facets: kind=print · state=us
region: The American South, The Carolinas
what: A small group of American political prints from the 1830s in which the barbecue is the joke and the pig is the politician. A lithograph — a print pulled from a drawing made on stone, the cheap illustrated medium of the period — could be sold loose from a shop window within days of the news. H. R. Robinson of New York issued The Political Barbecue in 1834, laying Andrew Jackson on a grid iron over a brick pit lettered PUBLIC OPINION, with one bystander remarking that in South Carolina it is called barbecue. Others draw out the campaign phrase going the whole hog. They are the oldest barbecue pictures this project can show.
- kin → political-barbecue (event): the institution the prints are drawing: the candidate's free pig and the crowd it gathers.
- kin → whole-hog (pit): the cooking the phrase is a pun on, and the meat of the colonial rally.
- kin → hog (term): the word doing the work in every one of these prints.
- kin → robert-moss (person): the historian who puts the whole-hog political rally in the colonies by the 1700s.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word a bystander in the 1834 print says South Carolina uses, while Massachusetts says roasting.
- kin → cannibal-pig-sign (art): the later American habit of putting a pig on a sign and giving it a part to play.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the surviving form of the free feed that gathers a crowd for a purpose.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/political-barbecue-prints/political-barbecue-prints-andrew-jackson-barbecue-cartoon.jpg · Public domain · Henry R. Robinson · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAndrew_Jackson_Barbecue_Cartoon.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/political-barbecue-prints/political-barbecue-prints-democratic-ticket-going-the-whole-hog-lccn2008661288.jpg · Public domain · Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ADemocratic_ticket._Going_the_whole_hog_LCCN2008661288.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/political-barbecue-prints/political-barbecue-prints-going-the-whole-hog-lccn2008661311.jpg · Public domain · Henry R. Robinson · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AGoing_the_whole_hog_LCCN2008661311.jpg
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/political-barbecue-prints/political-barbecue-prints-the-political-barbecue-going-the-whole-hog-c-1832-1833-by-an.jpg · Public domain · Unknown authorUnknown author · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AThe_political_barbecue%2C_Going_the_whole_hog%2C_c._1832-1833%2C_by_an_unknown_artist%2C_from_the_Digital_Commonwealth_-_commonwealth_9880w959q.jpg

## Pigs in the City (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/pigs-in-the-city/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/pigs-in-the-city.json
id: pigs-in-the-city
aliases: Lexington's painted pigs · Pigs on Parade
said: Everybody in Lexington can name their favourite one.
facets: kind=statue · state=NC
region: North Carolina, The North Carolina Piedmont
what: Life-sized pig sculptures, painted by artists and set out on the sidewalks of Lexington, Davidson County. Uptown Lexington, Inc. — the non-profit set up to bring business back to the town centre — ran the first exhibition in 2003 with twenty pigs, each sponsored by a business for $1,000, which paid for the whole thing. More than 40,000 people came that first year. The pigs are fibreglass blanks, identical until the artist gets them, and they come back painted as anything: a fire engine, a bulldozer, a jigsaw puzzle, a winged horse. Retired ones stay out around town.
geo: 35.824, -80.2534 (town)
- kin → lexington-barbecue-festival (event): the October Saturday most people meet the pigs, because Main Street is closed and everyone is on foot.
- kin → lexington (style): the style that gave the town the animal: shoulders, dip, red slaw.
- kin → pig-mascot (art): the same smiling pig, standing on a sidewalk instead of a roof, with nothing to sell.
- kin → cannibal-pig-sign (art): the genre these sculptures leave out: a Lexington pig is a character, never a cook.
- kin → hog (term): the word the puns are built on, once per pig.
- kin → bar-b-q-center (place): one of the Main Street restaurants the pigs stand among.
- kin → lexington-barbecue (place): the town's best-known pit, a mile from the pigs.

## roadside barbecue signs (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/roadside-barbecue-signs/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/roadside-barbecue-signs.json
id: roadside-barbecue-signs
aliases: Bar-B-Q signs · the pylon sign · pit signs
facets: kind=sign · state=both
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: The sign a barbecue place puts at the road: a steel pylon with a lit box on top, neon or bulbs picking out a name, a bottler's disc above it, and a changeable letterboard underneath for the day's news. Most spell the word Bar-B-Q, hyphenated, because three short units fit a tall narrow cabinet better than nine letters do. What survives in photographs that anyone may reuse comes almost entirely from one man's slides: John Margolies drove American highways from the late 1960s to 2008 photographing exactly this, and the Library of Congress bought the archive and the rights with it.
- kin → cannibal-pig-sign (art): what goes on the crown of the pylon when the pit pays for its own sign.
- kin → pig-mascot (art): the house pig these signs carry, and the reason people recognise a pit from the road.
- kin → barbecue-postcards (art): the same buildings and signs, printed and mailed, thirty years earlier.
- kin → fsa-barbecue-photographs (art): the other federal picture collection this project draws on, from fifty years before Margolies.
- kin → barbecue (term): the word, spelled Bar-B-Q, because it fits a tall cabinet.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): West Columbia, the Carolina sign Margolies stopped for twice.
- kin → cheerwine (dish): the other Carolina bottler whose disc turns up over a pit's name.

## The FSA photographs of Carolina eating (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/fsa-barbecue-photographs/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/fsa-barbecue-photographs.json
id: fsa-barbecue-photographs
aliases: Marion Post Wolcott in the Carolinas · FSA/OWI Carolina photographs · the 1939 Farm Security Administration series
facets: kind=photograph · state=both
region: The Carolinas, North Carolina, South Carolina, The Lowcountry
what: The Farm Security Administration — a New Deal agency for rural poverty — kept photographers on the road from 1935, and their negatives went to the Library of Congress as federal work, free of copyright. Marion Post Wolcott worked North and South Carolina in 1939. What survives of Carolina eating is the occasion rather than the pit: a corn shucking at Tally Ho, near Stem in Granville County, North Carolina, with the tables that followed it; ministers and deacons at an outdoor picnic near Yanceyville; and a Fourth of July on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, shot on Kodachrome, which was new.
- kin → hog-killing (pit): the other November work party a Carolina farm held, and the one Wolcott did not photograph here.
- kin → fundraiser-barbecue (event): the church dinner the Yanceyville picnic is an early frame of.
- kin → pig-pickin (event): the gathering these photographs stand next to: a crowd, a yard, food set out on boards.
- kin → adrian-miller (person): whose Black Smoke follows the cooks the FSA caption sheet records as feeding two sittings.
- kin → sc-pee-dee (style): the style whose region reaches down to St. Helena Island; the Fourth of July frames are the Lowcountry's oldest colour pictures here.
- kin → eastern-nc (style): Granville County lies at its western edge, where the whole hog and the Piedmont shoulder meet.
- kin → roadside-barbecue-signs (art): the other government-owned picture collection this project draws on, from fifty years later.

## the pig mascot (art)
URL: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/art/pig-mascot/
JSON: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/api/art/pig-mascot.json
id: pig-mascot
aliases: the smiling pig · the house pig · Little Joe · the roof pig
said: A place with a pig on it does not need to say what it sells.
facets: kind=mascot · state=both
region: The Carolinas, The American South
what: One pig, drawn once, used everywhere a barbecue business puts its name: the sign, the menu, the sauce label, the takeout box, the trailer door, the roofline, the weather vane. It is standing, smiling and usually dressed. It has no job in the picture — it is neither cooking nor eating — and that is what separates it from the pig that serves itself. A mascot is an identity: a customer who sees a pig on a bottle in a grocery aisle is meant to think of a particular pit in a particular town.
- kin → cannibal-pig-sign (art): the same pig given something to do — a tray, a fork, a sandwich — which changes the joke.
- kin → roadside-barbecue-signs (art): the pylon, the neon and the bottler's panel the mascot rides on.
- kin → pigs-in-the-city (art): Lexington's sculptures, which are the house pig taken off the roof and set on the pavement.
- kin → maurices-piggie-park (place): Little Joe's home pit at West Columbia, and the sign that survived the 2024 fire.
- kin → maurice-bessinger (person): who took one drive-in's pig onto grocery shelves across the country.
- kin → wilbers-barbecue (place): whose pig turns on a weather vane over Goldsboro rather than standing on a sign.
- kin → carolina-gold (term): the sauce brand the pig went onto, and came off when the chains dropped it.
- kin → mustard-sauce (sauce): what is in the bottle the pig is standing on.
- kin → hog (term): the animal, and the word a customer reads off the picture without being told.
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/pig-mascot/pig-mascot-bessinger-s-bar-b-q-sign-west-columbia-south-carolin-825aefd.jpg · Public domain · John Margolies · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABessinger%27s_Bar-B-Q_sign%2C_West_Columbia%2C_South_Carolina_LCCN2017709630.tif
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/pig-mascot/pig-mascot-bessinger-s-bar-b-q-sign-west-columbia-south-carolin-897b1ae.jpg · Public domain · John Margolies · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3ABessinger%27s_Bar-B-Q_sign%2C_West_Columbia%2C_South_Carolina_LCCN2017709631.tif
- image: https://nanobotco.github.io/carolina-barbecue/images/pig-mascot/pig-mascot-wilber-s-bbq-pig-vane.jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Jay Cuthrell · https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AWilber%27s_BBQ_-_Pig_vane.jpg
sources: s:commons-margolies — John Margolies Roadside America Photograph Archive, 1972-2008; s:commons — Wikimedia Commons; s:wp-maurice-bessinger — Maurice Bessinger — Wikipedia; s:blog-suicide-food — Suicide Food; s:web-piggiepark-history — Uncover Our Rich History — Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ
